hearthbound.bond.can_follow: %s trusts you enough to travel with you. Ask them to follow you!
hearthbound.bond.can_move: %s would move to a village you rule, if you asked.
hearthbound.bond.follow_yes: Let me grab my things. Lead the way!
hearthbound.bond.gift_empty: Hold the gift in your hand.
hearthbound.bond.gift_liked: %s? For me? How did you know I love it!
hearthbound.bond.gift_ok: %s? Thank you, that's kind of you.
hearthbound.bond.gift_today: You already gave %s a gift today.
hearthbound.bond.go_home: I'll head back to %s. Come and see me soon.
hearthbound.bond.move_yes: A new home in %s... Yes. I'm ready for a new chapter.
hearthbound.bond.tip_move: %s: they would move to a village you rule
hearthbound.building.farm.desc: Fields and an irrigation channel. Feeds the village.
hearthbound.building.forge.desc: The smith sells tools and armour here. Better gear unlocks as your age advances.
hearthbound.building.hall.desc: The heart of the village: the elder keeps the contract board here and the builder plans what comes next.
hearthbound.building.house.desc: A family home. Every house brings new settlers.
hearthbound.building.mage_tower.desc: A tall tower full of books. The mage trades in lapis, amethyst and rarer things.
hearthbound.building.manor.desc: A two-storey home for a wealthier family.
hearthbound.building.market.desc: Open stalls where the merchant trades goods from afar.
hearthbound.building.shrine.desc: A quiet place of worship. The priest grants blessings for a small offering.
hearthbound.building.storehouse.desc: Barrels and chests. The village gathers materials faster.
hearthbound.building.tavern.desc: Food, drink and gossip. The innkeeper knows sellswords looking for work.
hearthbound.building.watchtower.desc: A guard keeps watch from the top and defends the village at night.
hearthbound.character.no_contracts: No active contracts. Talk to a village elder or open a hearth.
hearthbound.character.no_villages: You have not found any village yet. Explore!
hearthbound.character.title: Character
hearthbound.charter.not_flat: The ground here is too uneven.
hearthbound.charter.too_close: Too close to another village (min. %s blocks).
hearthbound.citizen.cooldown: You changed citizenship recently: wait %s more days
hearthbound.citizen.left: You are no longer a citizen of %s
hearthbound.citizen.perks: -%s%% prices, more trust from projects, respawn at the hearth
hearthbound.citizen.respawn: You wake up by the hearth of %s
hearthbound.citizen.switch: You are a citizen of %s: switching costs reputation there
hearthbound.citizen.title: Citizenship
hearthbound.class.artisan.desc: A builder at heart. Where you go, walls rise.
hearthbound.class.choose_sub: Your class gives a free skill rank and a passive talent. Choose carefully.
hearthbound.class.cleric.desc: A voice of faith that opens doors and hearts.
hearthbound.class.cleric.perk: Shrine blessings cost half and last longer.
hearthbound.class.noble.desc: Born to lead. People follow you, for coin or for glory.
hearthbound.class.noble.perk: One extra companion, and hiring is 25% cheaper.
hearthbound.class.ranger.desc: At home on every road, always looking for the next horizon.
hearthbound.class.ranger.perk: Discovering villages grants double XP and reputation.
hearthbound.class.rogue.desc: Quick hands and quicker words. Every deal is a small victory.
hearthbound.class.rogue.perk: Sell for 15% more to every village.
hearthbound.class.warrior.desc: A veteran of many battles. Villages sleep better when you are near.
hearthbound.class.warrior.perk: Defending villages grants 50% more reputation and XP.
hearthbound.contract.full: You can only take %s contracts at once.
hearthbound.contract.objective.defend: Slay %s hostile creatures inside the village
hearthbound.contract.ready: %s is ready to hand in at %s
hearthbound.contract.unfinished: That contract is not finished yet.
hearthbound.culture.brumaverde.desc: A secretive coven living on stilts above the bogs. They brew, they bargain and they never forget a favour, or a slight.
hearthbound.culture.durnhal.desc: Stout dwarves who carve their halls from dark stone and keep their forges burning day and night. Trade is honour; debt is shame.
hearthbound.culture.hrimfell.desc: Hardy northern clans who carve runes into their longhouses and settle every quarrel over mead. Courage earns their respect.
hearthbound.culture.solarys.desc: Desert mystics who read the stars over whitewashed terraces. Their bazaars trade in rare goods from beyond the dunes.
hearthbound.culture.sylvaran.desc: Long-lived elves who raise verdigris roofs among the old trees. They value patience, songs and those who protect the forest.
hearthbound.culture.valdoran.desc: Proud humans of the green plains. Their timber-framed villages grow around a stone hall, and their knights keep the roads safe.
hearthbound.diplo.mediate_need: You must be an Ally here and a Friend of the other village
hearthbound.flag.hold_banner: Hold a banner in your main hand
hearthbound.flag.name: Banner of %s
hearthbound.flag.set_tip: Hold a banner designed on a loom: it becomes the village banner
hearthbound.greet.builder.0: One more stone and it'll stand for a century.
hearthbound.greet.builder.1: Bring me timber and I'll bring you walls.
hearthbound.greet.builder.2: Every roof starts with a single beam.
hearthbound.greet.elder.0: The board has work for willing hands.
hearthbound.greet.elder.1: Sit, traveller. Tell me what you have seen.
hearthbound.greet.elder.2: Our village remembers those who help it.
hearthbound.greet.farmer.0: The harvest looks good this year.
hearthbound.greet.guard.0: Keep your blade sheathed in the village.
hearthbound.greet.guard.2: I've got my eye on the tree line.
hearthbound.greet.innkeeper.0: A warm meal and a warmer fire!
hearthbound.greet.innkeeper.1: Looking for sellswords? I know a few.
hearthbound.greet.innkeeper.2: Rooms are cheap, stories are free.
hearthbound.greet.mage.2: The stars were restless last night.
hearthbound.greet.priest.0: May the hearth keep you warm.
hearthbound.greet.smith.1: Need an edge? I've got plenty.
hearthbound.hire.days: For %s days. Right click to make them wait or follow.
hearthbound.lordship.offer: %s would accept you as its lord. Open the village ledger to claim it.
hearthbound.notify.build_cap: %s has thanked you enough for today
hearthbound.notify.build_praise: The people of %s admire your building
hearthbound.objective.citizen: Become a citizen of a village
hearthbound.origin.builder.0: My father raised half the roofs in this valley. I raise the other half.
hearthbound.origin.builder.1: I learned the trade from dwarven masons in Durnhal. They say I lay stone too fast; here they say too slow.
hearthbound.origin.builder.10: I was a stonecutter in the quarries of the north. I came down with the stone and never went back up.
hearthbound.origin.builder.11: I learned to build from a book I found in a ruin. Half the pages were missing, so I invented the rest.
hearthbound.origin.builder.12: I was a thief who broke into houses. Now I know exactly how to build them so nobody can.
hearthbound.origin.builder.13: I build what the village needs, not what it asks for. Usually it forgives me later.
hearthbound.origin.builder.2: A storm took our house when I was a child. I swore every house I built would outlast any storm.
hearthbound.origin.builder.3: I was a carpenter on ships until I got seasick one time too many. Houses don't sway.
hearthbound.origin.builder.4: I rebuilt my neighbour's barn for fun. Then the whole street asked, and suddenly it was my job.
hearthbound.origin.builder.5: I was an apprentice to a cathedral master in the capital. Here I build smaller things, but I sign every one.
hearthbound.origin.builder.6: I came from the desert of Solarys, where we build with clay and shade. Your wooden houses still scare me a little.
hearthbound.origin.builder.7: I owe my life to a well-built wall that didn't fall during a raid. Now I build walls.
hearthbound.origin.builder.8: I drew houses in the dirt with a stick as a child. The elder noticed and gave me a hammer.
hearthbound.origin.builder.9: I'm a roofer's grandchild, a roofer's child and a roofer. I'm not good at anything with my feet on the ground.
hearthbound.origin.elder.0: I sat on the council for thirty years before they made me elder. Mostly because everyone else was younger.
hearthbound.origin.elder.1: I founded this village with a handful of families and a stubborn mule. The mule is buried under the well.
hearthbound.origin.elder.10: I lost an election for the post and won the next one by a single vote. Mine.
hearthbound.origin.elder.11: I travelled the whole world and came back to die at home. Then I forgot to die and they made me elder.
hearthbound.origin.elder.12: I planted the oak in the plaza the year the village was born. We've grown old together.
hearthbound.origin.elder.13: I was a merchant who went bankrupt honestly. The village said honesty was the rarer skill.
hearthbound.origin.elder.2: I was a judge in the capital until I grew tired of judging. Here I only listen, and that's usually enough.
hearthbound.origin.elder.3: The last elder chose me on her deathbed. I still don't know what she saw in me.
hearthbound.origin.elder.4: I came from the elven groves of Sylvaran, where two hundred years is young. Here they think I'm ancient.
hearthbound.origin.elder.5: I was a soldier, then a prisoner, then a teacher. Leading a village is the hardest of the four.
hearthbound.origin.elder.6: I keep the village chronicle. Whoever writes the history ends up being asked to decide it.
hearthbound.origin.elder.7: I settled a quarrel over a cow so well that people kept bringing me quarrels. Forty years later, here I am.
hearthbound.origin.elder.8: I was the only one who could read when the plague came. Someone had to read the letters and the wills.
hearthbound.origin.elder.9: I was born in Durnhal, under the mountain. Dwarves respect age, and I brought the habit with me.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.0: These fields have been in my family for five generations. The soil knows our hands.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.1: I was a soldier until the war ended. I traded the sword for a hoe, and I sleep much better.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.10: The swamp folk of Brumaverde taught me which mushrooms heal and which kill. I grow only the first kind. Mostly.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.11: I bought this land with the money from my first and only horse race. The horse still lives with me.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.12: I plough by moonlight because I can't sleep. The neighbours think I'm strange; the harvest disagrees.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.13: I was born in a year of drought. I think that's why I love the rain so much.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.2: I came from the cherry groves of Sylvaran with a pocket full of seeds. Half of this orchard grew from them.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.3: I inherited a field of stones from an uncle I never met. It took me ten years to make it a field of wheat.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.4: I was a cook in a noble house. I got tired of complaining about the vegetables, so now I grow them.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.5: My grandmother taught me to talk to the plants. People laugh, but my tomatoes are the biggest in the valley.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.6: I was the youngest of nine and got the smallest plot. I've made it the most productive.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.7: I came to the village during a famine and swore nobody here would go hungry again while I could hold a hoe.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.8: I kept bees before I kept fields. The bees taught me patience; the fields are still testing it.
hearthbound.origin.farmer.9: I was a scholar who studied plants in books. One day I realised I had never grown one.
hearthbound.origin.guard.0: I joined the guard at fifteen, lying about my age. Nobody has ever asked me to lie again.
hearthbound.origin.guard.1: I served in the border companies for ten years. This village is the first quiet posting I've had.
hearthbound.origin.guard.10: My mother was the captain before me. Every recruit compares me to her, and I lose every time.
hearthbound.origin.guard.11: I was an archer in the elven woods of Sylvaran. I miss the trees, but not the politics.
hearthbound.origin.guard.12: A guard saved my life when I was lost in the snow. I became one to pay the debt forward.
hearthbound.origin.guard.13: I volunteered for one night watch and never stopped. That was nineteen years ago.
hearthbound.origin.guard.2: Raiders burned my village when I was a child. I became a guard so no child here sees what I saw.
hearthbound.origin.guard.3: I was a knight's squire until the knight died. I kept his shield and found a place that needed it.
hearthbound.origin.guard.4: I came from the war-clans of Hrimfell. Here they find my axe alarming and my manners worse.
hearthbound.origin.guard.5: I was the village troublemaker. The elder decided the only cure was to put me in charge of keeping the peace.
hearthbound.origin.guard.6: I was a hunter. I track monsters now instead of deer; they're less elegant but easier to find.
hearthbound.origin.guard.7: I lost a duel and my honour in the capital. Here, nobody cares about that, only whether I show up at night.
hearthbound.origin.guard.8: I was the smallest in my training company. I'm still the one who's never lost a fight.
hearthbound.origin.guard.9: I guarded a merchant prince's vault for years. A village is harder: people are worth more than gold.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.0: The inn has been in my family since my great-grandmother poured the first ale. The stains on the bar are historic.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.1: I was a traveller who stayed one night too many. The old innkeeper handed me the keys and left.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.10: I learned to cook in the longhouses of Hrimfell, where a feast lasts three days. Here, three hours feels short.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.11: Everyone tells their secrets to an innkeeper. I keep them better than any vault.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.12: I was a fisher until the lake froze for a whole year. I sold the boat and bought the tavern.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.13: I built this inn at a crossroads because every road deserves a warm place to stop.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.2: I was a cook in a noble's kitchen. Here nobody complains about the food, they just eat more.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.3: I won the inn in a card game against a dwarf. He comes every week to try to win it back.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.4: I was a bard with a terrible voice. Now I listen to other people's songs, and I'm much better at that.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.5: I came from the desert of Solarys, where a guest is sacred. I brought that rule and the spices.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.6: I opened the inn after my husband died, so the house wouldn't be empty. It's never been empty since.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.7: I was a soldier who swore that if I survived, I'd pour drinks for the rest of my life. I survived.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.8: I brew my own mead from the honey of my own bees. The recipe dies with me, unless you earn it.
hearthbound.origin.innkeeper.9: I was an orphan who washed dishes here. Now I own the dishes, the sink and the building.
hearthbound.origin.mage.0: I studied at the academy of the capital until they expelled me for asking too many questions. Here I can ask all I want.
hearthbound.origin.mage.1: People call me the village mage. I just mix, measure and write things down.
hearthbound.origin.mage.10: I inherited a tower full of dusty jars from an uncle. I've spent ten years labelling them.
hearthbound.origin.mage.11: I was a dwarven assayer in Durnhal, testing ores. Now I test everything else.
hearthbound.origin.mage.12: I lost my sight in one eye to a failed experiment. The other eye sees much more carefully now.
hearthbound.origin.mage.13: I wanted to be a knight but was hopeless with a sword. A book, however, I can wield.
hearthbound.origin.mage.2: I was apprenticed to an old herbalist from the swamps of Brumaverde. She taught me that every poison is a medicine in the right dose.
hearthbound.origin.mage.3: I read every book in the monastery by the age of twelve. Then I came here to find new ones.
hearthbound.origin.mage.4: I was a star-watcher in the desert of Solarys. The sky here is cloudier, but the stars are the same.
hearthbound.origin.mage.5: I blew up my father's kitchen at nine. He decided I needed a proper laboratory before I blew up the house.
hearthbound.origin.mage.6: I was an elven archivist in Sylvaran. I left because I wanted to write new things, not copy old ones.
hearthbound.origin.mage.7: I came to cure a sick child and stayed because the whole village kept getting sick. They're healthier now.
hearthbound.origin.mage.8: I was a court astrologer. I predicted the king's fall, which is why I had to leave quickly.
hearthbound.origin.mage.9: I collect stones, bones and strange lights. Someone has to understand them.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.0: I was born on a caravan and learned to count before I could walk. Numbers are my mother tongue.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.1: I sold my first apple at six years old, at twice its price. I've been improving ever since.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.10: I was a sailor. When I came ashore I only knew how to do one thing: bargain with everyone at the port.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.11: I trade with elves, dwarves and witches alike. Gold has no accent.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.12: I lost everything in a fire and started again with one basket of eggs. I still keep that basket.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.13: My shop was my grandfather's. The sign still has his name, and I'm not changing it.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.2: I came from the bazaars of Solarys, where haggling is an art. Here people pay the first price. It breaks my heart.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.3: I was a noble's accountant until I found out who he was stealing from. I left with the ledger and opened a stall.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.4: I inherited debts, not money. I've paid half of them and made friends with the rest of the creditors.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.5: I was a pirate's cook. I'll say no more about it, except that I learned what everything is worth.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.6: I traded furs with the clans of Hrimfell for twenty winters. I have enough stories to sell as well.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.7: I opened this stall to pay for my sister's medicine. She's well now; the stall stayed.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.8: I was a thief who got caught. The judge sentenced me to honest work. Turns out I'm good at it.
hearthbound.origin.merchant.9: I sell a bit of everything because I could never decide what I liked most.
hearthbound.origin.priest.0: I tend the shrine as my grandmother did. I don't know if anyone listens to the prayers, but the people who say them feel better.
hearthbound.origin.priest.1: I was a soldier who saw too much. I came to the shrine to find peace and ended up sweeping it every morning.
hearthbound.origin.priest.10: I carve the names of the dead on the shrine's stones. Every name is a story I make sure isn't forgotten.
hearthbound.origin.priest.11: I was a rune-reader among the clans of Hrimfell. Here I read people instead of runes.
hearthbound.origin.priest.12: I came to the shrine to ask for a miracle. It didn't come, so I stayed to help others wait for theirs.
hearthbound.origin.priest.13: I keep the shrine's garden. The flowers are my prayers; I've never been good with words.
hearthbound.origin.priest.2: I was left at the shrine's door as a baby. It's the only home I've ever known.
hearthbound.origin.priest.3: I travelled from the dunes of Solarys following a dream. The dream ended here, at this altar.
hearthbound.origin.priest.4: I was a thief who stole the shrine's candlesticks. The old keeper caught me and put me to work polishing them.
hearthbound.origin.priest.5: I sang in the choir of a great temple. Here I sing alone, but the echo keeps me company.
hearthbound.origin.priest.6: I promised a dying friend I'd look after the shrine. That was supposed to be for a year. It's been twenty.
hearthbound.origin.priest.7: I come from the witch-covens of Brumaverde. People here were suspicious at first; now they bring me their troubles.
hearthbound.origin.priest.8: I was a healer before I was a keeper. Sometimes a kind word does more than any herb.
hearthbound.origin.priest.9: I lost my faith in the capital and found it again in this little shrine full of wildflowers.
hearthbound.origin.smith.0: I was born beside the forge; my first lullaby was the hammer. It still helps me sleep.
hearthbound.origin.smith.1: I learned from a dwarven master in Durnhal who never praised anyone. Once he nodded at my work. Once.
hearthbound.origin.smith.10: I was a miner until the tunnel collapsed. I decided I'd rather work the metal than dig for it.
hearthbound.origin.smith.11: I talk to the metal while I work. It never answers, but it listens better than most people.
hearthbound.origin.smith.12: I learned the trade in the desert forges of Solarys, where the fire is the sun itself.
hearthbound.origin.smith.13: I became a smith because the old one couldn't lift the hammer anymore. I was the only one strong enough and foolish enough.
hearthbound.origin.smith.2: I made weapons for a war I didn't believe in. Now I make ploughs, and I'm happier for it.
hearthbound.origin.smith.3: I was a farrier's apprentice. The horses liked me more than the farrier did.
hearthbound.origin.smith.4: I found an old anvil in a ruin and carried it here on my back. The village was built around it, more or less.
hearthbound.origin.smith.5: My mother was the smith, and her mother before her. The forge has never been cold for a hundred years.
hearthbound.origin.smith.6: I came from the snowy clans of Hrimfell, where a bad blade means death. I don't make bad blades.
hearthbound.origin.smith.7: I was a jeweller in the city. Iron is less delicate than gold, and so are the customers.
hearthbound.origin.smith.8: I burned my hands in my first week and nearly quit. The scars are the first thing I teach apprentices about.
hearthbound.origin.smith.9: I fixed a traveller's broken sword for free. He turned out to be a lord, and paid for this forge.
hearthbound.origin.villager.0: I do a bit of everything: carry water, fix fences, find lost goats. Nobody else wants the odd jobs, so they're mine.
hearthbound.origin.villager.1: I arrived with a travelling fair and missed the wagons when they left. That was eleven summers ago.
hearthbound.origin.villager.10: I am the one who rings the bell at dawn. Twenty years without missing a morning.
hearthbound.origin.villager.11: My parents were travelling actors. I got tired of the road and stayed where the bread was good.
hearthbound.origin.villager.12: I came to deliver a single letter and stayed for a wedding. That was a long time ago.
hearthbound.origin.villager.13: I sweep the plaza, feed the cats and know everyone's secrets. It's a living.
hearthbound.origin.villager.2: My family has lived on this hill since before there was a village. We were here first; the walls came later.
hearthbound.origin.villager.3: I was a noble's servant in the capital. One day I simply walked out the door and kept walking until I got here.
hearthbound.origin.villager.4: The elder found me asleep in a haystack as a child and nobody ever came looking for me. The whole village raised me.
hearthbound.origin.villager.5: I came from the swamps of Brumaverde. People here still check my cooking for frogs.
hearthbound.origin.villager.6: I used to guard caravans until a bad knee retired me. Now the heaviest thing I carry is gossip.
hearthbound.origin.villager.7: I won my house in a game of dice. The previous owner still waves at me, somewhat bitterly.
hearthbound.origin.villager.8: I was a shepherd in the high pastures of Hrimfell. Down here the winters feel like spring.
hearthbound.origin.villager.9: I tried five trades and was bad at all of them. The village kept me anyway.

hearthbound.person.keepsake: Keepsake: a unique item from their story

hearthbound.person.no_quest: They have nothing to ask of you. For now.

hearthbound.person.tomorrow: That's enough for today. Come back tomorrow and I'll tell you more.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.bio.0: I grew up in the forest. I read tracks before letters, and I still trust the former more.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.bio.1: Something poisons the deer by the marsh. Dead animals, no wounds. Only one creature does that.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.bio.2: The witch of the marsh took my brother's eyesight when we were children. I've waited years to face her.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.dialogu: Walk softer. The forest hears you coming a mile away. There, see? The jay has already told everyone.
I grew up out there among the pines. I read tracks before letters, and I still trust tracks more.
Only one creature kills like that. I won't say its name yet. Saying it aloud feels like calling it.
But first, closer trouble. Spiders are nesting near the old oak. Keep your eyes up when you walk there.
I counted the webs this morning: thick as sailcloth, strung between the branches like a fishing net.
The village children gather mushrooms under that oak every autumn. Their mothers don't know about the nest yet.
Clear that nest. Six of them at least, before some child walks in there with a basket.
That print? Fox, limping on the left forepaw, passed at dawn. Letters never tell you that much.
You hunt well. For a townsfolk. Don't let it go to your head; the rabbits are slow this year.
I don't do well indoors. Walls make me deaf. I sleep in the loft with the window open, even when it snows.
I have a brother, Wren. Older than me. He carves wooden birds so real the cats stalk them.
He's blind. Has been since we were children. He knows the forest by its sounds better than I know it by sight.
We grew up by the marsh, at the forest's edge. Mother told us never to follow the lights over the water.
Wren followed them once. I followed Wren. That's all I'll say about it for now.
Something's wrong at the marsh lately. I found three deer dead by the reeds. No wounds. No bites. Just dead.
Clean work at the oak. You'd make a decent hunter. Don't grin like that; I said decent.
The children are back under the oak with their baskets. They don't know. That's how it should be.
Now she's back. The deer, the silent deaths, green lights at the last new moon. I've seen them.
But I won't go in half-ready like a frightened child. Not this time. I need gear that won't fail in the mud.
My boots are rotting through and my quivers are split. The marsh eats leather the way a goat eats rope.
The good kind of hide, thick and supple, that's what I need. Cured properly, not market scraps.
Bring me leather, ten pieces, and I'll make new quivers and boots. I'll owe you a favour, and I pay my favours.
I promised you the story. Wren was nine, I was seven. The lights over the marsh were green and dancing.
He waded in after them. I ran after him. There was a hut on stilts that smelled of boiled nettles and something sweeter.
She came out smiling. Grey skin, crooked hat, a bottle in her hand. She said, 'Look closer, little one.'
She threw the bottle in Wren's face. It smoked. He screamed. I dragged him home through the reeds by his collar.
When the smoke cleared from his eyes, he couldn't see. Never again. He was nine.
Mother went to the elders. They said the witch had lived there before the village. Leave her be.
So I learned to hunt. Every track, every bowstring, every snare. I told myself it was for food. It wasn't.
Wren never blamed anyone. He just learned to carve. He says his hands see better than my eyes. He may be right.
Fine hides. These will last me years. The boots are already stitched; they don't squeak, which is everything.
I made a spare quiver. It's yours. Don't argue; you'll thank me when you're three arrows short in a cave.
I've watched her hut from the treeline for three nights. She leaves at dusk and comes back before dawn.
She still throws bottles, like before. Poison, weakness, slowness. Bring milk if you can; it clears the worst of it.
I'm a good shot, but my hands shake when I see that hat. I'd miss. I know I would. I hate knowing it.
You don't carry that old fear. You'd see her for what she is: an old poisoner in a hut on stilts.
She's back, and the animals die one by one. I can't face her alone. Not after what she did. Will you?
I went to see Wren yesterday. He ran his fingers over the new boots and said, 'You're going back there.'
I didn't answer. He knew. He always knows. He said, 'Don't go back for me. Go for the deer.'
Here's the truth: I'm afraid. Not of her claws or her bottles. Of being seven again, running through the reeds.
I've faced wolves, bears, a cave full of spiders. And a crooked hat in a dream still wakes me in a sweat.
The marsh is worse now. The frogs have gone quiet. Herons gone. Fish floating belly-up. She's brewing something big.
Two hunters from the next village went in last week. One came back. He won't talk. He just shakes.
My dream, if you want to know? A quiet marsh. Wren sitting on the bank, listening to the frogs again.
And then I'd teach you to call the owls. It's the only music I know. Wren taught me, after he went blind.
It's over. I stood at the edge of the reeds and heard the frogs start up again. Nothing ever sounded so good.
Take my bow. Your aim deserves it. I carved the grip myself; Wren says it's crooked, and he's right.
I'll keep my promise. Tonight at dusk, meet me at the old oak. Cup your hands like this and blow. Softly.
Hear that? An owl answered. No, don't laugh, you'll scare it. Again. There. That one was yours.
Wren's wooden bird is finished. It's an owl. He says it's you. The mud is on the claws, apparently.
I still don't like walls, or towns, or people much. You're the exception. Don't tell anyone.
Go well, and walk softly. When you hear an owl on your road, it might be me saying hello.
I told Wren. He said nothing for a long while. Then he laughed, the way he laughed before the marsh.
He wants to carve you something. He asked what you look like. I said, 'Muddy.' He's working on it.
The deer are back at the marsh edge, drinking at dawn. A doe with two fawns. I didn't even reach for my bow.
Some mornings you may find fresh game at your door. A rabbit, a pheasant. I've no idea who leaves it there.
Don't thank me for it. I said I've no idea. Nobody saw anything. The forest keeps its secrets.
Remember how you walked when we met? Like a cart full of pans. You're quieter now. Almost a forest creature.
I burned her hut. The stilts, the bottles, the nettles. The smoke went green for a moment, then just grey.
Now the children dare each other to go near the marsh. Before, nobody dared. I call that progress.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.epilogu: The marsh is quiet again. The hunter leaves fresh game at your door and never says it was them.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.stage.0: Spiders have nested by the old oak and the children gather mushrooms there. Clear the nest.
Clean work. You'd make a decent hunter.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.stage.1: I need leather for new quivers and boots. The good kind. Bring me some and I'll owe you a favour.
Fine hides. These will last me years.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.stage.2: She's back. The animals die one by one. I can't face her alone... not after what she did. Will you?
It's over. My brother will sleep better. Take my bow; your aim deserves it.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.talk.0: Walk softer. The forest hears you coming a mile away.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.talk.1: Spiders are nesting near the old oak. Keep your eyes up.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.talk.2: You hunt well. For a townsfolk.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.talk.3: When this is over, I'll teach you to call the owls. It's the only music I know.
hearthbound.persona.beast_hunter.title: Beast Hunter
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.bio.0: At fifteen I pulled a blade out of a boulder by the mill, just to fetch it for someone else. Since then the elders keep asking me to decide things.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.bio.1: I never wanted a crown. I wanted a table where nobody sits at the head, and a village where the strong protect the weak because they choose to.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.dialogue: Don't bow, please. I still muck out the stables on Thursdays, and the horses don't bow either.
Welcome. If anyone asks you to settle an argument, send them to me. Everyone else does.
Here is the trouble: every quarrel in this village begins with who sits where.
At the harvest supper, the miller sat above the smith, and they didn't speak for a season.
I've been thinking of something simpler. A table with no head and no foot.
If nobody sits at the top, then nobody sits at the bottom. It's carpentry, not magic.
Bring me logs, and I'll build a round table. Everyone sits as an equal, and we'll see what happens.
I like mornings here. The mill wheel turns, the bread rises, and nobody needs a ruling yet.
Do you know how to mend a fence? I ask everyone. Fences are how neighbours stay friends.
The elders call me 'young master'. I'm neither very young nor anybody's master.
When I was fifteen, my foster brother forgot his sword before a tournament. I ran to fetch one.
There was a blade stuck in a boulder by the mill. I pulled it out without thinking. It came like a loose tooth.
Nobody else could put it back in, or pull it out again. Suddenly everyone was staring at me.
The old storytellers have a tale like that, of a boy king in Britain. I only wanted to help my brother.
Since that day the elders keep asking me to decide things. Wells, weddings, whose goat ate whose cabbage.
Look at them, all sitting as equals and still arguing. That's progress, believe it or not.
The miller and the smith shared a loaf yesterday. Neither would admit it was pleasant.
Lately something tests our walls at night. The dead, the creepers, things with red eyes.
And the young ones watch us. They want to know whether grown-ups run.
I could order the guards to stand. But orders aren't what I want the children to learn.
I'll stand myself, and I'd rather not stand alone.
Stand with me inside the village when the monsters come. Let the children see what a village does.
Now I'll tell you the part I don't say in the square: I never wanted a crown.
When the sword came out, an old sage whispered, 'This is only the start.' I wished it were the end.
People think the stone chose me. I think it chose someone willing to carry things for others.
What I want is a village where the strong protect the weak because they choose to, not because they're told.
The table helps. But a table is only wood if nobody sits at it when times are hard.
My foster brother still teases me. 'You were only fetching my sword.' He's right, and I love him for it.
Some nights I dream of a boat on a misty lake. I wake very calm, and I don't know why.
I'm not afraid of dying. I'm afraid of leaving behind people who only obeyed and never chose.
Nobody fled. Did you see? That's what a village is: people who don't flee.
The baker's girl held a torch all night and never once shook. I've never been prouder.
I want a blade waiting for them. Not to make them a ruler. To remind them they can be trusted.
The smith has agreed to help me forge it, if I bring the iron myself.
It must be good iron. A sword that waits for years has to be patient metal.
I'm told you know where the iron hides in the hills.
Bring me iron, and I'll forge a blade for the next one and leave it waiting in the stone.
Now that we've fought side by side, I can tell you what keeps me awake.
I won't be here forever. Nobody is. And I worry about what happens when I go.
If the village only holds together because of me, then I've built nothing at all.
There's an old legend that a king sleeps under a hill, waiting to return. I'd rather be forgotten and not needed.
My dream is simple: that one day nobody remembers who pulled the sword, only what the table was for.
I think about that boulder by the mill often. Everybody tries it once. It's just a rock now.
But one day someone else will need a sword from a stone. Someone who doesn't expect it.
Some shy child, some stable hand, somebody fetching things for others, like I was.
You still have my sword, I hope. Don't look at me like that; I meant it.
The new blade sits in the boulder now. Children try it every morning before chores.
I don't dream of the misty lake as often now. When I do, the boat is empty, and that's fine.
You came here a stranger and sat at our table like you'd always had a place. You did.
If I'm remembered at all, I hope it's as the one who built a table and then pulled up a chair.
Come to supper on feast days. There's no head seat, so you can't be late for it.
Go on, then. There's a quarrel about a goat waiting for me, and I intend to lose it gracefully.
One of them will pull it someday. I hope they laugh when it happens, instead of being frightened.
The round table is in the square now. Rain or shine, someone is sitting at it.
I sit at it too, like anyone else. Last week I lost an argument about turnips. Wonderful.
The elders have started deciding things among themselves. They barely ask me anymore.
Do you know how good that feels? Like setting down a load you forgot you were carrying.
I still muck out the stables on Thursdays. The horses remain unimpressed by legends.
Remember the night on the walls? The baker's girl tells it every supper, bigger each time.
In her version you slew forty monsters. I slew three and tripped over a bucket.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.epilogue: Now the round table stands in the square, and the one who drew the sword sits at it like anyone else.
Every quarrel in this village starts with who sits where. Bring me logs and I'll build a round table. No head, no foot.
Look at them, all sitting as equals and still arguing. That's progress.
Monsters test our walls at night, and the young ones watch to see what we do. Stand with me inside the village.
Nobody fled. That's what a village is: people who don't flee.
One day someone else will need a sword from a stone. Bring me iron: I'll forge one and leave it waiting.
Actually... take mine. The stone can keep the new one for whoever comes after you.
A blade for the next one
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.talk.0: Don't bow, please. I still muck out the stables on Thursdays.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.talk.1: The boulder is still by the mill. Everybody tries it once. It's just a rock now.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.talk.2: A leader is only someone who stays when everyone else has a reason to leave.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.talk.3: Some nights I dream of a boat and a lake mist. I wake up very calm.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_arthur.title: The sword in the stone
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.bio.0: When I was young, a thing from the moors dragged people out of the mead hall every night. I crossed the sea, waited in the dark and fought it bare-handed.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.bio.1: Then its mother came up from the black lake, and I dove after her. Fifty years later, a fire-drake woke. Every hero gets one monster too many.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.dialogu: Sit, sit. My knees creak louder than the door, but they still carry me to the inn.
Fame is the only thing that outlives us. Still, I'd trade some for a warm hearth.
Now something prowls our own inn at night. Drinkers go out for air and don't come back.
The dead, mostly. Shambling things that hate laughter and music, just like the one on the moors.
The innkeeper wants to stop the music altogether. I told her that's how the monster wins.
My hands aren't what they were. I can still hold a door, but not all night, not every night.
Help me make the nights safe? Let the inn sing again without counting empty chairs in the morning.
Young ones ask how to be brave. I tell them: be scared, and go anyway.
I once swam for five days in armour. Don't try it. The fish laugh at you.
You've got a good grip. I noticed when you shook my hand. Most people flinch.
Long ago I crossed the sea to a king's great hall. Something from the moors was eating his warriors.
Every night it came, and every morning there were empty benches. It hated their singing.
I told the king: no sword, no shield. If the thing fights bare-handed, so will I.
I waited in the dark, pretending to sleep. When it grabbed me, I didn't let go. Neither did it, at first.
In the end it tore free and ran home to die. It left its arm behind. We hung it from the rafters.
Silence at last... then music again. That's how it should be. Did you hear the fiddler?
I bought you a drink. I also drank it, because you took too long. I'll buy another.
I've never told anyone how afraid I was down there. Colder than fear. Like being forgotten.
Lately the lake past the marsh has gone dark again. The drowned walk out of it at dusk.
The creatures came from there, and there's worse at the bottom. I can smell it on the wind.
I'm too old to dive alone. That's hard to say. It took me three mugs and a week.
Come with me down into the mere? Watch my back in the water. I'll watch yours.
Now I'll tell you what came after the moor-thing. The part I tell less often.
The next night its mother came. Quieter. Angrier. She took the king's dearest friend.
She lived at the bottom of a black lake where the trees hang over the water like old men.
Even the deer, hunted by dogs, would rather die on the bank than jump into that water.
I jumped. It took most of a day to reach the bottom. The water was full of teeth.
The sword they lent me bent on her hide. I found an old giant-blade on her wall and used that.
The blade melted in my hand from her poison blood. I came up holding only the hilt.
Everyone on the bank had gone home, sure I was dead. Only my own companions waited.
The water ran clear afterwards. Down there I found another old giant-sword. It melted too.
Two melted swords in one life. The smiths say I'm bad for business. They're not wrong.
Now a thief has stirred fire-beasts near an old hoard again, out in the burning lands.
Blazes, spinning and spitting fire. Everyone runs. I'm not running. I've done this before.
But I'm not going alone. I learned that from Wiglaf. A hero alone is just a story about a grave.
If I don't come back, build a tall mound by the sea. Sailors like a landmark. So do I.
I'm going to fight the fire-beasts. Stay by me like Wiglaf did? That's all I'll ever ask of you.
You swim well. Better than me at your age. I wore armour, which, as we said, the fish found funny.
Now let me tell you the last story. The one I haven't finished living.
I was king myself for fifty years. Peaceful years. Then a thief took one cup from an old hoard.
A fire-drake woke under the hill, and burned my hall to the ground over one cup.
I went to fight it with eleven warriors. Ten ran into the woods. Only one young friend stayed.
Wiglaf, his name was. He stood by me in the smoke while the dragon's fire melted his shield.
The tales say that was my last fight. Maybe it was. Maybe an old one got lucky and walked away.
My fear isn't dying. It's that every hero gets one monster too many, and I don't know which one mine is.
Still alive! Unexpected. Keep my helm: it went down into the mere and came back up. So did I.
My mound will have to wait. The sea's in no hurry, and neither am I anymore.
Remember the black water? I still dream of it, but in the dream you're there, holding the rope.
I've started teaching the smith's children to swim. Without armour. I learned something at least.
When I'm gone, burn nothing, raise the mound, and tell the story wrong. Make the monsters huge.
But not yet. Not yet. There's still ale in the barrel and songs I haven't heard twice.
Go on, walk your road. If anything crawls out of a lake near you, you know where the inn is.
I tell the three fights at the inn every week now. The children bring their own benches.
Each year the monsters grow a little bigger. The moor-thing is now as tall as the church.
The fire-drake had one head last spring. By winter it had three. I blame the ale.
You come into the story too, you know. As the one who stood when the others ran.
The innkeeper gave up trying to stop the music. There's singing until late. The dead stay away.
I sleep through the night now. First time in fifty years. I'd forgotten what dawn looks like from bed.
Some young ones want to become monster-slayers. I tell them to become good friends first.
A good friend beside you in the smoke is worth more than any giant's sword. Those melt.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.epilogu: Now the old monster-slayer tells the story of three fights at the inn, and each year the monsters grow a little bigger.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.stage.0: Something stalks the tavern at night, dragging off drinkers. It hates laughter and music. Help me make the nights safe.
Silence at last... then music again. That's how it should be.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.stage.1: The creatures came from the dark lake, and there's worse down there. I'm too old to dive alone. Come with me.
The water ran clear afterwards. Down there I found an old giant-sword, and it melted in my hand.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.stage.2: A thief woke fire-beasts guarding an old hoard. Everyone ran but one young friend. I'm going. Stay by me like they did.
Still alive! Unexpected. Take my helm: it went down into the mere, and it came back up. So did I.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.talk.0: Fame is the only thing that outlives us. Still, I'd trade some for a warm hearth.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.talk.1: I once swam for five days in armour. Don't try it. The fish laugh at you.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.talk.2: Young ones ask how to be brave. I tell them: be scared, and go anyway.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.talk.3: When I'm gone, burn nothing and build a tall mound by the sea. Sailors like a landmark.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_beowulf.title: Three monsters, one life
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.bio.0: I swore to wed only someone brave enough to ride through fire, and strong enough to beat me at stones. One did. Then another took the credit, in borrowed face.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.bio.1: I learned of the trick at a riverbank, from a rival's mocking words. My anger burned half a kingdom. I've had many cold winters to regret it.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.dialog: You have a thrower's shoulders, or you will once I'm done with you. Everyone here loses to me eventually; you might as well start today.
I keep watch at the edge of the village. Old habit. I once guarded something far stranger than turnips.
Some nights I still dream of that wall of flame. In the dreams it isn't empty. Things hop inside it like living coals.
The miners swear they've seen those same burning lumps deep below, bouncing in the heat. So I'm not imagining them.
I'm too old to go into the depths and leap about with a spear. My knees filed a complaint years ago.
If those fire-things were gone, perhaps my dreams would go quiet too. It's foolish. I'd still like to try.
Go below for me and put a few of them out. Come back unburned, and I'll tell you who really crossed my flames.
Don't swear anything to me lightly. I remember every oath spoken near me, even the ones mumbled into soup.
The smith complains I throw his whetstones into the river. I call it training. He calls it theft.
I can't sit near a hearth for long. The crackle makes my hands itch for a spear.
When I was young I slept a long while behind a wall of flame. Not by choice. Someone older than me decided I needed humbling.
The fire never burned me, but it kept everyone out. For years I heard hooves stop at its edge and turn around.
I made a vow in there: only someone who crossed the flames would have my hand. It seemed a clever lock at the time.
Then one rider did cross. Golden hair, easy laugh, horse wreathed in sparks. I remember thinking the fire looked jealous.
Later the flames parted again, for someone wearing the face I'd been promised. I kept my oath. I shouldn't have trusted my eyes.
You came back smelling of smoke and grinning. I slept all night. Not one hopping light in my dreams.
I promised you the truth. The one who crossed my flames was honest. The one I married was that rider's friend, and afraid of fire.
I've wondered since whether I loved the honest one or only the fire he crossed. Probably both. Probably neither.
Enough gloom. The young ones saw me hurl a rock over the well yesterday, and now they won't leave me alone.
They want a real contest: throwing stones, then leaping to where they land. The old way. My way.
I expected to hate the idea. Contests brought me nothing but lies. This time nobody throws in a borrowed face; I'll make sure of it.
We need stones, heaps of them, heavy cobbles for the throwing lines. Bring me a good pile and I'll mark out the field.
The friend wanted me but couldn't make his horse face the flames. So the honest one crossed for him, wearing his face like a borrowed cloak.
The one in the borrowed face lay beside me three nights with a bare sword between us. I thought it was courtesy. It was loyalty to a friend.
I had also demanded a contest: beat me throwing stones and leaping after them. Nobody had ever managed it.
That day an arm threw further than any I'd known. I lost, and I was proud to lose. That pride lasted years.
We exchanged rings in the dark. I wore mine believing it honestly won. Never trust a ring you didn't see forged.
The truth came at a riverbank. A rival and I bickering over who should wade upstream, whose spouse was greater.
She laughed, and showed me the ring I had given away behind the fire. My own ring, on her finger. I didn't shout. That was worse.
The saga-singers give everyone grand names now. To me they were only ever the honest one and the clever one.
Did you see her throw? That skinny girl from the mill nearly beat me. I haven't been so delighted to almost lose.
I train her at dawn now. She argues with everything I say. Good. Obedient throwers never improve.
My fear is simple: dying having only regretted, without ever doing one small right thing about it.
The old hall stood on a hill not far from here. Only blackened stones remain, but I know where his seat was.
My dream is foolish for an old warrior. I want to light something up there that isn't a pyre or a war.
One candle feels like an apology. Three feel like a vigil: one for him, one for the wife I wronged, and one for me.
Bring me candles, would you? Three. I'll carry them up that hill myself, however long my knees take.
I gave her one rule above all: never swear anything while angry. She asked why. I didn't answer her yet.
The truth is my anger burned half a kingdom. After the riverbank I wanted someone to pay, and I barely cared who.
I told my husband the honest one had betrayed him. It was a lie wrapped around a small true thing. Those are the worst kind.
They killed him in his bed. The one who'd laid a sword between us out of loyalty. I laughed when I heard. Once.
Then I didn't laugh for years. The hall went quiet, and I learned that revenge has no taste at all.
The singers say I threw myself on his pyre. I didn't. I walked away from the ashes, which takes much longer.
I've had many cold winters to regret it. Winters are long when you spend them talking to someone who can't answer.
That's who the autumn candle is for. You'd guessed, I think. You have a way of not asking that I appreciate.
Three small lights on that hill. The wind tried all night and couldn't put them out. I watched till dawn to be sure.
It doesn't undo anything. I knew it wouldn't. But I came down the hill lighter than I went up.
Anger still visits. I let it sit by the fire but never let it make promises. It leaves sooner that way.
I kept one of your cobbles from the contest. It sits on my windowsill. Ugly thing. I'm very fond of it.
If you ever want a rematch at stones, I'm here. You'll lose, of course. Tradition.
Take care of your oaths out there. Keep the few that matter, and let the rest burn out harmlessly.
Go on, the youngsters are waiting at the throwing line. Come back soon, and bring someone who can beat me. Nobody has yet.
The mill girl threw past the well this morning. Past it! I've told her she may gloat for exactly one day.
I've added a lesson to training: before you swear anything, ask twice. Once to the other person, once to yourself.
Now the children swear oaths about chores and then ask twice. Their parents think I'm a genius. I let them.
Remember the burning lumps you put out below? I dreamed of the flame wall last night. Just fire. Warm, quiet, empty.
You're the first person in years I'd let watch me lose. From me, that's the biggest compliment there is.
Sometimes I think of the honest one when you walk into the square. You carry yourself the same way: no borrowed faces.
Someone asked if I was the one from the old saga. I said the one in the saga was much taller, with better hair.
I light the autumn candle openly now. The young ones bring me a spare each year and never ask who it's for.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.epilog: Now the old stone-thrower trains the village youth, and teaches them to ask twice before they swear anything.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.source: The Saga of the Volsungs — anonymous (c. 1260)
In my youth I lived beyond a wall of flame. Its creatures still haunt my dreams. Go below and put some out for me?
You came back unburned. Few could. I'd have married you on the spot, back then.
The young ones want a contest: throwing stones and leaping after them, like in my day. Bring me stones!
I won, of course. But one girl came close. I'll train her.
Long ago I brought ruin on someone who had never lied to me. Bring me candles; I'll light them where the old hall stood.
Three small lights. It doesn't undo anything. It helps me live with it.
A candle for the wrong one
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.talk.0: I can throw a stone further than anyone in this village. Want to lose to me?
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.talk.1: Oaths are like fire: easy to light, hard to put out.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.talk.2: The one who crossed my flames was honest. The one who deceived me was their friend. I hated the wrong one.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.talk.3: I light a candle every autumn. I don't say for whom.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_brunhild.title: Behind the ring of fire
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.bio.0: Slanderers turned the king against me and I was banished with nine days to leave. No inn would open its door. A little girl begged me to ride on, for her family's sake.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.bio.1: To feed my people I pawned two chests 'full of gold' to the moneylenders. They were full of sand. I paid it all back, with interest. I still blush.
A bad lord can't make a good vassal bad. Remember that, whoever you end up serving.
My beard has never been cut in anger. Long story. Very long beard.
I left my wife and daughters at a monastery gate. Parting was like tearing a nail from the flesh.
A band of loyal people followed me into exile. Sixty lances, and not a loaf between them.
We leave at dawn, and they must eat on the road. I've no money, and no lender trusts an exile.
So I've had an idea. A shameful one. It needs two sturdy chests, heavy and well locked.
Bring me two sturdy chests. What goes inside is my business... and my shame.
I keep the gate, advise the elders, and haggle at market. Old soldiers need three jobs to stay out of trouble.
You stand like someone who's slept on the road. I know the posture. I wore it for years.
Don't let the grey fool you. I can still sit a horse from dawn until the owls.
Once I served a king faithfully. Then slanderers whispered in his ear, and he believed them.
I was banished with nine days to leave his lands. Nine days, and no inn allowed to open its door.
I rode into a town and every shutter was closed. A little girl of nine came out alone.
She begged me to ride on, for her family's sake. The king had threatened any who helped me. I rode on.
The old Castilian song of the Cid tells a tale much like it. I've heard the minstrels. They get my horse's name wrong.
Heavy with sand, sealed with honour. The moneylenders will be repaid, I swear it on my beard.
You've helped me with the worst thing I've ever done, so you deserve to know it all.
But the sand only bought us days. Exiles only eat what they win, honestly or not at all.
Raiders plague the border villages. Crossbow men burning barns, taking what little there is.
The villages can't pay soldiers. But they'll feed anyone who frees them. That's honest bread.
We'll clear them out, and earn our keep with our swords instead of sand.
Ride with us against the raiders? Help us win our bread honestly.
To feed my people, I pawned those two chests to the moneylenders in the town, 'full of gold'.
I told them they mustn't open them for a year. They were so pleased they gave me six hundred marks.
They were full of sand. Every grain of it. I filled them with my own hands in the riverbed.
My people ate that night. I didn't. I couldn't swallow for shame.
I've paid it all back since, with interest. I still blush whenever I see a chest.
Loyalty to someone who wronged you is foolish. Or it's the only thing that heals. I still don't know.
I never spoke against the king. Not once. Even in exile, I called him my lord.
People asked why. I told them: if I become bitter, then the slanderers were right about me.
The villages cheer, and my people eat tonight. Better than any sand. Thank you.
An old woman kissed my beard. I didn't have the heart to tell her it's not done.
I can't carry it myself. A banished soldier at the king's door would be arrested, or worse.
It needs someone honest, who owes the king nothing and me very little.
You've seen how I pay my debts. You know I don't lie, except to moneylenders, once.
The king holds court in a village not far from here. Take the message there.
Carry one more message to the king: I ask nothing but my family back.
Now I'll tell you what still keeps me awake, after all these battles.
My daughters have grown up without me. My wife writes letters I read until they fall apart.
Every victory I've had, I've sent a share to the king. Horses, swords, a banner once.
Three times. Not to buy his favour. To show him that I'm still his, even banished.
I'm afraid he'll never answer. That I'll die a stranger's death on some border with my beard uncut.
My dream isn't lands or titles. It's a table, my family at it, and the right to sit down.
I've written one more message. It asks nothing. No lands, no pardon, no gold.
Only my wife and daughters back. Only to be allowed to be their family again.
Pardoned! After all this time. Keep that blade; it won me everything but the one thing, and now I have that too.
My wife came through the gate first. She said, 'You're thinner.' I said, 'You're lovelier.' We both cried.
You carried my last message, and brought my family home. My beard and I are in your debt.
If anyone ever banishes you, come here. My door will open, whatever the king says.
Come eat with us on feast days. My daughters will interrogate you. Answer bravely.
I still keep the gate, but only by day now. At night, I have somewhere much better to be.
Go well. And if you ever see a chest full of sand, think of me, and plant something in it.
My daughters are grown women with opinions. They've taken over my accounts. I'm not allowed to haggle anymore.
The moneylenders were repaid double. They sent me a thank-you letter. It's framed in the hall.
And the chests of sand? They hold seeds for the spring now. Beans, barley, onions.
Every time I open one, I laugh. The shame has turned into something that grows.
The king visited last month. We didn't speak of the past. We spoke of horses, which is safer.
Remember the raiders at the border? Those villages send us cheese every harvest. Too much cheese.
The little girl who begged me to ride on is grown now. She came to my table. I gave her the best seat.
I still say: a bad lord can't make a good vassal bad. But a good friend can make a bad day better.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.epilogue: Now the exile is home, the moneylenders were repaid double, and the chests of sand hold seeds for the spring.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.source: The Song of My Cid — anonymous (c. 1200)
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.stage.0.ask: We leave at dawn and the band has no bread. Bring me two sturdy chests. What goes inside is my business... and my shame.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.stage.0.don: Heavy with sand, sealed with honour. The moneylenders will be repaid, I swear it on my beard.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.stage.1.ask: Exiles only eat what they win. Raiders plague the border villages: we'll clear them and earn our keep honestly.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.stage.1.don: The villages cheer, and my people eat tonight. Better than any sand.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.stage.2.ask: Three times I've sent the king horses from my victories. Carry one more message: I ask nothing but my family back.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.stage.2.don: Pardoned! After all this time. Take this blade: it's won me everything but the thing I wanted, and now I have that too.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.talk.0: A bad lord can't make a good vassal bad. Remember that.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.talk.1: My beard has never been cut in anger. Long story. Very long beard.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.talk.2: I left my wife and daughters at a monastery gate. Parting was like tearing a nail from the flesh.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.talk.3: Loyalty to someone who wronged you is foolish. Or it's the only thing that heals.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_cid.title: Chests full of sand
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.bio.0: An old wanderer calls me a princess in every village square, and swears great deeds in my name. We have spoken once, about the price of pigs.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.bio.1: At first it made me furious. Now I read the poems at night. Nobody ever saw anything in me but a pair of strong arms for the threshing.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.dialog: Watch your step, there's chaff on every board. I sweep twice a day and it still wins.
You're new. Good. New people haven't heard the rumours about me yet.
At first I wanted to find him and throw him in the pond, horse and all.
Lately, though, something has changed. I can't stop wondering what he saw in one talk about pigs.
But first things first. The harvest doesn't care who is a princess.
My threshing floor is empty and my hands are restless. Grain calms me when I think too much.
Bring me wheat to winnow, and I'll tell you how I became a legend by accident.
I thresh, I sell a bit of grain, I bargain hard for pigs. That's my whole life, or it was.
My arms are the strongest in the village. Nobody writes songs about arms, though.
Do you like pork? Don't answer, I just like knowing who to sell to.
Some seasons ago an old wanderer came through on a bony horse, wearing a pot for a helmet.
We spoke exactly once. About the price of pigs. He nodded very seriously the whole time.
A month later travellers started asking for 'the peerless princess' who lives here. Meaning me.
In the square of every village, he swears great deeds in my name. People laugh at both of us.
I've heard he calls himself a knight of La Mancha, and me a lady from the old books. I can't even read those books.
Good wheat! Look how the chaff flies off. That's the best part: what's left is honest.
The wanderer says my hands smell of amber. They smell of work. I've decided both can be true.
Maybe that's why it hurts a little. Being admired by someone who's never really met you.
So I thought: what if he met me? The real one, with chaff in the hair and mud on the boots.
I've decided to answer him. In writing. Me, who only knows how to spell wheat.
The trouble is paper. A single sheet costs more than a basket of eggs, and hens are stubborn.
Would you bring me some paper? Eight sheets should hold everything I'm too shy to say aloud.
Now the secret you earned: he sends poems. Every week, with some carter or pilgrim.
At first I burned them. Then one night I ran out of kindling and read one instead.
He writes that I sift pearls, not grain. I laughed so loud the dog barked.
Then I kept reading. Nobody ever saw anything in me but two strong arms for the threshing.
Now I read them all at night, by the last candle. I hide them under the flour sacks.
My brother found one and read it out at supper. I didn't speak to him for a week.
Don't misunderstand me. He's mad as a hare. But his madness looks at me kindly.
Sometimes I wonder if he loves me, or a girl he invented who wears my name.
Eight sheets! I'll fill them with nonsense, and every word will be mine.
I've already ruined two. One with a tear, one with a blot shaped like a pig.
My letter says I have calluses, that I snore, that I once sold a pig twice by accident.
It doesn't say I'm a princess. It says I'm real. And it says thank you.
They say the wanderer is resting in a village nearby, nursing bruises from some windmill or other.
I can't leave the harvest, and I'd lose my nerve on the road anyway.
Will you take my letter there for me? Put it in his hands, not the squire's.
Writing is harder than threshing. With the flail, at least, you know where to hit.
Here's something I've never told anyone: I always wanted a story of my own.
As a child I told tales to the geese. They were a patient audience, if a hissing one.
Then I grew up, and the tales stopped. Someone had to bring the harvest in.
His poems woke that child up again. That's what I can't forgive him for, and what I thank him for.
I'm afraid, though. What if he reads my letter and stops writing? What if he prefers the princess?
Or worse: what if he laughs? I've been laughed at in squares for a year now.
But I'd rather be real and alone than a princess in someone else's dream.
They read it aloud in the square? Oh, heavens. Tell me everything, slowly.
He cried, you say? And then he stood up and bowed to the whole village. That's him.
I don't think the wanderer and I will ever marry. I think we'll write until one of us runs out of ink.
You carried my first true words across the hills. That makes you part of every story after.
If I ever write one about you, I'll give you a better horse than his.
Come by at harvest. I'll winnow, you'll listen, and we'll both pretend it's not a story hour.
Go on, then. I have a page to finish, and the pig in it is about to become mayor.
His squire wrote back for him. The spelling is worse than mine. I love it.
He calls me 'real lady of the threshing floor' now. It's a promotion, I think.
I gave that blank book to a shepherd child who draws goats on every wall.
Now I write every night. Stories about farmers, millers, and one very clever pig.
Nobody in my stories needs rescuing. They rescue themselves, and then they have lunch.
The villagers ask me to read aloud on market days. My brother sits in the front row. Traitor.
Remember when you first came and I warned you about the chaff? It's in my ink now, too.
Sometimes a traveller still asks for the peerless princess. I say, 'She's busy writing.'
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.epilog: Now the thresher of the village writes stories of their own, and no one in them needs rescuing.
Before any princess business, there's the harvest. Bring me wheat to winnow, and I'll tell you how I became a legend by accident.
Good grain. The wanderer says my hands smell of amber. They smell of work, and that's fine too.
Every week another poem arrives. I've decided to answer, but paper costs more than I earn. Bring me some?
Eight sheets! I'll fill them with nonsense and every word will be mine.
The wanderer is in a village nearby. Take my letter there. It doesn't say I'm a princess. It says I'm real.
They read it aloud in the square, you say? Then take this blank book: someone else deserves a story of their own.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.talk.0: Mind the chaff, it gets everywhere. Even in poems, apparently.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.talk.1: A knight came by asking for 'the peerless beauty'. I sent him to the pigsty.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.talk.2: Tell me honestly: do I look like someone worth a war?
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.talk.3: I've started writing back. Badly. I only know how to spell wheat.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_dulcinea.title: Someone else's princess
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.bio.0: One midwinter feast a green stranger walked into the hall and offered a game: strike once now, receive the same blow in a year. I was the only fool who stood up.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.bio.1: I kept my word and went to meet the blow. I also kept a green sash I was given, hoping it would save me. I've never forgiven myself that little cowardice.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.dialogue: Never accept a game at a feast. Especially from someone green. First rule of a long life.
Welcome! Sit by the fire, the ale's warm and the stories are mostly true.
An old English poem tells nearly the same tale. I prefer my version. I'm in it.
Every winter since, green things come hissing at the walls. The creepers, you know them.
They remind me of that old debt every time. Green, patient, and ready to go off.
My knees aren't what they were, and the young guards run when one hisses.
Deal with a few of those green visitors for me? Just three. Let's show them who stands up.
I always pay my debts. Well, almost always. We'll get to that, if you stay long enough.
I keep the gate by day and the inn by night. Both involve throwing out people who shout.
You have a steady look. Good. You'd be surprised how many travellers flinch at my collar.
The scar on my neck is tiny. The one on my pride is enormous. I wear a high collar for both.
One midwinter feast, long ago, a green stranger walked into the hall. Green skin, green beard, green horse.
He offered a game: strike him once now, and receive the same blow in a year and a day.
Everyone stared at their plates. I was the only fool who stood up. Youth, and too much wine.
I struck his head clean off. He picked it up, laughed, and said: 'See you next winter.'
Ha! Green, loud and gone. If only my old debt were so easy to scatter.
The young guards saw you do it. Now they want to be you. Careful, it's an awful job.
Now listen. The year has turned again for me, in my way. I've been dreaming of that green face.
I want to face him, or at least face the place, and end this properly.
Before he left all those years ago, the stranger said to find his chapel 'beyond the next village'.
I've never known which village. Every road looks like the wrong one in winter.
Find the green chapel for me? Scout beyond the next village, and I'll go when you've found it.
You've earned the rest of the story. The part I don't tell after the third ale.
I spent that year travelling to find the stranger. Snow, wolves, nights sleeping in armour.
On Christmas Eve I found a castle. The host welcomed me like family and proposed another game.
He'd hunt each day, I'd rest; each evening we'd trade whatever we'd won. Kisses included. Awkward story.
His lady kept visiting while he hunted. I paid back every kiss to the host, honestly. Red-faced, but honestly.
On the third day she offered me a green sash. She said whoever wore it couldn't be killed.
I took it. And I didn't give it to the host that evening. I kept it, hoping it would save me.
That little silence is the only debt I never paid. It weighs more than the blow ever did.
So it's there. I'll go at dawn, and I'll try to look braver than I am.
Actually... I've already been. Sit down. I need to tell someone before I lose my nerve again.
My fear is that if I stop punishing myself, I'll forget the lesson. And become proud again.
My dream is to turn that shame into something useful. Something honest that others can wear.
A belt, maybe, of good leather, with a strip of the green sash sewn inside.
Not to hide the fault. To remember it without being crushed by it.
Bring me leather, and I'll make something honest out of that green sash of shame.
I went to the chapel. Just a mound with a hole in it, grass grown over. And a sound of a blade on stone.
When I first met him, he let the axe fall three times. Two feints, and one tiny nick on my neck.
He said: 'The first two for the kisses you returned. The nick for the sash you kept.'
He knew everything. The host was him all along. The whole game was a test of my honesty.
And I failed it by the width of a ribbon. Not for greed. Just because I loved my own life.
He forgave me on the spot. Laughed, even. I couldn't forgive myself.
I've worn the sash under my shirt for years since. As a punishment. It itches terribly.
Yesterday at the chapel, the grass seemed to say: 'Enough.' Perhaps it's time I listened.
There. Wear it, and remember: the knight who admits a small fault is worth more than one who hides it.
I took off the old sash at last. My neck breathes. My pride is still enormous, but it's honest now.
Well, apart from cards. We play for walnuts. I cheat terribly and confess immediately.
You carried my shame to a mound in the woods and came back with my freedom. Odd trade.
If you ever keep something back out of fear, come find me. We'll laugh about it and fix it.
Come for the midwinter feast. Wear your green. Accept no games from strangers. Except mine.
Off you go. My debts are paid, all of them, and you're the only one I'm happy to owe.
At midwinter I told the whole inn the story. Kisses and all. They laughed until they cried.
Then the baker tied a green ribbon on her wrist. And the smith. And the children. And everyone.
Now the whole village wears a green ribbon at midwinter. Nobody is quite sure who started it.
I know, of course. It was the baker. But I let people think it was a green stranger.
The young guards stand up now when the creepers hiss. They say they learned it from you.
Remember that chapel you found? Someone's put a bench there. I sit on it sometimes and say nothing.
Last winter I thought I saw a green horse on the far hill. It waved. Or the snow did.
I still keep the gate by day and the inn by night. Nobody throws a game at my feasts anymore.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.epilogue: Now the whole village wears a green ribbon at midwinter, and nobody is quite sure who started it.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight — anonymous (c. 1390)
Every winter green things come hissing at the walls. They remind me of an old debt. Deal with a few for me?
Ha! Green, loud and gone. If only my old debt were so easy.
My year is up. The stranger said to find his chapel, 'beyond the next village'. Find it for me?
So it's there. I'll go at dawn, and I'll try to look braver than I am.
I came back with a nick on my neck and a green sash of shame. I want to make something honest out of it. Leather, please.
There. Wear it, and remember: the knight who admits a small fault is worth more than one who hides it.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.talk.0: Never accept a game at a feast. Especially from someone green.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.talk.1: I always pay my debts. Well, almost always. We'll get to that.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.talk.2: A host once asked me to trade whatever I won each day. Kisses included. Awkward story.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.talk.3: The scar on my neck is tiny. The one on my pride is enormous.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_gawain.title: The green bargain
hearthbound.persona.chiv_guinevere.bio.0: The whole village watched my wedding and then watched me every day after. Two good people loved me, and I was blamed for both.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_guinevere.bio.1: I don't regret loving. I regret the war it became. When the noise ends, I'll go somewhere quiet and learn to be only myself.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_guinevere.dialo: Welcome in. Sit anywhere except by the window; that's where the gossips like to watch from.
Every May I go out at dawn to gather flowers. It's the one custom nobody can take from me.
Tomorrow is the first of May. When I was a child, we crowned every child in the lane.
Nobody does it anymore. The grown-ups are too busy watching each other.
I'd like to bring it back. Crowns of daisies and poppies, a little procession, singing badly.
Let them talk about that instead of me. A village full of flower crowns can't stay sour.
Bring me flowers, and I'll weave crowns for every child in the village.
The soup is leek today. I'm told it's too plain. I'm told everything I do is too something.
You have a kind face. Careful, in this village that's enough to get you talked about.
Gossip travels faster than any horse. I should know: I'm usually the cargo.
When I married, the whole village came to watch. Flowers, bells, cheering in the square.
And then they kept watching. Every day after, as if the wedding had never really ended.
My husband is a good man. So is the other. That was never the difficulty.
The old storytellers tell of a queen at a round table who went a-Maying with her knights. I always liked that she went at all.
Some days I think the flowers are the only thing that ever looked at me without judging.
Look at them running in their crowns. That's the only court I ever wanted.
The miller's twins fought over who got the red poppies. I made them trade halfway through.
Except there's one thing I can't forget. Last spring, I rode out to gather May flowers.
Brutes with axes dragged me from my horse on the road. I was lucky to be found.
I've never forgotten their axes, or the sound they made on the saddle.
Now they're back near the road. I saw their smoke from the hill this morning.
Please. Drive them off, so I can gather flowers without looking over my shoulder.
You've been kind, so I'll tell you what the gossips only guess at.
Two good people loved me. One I married. The other was his closest friend.
I didn't choose to love twice. I'd have given anything to feel it only once.
Nothing happened that the gossips invented. What happened was worse: people took sides.
Friends stopped speaking. Old companions drew swords over an argument that was mine.
And I was blamed for both loves, as if I'd stolen them like apples from an orchard.
I stayed quiet for years. Quiet looked like guilt to some, and like pride to others.
Here, at least, I pour ale and nobody asks me to choose between anyone.
Gone. I can gather flowers without looking over my shoulder. I did it this morning. I cried a little.
Not from fear. From the smell of hawthorn and nobody behind me.
They don't ask who you were. They hand you a broom and a lamp and let you think.
I'll join them for a season. Long enough for the noise in my head to end.
Then I'll come back, or I won't. I don't know yet, and that feels like freedom.
The road is long and the nights are dark. The sisters say bring your own light.
Candles, for the road? Enough to think by, that's all I ask.
Let me tell you my deepest confession, since you've given me back the road.
I don't regret loving. I regret the war it became. That war is my real wound.
Good people died for a quarrel about my heart. I think about them every May.
I'm afraid I'll always be a story someone else tells. Never a person who lives her own life.
I'd like, just once, to be known for something I made rather than something I caused.
When I'm old, I'd like to be known for a garden. Only a garden.
Roses, maybe. Or herbs for the sick. Something that grows because you tend it, not because you're fought over.
There's a convent over the hill where the sisters keep lamps lit all night.
