Enough light to think by. Did you keep the apple? In the old tales it means 'no hard feelings'.
I came back from the convent with dirt under my nails and three packets of seeds.
You gave me that. Please don't wave it away; I've learned to say thank you properly.
If you ever need somewhere quiet, the garden gate latches but doesn't lock.
When I'm gone, I hope they say: 'That person grew the best roses in the valley.' And stop there.
Come in May. I'll put a crown on your head, and you'll have to wear it all day.
Go on. The roses need water, and they're the only ones allowed to gossip here now.
There's a walled garden behind the inn now. Roses along the south side, thyme along the north.
The gossips stand by the gate. You'll never guess what they talk about. Roses. Only roses.
Last week they argued for an hour about whether red or white roses smell sweeter. I nearly cried with joy.
My husband helps with the digging. The other friend sends cuttings from far away.
We're all older now. Old enough to be kind to each other without it meaning anything but kindness.
Every first of May the children still wear crowns. They make them themselves now.
The miller's twins ran the procession this year. They didn't fight once. Nearly once.
I still ride out at dawn for flowers. Nobody follows, nobody waits by the road. Only birds.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_guinevere.epilo: Now the village's former queen of May tends a walled garden, and no one gossips about anything but roses.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_guinevere.stage: Tomorrow is the first of May. Bring me flowers and I'll weave crowns for every child in the village.
Look at them running in their crowns. That's the only court I ever wanted.
Last spring, brutes dragged me from a May ride. I'll never forget their axes. Now they're back near the road. Please.
Gone. I can gather flowers without looking over my shoulder.
There's a convent over the hill where the sisters keep lamps lit all night. I'll join them for a season. Candles, for the road?
Enough light to think by. Take this apple: in the old tales it's a gift that means 'no hard feelings'.
Every May I go out at dawn to gather flowers. It's the one custom nobody can take from me.
Gossip travels faster than any horse. I should know: I'm usually the cargo.
My husband is a good man. So is the other. That was never the difficulty.
When I'm old, I'd like to be known for a garden. Only a garden.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_guinevere.title: A crown of May
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lady_lake.bio.0: I keep the lake behind the village. Long ago I lent a great sword to a young ruler, on one condition: that it come back to the water.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lady_lake.bio.1: I also raised a foundling by the shore, who grew into the finest knight alive and broke my heart. The lake gives, and the lake asks back.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lady_lake.dialo: Don't throw stones in the lake. It throws them back. Ask the miller's boy about his forehead.
The water is very clear today. That means someone nearby is telling the truth. Perhaps you.
Lately the lake has grown murky. The fish hide in the deep, and the frogs have gone silent.
Drowned things have crept in from the river. The dead that walk underwater, dripping and slow.
They stir up the mud and scare the herons away. The water can't see itself anymore.
A lake that can't see itself forgets what it's for. I can't let that happen.
Clear the drowned out of my lake, and the fish will come back. The lake remembers its friends.
I grow reeds and watercress along the shore. The lake feeds whoever doesn't take too much.
You walk softly on the jetty. Good. The planks are old, and so am I.
In the evenings I bless the nets. Fishermen pretend they don't believe in it, then come anyway.
I keep the lake behind the village. I have for longer than anyone can remember.
Everything lent must be returned. Swords, children, even summers. The water taught me that.
Long ago I lent a great sword to a young ruler, on one condition: that it come back to the water.
The old storytellers still speak of an arm in white silk rising from a mere. They make it sound grander than it was.
I once held a sword above the water for three days waiting for the right hand. My arm still aches.
Listen: the frogs are singing again. The lake says thank you, and so do I.
A heron came back this morning and stood on one leg for an hour, judging me. I've missed that.
That was my mistake. You can't raise a child to be a legend and expect them to stay gentle.
And now, last night, just like long ago, someone left another baby by the reeds.
Crying, hungry, wrapped in a sack instead of a cloak. I held it until dawn.
The village is looking for a family. Until then, the little one needs milk, fresh and often.
Bring me fresh milk for the foundling. This time I'll do things differently.
Since the water trusts you, I'll tell you what else the lake gave me once.
Many years ago, someone left a baby by the reeds. A boy, wrapped in a king's cloak.
His father had died fleeing. His mother fainted on the hill. I picked him up before anyone came.
I raised him by the shore. Taught him to swim, to fight, to be courteous to the smallest creature.
He grew into the finest knight alive. Everyone said so. I believed it more than anyone.
And then he loved where he shouldn't, and a whole kingdom cracked around him.
He broke my heart. Not by failing, but by being so great that his fall broke others too.
The lake gives, and the lake asks back. I gave him everything, and I asked him to be perfect.
Asleep and full. I'll raise this one to be kind rather than great. I've learned.
The child grabbed my finger and wouldn't let go. The lake did the same thing to me, once.
But the water doesn't need the same sword. It needs a sword given freely, with the right heart.
Bring me a blade, and I'll give it to the water in his name. The debt will be paid.
Iron will do. The lake cares about the promise, not the shine.
Stand with me when it goes in. Someone should witness it who isn't a heron.
Please. Bring me a sword to give the water, so an old friend can rest.
Now, my deepest trouble. It comes by messenger, as the worst news always does.
An old friend is dying. The young ruler I lent the sword to. Not young now, of course.
He wants his sword thrown back into the lake, as promised. He remembers. I'm so glad he remembers.
But his arms are too weak to lift it, and his last companion is too sad to let it go.
I'm afraid the promise will die with him. That the sword will rust on a hillside instead of coming home.
Things not returned leave holes. In the water, in the world. I've seen it happen.
My dream is simple: to see one thing end the way it should. Cleanly. With nothing owed.
I can't leave the shore; the lake won't let me. And his sword is far away with him.
A hand rose and took it. Or the light tricked you. Keep that fishing rod; the lake always pays its debts.
My old friend died the same evening, peacefully. His companion wrote to tell me. He smiled at the end.
My arm doesn't ache anymore. I think it was waiting for that last sword to go home.
You returned something for me that I couldn't return myself. That makes you part of the lake's memory.
If you ever lose something precious, come to the shore. Sometimes the water gives back.
Come swim in summer. The lake says you're welcome. It's very clear about it.
Go on. The child's calling, and the frogs need someone to argue with.
The foundling can swim now. Paddles like a puppy and shrieks at every fish.
I've taught the little one nothing about swords. Only about frogs, and sharing, and saying sorry.
The village didn't find another family. I've decided the lake is family enough.
The water is clearer than anyone remembers. You can count the pebbles at the deepest point.
The miller's boy threw a stone again yesterday. It came right back. He's learning.
Remember when you waded in after the drowned? You smelled of weed for a week. I noticed.
Sometimes the child asks where babies come from. I say: 'The reeds, obviously.' They believe me.
I still bless the nets in the evenings. Now the foundling helps, and splashes everyone.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lady_lake.epilo: Now the keeper of the lake has taught the foundling to swim, and the water is clearer than anyone remembers.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lady_lake.stage: Drowned things have crept into my lake and muddy it. Clear them out, and the fish will come back.
Listen: the frogs are singing again. The lake says thank you.
Someone left a baby by the reeds last night, just like long ago. I need fresh milk until a family is found.
Asleep and full. I'll raise this one to be kind rather than great. I've learned.
An old friend is dying and wants his sword thrown back into the lake, as promised. He can't lift it. Bring me a blade to give the water.
A hand rose and took it. Or the light tricked you. Take this rod: the lake always pays its debts.
Don't throw stones in the lake. It throws them back.
The water is very clear today. That means someone nearby is telling the truth.
Everything lent must be returned. Swords, children, even summers.
I once held a sword above the water for three days waiting for the right hand. My arm still aches.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lady_lake.title: What the lake keeps
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.bio.0: Everyone says nobody fights better than me. It's true, and it's the problem. I have never lost a duel, only the things that matter.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.bio.1: I loved someone promised to my dearest friend. We never meant harm. The harm came anyway, and split the whole hall in two.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.dialog: I train at dawn. Not to get better. To get tired, so the mind goes quiet.
You hold your weight well. Most people lean forward when they meet me, as if bracing.
I don't tell these to boast. I tell them because I used to be proud of them.
Now the stories feel like armour that no longer fits. Too heavy, and full of dents.
Yesterday, raiders with axes took a traveller on the east road. The family came to me first.
I once crossed a bridge of blades for less. But I'd rather not go alone this time.
Help me bring the traveller back? Those axe-men won't stop at one prisoner.
Don't ask me to judge the village contests. I always pick whoever fought fairly, not whoever won.
The smith lets me work the bellows. It's the only fire I trust myself near.
I say prayers at the little altar most evenings. Not for forgiveness. For patience.
Everyone says nobody fights better than me. It's true, and it's exactly the problem.
I have never lost a duel. Only the things that matter, one by one, without a single blow.
Once I rode in a criminal's cart to reach someone who'd been taken. People still mock me for it.
The old French poets tell of a knight who shamed himself in a cart for love. I'd do it again, gladly.
Another time I crossed a bridge made of a single sword blade. My hands bled for a month.
Freed, and not a scratch on either of us. Some debts still get paid cleanly.
The traveller's mother tried to kiss my hands. I let her kiss yours instead. You earned it.
And now, of all things, my friend has written to me. The hand was shaky but it was his.
Raiders gather in the hills near his lands. More than his guards can handle.
He asked me to lead the defence, as if nothing had happened. As if I were still his.
I don't know if it's trust or a test. I've decided it doesn't matter. So I will.
Ride with me against the raiders in the hills? I'd like one honest person at my back.
Since you've bled beside me, I owe you the truth about why I train until I'm numb.
I loved someone promised to my dearest friend. The one who gave me a seat at his table.
We never meant harm. We never even meant to love. It came in like weather.
The harm came anyway. Whispers, then accusations, then the whole hall split in two.
Half the knights stood with him, half with me. Brothers who had shared bread drew swords.
I fought well that day. I always fight well. It's the only thing I've never failed at.
Afterward I came here, far from all of it. Nobody knew my face. I liked that.
Friendship is heavier than armour. Believe me, I've carried both up very steep hills.
We won. He clasped my arm and said nothing. That silence was the best thing he could give me.
No speeches, no apology from either of us. Just his hand on my arm, like when we were young.
People will say the best fighter in the realm has gone soft. Let them. Soft is what I need.
The smith offered to take my sword and melt it into horseshoes. I said yes before I could think.
I'll keep a vigil the first nights, to make the place mine. It needs many candles.
I can't buy them without the whole market asking why. You understand.
Bring me candles for the vigil, and I'll go to the chapel and keep it lit.
I've been thinking about it every night since. I think it was forgiveness. Or the start of it.
Now I'll tell you the deepest thing, the one I haven't told the priest.
I'm afraid that if I keep a sword, I'll keep being the man who fights instead of the one who mends.
Every duel I won made me more famous and less whole. I don't want to win anything else.
There's an empty chapel in the woods, past the birches. The roof leaks, but the altar stands.
I've walked there some evenings. It's so quiet you can hear the candles think.
My dream is small: to keep a light burning there, for anyone who walks the forest at night.
A lost woodcutter, a child, a knight who's had enough. A light doesn't ask who you are.
The flame doesn't judge. For the first time in years, I can sleep through the night.
I've fixed the chapel roof. Badly. Rain still gets in, but only over the one bench.
You fought beside me when I was still trying to be the best. Thank you for not needing that.
If you ever need a quiet place, the candle will be lit. No questions. That's the whole rule.
I pray for patience still. Lately it's for the bees.
Go gently. And if you meet someone carrying too much armour, send them to the woods.
The light will be burning. It always is now. That's something I've finally learned to keep.
The children come on feast days. We fight with sticks. I let them win. They know. They don't care.
A woodcutter got lost in the snow last month and found the light. He brought me a cake.
My friend visited. We sat by the candles and didn't talk about the past. We talked about bees.
Bees! Two old fighters, arguing about honey. You'd have laughed.
The smith really did turn my sword into horseshoes. The miller's mare wears them proudly.
Remember the east road? The traveller we freed comes to the chapel every spring with flowers.
I still train at dawn, but with an axe, on firewood. It tires me just the same.
People say I've grown gentle. I think I've grown honest. From the outside they look similar.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.epilog: Now the best fighter of the realm keeps a small chapel in the woods, and lets the children win at sticks.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.source: Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart — Chrétien de Troyes (c. 1180)
Raiders with axes took a traveller on the east road. I once crossed a bridge of blades for less. Help me?
Freed, and not a scratch on either of us. Some debts still get paid cleanly.
More raiders gather in the hills. My friend asked me to lead, as if nothing had happened. So I will.
We won. He clasped my arm and said nothing. That silence was the best thing he could give me.
I'm done with swords. There's an empty chapel in the woods; I'll keep it lit. Bring me candles for the vigil.
The flame doesn't judge. For the first time in years, I can sleep through the night.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.talk.0: I train at dawn. Not to get better. To get tired.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.talk.1: Don't ask me to judge contests. I always pick the one who fought fairly, not the winner.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.talk.2: Once I rode in a criminal's cart to save someone. People still mock me for it. I'd do it again.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.talk.3: Friendship is heavier than armour. Believe me, I've carried both.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_lancelot.title: The best of them
hearthbound.persona.chiv_little_john.bio: I'm the tallest person in the village, so naturally everyone calls me Little. It started on a narrow bridge, with a stranger and two staves.
Neither of us would step aside. I knocked the stranger into the stream, laughing. They came up laughing too, and I've followed them ever since.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_little_john.dia: Mind your head on the doorframe. Everyone bangs it, except me: I've learned.
Yes, they call me Little. Yes, I'm the tallest in the village. No, it's never stopped being funny.
The best friendships start with a fight you both lose. We both lost our dignity that day.
That old footbridge is still out past the mill. I walk by it most mornings.
It's rotting now. Moss on the log, cracks down the middle. Last week a goat fell through.
I'd like it rebuilt, but better. Wide enough for two, so people can meet in the middle.
Bring me logs, and we'll build the narrow bridge wide enough for two.
I build walls, shoe horses, and stand at the gate looking large. Mostly the last one.
A quarterstaff is just a stick with opinions. Mine has very strong opinions.
You shook my hand without flinching. Most people count their fingers afterwards.
It started on a narrow bridge over a stream, with a stranger and two staves.
The bridge was one log wide. I was on one end, the stranger on the other. Neither would step aside.
We fought right there, on a slippery log, for the best part of an hour.
The old ballads say the outlaw of the greenwood met his big friend exactly so. I'll let them have it.
I knocked the stranger into the stream at last, laughing. They came up laughing too, soaked to the ears.
Wide enough for two... but I think I'll still make people fight for it. Tradition.
The miller and the baker met in the middle yesterday and just nodded at each other. Disappointing.
Wherever it lands, that's where they'll rest. It's a big promise for a big person.
But there's a closer worry now. Brutes with axes are waiting at the ford for the market carts.
They jump out of the reeds, smash the carts, take everything. Two drivers are hurt already.
The ford is narrow, like the old bridge. You need two to hold it: one big stick and one sharp edge.
My staff and your blade? Let's clear the axe-men from the ford.
Sit down on the new rail. It'll hold. I tested it with my entire self.
Let me tell you the rest. That stranger I knocked in the stream became my leader, my best friend.
They led a band of outlaws in the woods. I joined the same afternoon, still dripping.
We've been through winters, hangings nearly, a whole sheriff's army. I've never once regretted it.
When I joined, they 'christened' me Little over a feast. Roast meat and too much ale. I cried laughing.
People think I'm the muscle and they're the brains. It's nearer the other way round some days.
Here's something I don't say aloud. My friend is getting old. Slower on the bow, quieter at night.
I've promised: when they go, I'll carry them to the window to shoot one last arrow.
Down they went, like I did once. Only they didn't come up laughing.
The carts are rolling again. A cheesemaker gave me a whole wheel. I've eaten half already.
When I joined, they christened me Little over a feast. Now it's my turn to christen someone.
We need a proper feast. Roast beef, heaps of it. Outlaws don't do small portions.
I'm already thinking of names. Tiny, maybe. Or Sprout. Or Wee Thomas.
If there isn't enough meat, the band will sulk, and I'll never live it down.
The christening feast needs meat, lots of it! Cooked beef, as much as you can bring.
Since we've fought together now, I'll tell you the thing that sits heaviest on me.
I'm afraid of the day I keep that promise. Of carrying my friend to the window.
I'm big. I can carry anyone. But I don't know if I can carry that.
Every time they cough in the night, I sit up in bed like a startled bear.
And I'm afraid of what comes after. A band without its heart. Just a lot of large people in green.
My dream is that the band goes on without either of us. New faces, new names, same laughter.
That's why I care so much about the new ones. Somebody took me in; I have to take others in.
Speaking of which: a new lad joins the band tomorrow. Big fellow. Shy. Hands like shovels.
They named the lad Tiny. He's the size of a barrel. Perfect. He cried laughing, like I did.
Tiny hit his head on the doorframe twice on the first day. I've started teaching him.
You built a bridge with me, and held a ford, and fed a christening. That's a whole life, for outlaws.
If anyone blocks your way on a narrow path, remember: fight them, lose, laugh, and make a friend.
Come fight me on the bridge some morning. I'll go easy. I won't, actually.
Mind the doorframe on your way out. Ha! Told you.
Off you go. And whenever you hear a splash and laughter, you'll know someone's made a friend.
The bridge is wide enough for two, and the village settles every quarrel on it now.
Two staves, one splash, and then everyone laughs and goes home. The baker's lost three times this month.
My friend is still here. Slower, but still laughing. We sit on the bridge and dangle our feet.
The promise about the window stands. But I don't lie awake about it anymore.
Tiny says he'll help me carry them, when the time comes. It makes the weight easier somehow.
Remember the goat that fell through the old bridge? It crosses the new one every morning like a queen.
The ford's still clear. The cheesemaker sends me a wheel every month. I've gotten larger. Somehow.
The band calls you 'Little Too' now. It's the highest honour we give. Don't laugh.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_little_john.epi: Now the bridge is wide enough for two, and the village settles every quarrel on it with a laugh and a splash.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_little_john.sou: Robin Hood and Little John — traditional ballad (17th century)
hearthbound.persona.chiv_little_john.sta: The old footbridge where I met my best friend is rotting. Bring logs, and we'll build it wide enough for two.
Wide enough for two... but I think I'll still make people fight for it. Tradition.
Axe-men are waiting at the ford for the market carts. My staff and your blade?
Down they went, like I did once. Only they didn't come up laughing.
When I joined the band, they 'christened' me Little over a feast. A new lad joins tomorrow. We need meat, lots of it!
They named the lad Tiny. He's the size of a barrel. Perfect.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_little_john.tal: Mind your head on the doorframe. Everyone does, except me: I've learned.
A quarterstaff is just a stick with opinions.
The best friends start with a fight you both lose.
When our leader goes, I'll carry them to the window to shoot one last arrow. I've promised.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.bio.0: When my beloved was outlawed, I didn't wait at home. I cut my hair, put on a stranger's clothes, and went into the forest to find them.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.bio.1: We met on a path, didn't recognise each other, and fought for an hour. I was winning. Then we laughed so hard we couldn't hold our swords.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.dialogue: The best disguise is confidence and muddy boots. Most people never look higher than your knees.
Welcome to the stall. Apples, cheese, honest prices. Well, honest-ish on market days.
Now an old friend of the band needs to cross the sheriff's lands without being recognised.
They've a face half the county knows. A price on their head and a very recognisable nose.
A disguise needs to be more than a hood. It needs a whole other person inside it.
Boots, a jerkin, a pedlar's pack. Something that makes a guard look away out of boredom.
Bring me leather, and I'll make a disguise even their mother wouldn't see through.
I keep accounts for half the village. Numbers are easy. People are the hard sums.
You're sizing me up. Good. I do the same with everyone who walks in.
Never marry someone you haven't fought at least once. You learn everything that way.
When my beloved was outlawed, the whole village expected me to wait at home and weep.
I waited one night. Then I cut off my hair with the bread knife and took a stranger's clothes from the line.
I went into the forest with a sword I barely knew how to hold, looking for them.
The old ballads tell of a maid of the greenwood who did the same. They leave out the blisters.
I still keep the band's accounts. Outlaws are terrible with numbers. They count arrows on their fingers.
Perfect. They walked past the gate guard and asked him for directions. He gave them.
I laughed so hard I had to hide behind a haystack. Thank you. That leather was perfect.
The band took me in that night. Nobody asked me to cook. They asked me to count.
But the sheriff has learned new tricks. Crossbow men hunt our messengers on the forest road.
Two messengers haven't come back this month. One was only fifteen.
I'll go myself, in disguise, as a pedlar with a heavy pack. They'll think I'm easy prey.
Come watch my back? When they come for the pedlar, I'd like a friend in the trees.
You've earned the rest of the forest story. It's my favourite, and my most embarrassing.
After days of wandering, I met a figure on a narrow path. Hood up, sword drawn. An outlaw, I thought.
They thought the same of me. Neither of us would give way. So we fought.
For an hour. Up and down the path, through bracken, over a stream. I was winning.
I cut them across the arm. They cut me across the cheek. Then they called out a name to their friends.
It was my beloved's voice. I dropped my hood. They dropped their sword. We just stared.
Then we laughed so hard we couldn't hold our swords. We sat in the mud and laughed until dark.
I still have the scar from our duel. So do they. We compare them on anniversaries.
Nobody expected the pedlar to draw a sword. Especially not the pedlar's friends.
The fifteen-year-old messenger was in their camp, tied up but alive. He's home now, eating everything.
My dream is a wedding with no disguises. Real names, real faces, and apples for everyone.
Not just for the band: for the charcoal-burners, the widows, every family who hid us.
The whole forest, fed, under the apple blossom. That's the only feast I've ever wanted.
But the orchard's been picked bare by winter. We need baskets and baskets of apples.
Finally, a wedding under the apple trees, as we always said. Bring apples for the whole forest!
Now that you've stood in the trees for me, I'll tell you what I haven't told anyone in the band.
We've never married. We always said: 'Under the apple trees, when it's safe.'
It's never been safe. Every spring there's a new sheriff, a new price, a new reason to wait.
I'm afraid we'll wait so long that one of us won't be there when it's finally safe.
I'm not the waiting kind. I cut my hair and ran into the forest, remember? Yet here I am, waiting.
Well, not anymore. I've decided. Safe or not, this spring we'll marry in the orchard.
The friar has agreed. He's a round, cheerful man who once fought my beloved in a river.
Everybody fights everybody in this band. It's how we say hello.
The friar married us in the rain and nobody minded. Did you keep your golden apple? Every guest got one.
The first dance was a duel, of course. I won. They let me. I let them think I didn't notice.
You helped me stop waiting. That's the best gift anyone's given me, and I've had a golden apple.
If you ever love someone, fight them once. Fairly. Then laugh in the mud together.
Come to the orchard in spring. Bring someone. Or come alone and duel me for the first dance.
The stall's always open. Apples, cheese, honest prices. Even on market days, for you.
Off you go. Mind the mud on your boots. It's the best disguise, remember?
The charcoal-burners' children danced on the tables. One fell into the cake. Nobody minded that either.
Now the orchard hosts a wedding every spring. Farmers, millers, a very old shepherd last year.
And the first dance is always a friendly duel. It's become the rule. The priest in the village disapproves.
I still keep the band's accounts. They still count arrows on their fingers. Some things never change.
The disguise I made for our old friend? They wear it for fun now, and fool their own family.
Remember watching my back from the trees? The messenger boy wants to be you when he grows up.
We compare scars every anniversary. Mine's fading. Theirs is somehow getting bigger in the telling.
My hair's grown back. Sometimes I cut it short again, just to remember who I was that night.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.epilogue: Now the orchard hosts a wedding every spring, and the first dance is always a friendly duel.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.source: Robin Hood and Maid Marian — traditional ballad (17th century)
An old friend has to cross the sheriff's lands unseen. Bring me leather and I'll make a disguise even their mother wouldn't see through.
Perfect. They walked past the gate guard and asked him for directions.
Crossbow men are hunting the band's messengers on the forest road. I'll go myself, in disguise. Come watch my back.
Nobody expected the pedlar to draw a sword. Especially not the pedlar's friends.
Finally, a wedding under the apple trees, as we always said. Bring apples for the whole forest!
The friar married us in the rain and nobody minded. Take this: every guest gets a golden one.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.talk.0: The best disguise is confidence and muddy boots.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.talk.1: I keep the band's accounts. Outlaws are terrible with numbers.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.talk.2: Never marry someone you haven't fought at least once. You learn everything.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.talk.3: I still have the scar from our duel. So do they. We compare them on anniversaries.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_marian.title: The disguise in the woods
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.bio.0: I live the wrong way round: I remember what hasn't happened yet and forget what did. It makes me a decent sage and a terrible neighbour.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.bio.1: I have already seen how I end: taught too well, sealed under a stone by my best pupil. I'll teach them anyway. Knowledge was never meant to be kept.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.dialogue: Ah, you. We met next week. You were very kind, and you had mud on your left boot.
Don't eat the mushrooms by the east well. Trust me. Or rather, trust Thursday.
For years I used a crystal to look ahead more clearly. My memory of tomorrow is foggy without it.
Last winter it showed me too much at once. There was a crack like thunder, and then nothing.
Since then tomorrow comes to me in pieces. A cup, a storm, a face. Very untidy.
I'd like to see properly again. There are things coming I should warn people about.
Bring me amethyst, and I'll grind a new seeing crystal. Purple is the only colour that doesn't lie.
Sorry, what did I have for breakfast? No idea. But I know it rains the day after tomorrow.
Neighbours find me tiring. I congratulate them on weddings before the proposals.
Sit, sit. I'll make tea. I'm fairly sure I already enjoyed this conversation.
I live the wrong way round. I remember what hasn't happened yet, and forget what did.
It makes me a decent sage and a terrible neighbour. I return borrowed tools before they're lent.
In the old chronicles of Britain there's a boy with no father who saw dragons under a tower. I like that tale. It feels familiar.
Some stones remember songs. I once moved a whole circle of them by singing back. Don't ask which key.
I have a pupil now. Clever, hungry, quick. Faster than I'd like. I smile anyway.
Clear as rain. Oh dear. You should buy candles before winter. Trust me on that one.
Thank you. The crystal hums when I hold it. It knows you, I think. Or it will.
Kings thought it was a monument to them. It was a calendar. I let them believe what they liked.
I'd like to show my pupil how it works. Not in books: under the real sky.
A small circle would do. Enough to catch the midsummer sunrise through one gap.
I remember we build it together, you and I. I also remember you complaining about the weight.
Bring me stone bricks, and I'll raise a small circle here, to teach the stars properly.
Now that I can see again, I owe you honesty. So, a secret.
I have already seen how I end. Not in dreams: remembered, like you remember a meal.
I teach too well. My best pupil learns everything, and at last seals me under a stone.
Please don't make that face. I've had years to get used to it, or years in the other direction.
The strange part is that I don't hate the pupil. In my memory, they cry while doing it.
I could refuse to teach. I've thought about it. But knowledge was never meant to be kept.
Knowledge locked away is just a treasure for rats. I'd rather be a stone with a good student outside.
Once, long before this village, I raised a ring of standing stones to count the stars.
At midsummer the sun will rise exactly through that gap. You'll see. I already did, and it was lovely.
My pupil sat in the middle all night with a candle, counting. I've never seen such joy.
I could lie. I could teach it wrong. But a teacher who lies is only a jailer with a beard.
The spell needs ender pearls, the eyes of those tall shadows that walk at night.
They're dangerous to gather. I wouldn't ask if I didn't already remember you coming back.
Whatever happens after, promise me you'll be kind to my pupil. They'll need it.
Bring me ender pearls, and I'll teach the last lesson. Let tomorrow do what it likes.
That's the thing about teaching. You hand someone a key and hope they open good doors.
Now I'll tell you what frightens me. It isn't the stone. It's being wrong about the pupil.
What if I've taught them to be clever and forgotten to teach them to be kind?
My memory of the end is so clear. Yet my memory of kindness in them is clearer.
I have a dream, which is rare for someone who remembers tomorrow: to be surprised. Just once.
Imagine. Waking up and not knowing what the day holds. People complain about that. I envy it.
My pupil has asked for the last secret: how to shut a door no one can open.
It's the very spell that closes the stone over me. I know how this ends.
Well, it's done, and I'm still here. Perhaps I misremembered. Isn't that marvellous?
My pupil cast the spell perfectly, looked at me, and shut the door on an empty cave instead.
I've started keeping a diary. For me it's a book of surprises, since I forget the past.
Most pages say: 'The traveller came by. Pleasant.' I don't need to remember more than that.
You helped me teach the last lesson, and it turned out the last lesson was mine.
Come back at midsummer. The sun will pass through the gap. I think. I'm not sure. Isn't it lovely?
Off you go. I'll see you soon, or saw you, or both. Either way, it was a pleasure.
They said, 'I learned how. I didn't learn why I'd ever use it on you.' I had no answer. Wonderful.
For the first time in my life, I don't know what happens next. I keep laughing at breakfast.
I still get tomorrow wrong now and then. Yesterday I greeted the baker's wedding. There isn't one.
Well, there isn't one yet. We'll see. I've stopped betting.
The glass I gave you: look far, but look kindly. That advice cost me forty years.
Did you buy candles before winter? Good. Nobody else did, and the whole village borrowed yours.
My pupil teaches the children now, in the stone circle. They argue with the stars. Excellent.
The crystal still hums when you walk by. It's decided you're a friend.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.epilogue: Now the old sage still gets tomorrow wrong now and then, and seems delighted every time.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.source: History of the Kings of Britain — Geoffrey of Monmouth (c. 1136)
My old crystal cracked when it showed me too much. Bring me amethyst and I'll grind a new one.
Clear as rain. Oh dear. You should buy candles before winter.
Long ago I raised a ring of standing stones to count the stars. Bring me stone bricks and I'll raise a small one here.
At midsummer the sun will rise exactly through that gap. You'll see. I already did.
My pupil wants the last secret: how to shut a door no one can open. It needs ender pearls. I know how this ends.
Well, it's done, and I'm still here. Perhaps I misremembered. Take my glass: look far, but look kindly.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.talk.0: Ah, you. We met next week. You were very kind.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.talk.1: Don't eat the mushrooms by the east well. Trust me. Or rather, trust Thursday.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.talk.2: Some stones remember songs. I once moved a whole circle of them by singing back.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.talk.3: My pupil learns fast. Faster than I'd like. I smile anyway.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_merlin.title: Remembering tomorrow
hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.bio.0: The village calls me the dark healer. I cure what others can't, and I don't smile while doing it. That's enough to make a villain of anyone.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.bio.1: My half-brother and I have spent our lives crossing each other. But when the end comes for him, I'll be the one who carries him home.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.dialogue: Whatever you've heard about me is true. Also, the opposite is true. Come in anyway.
Tea? It's only nettle. Mostly. The rest is between me and the nettle.
Right now the miller has a cough that rattles like dice in a cup. He won't admit he needs me.
His daughter came last night, crying. I said yes before she finished.
The remedy needs berries that glow in the dark. They only grow in caves, hanging from the roof like lanterns.
Few people dare go that deep. Things live down there that don't like visitors.
Bring me glowing berries from underground. You look like you might dare.
Don't touch the jar with the blue lid. Not poison. Just my grandmother's temper, bottled.
You walk in without crossing yourself. That makes you either brave or new. I like both.
People come to my door at night, so no one sees them. They leave cured and pretend I don't exist.
The village calls me the dark healer. I cure what others can't, and I don't smile while doing it.
That's enough to make a villain of anyone. A healer who frowns is a witch; one who grins is a saint.
There's an island in the west where apples grow all year. I was born there, or I dreamed it.
An old Latin poem tells of nine sisters on an isle of apples who heal the wounded. I've always felt I was the ninth.
Family is the only wound I can't close with herbs. I'll tell you why another day.
Perfect. Now the miller's cough will stop, and he'll still call me a witch. Watch.
He did, by the way. Loudly, in the square, while breathing perfectly. I nearly laughed.
Some women in the swamp brew poisons and sign my name to them. Little notes, in my style.
Last week a shepherd drank one. He's alive only because I got there first.
They want the village to hang me so they can take my trade. Clever. Not clever enough.
I'd rather they stopped. Permanently. I'm a healer, but I'm not a fool.
Deal with the swamp witches for me. Three of them. Then maybe people will see which of us is poison.
You've earned a real answer about the wound I can't close. Sit down.
I have a half-brother. Same mother, different fathers, and different luck.
He was raised to be admired. I was raised to be useful. Guess which one of us got the stories.
We've spent our lives crossing each other. Stolen horses, broken promises, a scabbard I once hid from him.
Everyone says I hated him. It was never hate. It was being always the shadow beside his sun.
When he fought, I patched up his men. When he won, nobody mentioned who stitched the victory.
I left that court long ago. I came here, where nobody knew him or me.
And still, somehow, my name rots on other people's tongues. Now there's a new reason.
Good. My reputation is dark enough without help. Thank you, truly.
The shepherd came to thank me himself. In daylight, with his cap in his hands. That's a first.
To see him across, I need a golden apple. The old tales say it's food for the crossing.
Gold and apple, sweetness and weight. It's the only medicine for a journey with no return.
I can't make one myself. My hands shake when I think about why I need it.
Please. I'd go myself if I trusted my knees.
Bring me a golden apple, so I can see my brother across the lake.
Now the last secret, the one I keep under the floorboards of my heart.
My half-brother is dying. An old wound from his last war that never closed properly.
I'm the only one who could heal it, and he's too proud to ask. Some things run in families.
But I've always known how this ends. When the end comes for him, I'll be the one who carries him home.
Not to his castle. To the isle of apples. That's the only place he can truly rest.
There's a boat at the lake, waiting for years now. I've kept it caulked and dry, just in case.
I'm afraid he'll look at me the way he always did: suspicious, as if I'd poisoned the water.
My dream is ridiculous for someone my age. I want him to smile at me. Once. Without a reason.
He smiled at me. After forty years. Tell no one I cried. I mean it. No one.
He said, 'You always did carry me, didn't you?' Then he closed his eyes, and the mist took the boat.
Sometimes I row out on the lake at dusk. Not far. Just enough to wave.
You went into the dark for my berries and into the swamp for my name. I won't forget that.
Come by for tea. Nettle only. Truly only nettle, this time.
When the orchard fruits, the first apple is yours. It won't be gold, but it'll be sweet.
Off you go. And if anyone calls you a villain, tell them the one by the lake says otherwise.
I planted the apple's seeds by the lake shore when I came back. Now there's an orchard.
Young trees, crooked and stubborn. They remind me of both of us.
The village sends its sick to the orchard now, in daylight. They sit under the trees while I work.
Nobody says witch anymore. They say 'the one by the lake.' I've decided I prefer it.
The miller brings me flour every week. He still grumbles. He also still breathes.
The swamp's quiet since you went. The frogs have taken over. Much better neighbours.
Do you remember the jar with the blue lid? I opened it at last. It was just honey. Grandmother.
I still don't smile much while I heal. But I smile afterwards, where people can see it.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.epilogue: Now the dark healer tends an orchard on the lake shore, and the village has quietly stopped using the word witch.
My remedies need berries that glow in the dark, gathered underground. Few people dare. You look like you might.
Perfect. Now the miller's cough will stop, and he'll still call me a witch.
Some women in the swamp brew poisons and sign my name to them. I'd rather they stopped. Permanently.
Good. My reputation is dark enough without help.
My brother is dying of an old wound. There's a boat at the lake. I need a golden apple to see him across.
He smiled at me. After forty years. Tell no one I cried.

hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.talk.2: There's an island in the west where apples grow all year. I was born there, or I dreamed it.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.talk.3: Family is the only wound I can't close with herbs.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_morgan.title: The isle of apples
hearthbound.persona.chiv_percival.bio.0: My mother raised me deep in the forest so I'd never see a knight. I saw five on the road one day and thought they were angels. I followed them.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_percival.bio.1: Once I sat at the table of a wounded old lord while a marvel passed before us. I was taught not to ask questions. I didn't. That silence haunts me.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_percival.dialog: I didn't know what a fork was until I was nineteen. I'm still suspicious of them.
Is that thing on your belt for cutting or for eating? Sorry. I ask a lot of questions now. It's a long story.
I've never been anywhere except that forest and this village. I don't have names for half the world.
When a traveller says 'mesa' or 'savanna', I nod, and go home and wonder what they meant.
Mother said the world beyond the trees was only dangerous. I'd like to know if she was right.
There must be other villages, other houses, other people eating with forks.
Would you go out and find one for me? Another village. Tell me what it looks like.
I tend the bean rows and help the priest ring the bell. Both need patience and strong arms.
My mother told me: help anyone who asks. Nobody told me to help those who don't.
You've travelled far, haven't you? You have that look. Road-dust in the eyelashes.
My mother raised me deep in the forest so I'd never see a knight. My father and brothers died as knights.
One day I saw five of them on the road, all shining. I thought they were angels. I asked if they were God.
They laughed at me and told me what a lance was for. I followed them the same afternoon.
I didn't even say goodbye properly. Mother fell down at the bridge as I rode off. I didn't turn around.
An old French poem tells of a forest boy who did exactly that. I didn't need a poem. I remember her falling.
Real houses, far away? Then my mother was wrong: the world isn't only dangerous.
Tell me again about the bell tower. And the well with a roof. I want to picture everything.
Have you ever missed a chance so small you only saw it years later? That's what I carry.
And now I've heard of an old man at the river near here. He can only fish, because of a wound that never heals.
Maybe it's him. Maybe it's someone like him. Either way, I won't walk past a second time.
He's been fishing for days to feed himself, and can barely hold the rod.
Bring him salmon, so he can rest. I'll go with you, but my hands shake around him.
You've done so much for me, so I'll tell you my secret. The thing I didn't do.
After I left home, I wandered and learned to fight. Then one evening I came to a castle by a river.
An old lord lived there, wounded long ago so badly he could only sit in a boat and fish.
He invited me to dine. And while we ate, a marvel passed before the table. Light, a dish, a bleeding lance.
Everyone went silent. I wanted to ask what it was, and whom it served. I didn't.
An old knight had told me not to chatter, that good manners meant no questions. So I held my tongue.
In the morning the castle was empty. I rode away, and later learned my question would have healed him.
That silence haunts me more than any battle. It was such a small thing not to say.
He nodded without a word. I almost asked him. Almost. My mouth opened and nothing came.
I'm so angry at myself. I've practised the question every night. Out loud, to the pigs.
I'm going back to his table. This time I'll bring a warm meal and ask the question.
Nothing fancy. Mushroom stew, the kind my mother made in the forest, thick enough to stand a spoon in.
Three bowls: one for him, one for me, one for whoever else is sitting silent at that table.
If I'm carrying food, my hands won't shake. And I'll have a reason to stay long enough.
Help me carry stew to his table? I'll ask. I promise I'll ask.
Let me tell you the fear underneath. It's not being wrong. It's being right and too late.
What if I ask, and it doesn't help? What if the marvel was only a story and he just hurts?
Then I'd have hope in my hands and nothing to put it in.
But I think the real marvel is to ask someone: what hurts? And then stay to hear the answer.
My mother never asked me why I wanted to leave. I never asked her why she was so afraid.
I went back once, years later. She was gone. I stood in her garden asking everything, too late.
So this time I'm not waiting for the right moment. There isn't one. There's only the moment.
My dream is to be the kind of person who asks. Of everyone. The miller, the children, the priest.
I asked 'what ails you?' and he wept, and laughed, and stood up. The marvel was the question all along.
He walked to the river on his own feet and caught a fish just by laughing at it. Well, nearly.
So: how are you? Truly? No, don't say 'fine'. I'll wait.
See? That wasn't so hard. Now you owe me a longer answer tomorrow.
If I ever find another marvel, I won't stare at it. I'll ask it its name.
Come back often. I'll have new questions. I always do now.
Go gently. And if you see someone sitting silent at a table, you know what to ask.
Now he comes to the village on market days. He asks me how I am, too. Imagine.
I ask everyone now. The baker says I'm a nuisance. Then she tells me for twenty minutes.
Most people only need someone to wait for the whole answer. It's usually longer than you'd think.
The priest says I've become the village's second bell. I think it's a compliment.
I've stopped being suspicious of forks. I'm still suspicious of spoons with holes in them.
Remember when you described that other village to me? I've visited now. You were right about the well.
I planted a small garden like my mother's. I talk to it sometimes. It doesn't answer, but I ask anyway.
You helped me say three words I'd owed for years. That's worth more than any lance.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_percival.epilog: Now the forest child asks everyone in the village how they are, and waits for the whole answer.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_percival.source: Perceval, the Story of the Grail — Chrétien de Troyes (c. 1190)
I've never seen another village. The world must be full of things I don't have names for. Find one for me?
Real houses, far away? Then my mother was wrong: the world isn't only dangerous.

hearthbound.persona.chiv_quixote.bio.0: I sold half my land to buy books of knights errant. I read them by candle until dawn, and one morning the world outside began to look exactly like them.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_quixote.bio.1: I know the neighbours laugh. But someone has to believe the world can still be righted, one wrong at a time. Why not a person with an old lance?
hearthbound.persona.chiv_quixote.dialogu: Good day, traveller. Have you seen any enchanters pass this way? They leave a smell of sulphur.
That inn over there is a castle. Do not let the innkeeper tell you otherwise. He's under a spell.
Have you heard of the old tale of the gentleman of La Mancha? Some say it's about me. It isn't. Probably.
I've decided to ride out and right wrongs. The world is crooked. Someone must straighten it, one wrong at a time.
But look at me. Armour of rust and patches. My helmet crumbled like old bread when I tried it on.
The books say there's a golden helm, the helm of Mambrino, that makes its wearer unbeatable.
Every knight needs a helmet. Bring me a shining basin... I mean, the golden helm of Mambrino.
You have the look of a squire. Or of a hero. Hard to tell in this light. Stand closer.
My old horse is thin as a rake, but nobler than any warhorse in the king's stables. Don't laugh.
Sometimes, just before sleep, the giants look like mills again. I don't like that moment.
I was not always like this. I did my trade, paid my dues, went to bed at a sensible hour.
Then I found a book in a trader's cart. A knight errant, a dragon, a lady in a tower. One book.
Then ten. Then fifty. I sold half my land to buy them. The neighbours thought I'd lost my wits.
I read by candle until dawn, every night, for years. Knights, giants, oaths, enchanted islands.
And one morning I opened the door and the world outside looked exactly like the pages. Exactly.
It fits perfectly! Do not call it a bucket in front of the enchanters. They're listening.
Thank you, noble squire. Yes, I've made you my squire. You didn't object quickly enough.
Now listen. Something is stalking the fields at night. Tall as a tower. Dark as a well.
Its eyes burn violet, and it carries stones from the earth as if they were feathers.
If you look at it, it comes for you. The shepherds have seen it. They won't graze after dark.
My lance trembles. I'll admit that to you, and to no one else. It's a real giant this time. I think.
Would you ride at my side against the tall dark giant? Two lances are braver than one.
A barber once swore that helm was his shaving basin. Enchanters. They change what others see.
Now that I'm armed, let me tell you what the neighbours say behind my back. I hear them.
They say the books rotted my mind. The priest and the barber wanted to burn my library.
They did burn some. They walled up the room and told me an enchanter had carried it off.
I believed them. Isn't that funny? I believed the enchanter part more than I believed them.
Still, I have my reasons. Someone has to believe the world can still be righted. Why not someone with an old lance?
I saw a merchant beat a shepherd boy in the road. Everyone walked by. I didn't. I got a black eye for it.
The boy got his wages, that day. Maybe he lost them later. But that day, the wrong was righted.
It vanished in a flash and left this pearl behind. You see? Giants are real, whatever the priest says.
I've shown the pearl to everyone. Even the priest held it. He went very quiet. Victory.
She was carrying a sack of grain. She laughed at something. I've built her a palace in my mind since.
The old tales call such a lady Dulcinea. I call mine that too. I don't know her real name. I never asked.
I've written her a letter listing every deed: the helm, the giant, the shepherd boy. All true. Mostly.
I'm afraid, squire. Not of giants. Of finding out she doesn't exist. Or worse, that she does, and laughs.
Carry this letter to my lady in the next village. She lives... somewhere there, I'm sure.
You fought well. I shouted a great deal. Between us, I think that's a fair division of labour.
Can I confess something? Sometimes I know. I know the windmills are windmills and the basin is a basin.
It comes in the morning, before I've had bread. A cold, grey clarity. I hate it.
In that moment I'm just an old person with sold land and a thin horse. Nothing more.
So I choose. Every morning, I choose the giants. Because a world with giants needs knights.
And a world with only windmills needs nobody. I would rather be needed, even foolishly.
Every knight must have a lady of their thoughts. Someone to dedicate every deed to.
Mine is the fairest in all the land. I saw her once, years ago, in the neighbouring village. Just once.
She read it? She laughed? Then she is alive and real. That's all I needed to know. Truly.
You say she laughed kindly? Then she's even fairer than I thought. And I thought a great deal.
The children play knights in the square now, with sticks and buckets. I judge the tournaments.
I've started writing my own book. Not a true one. The best ones never are, entirely.
You're in it, of course. The faithful squire who was really the hero. The reader will figure it out.
The world is still crooked. But it's a little straighter here. That will do for an old lance.
Farewell, squire. Should you meet an enchanter on the road, tell them I send my regards. And a warning.
How is the shield? Its face is sad, I know. The Knight of the Sad Countenance. It has never failed me.
I'll tell you a secret now, since you've earned it. The giants were windmills. I know. I've always known.
But I still bow to every one of them, just in case. You never know which one is enchanted.
The priest visits now. We argue about books. He's read more of mine than he admits.
I found the walled-up room. I left it closed. Some libraries are better as legends.
My old horse and I ride out less. Short errands. Carrying letters, mending fences. Small wrongs.
The shepherds graze after dark again. They wave at me. One called me 'sir knight'. I nearly wept.
I keep the giant's pearl on the windowsill, next to the helm. Well. The basin. The helm.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_quixote.epilogu: Now the old dreamer admits the giants were windmills, and still bows to every one of them, just in case.

hearthbound.persona.chiv_robin.bio.0: Officially I'm a guard. Unofficially, what's taken from the poor on the king's road sometimes finds its way back to them. I have no idea how.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_robin.bio.1: I was outlawed once, for a deer I didn't kill. The forest took me in. I owe the woods, and the poor who hid me, more than any lord.
Lovely day for walking through a forest with a heavy purse. Not that I'd know.
Never trust a sheriff who smiles at breakfast. Or a steward who smiles at all.
Lately there's a new problem. Crossbow men on the road, stripping travellers bare.
They wear some lord's colours and call it tax. The farmers pay twice and eat once.
Yesterday they took a pedlar's whole cart and his mule. The mule was the only thing he loved.
I could go alone, but I'd rather not carry a pedlar's mule back by myself.
Crossbow men on the king's road. Let's have a word with them, you and I.
Officially I guard the gate. Unofficially I count the geese. Somebody should.
You've got good boots. Quiet soles. I notice things like that. Professional habit.
I split an arrow with an arrow once. I've told the story so often it's now three arrows.
Funny thing about this village: what's taken from the poor on the king's road sometimes finds its way back to them.
A widow's rent turns up in her bread bin. A cobbler's stolen tools reappear on his doorstep. I have no idea how.
Don't look at me like that. I'm a guard. I guard things. Sometimes I guard them all the way home.
Old ballads tell of an outlaw of the greenwood who did the same. Songs exaggerate. Mostly.
Riches are fine. Friends who'd hide you in a hollow oak are better. Take it from someone who knows oaks.
The road's clear, and the purses are going back to their owners. Somehow. Don't ask how.
The pedlar kissed his mule on the nose and then, horribly, me. I've had worse thank-yous.
So I came back and put on this guard's coat. But I never forgot the oak.
This winter there are families hiding in those same woods. Debts, bad landlords, one burnt farm.
The steward pretends they don't exist. They're going hungry, and the snow's already here.
I can't be seen carrying food there. My coat would be a very short-lived coat.
Bring bread for the families in the hollow. Lots of it. And don't tell the steward.
You fight well and you don't brag. That's rare. So I'll tell you why I care so much.
I wasn't always a guard. Once I was outlawed, for a deer I didn't kill.
The steward needed someone to blame. I was poor, I was loud, and I had a bow. That was enough.
I ran into the forest with nothing. It was winter. I thought I'd die by the second night.
Then a charcoal-burner's family found me. They had one pot of soup and they split it five ways, not four.
They hid me in a hollow oak when the steward's men came by. The children giggled at me all night.
The forest took me in. I owe the woods, and the poor who hid me, more than any lord.
Years later I was pardoned. Nobody knows why. I suspect a certain abbot lost a bet.
Warm bread under the oaks. You'd think it was a feast day. The children called you 'the bread saint'.
Don't let it go to your head. They called me 'the hat' because of my hat.
I'll go anyway. A silver arrow melts down into a lot of bread.
And I'll wear a disguise. A beard, maybe. A limp. A terrible accent.
But I need arrows. Good ones, straight and fletched true. Many, for practice and for the way out.
If they close the gates, I'll want enough to keep their heads down while I climb.
Arrows, please! Plenty of them. I've a contest to win and a trap to walk out of.
Now I'll tell you what worries me. It's that they've guessed who I am.
The steward's been asking questions. Who clears the roads? Who feeds the woods?
I'm afraid that if they catch me, the families lose their only friend in a guard's coat.
My dream? That one day nobody needs a hollow oak. That the poor box by the gate is always full.
Until then, I'll keep doing things I have no idea how I did.
Now listen to this. The sheriff has announced an archery contest. The prize is a silver arrow.
Anyone may enter. Anyone. He's practically written my name on the notice.
It's a trap to catch me, of course. The best archer in three valleys wins, and they know who that is.
Won, and out through the back gate before they closed it. Keep that bow; the woods would want you to have it.
The sheriff presented the silver arrow to a limping bearded stranger with a terrible accent. Priceless.
You walked the king's road with me when it was dangerous, and carried bread when it was forbidden.
If you ever need hiding, come to the woods and whistle twice. Somebody will find you.
The split arrow story now has four arrows, by the way. Don't correct me in front of people.
Come to the spring contest. Try to beat me. You'll lose, but it'll be fun to watch.
Off you go. Mind your purse on the forest road. Or don't. It'll find its way back either way.
It became forty loaves, eleven blankets, and a new roof for the charcoal-burners.
The steward has stopped asking questions. I think someone left him a very clear note.
The families came out of the woods in spring. Two of them live in the village now. One makes cheese.
I still win every archery contest. The children say I cheat. I say the wind likes me.
The poor box by the gate is never empty. People fill it without being asked. That's my real prize.
Remember the pedlar's mule? It follows me on my rounds now. The pedlar's quite jealous.
I visited the hollow oak last week. Somebody had carved a little bow in it. And a loaf.
The loaf is you, in case you wondered. The children insisted.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_robin.epilogue: Now the village guard still wins every archery contest, and the poor box by the gate is never empty.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_robin.source: A Gest of Robyn Hode — anonymous (c. 1450)

hearthbound.persona.chiv_robin.talk.3: Riches are fine. Friends who'd hide you in a hollow oak are better.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_robin.title: Taxes and arrows
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.bio.0: Once I held a mountain pass with a handful of friends against an army. I had a horn to call for help. I was too proud to blow it.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.bio.1: When I finally blew, it was too late, and I blew so hard it nearly killed me. My wisest friend had begged me from the start. I think of that every day.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.dialogue: You walk like someone who's been in a fight or two. Me too. We'll get along.
I check the fence every evening. Twice. Once for the village, once for my own peace of mind.
Lately I dream of that pass. And lately the dead gather at night by the gap in our fence.
They come the same way the army came: through the one narrow opening, hungry and many.
I could hold that gap alone. That's what my pride says. My pride has been wrong before.
So I'm doing something new. I'm asking before the first shadow falls, not after the last friend.
Stand with me inside the walls tonight? They'll come through the gap. I don't want to hold it alone.
Being brave and being wise are cousins. They don't always speak to each other.
The children call me 'the old wall'. I pretend to be offended. I'm secretly delighted.
Do you hear the wind in the gap between the hills? It sounds like something calling from far away.
I once had friends who'd follow me anywhere. Twelve of them. I led them into a narrow place.
A mountain pass, long ago. Rocks on both sides, an army in front, and us in the middle.
I carried a horn at my belt, carved from ivory. One blast, and help would have come running.
My wisest friend, Oliver, asked me to blow it. Three times he asked. Three times I laughed.
I told him a true fighter doesn't call for help. I believed it. That's the worst part.
We held. And I sent a runner at the first shadow. Do you know how strange that felt?
My hand kept reaching for my belt, for a horn that isn't there. Old habits have long arms.
Sometimes I wonder if I'm really wiser now, or just older and more tired of burying friends.
Last night I saw tracks behind the eastern hills. Heavy boots, and the marks of axes dragged.
Axe-men are camped there. They're waiting for the carts to leave for the market road.
That's a rearguard fight. Exactly the kind I lost once. My stomach turns just saying it.
I'll take the rear this time. Will you take the front? Two sides watched, nobody left behind.
Let me tell you the rest of the pass. We fought all day. The rocks turned red.
When I finally blew the horn, only a few of us were still standing. Oliver wasn't one of them.
I blew so hard my temples burst. The sound carried thirty leagues. It carried too late.
The king came, with his whole host. He found us among the rocks, facing the enemy's road.
Before the end, I tried to break my sword on a stone so no enemy would take it. The stone broke.
I lay down under a pine tree, facing the enemy, so they'd know I never ran. Proud to the last.
The old songs made me a hero for that. The songs were kinder to me than I deserve.
Oliver told me: courage with good sense isn't madness. I only understood it once he was gone.
Everyone arrived. Every cart, every driver, every mule. That's the victory I never had.
I counted heads at the market three times. The drivers thought I'd lost my mind. I'd found it.
No asking permission. No deciding whether it's serious enough. Ring, and people come.
If it rings for nothing, fine. I'd rather run a hundred times for nothing than once too late.
Oliver would laugh at me. A bell, from the one who wouldn't blow a horn. He'd laugh kindly.
I've already built the frame for it, by the well. It's standing there empty, waiting.
Bring me a bell for the square? One that anyone can ring. No pride, no waiting. Please.
Now I can tell you what I never tell anyone: I still hear Oliver's voice when I hesitate.
He'd say, 'Friend, blow the horn.' Quietly. As if he already knew how it would end.
My fear isn't death. It's being the one who could have called, and didn't, again.
There are people here who'd rather suffer in silence than knock on a neighbour's door.
The widow by the mill froze through half a winter before anyone knew her fire had gone out.
I recognised it. That silence is just pride dressed as good manners. I wore it for years.
So I've been dreaming of something better than a horn. Something that belongs to everyone.
A bell. Right in the square. Anyone can ring it: a child, a drunk, an old guard like me.
The first child rang it just to hear it. I ran all the way from the fence. Best run of my life.
Keep my sword well. It never breaks, which is more than I can say for me.
I'm teaching the young guards the first rule: call for help at the first shadow, not the last.
The second rule: bring snacks. Holding a wall is hungry work. Oliver taught me that one too.
If you're ever outnumbered, far from here, ring whatever you have. Shout. I'll hear it somehow.
You gave me back a thing I lost in a mountain pass. I won't lose it again. Not with you around.
Go on, then. The fence is solid, the bell is hung, and I'll be here when it rings.
The bell has rung eleven times this month. Twice for fires, once for a lost goat, the rest for fun.
I'm always the first to arrive. The baker says I sleep with my boots on. The baker is right.
Yesterday the widow by the mill rang it. Her roof was leaking. We fixed it before supper.
She cried, and said she'd never have dared knock on anyone's door. That's the whole point.
I think Oliver would like this village. It asks for help early. It's wise and brave at once.
I don't dream of the pass so often now. When I do, somebody in the dream is ringing a bell.
Remember when you took the front and I took the rear? The drivers still sing about it. Badly.
The song gets longer every time. By next spring we'll have fought a hundred axe-men.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.epilogue: Now the bell hangs in the square, and the old defender of the pass is always the first to answer it.
They'll come tonight through the gap in the fence, like they did at the pass. Stand with me inside the walls.
We held. And this time, I sent a runner for help at the first shadow. Progress.
Axe-men are camped behind the hills, waiting for the carts to leave. I'll take the rear. You take the front?
The carts arrived. Everyone arrived. That's the victory I never had.
I want a bell in the square that anyone can ring when they need help. No pride, no waiting. Bring me one?
The first child rang it just to hear it. Good. Take my sword: it never breaks, which is more than I can say for me.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.talk.0: Being brave and being wise are cousins. They don't always speak to each other.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.talk.1: I tried to break my old sword on a rock so no enemy would take it. The rock broke.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.talk.2: If you're ever outnumbered, ask for help early. It's not cowardice. I learned that the hard way.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.talk.3: My friend was wise and I was brave. Together we'd have been perfect.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_roland.title: The horn I didn't blow
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.bio.0: I followed a mad old neighbour down every road in the kingdom because they promised me an island to govern. I still don't know what an island is, exactly.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.bio.1: I say I went for the island. Truth is, I went because nobody else would, and a dreamer should not travel alone.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.dialogue: A full belly makes a brave heart. An empty one makes proverbs. I have plenty of both today.
My donkey is the wisest creature in this village. He never argues with a hill. He just sits down.
They fought windmills. Sheep. A barber. I held the saddlebags and prayed very quickly.
At one inn they tossed me in a blanket, up and down, like a pancake. I don't talk about that inn.
Now my old friend has that look again. Staring at the horizon. Polishing the basin. I know what it means.
They're going to ride out. And a squire's first duty isn't the lance. It's the saddlebags.
Bread, lots of it. Knights forget to eat, and then they see giants. Will you bring me some?
You look like someone who walks a lot. Sit. Feet first, talk later. That's a proverb. I just made it up.
You know what I learned on the road? Everyone is a little mad. Some just hide it better.
If I ever get my island, you shall be minister of bread. Nobody else, I swear on my donkey.
My neighbour down the lane, the one with the old lance and the sad shield? We go back a long way.
Years ago, they knocked on my door with a promise. 'Come as my squire, and I'll give you an island to govern.'
An island! Me! I'd never seen a lake bigger than a puddle. I said yes before my wife could say no.
I still don't know what an island is, exactly. Something with water around it and a lot of taxes, I think.
We rode down every road in the kingdom. They on a thin horse, me on my donkey, both of us hungry.
Bags full, heart light. Now we can chase any giant you like. As long as we're back for supper.
Thank you. I ate one loaf already, as a test. A squire must be sure of the equipment.
Since then, he eats before I do. Every day. That's the rule. My wife says I love him more than her.
I tell her that's nonsense. Then I lower my voice so the donkey can't hear me.
He's getting old now, and his teeth aren't what they were. Soft things suit him best.
He has earned a feast. A proper one. Crunchy, sweet, the kind that makes his ears stand up.
Carrots, please. A good pile of them. For the wisest creature in the village.
My old friend patted the bags and said, 'You think only of your stomach.' They took the first loaf.
Did I tell you about the donkey? No? Sit. This one deserves both ears.
One night on the road, a thief crept in while I slept and stole him right from under my saddle.
I woke up sitting on four sticks. Four sticks! Where my donkey had been. I've never felt so cheated.
I cried like a baby. Out loud, on the road, in front of a knight. I'm not ashamed of it.
I walked for days, carrying the packs myself. Every step I talked to him as if he were there.
Then one morning, there he was, coming down the road with a stranger on his back. I ran and hugged his neck.
The thief ran off. My donkey just looked at me as if to say, 'Where have you been?'
Look at him eat! His ears haven't stood that high since the day I found him again.
Do you like the saddle? I won't sell the donkey, but I'll gladly share his luck. It's a good saddle.
Could that be my island? After all these years? My stomach turns over just thinking about it.
What if it's grand, and I'm not? What if they take one look at this belly and laugh?
Worse, what if it's wonderful, and I have to leave my donkey, my wife, my old mad friend?
I can't look at it myself. I'd lose my nerve halfway and come home with nothing but blisters.
Go and see it for me? Tell me if it's an island worth governing. I'm too scared to look.
Now I'll tell you the truth, since you've been kind to him. The island was never why I went.
I say I went for the island. Everybody laughs and I laugh too. It makes a better story.
Truth is, I went because nobody else would. And a dreamer shouldn't travel alone.
They'd have ridden into a river thinking it was a moat. Someone had to hold the reins.
I'm a simple person. I can't read. But I can see when a friend is about to walk off a cliff.
Still, the island stuck in my head. Some nights I dream I'm judging disputes. Very wisely. With lunch.
Imagine it. People bringing me their quarrels, and me, with my proverbs, sorting them out.
Now there's talk of a village far away that needs someone to govern. A trader said so at the tavern.
Wise folk, full barns and no sea at all? Then I'll stay here. A good roof is worth ten islands.
Now I govern only a small vegetable patch. Cabbages, beans, and a very ambitious row of carrots.
Every time I eat bread on the bench, I think of the saddlebags you filled. Best bread of my life.
Everyone is a little mad, I told you. The trick is to find good company for your madness.
I found mine on a thin horse. And then another on the road, bringing carrots. That's you.
Come eat with us someday. The donkey will let you have the second carrot. That's a great honour.
Off you go, then. A full belly makes a brave heart. Take a loaf, just in case you meet a giant.
I rule it very wisely. Justice for the cabbages. Mercy for the snails, mostly.
The donkey is my chief counsellor. He votes with his teeth. Usually for the carrots.
My old friend admits the giants were windmills now. Still bows to them. I bow too, to be polite.
We sit together on the bench at sunset. They talk about knights. I talk about lunch. We both listen.
My wife says I'm happier now than when I dreamed of islands. Don't tell her she's right.
The children come to me with their squabbles. Who stole whose marble. I judge fairly. With proverbs.
'Whoever lends a marble should count it first.' They look at me like I'm the wisest person alive.
You remember the minister of bread post? It's still yours. The patch needs a minister. Pay is carrots.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.epilogue: Now the would-be governor rules only a small vegetable patch, and rules it very wisely.
My old friend wants to ride out again, and a squire's first duty is the saddlebags. Bread, lots of it. Knights forget to eat.
Bags full, heart light. Now we can chase any giant you like.
Thieves took my donkey once, and I wept like a child until he came back. He has earned a feast. Carrots, please.
Look at him eat! Take this old saddle. I won't sell the donkey, but I'll share his luck.
They say a village far away needs a governor. Could that be my island? Go and see it for me: I'm too scared to look.
Wise folk, full barns and no sea at all? Then I'll stay here. A good roof is worth ten islands.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.talk.0: A full belly makes a brave heart. An empty one makes proverbs. I have plenty of both.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.talk.1: My donkey is the wisest creature in this village. He never argues with a hill.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.talk.2: You know what I learned on the road? Everyone is a little mad. Some just hide it better.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.talk.3: If I ever get my island, you shall be minister of bread. Nobody else, I swear.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_sancho.title: Promised an island
hearthbound.persona.chiv_siegfried.bio.0: I reforged a broken sword that no smith could mend and killed a dragon with it. I bathed in its blood, and now no blade can cut me. Almost.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_siegfried.bio.1: A linden leaf fell between my shoulders while I bathed. One spot, the size of a hand. Only I know where. And someone I trusted too much.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_siegfried.dialo: Mind the sparks. They don't hurt me, but they'll hurt you, and I'd hate that.
Gold is heavy. Friends are lighter to carry and worth more.
I've kept them all these years. Wrapped, in a box under my bed. Don't tell anyone.
Last week I held them again, and my hands knew what to do. File them to dust. Start over.
Every smith gave up because they tried to glue the pieces. You don't mend a sword like that.
You grind it all into filings, feed it to a goose, melt what's left. Or so the old tale says. I'll skip the goose.
I'll need iron, though, a lot of it, to temper the dust. Bring me iron? I want my father's sword back.
I understand birds, you know. They mostly complain about cats. And about me, for being loud.
That blackbird says you've got bread in your pocket. Do you? Then share, it's been nagging.
I've started sleeping with my back to the wall. Old habits. Don't ask why. Not yet.
My father had a sword that broke in his last battle. My mother kept the pieces for me.
When I was young, I brought the shards to every smith in the land. Each one said: impossible.
One smith raised me, and he was the worst of them: clever hands, crooked heart. He wanted me dead.
He wanted me to kill a dragon for him, so he could take its gold. I didn't know that then.
I still dream of those shards on a velvet cloth. Seven of them. The eighth was lost.
It split the anvil in two. I've never been so happy to ruin an anvil. The smith next door wept.
Now you've earned the truth. That sword killed a dragon. A real one, in a cave by a river.
The dragon was lying on a hoard. Gold and rings and a helmet that makes you invisible.
I took some. I left most. It was cursed, the birds said. They say that about most things.
But I've heard the hoard is hidden past the next village now. Someone moved it, or it moved itself.
Treasure has a way of owning its owner. I want to know where it sleeps, so I know where not to go.
Find the dragon's hoard for me? Just find it. Don't touch it. Cursed or not, I need to know.
I dug a pit on its path and waited inside. When it crawled over, I struck upwards.
Its blood poured over me. Hot as a forge. I bathed in it, as the old smith had told me to.
Since then no blade can cut my skin. Arrows bounce. Knives slide off. I stopped fearing anything.
And I tasted its heart, by accident, licking my burnt thumb. That's when the birds started talking.
The first thing they said: the old smith is coming to kill you. They were right. I was quicker.
Almost no blade can cut me. Almost. A linden leaf fell on my back while I bathed.
One spot between my shoulders, the size of a hand. The blood never touched it.
You're the second person I've told. That's how much I trust you. That scares me a little.
So it's real. Maybe I'll leave it there. Treasure has a way of owning its owner.
You went and came back with empty pockets. I'm impressed. Most people fill their boots.
The birds say he's been asking about me. They say he sharpens a spear every evening.
I could run. I'm good at leaving. But I'm tired of turning my back on everyone to be safe.
What I need is something simple, not magic. Something to put between my back and the world.
Then I'll know who stands behind me. The wrong friend won't get that close again.
Bring me a shield? I'll never again turn my back on the wrong friend. Just the right ones.
