Now the deepest thing. I told you you're the second. The first was someone I loved.
She asked me once, worried, where the weak spot was, so she could protect it. I told her.
She sewed a little cross on my tunic over the spot. To guard it, she said. She meant well.
But she told someone else. A grim man with one good eye who smiled like a closed door.
In the old songs, that man waited at a spring during a hunt, when the hero bent to drink.
I don't want to be that song. I don't sleep. I hear footsteps behind me in the forge.
Never tell anyone your weak spot. Not even the people you love. Especially not them.
I don't blame her. Love makes us careless with each other's secrets. I was careless too.
Thank you. Take the gold. I threw the rest of the hoard in the river, where it came from.
The river glints oddly on sunny days now. The fishermen say it's lucky. I say don't dive.
Remember the anvil splitting? The whole village thought lightning had struck the forge.
I kept one ring from the hoard. Just one. I'm melting it into a clasp for your cloak.
The birds say it'll be a long, easy winter. They lie sometimes, but they're rarely wrong about weather.
Gold is heavy. Friends are lighter. I told you that the first day. Now I know it's true.
Go on, then. Keep your back to good people, and your eyes on the rest. I'll mind the forge.
I sleep soundly with the shield on the wall. First night, I slept fourteen hours. The birds complained.
The grim man stopped by the village last month. He saw the shield, nodded, and rode on.
Sometimes the best fight is the one someone decides not to start. I learned that late.
My father's sword hangs over the forge. I use it to cut bread. Very thin slices.
The smith next door forgave me for the anvil. I made him a new one. Twice as heavy.
The blackbird still nags about your bread. You've spoiled it. It waits for you by the well.
I've told nobody else about the leaf. You and I are the only ones who know now. Good.
I don't need armour of blood anymore. A shield and a good friend at my back. That's enough.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_siegfried.epilo: Now the dragon-slayer sleeps soundly with a shield on the wall, and the river glints oddly on sunny days.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_siegfried.stage: My father's sword was shattered. Every smith gave up. I'll file it to dust and forge it anew. Bring iron.
It split the anvil in two. I've never been so happy to ruin an anvil.
The dragon's hoard is hidden somewhere past the next village, cursed or not. Find it for me?
So it's real. Maybe I'll leave it there. Treasure has a way of owning its owner.
I told someone where the leaf fell. Now I can't sleep. Bring me a shield, and I'll never turn my back on the wrong friend.
Thank you. Take the gold: I'm throwing the rest of the hoard in the river, where it came from.
Gold is heavy. Friends are lighter to carry and worth more.
I understand birds since I tasted the dragon's heart. They mostly complain about cats.
Never tell anyone your weak spot. Not even the people you love. Especially not them.
I've started sleeping with my back to the wall. Old habits.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_siegfried.title: A leaf on my back
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.bio.0: A cruel bailiff put his hat on a pole in the square and ordered everyone to bow to it. I walked past without bowing. My child was holding my hand.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.bio.1: As punishment he made me shoot an apple off my child's head at a hundred paces. I hit the apple. I kept a second bolt, for him, if I had missed.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.dialogue.0: You didn't bow when you came in. Good. I don't bow to hats, and I'm starting to think you don't either.
People here bow to each other, which is fine. People, sometimes. Hats, never. There's a difference, and it matters.
The guards grabbed me before I reached the fountain. My child asked why we were in trouble. I had no good answer.
My child laughs about that day now. I don't. I still see a certain apple in my sleep. I'll tell you another time.
Lately the little one has an idea: plant an orchard, 'so there are always spare apples'. I can't say no to that.
I think the child means: so no single apple ever matters that much again. Children understand more than we let on.
Bring us some apples, would you? We'll take the seeds and start an orchard behind the house.
My crossbow hangs over the door. It hasn't been fired in years. I oil it anyway, every Sunday, like a prayer.
Apples taste better when nobody is aiming at them. Try one. That's a joke you'll understand later.
My child follows me everywhere, asking what every plant is called. I've started inventing names. The turnips are now 'mountain moons'.
I come from a valley between high lakes, where the mountains decide the weather and the people decide nothing.
A new bailiff came, sent by a far-off lord. He wanted our taxes, our timber and, most of all, our heads bowed.
One morning he hung his own hat on a pole in the square and ordered everyone to bow to it as if it were him.
Grown men bowed to a hat. I watched them. I felt something in my chest turn over, like a stone in a stream.
I walked past it without bowing. My child was holding my hand. I didn't think; my knees simply refused.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.dialogue.1: Seeds in the ground, and the little one watered them twice before supper. One day there'll be too many apples to aim at.
I promised to tell you about the apple. Sit. It's not a long story. It only feels long.
They say in the old play I escaped a boat in a storm and leapt onto a rock. The play exaggerates. Slightly.
I thought it was over when I came here. I planted, I hunted, I kept my head down. Well, down but not bowed.
But traders say the bailiff's men are back in the hills, asking for someone with a crossbow and a child.
I never waste a bolt, and I always keep a second one. It's the habit that saved us, and the one I hate most.
I need arrows, a good bundle, just in case. I hope with all my heart they'll gather dust.
The bailiff had me brought before him. He'd heard I was the best shot in the valley. He smiled, and I knew.
He took an apple from a basket and placed it on my child's head. A hundred paces, he said. Hit it and you're free.
I begged. I've never begged anyone before or since. He said I could refuse, and then they'd both die. Me and the child.
My child stood still against a linden tree and said, 'Shoot, I trust you.' Those words weigh more than any bolt.
I took two bolts from my quiver. Everyone saw. Nobody asked why two. The bailiff did, afterwards.
I aimed. My hands shook, so I waited until they didn't. The whole square held its breath with me.
The apple split in two. My child laughed first, then cried, then ran to me. I don't remember the next minute at all.
The bailiff asked about the second bolt. I told him the truth: it was for him, if I had missed. He had me chained for that.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.dialogue.2: Enough arrows for a lifetime of 'just in case'. I stacked them where the child can't reach. Then I stacked them higher.
I haven't told you the worst part. It isn't the apple. It's the second bolt, and how easily I took it out.
Where the road climbs, there's a hollow way, a narrow pass with high banks. Anyone who comes through must come one by one.
I'll wait there, among the bushes. The old play says I waited in just such a place once. The play gets that part right.
I don't want to do it. I want to be the one who plants apples. But if I don't go, someone else's child will stand under a hat.
I can't hold the pass alone. Too many of them, and my eyes are not what they were at a hundred paces.
Help me end this, at the hollow way. Six of their crossbowmen should turn the rest back for good.
In that moment I had already decided who would die if I missed. I've never known if that makes me good or terrible.
The child knows about the second bolt. Asked me once, straight out. I didn't lie. We didn't speak for a day.
Then the little one said, 'You kept it for me, not for him.' Perhaps that's the way to see it. I try.
Freedom starts with small refusals, I always say. A hat, a tax, a lie. But the big refusals cost more.
My fear is that my child will grow up thinking freedom means a crossbow. It doesn't. It means not needing one.
My dream is plain: an orchard where the pole stood, and children who don't even know what the pole was for.
The bailiff's crossbowmen are on the mountain road now. A shepherd saw them, dozens, with banners and torches.
They're not coming for taxes. They're coming for the whole valley, the way they took mine.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.dialogue.3: The valley is free. I walked home through the pass and nobody stopped me. I kept waiting for a hand on my shoulder.
You have my crossbow now. It hit an apple once, and that's the only shot I'm proud of. Keep it that way if you can.
That's the kind of friend I didn't know I needed: one who asks the small question first.
The lord's men sent a letter. It says they 'reconsider the valley's status'. Fancy words for 'we're scared of your hollow way'.
When the first real harvest comes, you'll have the first basket. No aiming, no bowing. Just eating.
If ever someone makes you bow to a hat out there, remember: small refusals. And come home to the orchard.
Go on, then. Mind the crooked tree on your way out; the little one will ask if you said hello to it.
The old pole in the square is gone. We pulled it down together and used it for firewood. It burned badly. Fitting.
The orchard is sprouting. Twelve little trees, each with a name. The child named one after you. It's the crooked one.
Don't be offended. The crooked one grows fastest. It leans toward the sun like it has somewhere to be.
Every child in the valley now knows how to not bow to a hat. It's become a game. They bow to scarecrows instead, very deeply.
I still keep a second arrow, out of habit. It sits in a jar on the shelf. I think it'll stay there forever.
My child asked if we're heroes now. I said no, we're orchard-keepers. The child seemed disappointed, then pleased.
I dream of the apple less. Last night I dreamed of the orchard in blossom, and nobody was aiming at anything.
Do you remember the day you brought those first apples? I thought you'd ask about the pole. You just asked if they were sweet.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.epilogue: Now an orchard grows where the pole once stood, and every child in the valley knows how to not bow to a hat.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.stage.0.as: My child wants to plant an orchard 'so there are always spare apples'. I can't say no to that. Bring some?
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.stage.0.do: Seeds in the ground. One day there'll be too many apples to aim at.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.stage.1.as: I never waste a bolt, and I always keep a second one. The bailiff's men are back. I need arrows, just in case.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.stage.1.do: Enough for a lifetime of 'just in case'. I hope I never use them.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.stage.2.as: The bailiff's crossbowmen are coming up the mountain road. There's a narrow pass where I'll wait. Help me end this.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.stage.2.do: The valley is free. Take my crossbow: it hit an apple once, and that's the only shot I'm proud of.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.talk.0: I don't bow to hats. People, sometimes. Hats, never.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.talk.1: Apples taste better when nobody is aiming at them.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.talk.2: My child laughs about it now. I don't. I still see that apple in my sleep.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.talk.3: Freedom starts with small refusals. A hat, a tax, a lie.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tell.title: An apple on a head
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.bio.0: Years ago I was sent across the sea to fetch a bride for my uncle. On the voyage we shared the wrong cup, and we have loved each other ever since.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.bio.1: We've been apart longer than we've been together. I don't want a great ending anymore. I only want the right colour on the sail.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.dialogu: Honey wine is dangerous. Don't let anyone tell you it's just a drink.
I play the harp badly and sing worse. The seagulls forgive me. The neighbours don't.
Some loves are a choice. Mine was an accident that I would choose again. That's the hard part.
Still, I've always wondered. Was it the drink? Or would it have happened anyway?
If I brewed that cursed drink once more and poured it into the sea, would I be free?
I know the recipe; the servant who made it told me, years later, weeping. It starts with honey.
Bring me honey. I want to brew it once more, only to pour it into the sea and be free of it.
You've come from the coast road? Did you see any ships? No? Never mind. I always ask.
I mend nets and carry crates at the harbour. Hands busy, eyes on the horizon. It's a habit.
If you ever carry a message for lovers, never lie about the colour of anything. Promise me.
Years ago my uncle, a lord across the water, sent me to fetch his bride from over the sea.
I was proud to go. His most trusted kin, bringing home a queen. What could go wrong?
On the voyage, it was hot, and we were thirsty. There was a flask in the cabin.
It was a love drink, meant for her and my uncle on the wedding night. We shared the wrong cup.
The old Norman poets tell it as a doom. From inside, it felt like waking up.
I poured it out. Nothing changed. So it was never the drink.
I stood on the rocks for an hour afterwards. I didn't feel cursed. I felt answered.
My uncle has grown old and soft. I've heard he'd let her write to me now. Just write.
But she lives in a village too far for any stream to reach. Wood chips won't do.
I've written a letter. Six drafts. Most of them are just her name, in different moods.
I can't go myself. The last time I did, the whole valley ended up with swords drawn.
Carry my letter to the village where my love lives? Put it in her hands, and wait for an answer.
You've been patient with an old fool's heart, so here's the rest of it.
She married my uncle. Of course she did. We stole hours, then days, then we were caught.
My uncle is not a cruel man. That made everything worse. He wept when he banished me.
We've been apart longer than we've been together. Seasons, years, whole lifetimes of tides.
In the old days, when I hid in the woods near her garden, we sent notes carved on wood chips.
I'd drop them in the stream above her fountain. She'd see them float by and know I was near.
Such a silly, beautiful system. A bark chip with three letters on it could keep me alive a month.
I don't want a great ending anymore, the kind the harpers sing. I only want to know she's well.
An answer! Three words. I'll read them until the ink gives up.
No, I won't tell you the three words. You carried them; you can guess.
My dream is so small: to stand on the harbour and see the true colour, whatever it is.
So I'll make the sail myself. Nobody can lie about a sail they didn't make.
I'll weave it white, pure white, the whitest wool in the valley, and send it to her ship.
If it comes back black, it's the truth. If white, it's the truth. Either way, it's ours.
Bring me wool, and I'll weave the sail myself. No more lies about colours.
Now I'll tell you the thing I fear most, which is also the oldest story about us.
In the harpers' version, I lie dying and send for her. White sail if she comes, black sail if not.
And someone jealous lies. Says the sail is black when it's white. And I die of the lie.
I used to think that was just a song. Then I realised how many people love to lie about colours.
Now, truly: she's coming. My uncle has given leave. A ship will bring her here before summer.
White sail if she's aboard, black if not. We agreed that in the letter, half joking, half not.
I'm not dying. I'm only old. But my heart knows that song better than my head does.
I'm afraid someone will change the sail. A jealous sailor, a careless dyer, or just the dark.
Nobody could lie about that one. It came over the horizon white as a gull's wing.
She stepped off the ship with grey hair and the same laugh. I dropped my harp in the harbour.
You carried three words across the hills and wool across the fields. Both became a sail.
If you ever carry a message for lovers again, remember: the truth, and the colour.
Come by at dusk. I'll play something terrible and she'll correct me loudly.
Honey wine is still dangerous, mind. We only drink it on the anniversary. From separate cups.
Go on. The sail needs airing, and she's calling me something rude from the doorway. I love it.
We fished it out. It plays even worse now. She says it finally matches my singing.
We argue about harp music every evening under the sail. She's wrong about everything. It's wonderful.
The sail hangs in the village square now. Every spring we wash it in the stream, like the old days.
The children float wood chips down the stream with their names on them. Nobody told them to.
My uncle wrote to wish us well. In his own hand. Some wounds close if you're patient enough.
Remember the honey I poured into the sea? The fishermen swear the fish were friendlier for a week.
I still look at the horizon every morning. Habit. But now I look for weather, not for her.
She tends the fire and I mend nets. We've wasted enough time being a legend.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.epilogu: Now a white sail hangs in the village square, washed every spring, and two old lovers argue under it about harp music.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.stage.0: Bring me honey. I want to brew that cursed drink once more, only to pour it into the sea and be free of it.
I poured it out. Nothing changed. So it was never the drink.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.stage.1: We used to send notes carved on wood chips down the stream. Too slow now. Carry my letter to the village where my love lives?
An answer! Three words. I'll read them until the ink gives up.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.stage.2: A ship will bring my love back. White sail if aboard, black if not. I'm afraid someone will lie. Bring wool: I'll weave the sail myself.
Nobody can lie about this one. Whatever comes over the horizon, it'll be the truth.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.talk.0: Honey wine is dangerous. Don't let anyone tell you it's just a drink.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.talk.1: I play the harp badly and sing worse. The seagulls forgive me.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.talk.2: Some loves are a choice. Mine was an accident that I would choose again.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.talk.3: If you ever carry a message for lovers, never lie about the colour of anything.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_tristan.title: Black sail, white sail
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.bio.0: A greedy king once seized me for my skill, cut the tendons of my legs, and chained me to a forge on an island. I made his treasures for years.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.bio.1: While I hammered his rings I built something else, feather by feather. Revenge I had, and it tasted of ash. The flight was the part worth keeping.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.dialogu: Mind the sparks. They like new faces. So do I, though I show it less.
Yes, I limp. No, it doesn't slow the hammer. The hammer never needed my knees.
I made him cups, brooches, a sword for his hip. He praised the work and never once asked my name.
The iron here is good, but thin in my stores. I haven't made anything worth showing since I arrived.
I'd like to make one ring again, the way I made them for him. To see if my hands remember without the chains.
Some people think a smith is only as good as the iron they're given. Let's test that.
Bring me iron, a good heap of it, and I'll show you what I made for a king. And what I made for myself.
Hand me that tongs? Thank you. You hold iron like someone who's been burned once and learned from it.
Leave a coin on my anvil at night and your horse will be shod by morning. Don't try to watch. It spoils the custom.
Every ring I make has a tiny flaw on purpose. Perfection is for gods, and gods are poor customers.
I wasn't always a village smith. Once I made rings so fine a king heard of them in his sleep.
He wanted them all. When a king wants all of something, he usually wants the one who makes it too.
His men came at night while I slept. I woke up bound, with one of my own rings missing from the string.
I don't talk about my legs. Let's say the king made sure I'd never walk away from his forge.
They put me on an island, just me and an anvil and the sea. The gulls were my only visitors for years.
Look at that ring. The king never knew its twin was in my pocket the whole time.
Here, the twin. I've carried it for twenty years. Same flaw, same weight. The one thing he couldn't own.
I hid them in the ash pit, under the coals. The guards never looked there. Who digs through a smith's ashes?
Feather by feather, while I hammered his rings. Some nights I think I built the wings more than I built anything else.
I want to build them again. Not to escape. Just to know if I was right, or if I was only desperate.
Don't ask why. Well, you know why now. But don't tell the guards; they get nervous about smiths and heights.
Feathers, as many as you can gather. Big ones, clean ones, any bird. I'll find each a place.
It felt strange, working iron without a guard at the door. I kept looking up. Nobody was there. You were, once.
Let me tell you about the island. A black beach, a forge in a cave, and a boat that came once a month with ore and orders.
The king's daughter came once, with a broken ring. I mended it. She was the only one who ever said thank you.
The king's sons came too, greedy for treasure. I won't tell you what became of them. I'm not proud of it.
Revenge, they call it in the songs. I'll only say it tasted of ash, and the ash is still in my mouth some mornings.
Every evening the gulls came to the rocks outside my cave. I watched them lift off the cliff without a single step.
That's when it started. Not with a plan. With envy. I envied the gulls their legs that didn't need to work.
I began keeping feathers. One from the beach, one from a gull's quarrel, one from the king's own feasting table.
Perfect. Every feather has a place, and every place has a feather. I laid them out on the floor like a map.
I slept on the floor beside them. My back paid for it. I didn't mind.
This time I want wings built from something else. From patience. From the village. From you bringing feathers.
But feathers alone won't hold. On the island I ruined three sets before the wind taught me: you need a skin.
No bird has the right skin. But the night-flyers, the grey ones that hunt the sleepless, their wings are all skin.
I've seen them fall at dawn. Their membranes are tough as sailcloth and light as breath.
Bring me four of those membranes, and I'll finish what I started on that island. Honestly, this time.
On the island, the frame was the hard part. I used whale bone and the king's own silver wire. He paid for my flight.
The first time I tried, I only lifted a hand's width off the rock. I laughed so loud the guards came running.
I had to lie. I said a gull had stolen my bread. They believed it. Nobody thinks a lame smith laughs for other reasons.
The night I flew, I stopped above the king's hall and told him everything. The truth fell on him harder than any hammer.
Then I flew away, and never saw him again. The flight was the part worth keeping. The rest I'd trade for nothing.
I landed badly, on a hillside far away. Broke the wings, and nearly broke myself. I burned the feathers there.
I swore I'd never fly again. Too much of the island lived in those wings. Now I'm not sure that oath was fair.
My fear is this: the wings are still made of what I felt back then. Rage flies, but it doesn't land.
I flew over the roofs and landed in the pig trough. You saw. Everyone saw. The pigs have forgiven me; the baker hasn't.
Those boots I gave you, do you wear them? Good. Fall gently, wherever you go. I'd hate for you to land like me.
Leave a coin on my anvil tonight, if you like. I'll mend whatever you bring. For you, I might even let you watch.
Some nights I still dream of flying, and I wake smiling. My legs still ache. But now I know the dream was true.
I never thanked the gulls on that island. I leave crusts on the forge roof now. Late thanks are still thanks.
You helped a lame smith fly. Don't let it go to your head. Let it go to your feet, in those boots.
Go on. The forge is warm, the wings are quiet, and the pigs are watching. Come back and tell me how the world looks where you land.
The wings hang in the back of the forge now. I take them out on quiet evenings. Not far. Just over the roofs.
The village swears it sees a shape gliding over the forge at dusk. I tell them it's an owl. A heavy, limping owl.
Funny thing: in the air, I don't limp. It's the only place I've ever been equal to everyone else.
I made a ring for the miller's wedding last week. It has a flaw, of course. The bride found it and laughed. Good sign.
I still have the twin ring. I've decided to give it away one day, to someone who never tried to own anything.
The ash taste is fading. Not gone. But the mornings smell of bread and coal instead of the island.
Do you know what I remember from that first ring you watched? You asked what the flaw was for. The king never asked.
The children want me to teach them to fly. I teach them to shoe horses instead. Flight comes after patience.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.epilogu: Now the lame smith is the best in the land, and on quiet evenings the village swears it sees a shape gliding over the forge.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.source: The Lay of Völund, Poetic Edda — anonymous (c. 1270)
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.stage.0: They say a smith here is only as good as the iron. Bring me iron and I'll show you what I made for a king.
Look at that ring. The king never knew its twin was in my pocket.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.stage.1: Don't ask why. Feathers, as many as you can. And don't mention them to the guards.
Perfect. Every feather has a place, and every place has a feather.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.stage.2: The wings need a skin no bird has. Bring me the membranes of the night-flyers, and I'll finish what I started on that island.
I flew over the roofs and landed in the pig trough. Take these boots: fall gently, wherever you go.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.talk.0: I walk with a limp. My hammer doesn't.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.talk.1: Every ring I make has a tiny flaw on purpose. Only the gods should be perfect.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.talk.2: Leave a coin on my anvil at night and your horse will be shod by morning. Old custom.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.talk.3: Some nights I still dream I'm flying. I wake up smiling, legs aching.
hearthbound.persona.chiv_wayland.title: Wings from the forge
hearthbound.persona.curious_alchemist.bi: People think I do magic. I don't. I mix, I boil, I write down what happens. That's all alchemy is.
My master died looking for a remedy against the wasting cough. I inherited her notes... and her obsession.
I'm close. I know I'm close. The last ingredient grows in the realm of fire.
hearthbound.persona.curious_alchemist.di: Don't drink that. Or that. Actually, don't drink anything on this table. Or touch it.
Eyebrows grow back. I checked. Took about six weeks. I have notes.
I inherited her notes. And her obsession, I suppose. Some nights I think she's reading over my shoulder.
Her last page has a list of ingredients. Half are crossed out. The rest have question marks.
The first one is the least pleasant. It helps the body fight what's already inside. Poison against poison.
Spiders. Specifically, their eyes. Yes, eyes. Don't look at me like that; it's science.
Would you bring me some spider eyes? I'd go myself, but spiders and I have a history.
You're remarkably unharmed for someone who keeps visiting. I find that scientifically interesting.
People think I do magic. I don't. I mix, I boil, I write down what happens. That's all alchemy is.
That green smoke? Nothing dangerous. Probably. Open the window anyway.
These notebooks weren't mine at first. They belonged to my master. Twenty-two volumes, all cramped handwriting.
She took me in when I was a scrawny kid stealing apples. Said I had 'an eye for what goes wrong'.
She taught me to measure twice, pour once, and always write down failures. 'Failures are maps,' she said.
There's a sickness in these parts. The wasting cough. It starts as a tickle and ends in blood.
She spent her last ten years hunting a remedy. The cough took her before she found it.
Perfect. Slimy, but perfect. I've already dried two and dissolved one. Don't ask about the smell.
Thank you. You didn't even flinch handing them over. Most people drop the jar.
It needs something that holds light inside it. Something that keeps it awake.
There's a dust that glows on its own, from the stone that hangs in the burning realm's ceilings.
Traders sometimes bring it, for lamps. It's rare. Expensive. And I need rather a lot.
I know it's a strange thing to hunt for. I can explain the chemistry, if you have three hours.
The mixture needs glowstone dust. Will you bring me some? Then we'll see if she was right.
Let me tell you the rest. My master didn't just die of the cough. She died testing her own remedy.
She was sure she was close. She drank a batch that was wrong. I found her in the morning, pen still in hand.
Her last note says 'too dark. Needs light.' I've read it a thousand times. I didn't understand it.
I was angry with her for a long time. For being careless. For leaving me with twenty-two volumes and no answer.
Then last winter, the miller's youngest started coughing. And I stopped being angry and started working.
He's better now. Rest and warm broth. But it'll come back. It always comes back in the cold.
If the remedy works, no child in this village will cough blood again. That's the whole point.
I finally think I understand 'needs light'. The mixture goes black and dead after a day. It spoils.
Look how it glows! A week and it's still bright. My master was right. We're one step away.
I talked to her last night. Out loud, to her portrait. I told her 'light' worked. It felt good.
She wrote 'blaze?' and underlined it twice. It's the last word in her handwriting.
I'm an alchemist, not a warrior. I'd last about four seconds there. Three, if I tripped.
I'd never ask if it weren't important. Winter is coming. The coughing season.
You've come back from worse places. I've seen the scorch marks on your boots.
The last ingredient: blaze rods, from the burning realm. Please. For the children. For her.
The miller's youngest came by and held the vial. He said it looked like a firefly in a bottle.
Can I tell you what frightens me? Not the fire. Not the danger. Getting it wrong, like she did.
I've tested every batch on myself. Small doses. Don't tell anyone. My hands shake a little, that's all.
If I fail, all twenty-two volumes were for nothing. Her life's work. Mine too, now.
Sometimes I dream the cough is in me. I wake up and cough on purpose, just to check. Silly.
My master's last question mark is the hardest. The final ingredient doesn't grow here.
It comes from the realm of fire. From creatures made of flame, spinning in the heat.
Their rods carry fire that doesn't die. Mixed in, they'd bind everything together, give it strength.
It works. It works! The remedy works! I still say it every morning, just to hear it.
The miller's youngest took the first dose this winter. Not a single cough. Not one.
Failures are maps, she said. We walked through a lot of failures to get here, didn't we?
The children leave spider drawings on my door now. As thanks. I think. Could be threats.
The shelves are full of glowing vials. At night the workshop looks like a starry sky.
Thank you. For the eyes, the dust, the fire. For not drinking anything off my table.
Now go on, before I ask you to test something. And open the window on your way out.
The wasting cough is gone from the village. Gone. I didn't think I'd see that in my lifetime.
Did the potions I gave you help? They're the best thing I know how to make. Besides the remedy.
I wrote your name in the notes, next to my master's. Right on the title page of volume twenty-three.
She'd have liked you. She'd have scolded you for walking into the fire realm, then hugged you.
I've started copying the recipe for other villages. Carefully. With warnings in big letters.
The scholar says it'll go in their history. The alchemist and the traveller who beat the cough.
My eyebrows are fully grown back, by the way. For now. I'm working on something new.
Don't worry. It's only mildly explosive. Theoretically. I'll write it down either way.
hearthbound.persona.curious_alchemist.ep: The wasting cough is gone from the village. The alchemist's notes now carry a second name next to their master's: yours.
hearthbound.persona.curious_alchemist.st: I need spider eyes. Yes, eyes. Don't look at me like that; it's science.
The mixture needs something that holds light. Glowstone dust. Rather a lot of it.
Look how it glows! We're one step away.
The last ingredient: blaze rods, from the burning realm. I'd never ask if it weren't important.
It works... it works! The remedy works! Take these; they're the best thing I know how to make.
hearthbound.persona.curious_alchemist.ta: Don't drink that. Or that. Actually, don't drink anything on this table.
You're remarkably unharmed for someone who spends so much time here.
If the remedy works, no child in this village will cough blood again.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.bio.0: I taught history at the great academy, until I wrote the history that someone important didn't like.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.bio.1: They burned my books and banished me. I came here with nothing but what I remember.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.bio.2: I'm rewriting everything from memory. The true history. Someone has to.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.dialo: Ah, a visitor. Sit. Mind the stack of notes, it's in chronological order. Mostly.
Ink, paper and time. That's all a scholar needs. And tea. Would you like tea? It's terrible.
Then they banished me. I walked out of the city with the clothes I wore and nothing else.
Knowledge is the only thing they can't banish. It came with me. Up here.
I'm rewriting everything from memory. Every date, every name. Someone has to.
But I've filled every scrap: the backs of old letters, the margins of the tavern menu. I'm out.
I need books to write in. Blank ones, used ones, it doesn't matter. Would you bring me some?
Did you know this village is built on older ruins? Nobody asks. Nobody knows.
You have the eyes of someone who's seen a lot. One day you'll tell me, and I'll write it down.
The well stones by the plaza have carvings on the underside. Spirals. Older than any family here.
I used to teach history at the great academy. Six hundred students, a library with forty rooms.
I loved the smell of that place. Dust and candle wax and old leather. I still dream of it.
I spent twelve years on one book. The true history of the old wars, from the records nobody read.
It turns out someone important's great-grandfather did something shameful. The records said so.
They burned my books in the courtyard. My students watched. Some of them cheered. Some of them cried.
Pages! Glorious pages! I can write again. I filled the first book in two nights.
Thank you. You've no idea. It's like being handed back my own voice.
If those places are real, my memory is sound. If they're not... I'm just an old exile scribbling.
I'm too slow for the roads now, and the dead walk at night. The chronicles don't mention that part.
You travel. You notice things. I've seen you read a landscape the way I read a page.
I need eyes out there. Honest eyes that tell me what's really there, not what I hope.
Go and find another village. Tell me what you see, every detail. Especially the stones.
Let me tell you what they burned. Not just one book. My notes, my students' essays, my letters.
The chancellor stood by the fire and said, 'History belongs to those who pay for it.'
I said, 'Then you owe a great deal.' That's probably when the banishment became certain.
My hands still smell of smoke some mornings. I know it's impossible. I smell it anyway.
Some nights I wake and can't remember a date. A king's name. I lie there sweating until it comes back.
What if I remember it wrong? A false history in good faith is still a false history.
The chronicles I read at the academy spoke of other settlements. Villages built on older villages.
They described towers, bells, and a particular way of stacking stone. I copied the sketches once.
Just as the chronicles said. The stacked stones, the bell. My memory hasn't failed me.
I cried when you described it. Don't tell anyone. Scholars are supposed to be dry as parchment.
The old texts say they leave behind pearls that hold a little of the between. Green and cold.
I have never held one. I've written about them for years. That's not scholarship, that's guessing.
I will not end my history with a guess. Not after they burned the truth once.
I need to study their pearls. I know what I'm asking. They're dangerous, and you're my friend.
Bring me those pearls, from the walkers between worlds. Please, be careful. Don't meet their eyes.
I've written forty chapters now. The wars, the founders, the ruins under this very village.
Your description is in chapter twelve. I credited you as 'a reliable witness'. High praise, from me.
Can I tell you my deepest fear? That I'll finish, and nobody will read it. Or worse, they'll burn it again.
Books die in fires. Stories die in silence. I don't know which scares me more.
But I've started copying chapters for the tavern cook, the builder, the elder. Spread it thin, keep it alive.
There's one chapter left. The oldest one. The legends the first chroniclers wrote with trembling hands.
They speak of tall ones who walk between worlds. Dark and silent, with eyes like violet coals.
Look at them and they come for you. Leave them be and they carry stones from place to place.
My history is complete. Every page. I slept a whole night afterwards. First time in years.
You've read the first chapter of your journal? It's about you. You're part of history now.
Remember that terrible tea? I've improved it. Slightly. It's now merely bad.
I don't smell smoke in the mornings anymore. Only ink. That's a kind of healing, I think.
They can banish a person. They can burn paper. But they can't unwrite what's already been read.
Come back and tell me what you see out there. There's always another volume.
And do try to do something less heroic next time. The chapters are getting very long.
Don't make that face. Heroes always hate being written down. That's how I know I got it right.
The book is being copied by hand, village to village. The tavern cook says a trader asked for it by name.
Somewhere in the capital, I'm told, a student is reading it by candlelight in secret. Good.
The pearls are on my desk. I watch them some evenings. They seem to watch me back.
I wrote the last chapter with one of them beside the inkwell. It felt appropriate.
The children come by asking about the spirals under the well. I've started teaching again. Tuesdays.
Six students. Much smaller than the academy. Much better questions.
The elder asked me to record the village's founding. From living memory, while there's still time.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.epilo: The scholar's book is copied by hand from village to village. You appear in it, even if you'd rather not.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.stage: I need books to rewrite my work. Blank ones, used ones, it doesn't matter.
Pages! Glorious pages! I can write again.
The old texts speak of other settlements. Go and find another village; tell me what you see, every detail.
Just as the chronicles said... My memory hasn't failed me.
My last chapter is about the tall ones who walk between worlds. I need to study their pearls. Be careful.
My history is complete. Take this journal; the first chapter is about you. You're part of history now.
Did you know this village is built on older ruins? Nobody asks, nobody knows.
Ink, paper and time. That's all a scholar needs. And tea.
You have the eyes of someone who's seen a lot. Tell me about it one day; I'll write it down.
Knowledge is the only thing they can't banish.
hearthbound.persona.exiled_scholar.title: Exiled Scholar
hearthbound.persona.family_father.bio.0: I have three children and a roof that leaks. I work from dawn to dusk so none of them goes hungry.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.bio.1: My wife died the winter the river froze. Since then I am father and mother, and some nights I don't know if I'm doing it right.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.bio.2: My eldest wants to be a guard. I'm proud and terrified at the same time. I'd give anything to keep them safe.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.dialog: Mind the puddle by the door; the roof leaks there, and there, and there. I'll fix it when the day grows more hours.
The little one asked me where the stars go in the morning. I said they go to bed, like good children. She didn't believe me.
Harvest was poor this year. We'll manage... we always manage. That's what I keep telling myself, anyway.
The smith won't pay me for another ten days. I've counted the flour three times. It doesn't grow when you count it.
The children don't complain. That's the worst part. They say they're not hungry and stare at the empty pot.
Last night I gave Pip my crust and said I'd eaten on the way home. He's getting too clever for that lie.
I hate asking. But if you could bring bread, a dozen loaves, we'd reach payday. I'll repay you somehow, I swear.
I've got three: Tomas, the eldest, Pip in the middle, and Lina, who's almost seven and rules us all.
I work the fields at dawn, mend fences at noon and hammer nails for the smith by lamplight. A coin is a coin.
The children talk about you at every meal. Pip thinks you sleep up in the trees. I didn't dare ask.
Their mother used to sing while she kneaded dough. Since then the house has been too quiet for baking.
She died the winter the river froze. That whole season I couldn't get warm, no matter how much wood I burned.
Some nights I sit by the stove and wonder if I'm doing it right. Father and mother at once. Nobody teaches you both.
Tomas wants to be a guard. He practises with a broom handle. I'm proud of him and it scares me half to death.
Lina still sets out four spoons at supper sometimes. I don't correct her. I just put one back when she's not looking.
They ate until they fell asleep at the table, crumbs on their cheeks. I just sat and watched them. Thank you.
Lina hid a slice under her pillow for you. It's rather flat now, but she insists you must have it.
Lately the children won't sleep. They lie awake whispering. At first I thought it was ghost stories.
Then I heard it too. Scratching on the back wall after midnight. Slow. Patient. And that groaning.
The dead are coming down from the hills. I've counted shapes by the fence: five, six, more on some nights.
I sit up with the axe until dawn, then go straight to the fields. I can't keep it up much longer.
You fight better than any of us. Would you thin them out? Just enough that my children sleep through one night.
I'll tell you something I tell no one. The winter she died, I kept baking her bread. Badly. I burnt every loaf.
The children ate the burnt ones without a word. Tomas was nine. He said they tasted like hers. They didn't.
Her apron still hangs on the hook. I wore it once to cook. Pip laughed until he cried. So did I.
That year the river froze so thick you could walk across it. She went for water where the ice was thin.
I was at the smith's. A thousand times I've asked myself what would have happened if I'd gone instead.
Some nights I talk to her while I patch the roof. I tell her the children are fine. I hope I'm not lying.
Yesterday Tomas asked if you'd teach him to fight. I said no. Then maybe. Then I went for a long walk.
The house isn't much. But I built the cradle each of them slept in, and the table, and the benches. It's ours.
They slept straight through. All three in one bed, snoring like old dogs. First time in weeks. I owe you.
Tomas watched you from the window that night. Now he walks the fence every evening with his broom handle.
Since then I buy sweets at the market. She says thank you; she's polite. It's not the same, and she knows it.
She turns seven soon. Seven. Her mother always said seven is the year you stop being little.
I keep dreaming of the old kitchen, flour everywhere and her laughing. I wake up and the kitchen is cold.
I'm handy with a hammer and hopeless with an oven. My children deserve better than my sunken cakes.
Would you help me? A real cake for Lina's seventh. I want her to keep that tradition. I want her mother in that room.
I'll confess something: I was glad it was you out there and not him. And ashamed of being glad.
He'll be a guard, I know it. He has her stubbornness. When she decided something, the river itself moved aside.
I used to think keeping them safe meant keeping them close. Maybe it means teaching them to stand.
In the evenings I'm making something at the smith's. A shield. For the house, I tell myself. For the door.
Pip asked if his mother can see us. I said yes. He asked if she's cross about the roof. I said very.
Lina is the one I worry about. She was barely three. She doesn't remember her mother's face, only her cakes.
Every birthday her mother baked a honey cake with one candle on top, and let Lina lick the spoon.
The first birthday after, I tried. The cake sank in the middle like a boot print. Lina cried. So did I, outside.
She laughed. Did you hear it? Exactly like her mother. I had to step outside for a moment.
Lina wore frosting on her nose all evening and refused to wipe it off. 'It's the travellers' mark,' she said.
Remember when Pip thought you slept in trees? Now he swears you live in a cave with a dragon. I give up.
Payday still feels far away sometimes. But the pantry isn't empty, and nobody pretends not to be hungry.
If you ever need something mended, a hinge, a fence, a door, you come to me. That's what family is for.
There's always a seat for you at our table. Not a guest's seat, mind. The one by the stove, where she used to sit.
Go on, the road is calling you. Just come back for supper now and then. The children count the days.
That shield looks better on your arm than on my door. Keep it. You protect more homes than I ever will.
Did you see the drawings on your doorstep? That's you fighting the dead. The green blob is you, apparently.
Tomas trains with the real guards now. He comes home bruised and happy. I stand at the window every evening.
I've learned to bake. Proper bread. Pip says it's almost as good as the loaves you brought. Almost.
The house smells of fresh bread again. I didn't know how much I'd missed it until it came back.
I finally fixed the roof. Well, most of it. One leak is left. The children named it and won't let me touch it.
I talk to her less at night now. Not because I've forgotten. Because I have fewer worries to tell her.
Yesterday Lina set out five spoons at supper. One for her mother, and one for you. I left them both.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.epilog: The house smells of fresh bread again. The children leave you drawings on the doorstep, and their father greets you like one of the family.
The pantry is empty and payday is far away. Could you bring me some bread? The children won't complain, but I see it in their eyes.
They ate until they fell asleep at the table. Thank you, truly.
The dead roam near our house at night. The children hear them scratching at the walls and don't sleep. Please, thin them out.
Last night they slept straight through. First time in weeks. I owe you.
My youngest turns seven. Her mother always baked her a cake... I can't. Would you help me keep that tradition alive?
She laughed like her mother used to. Take this shield: I made it for the house, but you protect more homes than I do.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.talk.0: The little one asked me today where the stars go in the morning. I had no answer.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.talk.1: Harvest was poor this year... we'll manage. We always do.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.talk.2: You know, the children talk about you. "The traveller", they call you.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.talk.3: When they're asleep and the house is quiet, that's when I finally breathe.
hearthbound.persona.family_father.title: Family Man
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.bio.0: Four children, a husband who travels with the caravans and a garden that never stops asking for water.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.bio.1: People think I'm tough. I am. But when my husband is on the road I leave a candle in the window every night.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.bio.2: I was a weaver in the capital before I married. Sometimes I still dream of the looms.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.dialog: If you see a boy with scraped knees climbing the tower, that's Bran, my second. Tell him his mother is watching.
Four children, a garden that drinks like a thirsty ox, and a husband somewhere out on the caravan roads.
I sold my own loom to buy our first goat. I don't regret it. Most days.
Winter is coming early this year. I can smell it in the mornings, sharp, like cold iron.
Last night I pulled out the children's blankets. Threadbare. You could read a letter through Tob's.
I've patched them twice already. There's nothing left to patch; it's just holes holding hands.
If I had wool I could weave new ones, thick and proper. Would you bring me some? A dozen bundles would do.
Mara is the eldest, twelve and with my temper. Then Bran the climber, then Nell, who hums, and little Tob.
You always come back with mud up to your knees. Does anyone mend your clothes? No? Hm. We'll see about that.
Joren, my husband, drives caravans south. He's gone for months. Every time he returns the children have grown a finger.
He wrote! Three lines, but he wrote. 'Roads dry. Missing you. Buy salt.' That man, honestly.
People think I'm tough. I am. Somebody has to be, when the cart is gone and the well rope snaps.
But every night he's on the road, I leave a candle burning in the window. So he finds his way home. Silly, isn't it?
Before I married I was a weaver in the capital. Forty looms in one hall, clattering like a hailstorm.
I could weave swallows so fine you'd almost hear them sing. My hands still remember, even rough as they are now.
They'll sleep warm this winter. You should see Nell rolled up like a sausage in pastry. Thank you.
The weaving took me four nights. My fingers ached, but it felt like coming home.
Yesterday Tob came home crying, holding his arm. Two little red marks, swelling. A spider, near the old stumps.
He's fine now. I washed it with vinegar and he got honey on bread for being brave. But I didn't sleep a wink.
This morning I went to look. Webs everywhere between the trees, and eyes. Red ones. Far too many.
I'd take a broom to them myself, but somebody has to stay with four children who never listen.
Would you hunt them down? Half a dozen at least, so my little ones can play without me watching every leaf.
I'll tell you a secret. The first night Joren left, I didn't sleep. I sat by that candle until it drowned in wax.
I was young and new here. Nobody knew my name. That candle was the only company in the house.
Now the neighbours joke that my window is a lighthouse. Let them. Two lost caravans found the road by it last winter.
Mara asked why I never went back to the capital. I told her the capital had plenty of weavers and too few goats.
The truth? I was afraid of loving two things and losing both. So I chose one. And I'd choose it again.
Bran climbed the tower again, by the way. Came down with a pigeon stuck in his shirt. I didn't know whether to scold or laugh.
My husband's last letter had four lines. Four! He's getting sentimental out there on the road.
The children play at the edge of the woods, where the mushrooms grow. They know not to go any further. Mostly.
Tob is playing in the garden again as if nothing happened. A mother breathes easy, thanks to you.
Bran now tells everyone he killed the spiders himself. With a spoon. I let him keep the story.
I've tried cold cloths, willow bark, singing. The fever won't come down. It laughs at me.
My grandmother had a remedy for this. Honey and herbs, warm, spoon by spoon until morning.
I have the herbs. I have the pot and the patience. What I don't have is honey, not a single drop.
The bees are far from here, and I can't leave him. I won't. Not for anything in the world.
Please, hurry. Bring me honey, three bottles. I'll keep the candle and the fire going until you're back.
I've been thinking about the looms. I dreamt I was back in the great hall, and every thread was a colour of the sky.
Sometimes I wonder who I'd be if I'd stayed. A master weaver, perhaps, with soft hands and no mud on the floor.
Then Nell climbs into my lap and hums, and I know. I'd be poorer. Much poorer.
Do you know what frightens me most? Not the dead, not spiders. A fever in the night and no one to send for.
My mother used to say a mother has two hearts: one in her chest and one running about outside.
Joren's caravan is late. Only a week, but a week is long when you're the one lighting candles.
Tob has been coughing since yesterday. Just a little, I told myself. Children cough.
Tonight his forehead is hot as a bread oven. He says the ceiling is moving. He keeps asking for his father.
The fever broke at dawn. He woke up asking for pancakes, the little rascal. I cried into the batter.
Does the hood fit? I knitted it through the night while he slept. My hands needed something to do.
Your clothes are a disaster, as usual. Leave them here tomorrow. Don't argue; I've raised four, I win arguments.
Bran climbed the tower again yesterday. This time he waved at me from the top. I waved back. What else can you do?
People still think I'm tough. Good. I am. But I've learned it's all right to ask for help now and then.
You came when we needed you, three times. In this house that makes you family. No arguments there either.
Off you go, then. Mind the road, eat properly and come back with less mud. The candle will be in the window.
It has the swallow pattern from the capital. I hadn't woven it in fifteen years. My fingers found it anyway.
Joren came home three days later. He saw the hood on the peg and asked who I was knitting for. I told him everything.
He wants to shake your hand. Fair warning: he shakes hands like he's pumping water from a well.
There's soup on the stove. There's always soup on the stove now. If you walk past without a bowl, I'll know.
The children fight over who runs to greet you first. Mara usually wins. She cheats.
Tob says when he grows up he'll hunt spiders like you. Then he remembers the bite and says maybe crickets.
I bought a little loom at the market with the caravan money. Just a small one. It lives by the window.
I weave in the evenings now, beside the candle. It's still there for Joren. Maybe for you too.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.epilog: Her children run to greet you, and there is always a bowl of soup waiting for you in her kitchen.
Winter is coming and the children's blankets are threadbare. Bring me wool and I'll weave new ones.
They'll sleep warm this winter. Thank you, dear.
A spider bit my youngest while he was playing near the woods. He's fine, but there are more. Would you hunt them down?
He's playing in the garden again. A mother breathes easy thanks to you.
The little one has a fever that won't go down. Grandmother's remedy needs honey. Please, hurry.
The fever broke at dawn. I knitted you this hood through the night... it's the least I could do.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.talk.0: If you see my second son climbing the tower again, tell him his mother is watching.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.talk.1: Winter is coming and the blankets are thin... one thing at a time.
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.talk.2: You always come back with mud up to your knees. Do you have someone to mend your clothes?
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.talk.3: My husband wrote! Three lines, but he wrote. That man...
hearthbound.persona.family_mother.title: Mother of Four
hearthbound.persona.indebted_merchant.bi: I trade in everything: cloth, spices, rumours. Business is good. Well... it was.
A caravan lost in a storm. All my goods, and a loan from a very unforgiving guild in the next village.
If I don't pay by spring, they'll take the stall. It's been in my family for four generations.
hearthbound.persona.indebted_merchant.di: Welcome, welcome! Cloth, spices, rumours, all at fair prices. The rumours are free today.
Buying? Selling? Lending me a little something? Just kidding. Mostly. Somewhat.
A storm came down off the mountains. Carts, goods, the mule. Gone. The drivers lived, thank the sky.
To fill those carts I'd borrowed from the guild in the next village. They are not a forgiving guild.
They sent a letter. Very polite. Polite the way a knife is polite when it's still in the drawer.
They want a first payment in gold, and soon. I've counted twice. I'm short. Badly short.
I hate asking. Would you lend me the difference? I'll pay you back, I swear on this old counter.
You have an honest face. In my trade, that's rarer than gold, and I'd know.
This stall has four generations of elbows worn into the counter. Feel that groove? Great-grandmother.
I can tell a traveller's home by their boots. Yours say 'everywhere and nowhere'. Interesting.
Business was good. Very good. I had a caravan of my own, two carts and a stubborn mule.
Silk from the south, pepper from the coast. I used to smell of cinnamon all winter.
The shelves look thin, don't they? I tell people it's a new style. Elegant emptiness.
Numbers don't lie. They just keep me up at night, whispering in columns.
Last autumn I sent the caravan through the pass. Everyone said wait. I didn't wait.
You're a lifesaver. I've written it in the ledger, in red ink: I owe you. And I pay my debts.
The guild's rider took the gold and didn't even smile. I smiled enough for both of us.
I can't pay the rest by spring. Not in one piece. But with one more season, I could.
So I wrote them a letter. Nine drafts. I begged in the first. Threatened in the third. Burned both.
This one's honest. It asks for time and promises the rest. It's the best thing I've written.
But letters are easy to ignore. The guild respects people who show their face at the door.
My face owes them money. Yours doesn't. Would you take the letter to their village in person?
Now I can tell you the part I left out. If I don't pay it all by spring, they take the stall.
Four generations. Great-grandmother started with a blanket on the ground and a sack of salt.
Grandfather built the roof. Mother painted the sign. I... lost the caravan. Quite the legacy.
Some nights I sit here after closing and talk to the counter. It doesn't judge. Much.
I've sold my good coat, my silver buttons, the painted chest. Customers think I've gone simple.
Don't tell the tavern cook. I owe them for three suppers. They think I'm fasting for my health.
What eats me is that I knew. I knew the pass was dangerous. Pride sent that caravan, not sense.
Mother always said a merchant's first treasure is their word. The second is patience. I had neither.
One more season! They accepted! You have a way with people. I should hire you. I can't afford you.
What did you say to them? The rider came back almost cheerful. It unsettled everyone.
What's missing isn't gold anymore. The guild wants the last of it in emeralds. They trade in green.
Villagers pay in emeralds for good work. I have none to spare, and my work lately is mostly worry.
Just a few. A handful. That's all that stands between me and the rest of my life.
I promised I'd never ask you for anything again. I'm a merchant; I lie a little. Forgive me.
The final payment. A few emeralds and I'm free. Free! Will you help me one last time?
I've started trading small again. Wool, candles, gossip. Every coin goes into the red jar.
Do you know what I've learned? Customers come back for the talk, not the discount.
I used to think the stall was my family's. Now I think it's the village's. They just let us run it.
If I lose it, what do I tell the children who come for sweets on market day? Sorry, the numbers won?
I dream about the counter being carried off by guild clerks. It waves goodbye. Horrible dream.
When I'm free, I'll throw a feast. I've planned the menu. Twice. It helps me sleep.
You're invited, of course. Head of the table. Next to the tavern cook, so you eat well.
I've counted the jar every night. We're close. So close I can taste it, like copper on the tongue.
Free! Every morning I say it out loud before I open the shutters. Free!
The red ledger line with your name is still there. I crossed out 'owe'. I wrote 'friend'.
It says: 'Honest weights, honest words.' Took me four generations and one disaster to earn it.
I kept the old guild letter too. When I get proud, I read it and remember the knife in the drawer.
If you ever need anything, anything, come here first. I owe you more than coins.
Now then, a rumour for you, free of charge: there's a traveller everyone trusts. Guess who.
Go on, off you go. And come back soon. The counter misses your elbows.
Your prices are the best in the land, and they stay that way. Don't tell the other customers.
Well, they know. Everyone knows. Your discount is legendary. People try to borrow your face.
Did you enjoy the feast? The tavern cook outdid themself. The elder danced. I have witnesses.
I sang behind the counter yesterday and a customer paid double to make me stop. Good business.
The guild sent a note after the last payment. It said 'pleasure doing business'. I framed it.
I've bought a new mule. Grumpier than the old one. We understand each other.
No more caravans through the pass in storm season. I learned that one the expensive way.
Mother's sign got a fresh coat of paint. I added one small line underneath, in gold.
hearthbound.persona.indebted_merchant.ep: Out of debt, the merchant sings behind the counter. Your discount is legendary, and so is the feast they threw.
hearthbound.persona.indebted_merchant.st: The guild wants a first payment in gold. I'm short. Would you lend me the difference? I'll pay you back, I swear.
You're a lifesaver. I've written it down: I owe you, and I pay my debts.
I've written to the guild asking for more time. Take it to their village in person; they respect people who show their face.
They've accepted! One more season. You have a way with people.
Only the final payment is left. A few emeralds and I'm free. Free!
Free! Here, keep this. And from now on, you always get my best prices.
hearthbound.persona.indebted_merchant.ta: Buying? Selling? Lending me a little something? Just kidding. Mostly.
Numbers don't lie. They just keep me up at night.
You have an honest face. In my trade that's rarer than gold.
When I'm out of debt I'll throw a feast. You're invited, of course.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.bio.0: There's someone in the neighbouring village. We met at the harvest fair, danced once, and I haven't stopped thinking about it.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.bio.1: I've written forty letters. I've sent none. What if they don't remember me?
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.bio.2: My grandmother says love is like bread: if you don't knead it, it doesn't rise. I think she's right.
Do you think flowers are too much? Or too little? Don't answer. I'll overthink it either way.
I practised what I'm going to say. Out loud. To a goat. The goat left halfway through.
I've sent none. What if they don't remember me? What if that dance was just a dance to them?
My grandmother says love is like bread: if you don't knead it, it doesn't rise. I think she's right.
So I'm going to knead. I'm going to send one. The next one. Letter forty-one.
But a letter alone looks so bare. I want to send something with it. Something that says what I can't.
I want to send flowers with my letter. The prettiest ones. Would you help me pick them?
You've been to many places. Do they have fairs everywhere? With music and lanterns?
Someday I want a house with a garden, and someone to share the sunsets with. Is that too much to want?
Sorry, I'm staring at the road again. It goes east. East is... never mind.
Last autumn, at the harvest fair in the neighbouring village, there was a dance under the lanterns.
I don't dance. I have two left feet and both of them are shy. But someone held out a hand.
We danced once. One song. They laughed when I stepped on their toe and didn't let go of my hand.
They smelled of apples and woodsmoke. I haven't stopped thinking about it. Not for one day.
I've written forty letters since. Forty! They're in a box under my bed, tied with string.
They're perfect. Look at the colours. Now I just need the courage. Courage doesn't grow in meadows.
Thank you. I pressed one between the pages of my diary. For luck. Or for the memory, if it goes badly.
But the flowers you brought made something clear. I can't keep kneading dough nobody bakes.
So here it is. Letter forty-one. Short, true, with a pressed flower inside. Sealed with wax.
I can't carry it myself. I'd get to their door and turn around. I know myself. I'd bolt like a rabbit.
They respect people who come in person, I've heard. And you're braver than me by a mile.
Take it to their village. Please, before I change my mind! Go, go, go!
Can I read you something? Letter twelve. No, don't laugh. Fine, laugh. It rhymes 'heart' with 'cart'.
The early letters were terrible. Poems. Long ones. Letter nine was eleven pages about their eyebrows.
The later ones got shorter. Honest. Letter thirty just said 'I think of you when it rains.'
Grandmother caught me writing last night. She didn't tease. She told me about grandfather.
He courted her for two years with bread. A loaf every Sunday. She married him for the rye.
She says she'd have married him for the first loaf, but he didn't need to know that.
What stops me isn't them. It's me. I'm afraid of being the person who wanted more than one dance.
At night I imagine every answer. Yes. No. Who? The 'who' is the worst one.
They wrote back! They remember the dance! They remember! I've read it so often the paper's gone soft.
They said they looked for me at the fair the next morning. The next morning! I'd already left.
I'm going to ask. I'm really going to ask. Saying it out loud makes my knees go soft.
But a question like that needs something in your hand. Something that says 'forever' without words.
I've saved enough for the gold band. The smith will forge it. But a ring needs a stone.
A diamond. Just one. It's the only thing hard enough to last as long as I mean it to.
I need a ring, and a ring needs a diamond. Will you help me one last time?
They kept the ribbon I dropped. I didn't even know I'd dropped a ribbon.
We've written every week since. Their letters smell of apples. I sleep with them under my pillow. Don't tell.
Last week they visited. We walked by the mill. I didn't step on anyone's toes. Progress.
Grandmother met them. She gave them bread. Then she winked at me. I nearly fainted.
Can I tell you my fear now? It's not that they'll say no. It's that I'll ask badly.
I want it to be right. Not grand. Just right. A garden, a sunset, a question.
I've built a bench behind the house. Facing west. It's crooked. I'm hoping they won't notice.
The builder offered to straighten it. I said no. I want every crooked bit to be mine.
They said yes! Yes! I still wake up and say it to the ceiling. Yes!
The wedding was the talk of both villages. Two fiddlers, three pies, one very confused goat.
The diamond catches the sunset every evening. Your diamond, really. We call it 'the traveller's stone'.
If you ever want a quiet sunset, there's room on the bench. It's crooked, but it's sturdy.
I used to think courage was something you're born with. Turns out a friend can lend you some.
Next year's harvest fair, we're going back. We'll dance under the same lanterns. You should come.
Thank you. For the flowers, the letter, the ring. For the house with the garden I only used to dream of.
You sat at the head of the table, like I promised. You ate like someone who'd earned it.
I stepped on their toe during the first dance. On purpose, this time. For old times' sake.
Now there's a house with a garden, and every sunset there are two chairs outside. Well, the crooked bench.
They noticed it's crooked. They said they love it. I think that's what love is, mostly.
Grandmother says the bread has risen. She says it every time she sees us. Every single time.
The box of forty letters? I gave it to them. They read all forty. Even the eyebrow one.
They laughed so hard at letter nine they had to sit down. Then they kept it. Framed it, actually.
The goat I practised on came to the wedding. It still left halfway through. Some things don't change.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.epilogue: The wedding was the talk of both villages. Now there's a house with a garden, and every sunset there are two chairs outside.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.stage.0.ask: I want to send flowers with my letter. The prettiest ones. Would you help me pick them?
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.stage.0.don: They're perfect. Now I just need the courage.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.stage.1.ask: Here it is. Letter forty-one, the one I'm finally sending. Take it to their village. Please, before I change my mind!
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.stage.1.don: They... wrote back? They remember the dance! They remember!
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.stage.2.ask: I'm going to ask. I'm really going to ask. But I need a ring, and a ring needs a diamond.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.stage.2.don: They said yes! YES! You'll be at the wedding, and you'll sit at the head of the table.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.talk.0: Do you think flowers are too much? Or too little?
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.talk.1: I practised what I'm going to say. Out loud. To a goat.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.talk.2: You've been to many places. Do they have fairs everywhere?
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.talk.3: Someday I want a house with a garden, and someone to share the sunsets with.
hearthbound.persona.lovelorn.title: Lovesick Heart
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.bio.0: I was a lazy street kid until a stranger sent me into a cave for an old lamp. I rubbed it to clean it, and something answered.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.bio.1: I've made two wishes and wasted neither. The third I've saved for years, because I know exactly who deserves it, and it isn't me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.dialogu: Hello! Mind the basket, it's full of figs. Take one. Taking things when they're offered is fine. It's the other kind of taking that gets you in trouble.
Don't rub anything shiny you find in a cave. Trust me on this. Just don't.
Three days in the dark. I was dusty, starving, and the lamp was filthy, so I rubbed it to see it better. Something answered.
I won't tell you yet what answered. Just that it was very large, very polite, and it called me 'master'. I hated that word at once.
The cave where I found it has a second chamber. I saw a doorway in the rock that night, but I never dared go in.
It's been nagging at me for years. What if there's something in there that explains the lamp? Or frees it?
I need light first, lots of it. Would you bring me torches, a good bundle? I'm done fumbling in the dark.
My mother still thinks I found our money in a ditch. Let her. It's a nicer story for her than the true one.
I used to be the laziest kid in the market. I'd sleep in doorways and wake up only for food and trouble.
You see that old lamp on my shelf? Don't look at it too long. It gets shy. Well. Something does.
One day a stranger in a fine cloak called me 'nephew' and bought me sweets. I'd never met him. I ate the sweets anyway.
He took me out beyond the hills to a crack in the ground, lit a fire, spoke some words, and the earth opened.
He said: go down, touch nothing, bring me the old lamp at the end. I was small enough to fit. That's why he chose me.
The cave was full of trees whose fruit were jewels. Red, green, clear as water. I filled my pockets anyway.
At the top he wanted the lamp before he'd help me out. I said help me out first. He got angry and sealed me in.
Enough light to see the walls sparkle. I'd forgotten how beautiful it was down there. And how cold.
Now I can tell you properly. What answered the lamp was a spirit, bound to it for longer than any kingdom has stood.
Everyone wants three wishes. Nobody asks what the one granting them would wish for. I asked, once. It went very quiet.
Anyway. The second chamber. When I took your torches in, I heard scratching, and saw a lot of small red eyes.
Little poisonous spiders, nesting in every crack, like they're guarding something. One bit my boot clean through.
I'm not a fighter. The spirit could deal with them, but I won't waste a wish on spiders. That would be an insult to it.
Could you clear them out for me? Eight or so should do. Then I'll go deeper, with you watching my back.
It said it would grant what I asked. I asked to go home. Poof. There I was, in my mother's kitchen, covered in cave dust.
My first real wish came that winter, when we had nothing. I asked for bread and a warm roof. Nothing more.
The spirit looked at me strangely. It told me most people ask for palaces on the first try. I said we only needed bread.
My second wish was when my mother caught the fever. I didn't even think. I just rubbed and said, 'Make her well.'
She woke up hungry and cross, asking why I was crying. I've never been so happy to be scolded.
Two wishes, and I've wasted neither. The storytellers say I asked for a palace and a princess. They love a palace.
The third wish I've kept for years. I know exactly who deserves it. It isn't me. I'll tell you who, another time.
Some nights the lamp hums, as if someone inside were humming along to the rain. I hum back. It's our little talk.
The chamber was empty but for an old ring. Look: it's plain iron, scratched with the same signs as the lamp.
Treasure is never where you expect. I went in hoping for gold and came out with a clue. A better treasure.
The storytellers say this happened in the old tale too, with a wicked sorcerer. Maybe pedlars never change.
I ran to find him. He'd already heard the lamp hum. He knows it's something. But he's a trader first, not a sorcerer.
He'll trade it back, he says, for three fine lanterns. Not torches, lanterns. Proper ones, iron and glass.
I don't dare think of what he could wish for if he ever rubs it. Or what the spirit would have to do.
Please, bring me three lanterns, quickly. I'll give him lamps for old, and more, and never let it out of my sight again.
The signs on the ring are a binding, I think. Whoever made the lamp made this too. A lock, and its key's cousin.
Here's my secret: the spirit is tired. Centuries of 'master'. Palaces, armies, curses, for anyone who found the lamp.
It told me once that it can't remember the sky. Only the inside of the lamp and the faces of whoever rubs it.
That's who my third wish is for. It deserves to walk out. Not as a servant. Just out, into the square, into the sun.
My fear is that I'll hesitate. That some day I'll be hungry or scared and use the last wish on myself.
So I've been careful. Too careful, maybe. And while I was being careful, I made a very stupid mistake.
A pedlar came by the house last week shouting, 'New lamps for old! New lamps for old!' My family heard.
They thought they were doing me a favour. They traded my dusty old lamp for a shiny new one. Beaming, they showed me.
It's back. And that very night I said the third wish out loud: the one inside gets to walk out. And it did.
It came out slowly, rubbing its eyes like a child after a long nap. Then it looked up at the sky for an hour.
Like you. You brought torches and lanterns and cleared spiders, and never asked for a wish. Why not? Don't answer. I know.
My friend at the well asked me what I'd wish for, if it could still grant one. I said: nothing, I'm fine. It laughed for a minute.
Some nights I still hear humming in the rain. Now it comes from the well, and it's a new song.
If you ever find a lamp in a cave, bring it here. We'll open it together, gently, and ask what the one inside wants.
Go on, then. Take a fig for the road. Taking what's offered is fine. You've earned it, and nobody's sealing you in.
The first thing it said, free, was, 'It's much bigger than I remembered.' I think it meant everything.
Now an ordinary lamp burns in the square. Just oil and a wick. I lit it myself. It doesn't answer, and I love that.
Have you met the stranger at the well? Very old smile, draws water for the children every morning. That's my friend.
It chose to help at the well. It says carrying water is the first thing it's done in centuries because it wanted to.
My mother adores it. She thinks it's a cousin from the south. Let her. It's a nicer story for her.
The pedlar comes by now and then. He keeps offering me new lamps for old. I tell him I'm out of old lamps.
I kept the iron ring from the chamber. It does nothing. I wear it to remember that the best treasure was a clue.
I have no wishes left. It's wonderful. When I want something now, I have to work for it, or ask a friend.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.epilogu: Now an ordinary lamp burns in the square, and a stranger with a very old smile helps the children draw water every morning.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.source: The Thousand and One Nights — Anonymous (c. 9th–14th century)
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.stage.0: The cave where I found the lamp has a second chamber I never dared enter. I need torches, plenty of them.
Enough light to see the walls sparkle. I'd forgotten how beautiful it was.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.stage.1: Small poisonous things nest in that chamber, as if guarding it. Clear them out before I go any deeper.
The chamber was empty but for an old ring. Treasure is never where you expect.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.stage.2: A pedlar tricked my family: new lamps for old, he shouted, and they gave him mine. He'll trade it back for three fine lanterns.
It's back. And now I know what my third wish is: the one inside gets to walk out.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.talk.0: Don't rub anything shiny you find in a cave. Trust me on this.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.talk.1: My mother still thinks I found our money in a ditch. Let her.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.talk.2: Some nights the lamp hums, as if someone inside were humming along to the rain.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.talk.3: Everyone wants three wishes. Nobody asks what the one granting them would wish for.
hearthbound.persona.myth_aladdin.title: New lamps for old
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.bio.0: I was chopping wood when forty riders stopped at a cliff and spoke two words. The rock opened. I learned the words by heart.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.bio.1: I took a little gold, just enough. My greedy cousin took too much and forgot the words to get out. I still dream of that rock closing.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.dialog: Firewood's cheap today. Words, on the other hand, can be very expensive. Remember I said that.
Three donkeys, one axe, and a back that creaks like a cart. That's my whole fortune. Officially.
I waited until the dust settled. Then I climbed down, stood in front of that cliff, and said the two words myself.
