I won't repeat them. Not even whispered. There are some doors you shouldn't know how to open.
Some doors are better left closed, even the ones that open when you ask nicely. I learned that too late.
Lately I miss the simple days. Just wood, sweat, and a donkey that doesn't care what I know.
Would you help me be a plain woodcutter again, for one day? Bring me logs, and let's pretend I never heard anything.
Never shout at a cliff. You don't know who's listening, or what might answer.
The servant girl next door, Morgiana, is the cleverest person in the village. Don't tell the mayor. He thinks it's him.
She saved my life once with a jar of hot oil. Don't ask. Well, ask later. Not before lunch.
I used to cut wood in the hills every day. Up at dawn, down at dusk, a donkey load of pine to sell for bread.
One day I heard hooves. Dozens. I climbed a tree with my axe and hid among the needles, shaking like a leaf myself.
Forty riders. I counted twice. Hard faces, heavy saddlebags. They stopped at the foot of a bare cliff.
Their captain stepped forward and said two words to the rock. Just two. And the rock opened like a door.
They carried their bags inside. Later they came out with empty bags, the captain spoke again, and the rock closed.
Honest wood, honestly stacked. My back hurts in the most wonderful way. That's the pain of a simple life.
You deserve the rest of the story. Inside the cliff, there was a cave full of silks, carpets, and gold in heaps.
The riders found their cave lighter by one cousin's worth of gold. They knew somebody else knew.
Now strangers walk through the village at night. Morning comes and there are chalk marks on certain doors.
Morgiana noticed first. She chalked every door in the street the same way, so they couldn't tell which was mine.
Their scouts are around the houses now. Chalk in their pockets, crossbows on their backs. Clever, patient, cruel.
Deal with them for me, before they find my door. Six of their scouts should make the rest think twice.
I took a little gold. Just enough for my donkeys' saddlebags. Enough to stop my family worrying about winter.
My cousin noticed. He's the rich one in the family, or was. He measured my coins with a cup and saw gold stuck to it.
He made me tell him everything. The cliff, the words, the cave. I told him. I've regretted it every day since.
He went with ten mules. He said the words, the rock opened, he went in, and he filled every sack he could carry.
But the greed made him forget. When he turned to leave, he couldn't remember the words. He tried every grain but the right one.
Barley, wheat, millet. He shouted them all at the rock. The riders came back and found him there.
I still dream of that rock closing. And of his voice inside, calling out the wrong grains.
We buried him quietly. A tailor sewed him together blindfolded. That's a story for a darker evening.
They're gone. I've rubbed the chalk off every door in the street anyway, just in case. My sleeves are white for days.
The baker thinks I've gone mad, scrubbing his door at midnight. I told him it was a new custom. He now scrubs it himself.
I haven't gone. I won't. But I understand my cousin better every year, and that frightens me.
The captain has gathered new men. Big ones, with axes, the kind that break doors instead of marking them.
He's out there in the hills, and he'll come himself this time. He knows my face, and my house, and my street.
I can't fight him. I cut wood; I don't cut men. And I won't let Morgiana carry this again. She's done enough.
Please, end this. Stop the captain's axemen, three of the worst, so nobody else has to hide in a jar.
Now the jar of hot oil. The captain came to my house once, dressed as an oil merchant, with forty great jars on mules.
One jar held oil. The other thirty-nine held his men, waiting for his signal. He asked for a bed for the night, and I gave it.
Morgiana went to fill a lamp and heard a jar whisper, 'Is it time?' She didn't scream. She boiled oil instead.
I slept through it all. In the morning she showed me the jars. I have never felt so foolish and so grateful at once.
The captain escaped over the wall that night. He never forgets a face. I don't think he forgives one either.
That's my deepest fear: not for me, but for Morgiana, and the children on this street. He'll come back for all of us.
I dream of a morning when nobody has to hide in a jar, nobody boils oil, and I can say 'good day' without flinching.
My other secret: sometimes I still want to go back to that cliff. Just to look. That's how greed starts, with 'just to look'.
It's over. I'll never say those two words again. I'm already forgetting them... on purpose. Mostly.
The cave stays closed now. I walked past the cliff yesterday gathering pine. Just a cliff. Moss, birds, silence.
I learned something through all this: gold is heavy, but a secret is heavier. Only friends make it lighter.
You carried a lot of mine. Chalk, jars, axes, and a donkey-load of logs. I don't know how to repay that.
Actually, I do. Firewood, all winter, free. Words are expensive, but wood from a friend costs nothing.
If you ever stand in front of a cliff that listens, walk away. And if you can't, come find me. I'll forget the words with you.
Go on, then. The hills are quiet, the doors are clean, and I've got honest wood to split. Come back for supper.
Morgiana is free now. I paid her way, and she chose to stay as a friend and partner. She runs my accounts. Much better.
She sends her regards, by the way. She said anyone who clears thieves is welcome to dinner, but please, no jars.
My donkeys are fat and happy. So am I. Well, happy. The fat is mostly the donkeys.
Someone at the market said 'sesame' yesterday. I dropped a whole bundle of wood. They thought I'd tripped.
Don't look at me like that. I'm smiling because of the bread with seeds on top. Nothing else.
Remember the logs you brought, the first favour? I still have one. I carved a little donkey from it. Here, it's for you.
I think of my cousin often. I leave a cup of barley on the cliff each year. He'd have hated the joke. I think he'd laugh now.
The children play 'forty thieves' in the lanes. Morgiana always wins. They argue about who gets to be her.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.epilog: Since then the cave has stayed closed. The woodcutter swears the words are forgotten, but smiles oddly whenever someone says 'sesame'.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.source: The Thousand and One Nights — Anonymous (c. 9th–14th century)
Let me go back to being a simple woodcutter for a day. Bring me logs, and let's pretend I never heard anything.
Honest wood, honestly stacked. My back hurts in the most wonderful way.
The forty have noticed their gold is lighter. Their scouts mark doors with chalk at night. Deal with them before they find mine.
They're gone, and I've rubbed chalk marks off every door in the street, just in case.
Their captain is still out there, and he never forgets a face. Please, end this, so nobody else has to hide in a jar.
It's over. I'll never say those two words again. I'm already forgetting them... on purpose.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.talk.0: Firewood's cheap today. Words, on the other hand, can be very expensive.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.talk.1: Never shout at a cliff. You don't know who's listening.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.talk.2: The servant girl next door saved my life with a jar of hot oil. Don't ask.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.talk.3: Some doors are better left closed. Even the ones that open when you ask nicely.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ali_baba.title: Two words to a rock
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.bio.0: A storm threw me onto an island with nobody on it. I lived there twenty-eight years. I carved one notch on a post for every day.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.bio.1: I learned to grow barley, bake clay and talk to a parrot. The hardest part wasn't hunger. It was the day I found a footprint that wasn't mine.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.dialogue: Oh. Hello. Sorry, I don't talk to many people. I'm out of practice. Is this how it's done?
Never waste a nail. You don't know how long it has to last.
I lived on that island for twenty-eight years. Twenty-eight. That's a lot of notches.
The first thing I built was a wall. A double row of stakes, with a ladder I pulled in after me.
I didn't come out for months. Not because anything was there. Because anything might have been.
Now I'm here, among people, and I still can't sleep without a wall around me. I know it's silly.
Bring me logs, and I'll build a fence around my garden? I know it's silly. Please don't laugh.
I still count days. Old habits. Today is day eleven thousand and something.
People complain the village is too quiet. They have no idea what quiet sounds like.
You're the first person who's come back a second time. I noticed. I notice everything.
Years ago I went to sea against my father's wishes. He said I'd regret it. He was right, for a while.
A storm broke our ship on a reef. Everyone drowned but me. I crawled onto a beach with nobody on it.
The first night I slept in a tree, with a knife, too frightened to close my eyes.
I swam back to the wreck twelve times for tools, rope, bread, gunpowder. I even took the ship's cat.
I cut a post and carved a notch on it for every day. Every Sunday a longer one. So I wouldn't lose time.
A fence around my garden. I slept like a stone. Thank you for not laughing.
The neighbours think I'm keeping chickens in there. There's just me and some very safe cabbages.
I'd prayed for company for fifteen years. When it came, I was terrified of it. People are strange.
Last week, by the river, I found another strange footprint. Bare, broad, heading east.
Last time, it changed my life. I don't know if I want my life changed again. I think I do.
I can't follow it. My knees, my nerve. But you walk far. You could see where it leads.
Follow the trail and find where it leads? I need to know who left it. Before I hide again.
You've earned the rest of the island. Let me tell you how I learned to live, and not just survive.
A few spilled grains of barley sprouted by my wall. I thought it was a miracle. It was just luck.
I saved every grain for four years before I dared bake a single loaf. The best bread of my life.
I baked clay pots in a fire. The first ten cracked. The eleventh held water. I cried over a pot.
I taught a parrot to say my name. For years it was the only voice that said it.
I'd sit on the rocks at sunset, and it would say my name, and I'd answer. Silly. Necessary.
Then, one day, after fifteen years alone, I found it. A single footprint in the sand. Not mine.
The hardest part wasn't hunger. It was that day. I ran home and didn't come out for three days.
A whole village! And they want to trade! I'd forgotten how that feels.
They sent a basket of apples. I've eaten one a day. I carved a notch for each apple. Habit.
I realised it last week, with the apples. I was counting them instead of tasting them.
My deepest fear? That I'll die still counting. That I'll reach the end with a post, not a life.
I want to stop carving. But I can't just stop. My hands need something else to trust.
If something counted the hours for me, ticking away quietly, maybe I could let the days go.
Bring me a clock? So the days count themselves, and I can finally live them. I want to stop counting.
Now I'll tell you about my friend on the island. The footprint led to him, eventually.
He'd escaped from people who'd have killed him. I helped him. He stayed. For years.
A friend of mine on the island never learned my language fully. We understood each other perfectly.
He taught me which fruits were safe and how to paddle a canoe. I taught him bread and bad jokes.
When the ship finally came, he came home with me. He'd have hated this cold. He'd have loved you.
I never told anyone this: when I left the island, I took the notched post with me.
It's in my shed. Twenty-eight years of days, cut into wood. I still add a notch every night.
I've counted every day of my life for so long that I've forgotten how to just live one.
It ticks. I've burned my post. Keep my hoe; it dug an island into a farm.
I burned it at night, by the river. It smelled of salt, even after all these years.
Remember the footprint? I met the one who left it. A shepherd. Broad feet. Terrible singer.
I think my friend from the island would have liked it here. I think he'd have liked the shepherd.
People still complain the village is too quiet. I just smile and listen to it being full.
You walked where I couldn't, and brought me back a whole village. I'll never have enough notches for that.
Go on, then. Walk your road. My gate's open. The post is waiting for its next notch.
There's a new post by the door. It only gets a notch on the days you come to visit.
It has quite a few notches already. Don't let that go to your head.
I traded cabbages with the far village. They sent me seeds I've never seen. Round, purple, very rude.
My fence has a gate now. It's open most days. I only close it when the wind is wrong.
The children come to hear about the island. They always ask about the parrot. Never about the storm.
I've taught the miller's parrot my name. Now the whole village knows it. Shouted, mostly.
I don't know what day it is anymore. It's wonderful. I asked the baker yesterday. She laughed at me.
The clock sits on my shelf, ticking. Sometimes I forget it's there. That's the whole point.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.epilogue: Now there's a new post by the door, and it only gets a notch on the days the traveller comes to visit.
I can't sleep without a wall around me. Bring me logs and I'll build a fence; I know it's silly.
A fence around my garden. I slept like a stone. Thank you for not laughing.
I found a strange footprint by the river. Last time, it changed my life. Follow the trail and find where it leads.
A whole village! And they want to trade! I'd forgotten how that feels.
I want to stop carving notches. Bring me a clock, so the days count themselves and I can finally live them.
It ticks. I've burnt my post. Take my hoe; it dug an island into a farm.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.talk.0: Never waste a nail. You don't know how long it has to last.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.talk.1: I still count days. Old habits. Today is day eleven thousand and something.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.talk.2: A friend of mine on the island never learned my language fully. We understood each other perfectly.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.talk.3: People complain the village is too quiet. They have no idea what quiet sounds like.
hearthbound.persona.myth_crusoe.title: Twenty-eight years of notches
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.bio.0: I built a maze so clever that even I got lost in it. Then a king locked me in a tower so I'd never build another one for anyone else.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.bio.1: I made wings of feathers and wax to escape with my son. I told him not to fly too high. I built everything perfectly except his patience.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.dialog: Mind the plumb line. Everything in this village leans a little to the left. It drives me mad.
Every wall should have a door. I learned that the hard way.
I wasn't alone in that tower. My son was with me. He was very young and very loud.
He'd run up and down the stairs all day. I'd shout at him to stop. I'd give anything to shout again.
Lately the children here have been playing among the ruins of the old wall. Hiding, getting lost.
It gave me an idea. I want to build a maze again. A small one. But this time, with a way out.
Bring me stone bricks? Lots. I want to build a maze the children can play in, and always escape.
Measure twice, cut once, fly never.
I redesigned the baker's oven. Now it bakes in half the time. She still complains about the chimney.
You look at buildings the way I do. Top first, then the joints. I like that in a person.
Long ago I worked for a king on an island. He paid well. Kings always do, at first.
He asked me to build a prison for something terrible. I built a maze instead. My masterpiece.
Corridors that folded into themselves, doors that led to doors. I got lost in it myself, testing it.
I was proud. Too proud. I never asked who would be walking those corridors in the dark.
Afterwards the king locked me in a tall tower so I'd never build another one for anyone else.
Walls rising, and this time I drew the exit first. That's the whole secret. Always the exit first.
The children have already found three shortcuts I didn't design. I'm furious and very proud.
He laughed the whole way up. I still hear it when the wind hits the eaves.
And then he went higher. And higher. I called his name until my voice was gone.
I saw feathers on the water. Only feathers. I buried him on an island that carries his name.
I've spent years asking what I got wrong. The wax? The feathers? The words I chose?
Bring me honeycomb, please. I want to understand the wax. I want to know where I went wrong.
Now, the tower. You've been patient. Let me tell you how we got out.
Birds would land on the windowsill every morning. My son fed them crumbs. I watched their wings.
I collected every feather that fell. Big ones, small ones. I sorted them by length, like pan pipes.
I stitched the big ones with thread and fixed the small ones with wax. My son played with the wax.
He'd press his thumb into it and ruin my work. I let him. He laughed the whole time.
When the wings were ready, I strapped his on first. I told him: not too low, the sea spray will soak them.
And not too high. The sun will melt the wax. Follow me. Stay in the middle.
We flew. Over the sea, past the islands. Fishermen looked up and thought we were gods.
Good wax, soft and honest. It isn't the wax's fault. It never was.
I melted it and cooled it, a hundred times. It held exactly as long as it should have. I built well.
The night fliers have wings that never melt, never tear. Grey, papery, stronger than they look.
If I line a frame with them, the sun can shine on it all day. Nothing will drip. Nothing will fall.
I'm not building them to use them. I'm building them because I didn't, back then, build them right.
It's the last thing I owe him. Then I can put the tools down, maybe, for a while.
Bring me their membranes? I'm building one last pair, and this time, they won't fail.
That's the hardest thing to learn. My work was perfect. It was never going to be enough.
I built everything perfectly except his patience. You can't build that into a boy. You can only wait.
I'm the best builder alive, and I'd trade every stone I've laid for one more afternoon with him.
There's another secret. Before him, I had an apprentice. My nephew. Brilliant, better than me.
He invented the saw from a fish's spine. I was jealous. Something happened on a high roof.
The old tales say he fell, and the gods turned him into a partridge that never flies high.
I think about that bird often. Whatever the gods do, they have a very cruel sense of rhyme.
I don't want to fly again. But I owe my son one pair of wings that doesn't fail.
They're perfect. I'll never wear them. Keep my pick; I've finished building the one thing I owed him.
The wings hang over the maze's exit now. Every child who finds the way out gets to touch them once.
I've started teaching the baker's girl to build. She draws the doors first. Always the doors first.
If you ever build something, anything, draw the way out before you draw the walls.
You carried stone and wax and night-wings for a grieving old builder. That's a bridge, friend.
I built many famous things. The one I'm proudest of is the little gap in the hedge that leads out.
Go on, then. Wherever you go, find the exit first. And come back through the front door.
They touch them gently, like a sleeping animal. Not one has asked to try them on. Not yet.
The maze has become the most popular place in the village. The mayor wants a second one. I said no.
One maze with an exit is a gift. Two is showing off. I've done enough of that for one life.
A partridge nests near the maze now. It never flies high. I leave crumbs for it, like he did.
Remember when I measured your boots for the corridor width? The children still call it 'the traveller size'.
I stopped measuring everything twice. Now I only measure most things twice. Progress.
At night I sit by the exit and listen to the wind in the wing membranes. It sounds like breathing.
I don't hear him laughing only in the eaves now. I hear him in the maze, in every child.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.epilog: Now the wings hang over the maze's exit, and every child who finds the way out gets to touch them once.
I want to build a maze again, but one with a way out, for the children to play in. Bring me stone bricks.
Walls rising, and this time I drew the exit first. That's the whole secret.
My old wings failed because the wax melted in the sun. Bring me honeycomb; I want to understand where I went wrong.
Good wax, soft and honest. It isn't the wax's fault. It never was.
The night fliers have wings that never melt. Bring me their membranes. I'm building one last pair, and it won't fail.
They're perfect. I'll never wear them. Take my pick; I've finished building the one thing I owed him.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.talk.0: Every wall should have a door. I learned that the hard way.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.talk.1: Measure twice, cut once, fly never.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.talk.2: My son laughed the whole way up. I still hear it when the wind hits the eaves.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.talk.3: I'm the best builder alive, and I'd trade every stone I've laid for one more afternoon with him.
hearthbound.persona.myth_daedalus.title: Wings of wax and regret
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.bio.0: I have eaten breakfast at the same minute every day for twenty years. At the tavern I bet my fortune that I could go around the whole realm in eighty days.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.bio.1: I never cared for the sights. I cared for the timetable. Then, halfway, I rescued someone from a pyre, and the timetable stopped mattering.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.dialogue.0: Good day. You arrived at seventeen past nine. I note these things; it isn't rudeness, merely habit.
My tea is poured at eight, my toast buttered at eight and two. Twenty years without a single deviation.
Something troubles me, and I must confess it plainly: my clock stopped during the voyage. Salt water, I suspect.
Without it I wake at odd minutes. Yesterday I ate breakfast at eight and six. Six! I barely slept afterwards.
I've tried counting heartbeats instead. It works until someone surprises me, and then the whole day slips.
I need a proper clock, made of gold and redstone, the kind that follows the sun. I haven't the hands for such work.
Would you bring me a new clock? I'll set it by the sun at noon, and my heart will thank you to the second.
People call me cold. I prefer the word 'punctual'. It sounds warmer, somehow.
My valet sings in the mornings. Off-key and never on time. I keep him anyway, which should tell you something.
Have you heard the old tale of Phileas Fogg, who circled the world on a wager? I found him far too relaxed.
I once made a wager of my own, at a tavern table, over cards. My entire fortune on eighty days around the realm.
The other players laughed. I simply checked my watch and said the next coach left in forty minutes.
I crossed rivers on elephants, rode sledges pushed by the wind, and slept very little. Every hour was written down in advance.
I never looked out of the windows. The scenery was not on the schedule.
Then, halfway along, I saw a pyre being lit, and someone tied upon it. My notebook had no page for that.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.dialogue.1: Tick, tick. Do you hear it? Precise to the minute. My pulse has slowed to a most agreeable pace.
I set it at noon exactly, standing in the square with my shadow at its shortest. The children thought I'd gone mad.
Some mornings I wonder why I made that bet at all. To prove something? To whom? The card players have forgotten.
Perhaps I wanted, just once, to see whether a life measured to the minute could also be a good one.
There is a clause in the wager, you see. The route must pass through a village I've never set foot in.
I know every village on my charts. That's the trouble: I've visited them all, and the clock keeps running.
Would you ride ahead and find me a village I've never seen? Quickly, please. Every hour is already spoken for.
Now let me tell you properly about the wager. Twenty thousand in gold, half my fortune; the other half for the journey.
If I arrived one minute late, I'd be a pauper. I told no one how little I would have left.
My valet joined me on the very morning I hired him. He'd hoped for a quiet master. Poor fellow.
A detective followed us for half the voyage, certain I'd robbed a bank. I paid his fare more than once. He never thanked me.
I bought an elephant when the road ended. Absurdly expensive. My valet named it; I pretended not to hear.
Honestly? At night I did sums in the dark. Days left, miles left. The numbers never let me sleep.
I told everyone I was calm. My hands were calm. Inside, a thousand clocks were striking at once.
Once a ship left without us because my valet overslept. I didn't scold him. I simply hired another ship.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.dialogue.2: Found, charted and ahead of schedule! You'd make a splendid valet. Mine is jealous; he's sulking in the pantry.
I promised to tell you about the pyre. I haven't told it aloud in years. Forgive me if my voice slows.
She's waiting in the village where the bet was made. I told her I'd come when it was over. Win or lose.
But if I lose, I'll have nothing to offer her except a very accurate clock and an unpaid valet.
The wager ends tonight, when the tavern clock strikes. My card players will be sitting there, smirking.
I've written a letter declaring my arrival. If it reaches their table before the chime, the bet stands.
Carry it for me, please, faster than I can walk. I'll follow as quickly as these old legs allow.
They were going to burn a young widow beside her husband's body. The drums were so loud I couldn't hear my watch.
My valet dressed as the dead man and sat up in the smoke. The crowd screamed. We carried her off before dawn.
It cost me a day and an elephant. I wrote it in my notebook as 'unavoidable delay'. It was the best entry there.
After that, she travelled with us. She asked me questions about the stars. I didn't know the answers. I didn't mind.
For the first time I looked out of a window. There was a sea the colour of pewter, and I found it beautiful.
I began to be afraid, you see. Not of losing the money. Of arriving on time and finding nothing had changed in me.
Near the end the detective arrested me, by mistake. I lost hours in a cell, staring at the wall and thinking of her voice.
My dream isn't the fortune any more. It's to sit at breakfast and let the tea go cold, talking to someone.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.dialogue.3: Arrived in time! I still can't believe it. I'd miscounted the festival days; I had a whole day to spare.
I was sitting at home, sure I'd lost, when my valet burst in shouting the date. I'd never seen him run.
You're four minutes late today, you know. I noticed, and I didn't mind at all. Progress, wouldn't you say?
Sometimes I walk to the village you found, just to look at it. It was never on any map. Now it's on my heart.
If I ever wager again, it will be on something sensible. That you'll come for breakfast, for instance.
Around the realm in eighty days, and the best thing I found was waiting here, a few steps from my door.
Come by tomorrow, whenever you like. I won't look at the clock. Well... perhaps once.
Imagine it: eighty days of perfect sums, and the one mistake I made was the one that saved me.
The card players paid in full. One asked how I'd done it. I said, 'A friend with fast feet.'
She accepted my proposal that same evening. I asked at eight and three. She answered at eight and four.
Now I arrive five minutes late to everything. On purpose. It drives my valet to despair, and I adore that.
Yesterday I let my tea go cold while talking. Twenty whole minutes! I've never felt so rich.
The clock you brought still hangs above the hearth. I check it less often. It forgives me.
My notebook has a new page, titled 'Unscheduled'. It's already the fullest one.
The detective sent a letter of apology. I've invited him to dinner. He'll probably arrest the soup.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.epilogue: They won the bet thanks to a day they didn't know they had. Since then they arrive a little late everywhere, on purpose, and smile.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.source: Around the World in Eighty Days — Jules Verne (1872)
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.stage.0.as: My clock broke on the voyage and I can't bear it. Bring me a new one; I'll set it by the sun.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.stage.0.do: Precise to the minute. My heartbeat has calmed down noticeably.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.stage.1.as: The bet says I must pass through a village I've never visited. Go ahead of me and find one, quickly.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.stage.1.do: Found, charted and ahead of schedule. You'd make a splendid valet.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.stage.2.as: The wager ends tonight. Carry this letter to the village where the bet was made, before the clock strikes. I'll follow as fast as I can.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.stage.2.do: Arrived in time! I'd miscounted the festival days; I had a whole day spare. And I nearly didn't notice.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.talk.0: You're four minutes late. Don't worry, I've already accounted for it.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.talk.1: Every problem is a schedule that hasn't been drawn up yet.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.talk.2: My valet thinks I have no heart. He's wrong. It simply keeps excellent time.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.talk.3: I thought I'd lost the bet, you know. I was a whole day wrong. The best mistake of my life.
hearthbound.persona.myth_fogg.title: Eighty days exactly
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.bio.0: I've been a giant among people the size of my thumb and a toy among giants. I've seen a flying island full of scholars who never looked down.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.bio.1: In my last voyage I lived among wise, gentle horses. When I came home, people smelled strange to me. I still haven't quite got over it.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.dialog: Good day. You're a perfectly reasonable size. I say that as a compliment. I don't say it often.
Which end do you crack your eggs from? Careful. Wars have started over less.
Thousands died over it. Books were burned. Exiles fled across the water. All for the end of an egg.
I laughed at first. Then I watched the funerals. I stopped laughing. I've never settled the question.
It's bothered me for twenty years. Is there a right end? Did they die for something, or nothing?
I want to test it properly. Scientifically. Both ends, several eggs, a clean bowl and witnesses.
Bring me eggs? I want to crack them from both ends and settle, at last, the war I saw in that land.
Everything is the right size, it's just that you're the wrong one.
The horse in the paddock understands me better than the mayor does. No offence to the mayor.
You listen before you speak. That's rare. I once met a whole nation that forgot how.
I was a ship's surgeon once. Four voyages. Four shipwrecks, more or less. I'm very unlucky with boats.
The first time, I woke on a beach tied down with a thousand threads. The people were the size of my thumb.
They climbed on my chest with tiny spears. I sneezed. Three of them fell off. We became friends after that.
Their empire was at war with the island next door. Do you know why? Eggs.
One emperor decreed eggs must be cracked at the small end. Rebels insisted on the big end.
Both ends work perfectly. Two empires fought for years over nothing. Of course they did.
I made an omelette from the evidence. Delicious. Peace tastes of butter, it turns out.
Below them, the fields were ruined and the houses were falling down. They didn't notice. They were busy.
I've wondered ever since what they saw up there that was worth ignoring everyone below.
Maybe I've been unfair. Maybe the stars really are that interesting. I've never looked properly.
If I had a good glass, I'd look up once, just once, the way they did. Then I'd decide.
Bring me a spyglass? I want to see what the scholars of the flying island saw. Then I'll judge them.
Now the second voyage. After being a giant, I became a toy. A land where people were as tall as church towers.
A farmer found me in his field and sold me as a curiosity. His little daughter made me a doll's bed.
She called me her 'little mannikin'. She was kind. She was nine and forty feet tall.
A wasp the size of a hawk attacked me at breakfast. A monkey carried me up a roof. I've been humble since.
The king there listened to me boast about my homeland's wars and cannons. Then he called us vermin.
He wasn't wrong. That was the first time my own people started to look strange to me.
Then the third voyage. A flying island, floating above the land, full of scholars.
They studied the stars, music and mathematics so hard they never looked down. They needed servants to slap them awake.
Nothing up there but stars and a lot of sky. I'll keep looking down, thank you.
Well. The moon is very pretty. I'll grant them the moon. Nothing else. Fine, the moon and two comets.
That's my secret. I've been everywhere and never quite fit anywhere. Here, I'm starting to fit.
But I haven't ridden since. It felt wrong, sitting on the back of someone wiser than me.
The mare in the paddock looks at me the way they did. Patient. Like she's waiting for me to ask properly.
I want to ride again, if the horses will allow it. With respect. With a good saddle, not a rough one.
Bring me a saddle? I'll ask them nicely first. If they refuse, I'll carry it myself and walk beside them.
Now the last voyage. The one I don't tell at the inn. The one that changed me most.
My crew mutinied and left me on a strange shore. There I found a land ruled by horses.
Wise, gentle, honest horses. They had no word for a lie. They'd say 'the thing which is not'.
There were also wild creatures there, filthy and greedy, that looked horribly like people. Like me.
The horses took me in. They taught me their language. It's mostly soft neighs and very careful pauses.
I was happiest there. Truly. Then their council decided I was too like the wild ones. I had to leave.
When I came home, people smelled strange to me. I still haven't quite got over it.
I couldn't eat at the same table as my own family for a year. I spent hours in the stable, talking.
The mare said yes. Well, she snorted, which I choose to understand as yes.
We rode to the hill and back. She chose the path. I didn't argue. She has better judgement.
I've been a giant, a toy, a stranger and a nuisance. Here, I'm just the one who talks to horses.
That's the right size, I think. Not too big, not too small. The size of a friend.
If you ever wash up on a strange shore, be polite, learn the language and ask the horses first.
You helped an old wanderer finally unpack. I'd forgotten my bags had a bottom.
Go on, then. Travel well. And if anyone asks which end of the egg, tell them: the middle.
I talk to the horses more than to people now. The strangest thing is they seem to answer.
The mayor came to complain about the noise. The mare sneezed on him. We both enjoyed that.
I've noticed people here don't smell so strange anymore. Maybe I've got used to them. Or they bathe more.
I've written my voyages in a little book. Nobody believes a word. That's the best kind of book.
The children at the inn ask for the egg war every night. They always crack their eggs in the middle now.
The middle! Brilliant. No empire could fight over that. I've told them they've ended a war.
Remember the spyglass? I lend it to the mare at night. She seems to prefer the moon too.
I still set a place at the table for someone who isn't there. A little one. Just in case.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.epilog: Now they talk to the horses more than to people, and the strangest thing is that the horses seem to answer.
Bring me eggs. I want to crack them from both ends and settle, at last, the war I saw in the land of little people.
Both ends work perfectly. Two empires fought for years over nothing. Of course they did.
The scholars of the flying island studied the stars so hard they forgot their own feet. Bring me a spyglass; I want to see what they saw.
Nothing up there but stars and a lot of sky. I'll keep looking down, thank you.
I want to ride again, if the horses will allow it. Bring me a saddle, and I'll ask them nicely first.
The mare said yes. Well, she snorted, which I choose to understand as yes.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.talk.0: Which end do you crack your eggs from? Careful. Wars have started over less.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.talk.1: Everything is the right size, it's just that you're the wrong one.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.talk.2: The horse in the paddock understands me better than the mayor does. No offence to the mayor.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.talk.3: I've been everywhere and never quite fit anywhere. Here, I'm starting to fit.
hearthbound.persona.myth_gulliver.title: Giant, dwarf and stranger
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.bio.0: My grandmother told me of a boy who flew too close to the sun on wax wings. I'm the only one in the village who thinks he was right to try.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.bio.1: I fell off the mill roof twice and the bell tower once. I don't want to die. I just can't stand the thought of never seeing what's up there.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.dialogue: Look up! No, higher. See that cloud shaped like a boot? I've named it after you.
The clouds look solid from here. I'm going to check one day.
The second time I had a bedsheet tied to my arms. The miller still hasn't given me back the sheet.
Then the bell tower. I don't want to talk about the bell tower. My arm still clicks when it rains.
I don't want to die. I just can't stand the thought of never seeing what's up there.
So I've started a secret. A real one. Hidden in the hayloft behind the mill.
I'm building wings. Don't tell anyone. Bring me feathers, the biggest you can find? Lots of them.
My knees are all scabs, but my heart is all feathers.
I know every roof in this village by how it feels under my feet. The church is the slipperiest.
You climb things too, don't you? I saw you on the hill. You looked happy up there.
When I was small, my grandmother told me about a boy who flew on wings of feathers and wax.
His father made them. He told the boy: not too high. The boy went too high. The sun melted the wax.
Everyone in the village says the story means: obey your elders. I think it means something else.
I'm the only one here who thinks he was right to try. He saw what nobody else ever saw.
I fell off the mill roof twice. The first time I was trying to jump to the weathervane.
They're beautiful. The miller saw me with them and fainted. Worth it.
I tried them on the haystack. I flew for almost two whole heartbeats. Then hay. Lots of hay.
I was shaking for an hour. First time I've been really scared up high. I didn't like it.
If I jump with feathers and one of those things is waiting, I won't get a second try.
I'm brave, not stupid. Well. Mostly not stupid. Ask the miller, he'll say otherwise.
The sky isn't safe. Not yet. And I can't clear it myself, not with a broken arm's worth of luck.
Clear the night sky of those grey wings before I try? Please. I want the sky to be ours first.
Everyone tells me 'not so high'. You're the first who asked me why.
Do you want to know why? Because down here everything is fences and chores and 'be careful'.
Up there, I think, nobody tells you what size you're supposed to be.
My grandmother used to say I was born looking at the sky. The midwife had to turn my head.
She died last winter. She's the one who told me the story. I think she wanted me to finish it better.
But there's a problem. At night, the sky isn't empty. Something else flies there.
Grey wings, like rags. They come for anyone who stays awake too many nights. I stay awake a lot.
Three nights ago one dived at me on the mill roof. I only just rolled into the gutter.
The sky is ours again. I climbed the tower to celebrate. Then I climbed down. Carefully.
Carefully! Me! The baker dropped a loaf in shock. I'm keeping that as a trophy moment.
Through the crack, the sun looks like two suns. That can't be right. I need a proper one.
A spyglass. Brass, clear glass, the good kind. I'd study the sun from the ground first. At dusk, safely.
Look at me being sensible. My grandmother would laugh. Then she'd hug me. Then she'd laugh again.
The wings are hanging in the hayloft. They'll wait. Wings are patient, it turns out. I'm learning to be.
Bring me a spyglass? I've decided: I'll look at the sun properly before I ever fly to it.
Here's something I haven't told anyone. When that grey thing dived, I thought of my grandmother.
Not of the sky. Of her. Of who'd tell the story if I fell. That's the first time I thought that.
Maybe the trick isn't flying higher. Maybe it's knowing when to come down.
I still want to go up there. I haven't changed my mind. I've just started using it more.
In the old tale, the boy never looked at the sun before he flew towards it. He just went.
What if he'd studied it first? Measured it? Maybe he'd have seen how far it really was.
My dream isn't to touch the sun anymore. It's to see it properly, and still come home for supper.
The miller's son has a little glass for looking at birds. It's cracked. I've been borrowing it.
I spent all afternoon looking at it. It's much further than I thought. Keep these boots: for landing well.
Much further! Like, really far. The boy in the story never stood a chance. Nobody told him the distance.
I still think the clouds are solid. One day I'll check. With a spyglass first. And good boots.
The spyglass lives in my pocket. I've spotted three eagles, a hawk and the baker's lost hen with it.
When you're on a high place somewhere far away, look up. I'll probably be looking too.
You helped me love the sky without needing to fall out of it. That's a strange, lovely gift.
Go on, then. Walk your road. I'll be on the hill with a kite. Wave if you see one very high up.
Now we fly kites from the hill every windy afternoon. I made the first one from my old wings.
None of them go higher than is wise. Well, almost none. Mine got stuck in a cloud once. Probably.
The miller helps now. He holds the string and shouts 'not so high'. Then he lets out more string.
I tell the children my grandmother's story every week. I've added an ending. The boy comes home.
Remember the hayloft wings? The miller wants to hang them in the mill. He says they scared him into liking me.
My arm still clicks when it rains. Now I use it to predict weather. I'm very accurate.
The sky at night is full of stars again, not grey wings. I lie on the roof and count them. Lying down.
You asked me why, the first time. That question changed everything. Nobody had ever asked.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.epilogue: Now they fly kites from the hill every windy afternoon, and none of them goes higher than is wise... well, almost none.
I'm building wings. Don't tell anyone. Bring me feathers, the biggest you can find.
They're beautiful. The miller saw me with them and fainted. Worth it.
Something with grey wings attacks anyone who stays awake too long. The sky isn't safe. Clear it before I try.
The sky is ours again. I climbed the tower to celebrate. Then I climbed down. Carefully.
I've decided: I'll look at the sun properly before I fly to it. Bring me a spyglass, and I'll study it from the ground first.
I spent all afternoon looking at it. It's much further away than I thought. Take these boots: for landing well.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.talk.0: The clouds look solid from here. I'm going to check one day.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.talk.1: My knees are all scabs, but my heart is all feathers.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.talk.2: Everyone tells me 'not so high'. You're the first who asked me why.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.talk.3: Maybe the trick isn't flying higher. Maybe it's knowing when to come down.
hearthbound.persona.myth_icarus.title: Too close to the sun
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.bio.0: I teach the children letters and believe every ghost story I've ever read. Everyone here says a headless rider gallops through the hollow at night.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.bio.1: I rode home from a harvest feast once and something followed me, holding its head under its arm. It threw it at me. I haven't crossed the bridge since.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.dialogu: Come in, come in! Mind the slate on the floor; the children use it as a bridge. Don't ask what the floor is.
Reading is the finest thing in the world. Except, perhaps, pie. On a good day, reading with pie.
Our school has one book. One! A primer with a torn cover. The children know it by heart. So do the mice.
Little Hans recites it backwards now, to keep it interesting. His sister has started reciting me.
They do my voice, my walk, the way I jump at owls. It's flattering, in a humiliating sort of way.
Children who read think for themselves. Children who only memorise their teacher end up... well, like me.
Would you bring me more books? Three would change everything. Before they learn me by heart completely.
I teach the little ones their letters. They teach me which berries not to eat. A fair exchange.
Did you hear hooves just now? No? Neither did I. Definitely not. Let's keep talking. Loudly.
I think I've read every ghost story ever printed. I believe each one. It makes my evenings very eventful.
There's an old tale from over the sea, about a schoolmaster named Ichabod Crane. I've read it eleven times. It's no comfort.
Everyone here says a rider without a head gallops through the hollow at night, looking for the one he lost.
The old women tell it by the fire, and then they sleep soundly. I don't know how they manage it.
I take the long way home from the school now. The very long way. It avoids a certain bridge.
Some things I'd rather not explain yet. Let's say a harvest feast once ended very badly for me.
New stories for the little ones! I've hidden the scary ones. After reading them. Twice. By candlelight. A mistake.
Hans read the one about the sea voyage aloud, and nobody recited me all afternoon. Bliss.
He once blocked my chimney and smoked out a whole singing lesson. She laughed. At him or at me? I still wonder.
Honestly, I doubt I stand a chance. I'm all elbows and adjectives. He's all shoulders.
But the harvest feast is coming, and at her father's table a person is measured by what they bring.
I can't ride like him or lift what he lifts. But I can bring the best pumpkin pies the valley has ever tasted.
Would you bring me four pumpkin pies? The finest you can find. For the feast. And for... well. Pies.
Now, about the rider. The old women say he was a soldier whose head was taken by a cannonball in some forgotten war.
They buried him in the churchyard by the hollow. Every night he rides out to search for his head, and is back before dawn.
If he's late, they say, he gallops like a storm. And the bridge by the church is where he... stops chasing.
I know all the rules. Ghosts can't cross running water. Salt at the door. Never look back. I've written them in a notebook.
The notebook has forty pages. Thirty-nine are rules. One is a very bad poem I wrote for someone.
Yes, someone. She laughs like the first warm day of spring. Her father owns the finest orchard in the valley.
I tutored her in singing once. She sang beautifully. I sang for both of us, which was less beautiful.
There's a big loud fellow who courts her too. He rides a horse like thunder and plays pranks on everyone. On me, mostly.
The pies were a triumph! She smiled at me. Twice. Also at the big loud fellow, but twice at me. I counted.
He ate three slices and told everyone he'd baked them. She knew. She winked at me. I think it was a wink.
My fear isn't dying. It's being so frightened I run, and never come back, and they tell my story as a joke.
My dream? Not to run, for once. To see the thing in the dark with my own eyes and know what it is.
They say tonight he rides again. The anniversary. And the dark things come out with him, the dead and worse.
I won't hide behind the schoolroom door this time. The children sleep in this village. So does she.
Will you stand with me tonight and keep the village safe until dawn? I'll hold the lantern. You'll hold... everything else.
Now I owe you the truth about the bridge. It happened after a feast like this one, years ago. I've never told it all.
I left late, full of cake and hope. My borrowed horse was old and cranky. The moon was hiding. Everything was hiding.
Near the hollow, I heard hooves behind me. I sped up. They sped up. I slowed. So did they.
Then I saw him against the sky: huge, cloaked, and where his head should be, nothing. He carried it on his saddle.
I galloped for the bridge, because ghosts stop at the bridge. It's rule four. I reached it. He didn't stop.
He rose in the stirrups and hurled his head at me. It struck me, and the world went black.
In the morning they found my hat by the stream and me in a ditch, and beside me something smashed. I didn't look.
Some nights I think the rider wasn't a ghost at all. That someone wanted me gone. That's somehow worse.
We held until dawn! And by the bridge, nothing but a smashed pumpkin. I've examined it thoroughly. Definitely a pumpkin.
Does the helm fit? Keep your head, will you? I've grown very attached to it. Your head, I mean.
She asked what I was afraid of now. I said, 'Very little, and pumpkins.' She laughed at me, not at him. I checked.
The children have a new game called 'the rider'. Whoever plays me has to be brave now. It's in the rules.
I still believe in ghosts, mind you. Just not that one. And I sleep with the scary books under my pillow.
You stood in the dark beside a trembling schoolteacher and never once laughed. I'll write that in the school's own book.
Come by the school some afternoon. We're reading a new story. There's no rider in it. Only pie.
Here's the odd part. The big loud fellow laughs out loud whenever anyone mentions pumpkins. Every single time.
At the feast, someone said 'pumpkin pie' and ale came out of his nose. I've started keeping notes.
Years ago, a pumpkin by the bridge. Last night, a pumpkin by the bridge. A pattern, as we scholars say.
I'm beginning to suspect my headless rider had a very large head, firmly attached, and a very small sense of humour.
Strangely, it makes me braver. A ghost I can't fight. A prankster I can simply outlive and outread.
I crossed the bridge this morning. On foot, in daylight, whistling. The children applauded from the bank.
The notebook of rules has a new page: 'Rule forty. Check under the cloak.'
She came to the school yesterday with apples for the children. She stayed for the whole lesson. Then for tea.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.epilogu: Since then the big loud fellow from the feast laughs out loud whenever pumpkins are mentioned, and the teacher has begun to suspect why.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.source: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow — Washington Irving (1820)
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.stage.0: The school has only one book and the children know it by heart. Bring me more, before they start memorising me.
New stories for the little ones! I'll hide the scary ones... after I read them.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.stage.1: The harvest feast is coming, and I want to bring the best pies in the valley. There's someone there I'd like to... well. Pies.
The pies were a triumph. She smiled at me. Twice. Also at a big loud fellow, but twice at me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.stage.2: Tonight is the night the rider comes, they say. The dark things come with him. Stand with me and keep the village safe until dawn.
We held until dawn. And by the bridge, only a smashed pumpkin. Take this helm; keep your head, will you?
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.talk.0: Reading is the finest thing in the world. Except, perhaps, pie.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.talk.1: Did you hear hooves just now? No? Neither did I. Definitely not.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.talk.2: There was someone at that feast I hoped to impress. I impressed only the rider.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.talk.3: Some nights I think the rider wasn't a ghost at all. That's somehow worse.
hearthbound.persona.myth_ichabod.title: The rider without a head
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.bio.0: My uncle stole my family's seat and promised to give it back if I brought him a golden fleece from the end of the world. He expected me to die trying.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.bio.1: I gathered the finest crew that ever sailed. Heroes, twins, a singer. I've never admitted it, but I'm the least remarkable of all of them.
Ahoy! Sorry. Habit. We're nowhere near the sea, I know. Hello.
A ship is just trees that agreed to travel together.
He expected me to die trying. Everyone did. I was young enough to think that was a compliment.
The first thing I needed was a ship. The best ship ever built. Fifty oars, a talking prow.
I've been dreaming of that ship lately. Not the fleece. The ship. The smell of fresh-cut timber.
I want to build another. Smaller, for the river. For the village children to learn the oars.
No voyage without a ship, and no ship without timber. Bring me logs, the tallest and straightest?
Did you know rocks can clap? Big ones. At sea. Row faster.
I walk with one sandal loose. There's a reason. A prophecy, a river, an old woman. Long story.
You look like someone who's travelled. Good. People who travel don't ask why I stare at the horizon.
My family once had a seat of honour in a city by the sea. My uncle took it while I was a baby.
I was raised far away, in a cave, by a teacher who was half horse. He taught me herbs and patience.
When I came back to claim what was ours, I lost a sandal crossing a river, carrying an old woman.
My uncle had been warned about a man with one sandal. He went pale. Then he smiled, which was worse.
He said: bring me the golden fleece from the end of the world, and the seat is yours.
She'll be fast, and she'll talk back. Good ships always do. I've already named her.
The children rowed in circles for an hour. I've never been prouder. Circles are a start.
Everyone remembers the fleece. I only remember the faces at the oars.
But I'm getting ahead of myself. The fleece hung in a land nobody I knew had seen. The edge of maps.
I've been thinking of that again. There's a land out there where people have heard of the fleece.
I need someone to go ahead of me. Someone quicker. Someone who finds places without a crew.
Go ahead of me and find a village I've never heard of? A far one. We'll see if they know the fleece.
Now let me tell you about the crew. The finest that ever sailed. I didn't deserve half of them.
A strongman who could carry the ship on his back. Twins, one a boxer, one a horse-tamer.
A singer whose songs could calm the sea. Sons of the north wind, who flew. A helmsman who never slept.
And me. The one whose name was on the voyage. I've never admitted it, but I'm the least remarkable of all of them.
They followed me anyway. I've never understood why. Maybe because I asked nicely.
We rowed past clashing rocks that slammed together like hands. We sent a dove first. It lost its tail feathers.
Then we rowed like fools, and the rocks caught only our stern ornament. We laughed for three days.
My crew are scattered now. Sometimes I set out fifty cups, out of habit.
A far village, and they'd heard of the fleece! We're on the right course. I knew it.
You did in weeks what took my crew a year. And you didn't lose a single sandal. Show-off.
The keeper of the fleece set the task. Here, the closest thing to fire-bulls is out in the red lands.
The burning spirits there. Blazes. Spinning, snorting fire, guarding their dark fortresses.
I know what I'm asking. Go into the fire, for a sheepskin. It sounds mad when I say it out loud.
But it's not about the sheepskin. It never was. It's about finishing something the right way.
Hunt the burning spirits of the red lands? The fire-bulls of our time. Then the fleece will be ours.
Now the hardest part. When we reached the land of the fleece, the king there didn't want to give it.
He set me a task. Yoke two bulls with bronze hooves that breathed fire, and plough a field with them.
I couldn't have done it alone. The king's own daughter helped me, with an ointment against burning.
I've never told anyone how afraid I was. I stood in that field and wanted my teacher, my cave, anyone.
The bulls came at me snorting flame. I held the yoke. I ploughed. My hair smelled of smoke for a month.
The rest of that story is not a happy one. I made promises there I didn't keep. I carry that too.
My fear isn't fire. It's being the kind of leader who takes help and forgets who gave it.
This time I want to do it right. Face the fire myself. With a friend beside me I'll never forget.
Done! The fleece is ours. Keep this shield; it took more blows on the voyage than I did.
The fleece hangs in the tavern now. It turned out to be an ordinary dyed sheepskin.
I've stopped thinking of myself as the least remarkable. I'm the one who got everyone home. That counts.
My teacher used to say: a good captain is measured by the crew's laughter, not the treasure.
If you ever need a crew, for anything, send a message. There are a dozen idiots here who'd row for you.
You're part of the crew now, you know. The fiftieth cup has your name scratched on it.
Go on, then. Fair winds. Keep both sandals on. And if the rocks start clapping, row faster.
Nobody on the crew minds at all. We drink under it and argue about who rowed hardest.
Yes, the crew! Some of them found their way here. The twins came first. Then the singer.
I set out fifty cups last week, out of habit. Eleven were filled. That's more than I hoped for.
The children's river boat is in fine shape. They row straight now. Mostly. They still sing badly.
I told the singer about you. He wrote a verse. You have a very heroic nose in it.
Remember when you found that far village? They sent a letter. They want to visit the fleece.
I don't know what to tell them. It's a sheepskin. But the story is gold. Maybe that's enough.
I never got my family's seat back, in the end. I found a better one. That bench by the tavern door.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.epilogue: Now the fleece hangs in the tavern. It turned out to be an ordinary dyed sheepskin, and nobody on the crew minds at all.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.source: Argonautica — Apollonius of Rhodes (3rd century BC)
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.stage.0.a: No voyage without a ship, and no ship without timber. Bring me logs; the tallest and straightest you can find.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.stage.0.d: She'll be fast, and she'll talk back. Good ships always do.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.stage.1.a: The fleece hangs in a land nobody I know has seen. Go ahead of me and find a village I've never heard of.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.stage.1.d: A far village, and they'd heard of the fleece! We're on the right course.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.stage.2.a: The keeper of the fleece set a task: tame beasts that breathe fire. Here, the closest thing is the burning spirits of the red lands. Hunt them.
hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.stage.2.d: Done! The fleece is ours. Take this shield; it took more blows on the voyage than I did.

hearthbound.persona.myth_jason.title: A fleece of gold
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.bio.0: I'm the one they blame whenever the milk sours. Usually I'm guilty. Last spring I cut off the miller's wife's golden hair while she slept. For a laugh.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.bio.1: It wasn't funny. She hid for a month. I've made everything worse all my life, and just once I'd like to fix something before anyone makes me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.dialogue.0: Me? I was nowhere near it. Whatever it was. Oh, you're new. Hello. I was still nowhere near it.
Every rule has a crack. I'm just the one who finds it first.
Last spring I crept into the mill at night. The miller's wife was asleep, her hair spread on the pillow.
Golden hair. Everyone in the village talked about it. It glowed at the harvest dance like a lantern.
I cut it off. All of it. With her own sewing scissors. For a laugh. I thought it would be funny.
It wasn't funny. She hid for a month. The miller didn't speak to anyone. I heard her crying through the wall.
I'll make her a new head of hair, finer than the old. Bring me string? The dwarves of Durnhal will spin it.
I once bet my head with a dwarf. He won. I argued he couldn't take my neck. He sewed my lips instead.
The scars? Very fashionable where I come from. Nobody believes that. Worth a try.
You trust me. That's either very brave or very foolish. I'm touched either way.
Whenever the milk sours in this village, they look at me first. Usually I'm guilty. Usually.
I swapped the church bell rope for a sausage once. The priest rang it for a whole minute before noticing.
I've been the clever one my whole life. Clever is lonely. Nobody invites the clever one to dinner twice.
There's an old tale about a trickster among the gods. Always causing trouble, always fixing it at the last moment.
I used to love that tale. I thought: see, it all works out. Nobody gets hurt. It's all a laugh.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.dialogue.1: The dwarves are spinning. They charged double, because it's me. Fair.
You didn't ask why I wanted it. Or whether it was another trick. I noticed that. I'm still thinking about it.
Her hair used to glow like wheat in the evening sun. The dwarves say they can gild it if they have gold.
Real gold. Tiny pieces, hammered into the strands. It'll grow like real hair and shine like the sun.
I thought about stealing the gold. Easy. The merchant keeps a bag under the counter. I could...
No. I'm done with tricks. For this, at least. Everything that goes into it has to be honest.
Bring me gold nuggets to gild it? Real gold. Honestly found. I'm done with tricks, I swear. For this.
Now the part I don't say aloud. She came out of the mill last week. Wearing a scarf. Head down.
The children stared. One laughed. I wanted to throw that child in the pond. Then I remembered I was the cause.
I've made everything worse all my life. Pranks that go too far. Jokes nobody laughs at but me.
And somebody else always cleans up. Somebody else pays. I just slip away and wait for the next laugh.
In the old tale, the gods caught the trickster by the throat and said: fix it, or else.
Just once I'd like to fix something before anyone makes me. Before the threat. Because I want to.
The dwarves of Durnhal are the best spinners under any mountain. They spun thread fine as spider silk.
But thread is just thread. Pale, limp, lifeless. It has to shine. It has to be hers.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.dialogue.2: Hair that grows like real hair and shines like the sun. Even I'm impressed with me.
I held it up to the window. It caught the light and threw it across the room like water. I nearly cried.
So for once, I'm not playing. No bargaining. No words. I don't trust my mouth around them.
They brew poisons and throw them. They cackle. They cheat better than I do. That's saying a lot.
I need someone honest to deal with them. Someone who won't be tricked, because they won't try to trick.
That's you. You're the least tricky person I know. It's almost suspicious.
The swamp brewers want payment in her hair. For once, I'm not playing. Deal with them? Please.
But here's the mess I haven't told you. Years ago I owed a favour to some swamp brewers. Witches.
I lost a bet with them. I always lose bets. I'm clever, not lucky. They wanted payment in something precious.
They've heard about the hair. Of course they have. Everyone hears everything in a swamp. It's the damp.
Now they want the hair as payment. Her new hair. The one thing I've ever made that isn't a joke.
The old me would have handed it over and found a trick to steal it back. Laughing all the way.
But she's waited a month in the dark. I can't make her wait another month for my old debts.
My fear? That I'll be tempted. That I'll make some clever deal and trade her away without noticing.
I know myself. I'll talk, and twist, and bargain, and at the end I'll have sold something that isn't mine.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.dialogue.3: She got her hair, the brewers got nothing, and I got a thank-you. Strange feeling. Name something after me.
She hugged me. In the square. In front of everyone. I didn't know where to put my hands.
People invite me to dinner twice now. Some of them three times. I don't know what to do with my face.
I'm still a trickster. I'll always be. But now the cracks I find, I sometimes fill in.
If anything goes missing near you, it wasn't me. If anything turns up that you needed, maybe it was.
You trusted me when you had no reason to. That's the only trick that's ever worked on me.
Go on, then. Be careful of clever people. Except me. Well. Especially me. Come back soon.
Nobody knows if this was all a long prank to win your friendship. Not even me. Maybe it was.
The milk hasn't soured once since then. That's suspicious in itself. People keep checking.
The miller brought me flour yesterday. A whole sack. He didn't say a word. He didn't need to.
Her hair grows a finger a month and glows at dusk. The children follow her like moths now.
I still swap the church bell rope sometimes. With another rope. The priest is confused, not angry.
Remember the dwarves charging double? I paid them triple. They're very suspicious of me now.
The swamp brewers sent a letter. It said: 'We know it was you.' It wasn't. It was you. I'm very proud.
I've found that fixing things is also a kind of cleverness. The rarest kind. And nobody expects it.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.epilogue: Nobody knows if this was all a long prank to win the traveller's friendship. Since then the milk hasn't soured once, and that's suspicious in itself.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.stage.0.as: I'm going to make her a new head of hair, finer than the old one. Bring me string; the dwarves of Durnhal will spin it for me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.stage.0.do: The dwarves are spinning. They charged double, because it's me. Fair.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.stage.1.as: Now it has to shine like the old hair did. Bring me gold nuggets to gild it. Real gold. I'm done with tricks.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.stage.1.do: Hair that grows like real hair and shines like the sun. Even I'm impressed with me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.stage.2.as: The swamp brewers I owed a favour want it paid with her new hair. For once, I'm not playing. Deal with them.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.stage.2.do: She got her hair, the brewers got nothing, and I got a thank-you. Strange feeling. Take this; name something after me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.talk.0: Me? I was nowhere near it. Whatever it was.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.talk.1: Every rule has a crack. I'm just the one who finds it first.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.talk.2: I once bet my head with a dwarf. He won. I argued he couldn't take my neck. He sewed my lips instead.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.talk.3: You trust me. That's either very brave or very foolish. I'm touched either way.
hearthbound.persona.myth_loki.title: A prank too far
hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.bio.0: I once did a favour for a wandering old drunk, and his master offered me any wish. I asked that everything I touch should turn to gold. I'm a merchant; it seemed obvious.
hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.bio.1: My bread turned to gold. My wine. My daughter's hand, when she ran to hug me. I'd give every coin I own for one warm, ordinary loaf.
Welcome, welcome! Don't shake my hand. I mean it. Nod, please. Lovely nod.
Gold is lovely until you try to eat it.
The servants cheered. I cheered. We had a feast. And that's where the story stops being funny.
I still keep a little golden twig in my drawer. I take it out sometimes, when I'm tempted.
Tempted to what? To want it again. That shine. Merchants never quite stop wanting.
I've been feeling the itch lately. Coins in my dreams. I need to know if I'm cured or just scared.
Bring me gold. Lots of it. I want to see if the wish still works... no, I just want to count it. Humour me.
I wear gloves now. Very thick ones. The shopkeepers think I'm very elegant.
Best prices in the village, and I never touch the goods. Hygiene, I tell customers. Hygiene.
You have honest eyes. Merchants learn to read eyes. It's cheaper than reading contracts.
Once, far from here, my gardeners found an old drunk asleep in my roses. Wreathed in vines, snoring.
I fed him, housed him ten days, and walked him home. He belonged to a very important master.
The master was grateful. He offered me any wish. Anything at all. Can you imagine?
I'm a merchant. I asked that everything I touch should turn to gold. It seemed obvious.
The first day was glorious. I touched a twig: gold. A stone: gold. An apple: heavy, gleaming gold.
Look at it shine. And yet... it's cold. Why is it always so cold?
I counted it three times. It was exactly the same each time. Gold never surprises you. That's its sin.
I haven't tasted bread in weeks. It turns to gold at my lips. I survive on smells, mostly.
I stand outside the bakery at dawn and breathe. The baker thinks I'm courting her.
I'd give every coin I own for one warm, ordinary loaf. Every single one.
I've had a thought. If I don't touch it at all... if somebody else puts it in my mouth, with a spoon...
Bring me loaves? And feed me with a spoon, like a baby. Maybe one bite will survive. Please. I'm so hungry.
Now the feast. You've been patient. I sat down to dinner, delighted, and reached for the bread.
My bread turned to gold. My wine. It poured into my mouth as a stream of liquid metal. I spat it.
I sat there starving at a table covered in treasure. The servants backed away from me.
And then my daughter ran in, laughing, to hug me. I didn't think. I opened my arms.
My daughter's hand, when she ran to hug me. Gold. Her smile, gold. Silent, gleaming, still.
I begged the master on my knees. He took pity on her and gave her back. Warm again. Crying.
My daughter is flesh again, thank the gods. I still count her fingers every morning. Ten. Always ten.
But me, he said, I'd asked for it. I'd have to find my own way out. He was right, the brute.
You fed me like a baby and I don't care. Bread! Warm, soft, stupid, marvellous bread!
I ate eleven slices. Crumbs everywhere. I cried into the twelfth. The crumbs didn't turn. Nothing turned.
I ran to the river. And stopped. What if the water turns to gold when I touch it? Then I'd drown in wealth.
I've been too frightened to try for a week. Merchants are brave with money and cowards with hope.
If you brought me clear water, running water, in a bucket, I could pour it over my hands.
Not dip, pour. So it keeps moving. Moving water can't be caught. That's my theory. It's a merchant's theory.
Bring me a bucket of clear water, please, quickly. Before I lose my nerve. Before the wedding.
But I can't live forever with someone spooning bread into my face. You have roads to walk.
Here's my deepest fear. My daughter wants to marry next spring. She wants me to walk her to the altar.
Holding her arm. Ordinary. Like any parent. And I can't touch her without gloves as thick as boots.
What if I forget, just once, and reach for her hand? I dream of that. Every night. I wake up shouting.
I don't want the gold. I want the touch back. The ordinary, worthless, priceless touch.
Last week a river spirit spoke to me by the ford. A voice in the reeds. Very wet, very kind.
It said: wash your hands in running water, at the spring, and the wish will run off you.
Like the old tale, where the river's sand turned golden forever afterwards. I remember that tale now.
The gold slid off my hands into the bucket like sand. Keep the nuggets; I've had enough of the stuff.
I ate bread with my bare hands that same evening. I laughed so much I choked. Worth it.
If the reeds by the river ever start saying strange things about me, don't believe a word.
Remember feeding me bread with a spoon? My daughter still teases me. She calls me 'baby merchant'.
I count her fingers less often now. Once a week. On feast days. She lets me.
I've learned the only thing worth having is the thing you can hold without it changing.
Go on, then. Shake my hand! Properly! Ha! Warm, isn't it? Warm and worth nothing, and I love it.
I walked my daughter to the altar. I held her arm the whole way. I didn't let go until I had to.
The first thing I touched after the water? Your shoulder. You flinched. I don't blame you.
I sell bread now, too. With my own hands. The baker is furious. She says I'm poaching customers.
I threw away the gloves. Well, I keep one pair. For the cold. Only for the cold. Truly.
Oh, the cap? Nothing. A fashion. Why is everyone looking at my cap? It's a perfectly normal cap.
There was a little music contest last month. I judged it. I may have picked the wrong winner.
The winner was a god, apparently. The loser, I mean, was a god. Well. He was not happy with my ears.
Don't lift the cap. I mean it. The barber knows, and he's been digging holes in the field to whisper into.
hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.epilogue: Now the merchant eats bread with bare hands and laughs a lot. But a funny cap has appeared on their head, and rumour speaks of donkey ears.
hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.stage.0.a: Bring me gold. Lots of it. I want to see if the wish still works... no, I simply want to count it. Humour me.

hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.stage.1.d: You fed me like a baby and I don't care. Bread! Warm, soft, stupid, marvellous bread!

hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.stage.2.d: The gold slid off my hands into the bucket like sand. Keep the nuggets; I've had enough of the stuff.

hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.talk.1: Gold is lovely until you try to eat it.
