hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.talk.3: My daughter is flesh again, thank the gods. I still count her fingers every morning.
hearthbound.persona.myth_midas.title: Everything I touch
I once rode a cannonball into an enemy fortress, then hopped onto one flying back. I pulled myself out of a swamp by my own hair. All true.
Nobody believes me, and that's the whole point. The one story I never tell is the true one, about the day I ran away.
hearthbound.persona.myth_munchausen.dial: Ah, a new face! Sit, sit. Did I ever tell you about the time I went to the moon? Twice, in fact.
The second trip was easier. I knew where the good cheese was.
Speaking of cannonballs: I once rode one into an enemy fortress, then hopped onto one flying back. The view was superb.
The children don't believe it. They say I've never even seen a cannon. That hurts. Professionally.
So I've decided: I'll recreate the famous ride. For science. For the children. For my good name, what's left of it.
I have the cannon, more or less. It's a barrel with ambitions. What it lacks is a proper bang.
Bring me gunpowder, would you? Lots of it. Eight measures, at least. Heroes don't do things halfway.
Don't look at me like that. You don't believe me? Excellent. That means you're paying attention.
I once tied my horse to a stump in deep snow. By morning the snow had melted, and there it hung, from a church steeple.
I shot it down, naturally. The horse, not the steeple. The priest was very understanding.
They call me the Baron at the tavern. I was never a baron. I told them so, and they didn't believe that either.
In the old tales there was a Baron Munchausen who told stories like mine. Clearly he copied me. Or I him. Hard to say.
I've fought wars, survived shipwrecks and hunted ducks with a single piece of bacon. Every word true, mostly.
Children follow me through the square begging for stories. Grown-ups roll their eyes. The children are right.
There's one story I never tell. Don't ask which. It's the only one without a cannonball in it.
Well, the cannonball went up. I stayed down. A minor technical detail. The children cheered anyway.
One of them asked if I'd do it again tomorrow. I said the cannon needs to rest. Cannons are sensitive.
You never ask me to prove anything. You just listen. It's very unsettling. I rather like it.
Now, the swamp is real. I could take you there, if it weren't full of bouncing green nuisances.
Great wobbling blobs that split in two whenever you hit them. They've eaten three of my walking sticks.
I promised the children I'd show them the exact spot where I pulled myself out. My honour hangs on it, and my hair.
Would you clear those slimes out for me? Eight should do. Then the spot is ours, and the story too.
My eyebrows will grow back, I'm told. In the meantime I've drawn them on. Rather dashing, no?
Let me tell you properly about the swamp. My horse and I sank to the ears, and nobody was coming.
So I grabbed my own pigtail and pulled. Up I came, horse and all, clamped between my knees. Simple physics.
Then there was the duck hunt: one long string, one piece of bacon, twelve ducks swallowing it in a row. They flew me home.
And the stag I shot with cherry stones. Years later I met him again, with a cherry tree growing between his antlers.
You're smiling. Good. That's what they're for. A story that makes someone smile has done honest work.
Sometimes I wonder, though. If I stopped telling them, would anyone still sit at my table?
The tales are like a big coat. Warm, loud, full of pockets. Nobody sees who's inside.
There it is: the exact spot! Admittedly it looks a lot like any other puddle. The children loved it anyway.
One little girl stood in it and pulled her own hair. Nothing happened. She said I must be much stronger. I let her think so.
My dream is small. To stand in front of her once and not have to be anyone larger than I am.
In one letter, long ago, I promised her a pebble from the moon. She was seven. She kept an empty box for it.
She still has that box, I'm told. Someone from her village saw it on her shelf. Still empty. Still waiting.
I climbed a bean plant to the moon once, chasing my silver hatchet. The tall dark wanderers carry pebbles from up there, I'm sure of it.
Bring me three of those pebbles? I owe that little girl the one story of mine that ends up true.
You've earned something. Not a tall tale. A short one. The only one that's true.
When I was fifteen I ran away from home. No cannonball, no moon. Just a window, a sack, and a road at night.
My father drank and shouted. I was afraid, and I left. I left my little sister asleep in the next bed.
I told myself I'd come back for her with a fortune. All I gathered were stories, and I never really went back.
Instead I wrote to her. Every letter an adventure: sea serpents, giants, the moon. I couldn't bear to write the truth.
She believed every word. She wrote back asking for more. That's where the Baron was born, in those letters.
Every lie I tell in the tavern is really a letter to her. I've just forgotten how to write anything else.
My fear? That she knows. That she's always known I was a frightened child in a ditch, and was too kind to say.
Behold: moon pebbles! Nobody will doubt me now. Well, they will, but I'll have pebbles.
Is the crossbow treating you well? It really did shoot down a comet. A small one. Mostly sparks.
The exact spot in the swamp has a little sign now: 'Here the Baron pulled himself out.' The children painted it.
I don't need the big coat so much any more. I still wear it on feast days. It's very warm.
You know the funny thing? Your stories are the only ones I can't top. It's infuriating, and I'm grateful.
If anyone ever asks about me, tell them I went to the moon. Twice. And that once I came home, for real.
Sit, sit, the night is young. Did I ever tell you about the whale that swallowed a whole ship? Every word true...
I sent one pebble to my sister, in a box just the right size. And with it, a letter. A true one, this time.
I wrote about the window, the ditch, the fear. Four pages. It took me a week and most of a candle.
She answered: 'I always knew. I kept the letters because you were in them.' I read it standing, then had to sit down.
She's coming to visit in spring. I've told her the moon is lovely this time of year. Old habits.
I still tell the cannonball story in the tavern. But now there's a new one I tell very quietly, near the end of the night.
It's about a traveller who fought slimes in a swamp, brought pebbles from the sky, and never once exaggerated.
The children don't believe that one. Nobody could be that sensible, they say. I tell them I've met you.
My eyebrows grew back, by the way. Slightly crooked. I tell people a comet singed them.
hearthbound.persona.myth_munchausen.epil: Since then there's one story they tell very quietly, and it's the only true one: the one about a traveller who never needed to exaggerate.
hearthbound.persona.myth_munchausen.sour: The Surprising Adventures of Baron Munchausen — Rudolf Erich Raspe (1785)
hearthbound.persona.myth_munchausen.stag: I'm going to recreate the famous cannonball ride, for science and for the children. Bring me gunpowder. Lots.
Well, the cannonball went up. I stayed down. A minor technical detail.
The swamp I pulled myself out of by my hair is full of bouncing green nuisances. Clear them, so I can show the children the exact spot.
There it is: the exact spot! Admittedly it looks a lot like any other puddle.
I climbed to the moon on a bean plant once. I lost my silver hatchet up there. Bring me moon pebbles to prove it.
Behold: moon pebbles! Nobody will doubt me now. Take my crossbow; it once shot down a comet.
hearthbound.persona.myth_munchausen.talk: Did I tell you about the time I went to the moon? Twice?
I tied my horse to a stump in the snow. By morning it hung from a church steeple.
You don't believe me. Excellent. That means you're paying attention.
Your adventures are the only stories in this tavern I can't top. It's infuriating.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.bio.0: I built a ship that sails beneath the waves and lived in it for years, far from every king and every war. I swore never to set foot on land again.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.bio.1: The land took everything from me once: my home, my family. The sea gave me silence. I came ashore only because the sea began to feel lonely too.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.dialogue.0: You may stand there. Not too close. I'm still learning how close people stand on land.
The surface is noisy. Down there, even the fish whisper.
I kept my word for a long time. I ate kelp and fish, and dressed in silk spun from shellfish.
Everything on board was made by the sea. Even the ink I wrote with came from a squid.
My ship was shaped like a shell. The most perfect shell there is: the spiral of the nautilus.
I've been drawing it again, from memory. My hands keep getting it wrong. I need to hold one.
Bring me nautilus shells? I want to study how they hold the pressure of the deep. Two will do.
I don't give my name. Call me 'Nobody', if you need to call me something.
I've walked through forests of kelp and cities no one remembers. The village is almost as strange.
You walk softly. Good. Most people here stomp as though the ground owed them money.
I once built a ship that sails beneath the waves. Long, dark, shaped like a sea creature.
Sailors on the surface thought it was a monster. Harpoons bounced off. I let them believe it.
Inside there was a library of twelve thousand books, an organ, and a window onto the deep.
I lived in it for years. My crew spoke a language no one on land understood. That was the point.
I swore never to set foot on land again. No kings, no wars, no flags. Only the sea.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.dialogue.1: Perfect spirals. The sea knew how to build ships long before we did.
I sat all night with one to my ear. It still sounds like my old engine room. Or I imagine it.
Soon it was just me, and the ship, and twelve thousand books. The sea began to feel lonely too.
So I came ashore. Only because of that. I'm not cured of anything. I'm just very tired of echoes.
The drowned temples are guarded now. Spiked things with one eye, beams that burn in the water.
I want to go back, just once. To the coral garden. To say something I didn't say then.
Clear a few of the guardians of the ruins? I want to go back, just once. Only once.
You brought me something from the sea without asking why. So I'll tell you why I left the land.
The land took everything from me once: my home, my family. A war. A flag I won't name.
I came home to ashes. The one I loved, my children. After that, I wanted nothing that walked on dry ground.
So I went down, where no king could follow. The sea gave me silence. I thought silence was peace.
I sank ships that carried soldiers. I'm not proud of that. I'm not sure I'm ashamed either.
Down there I found drowned temples. Old, older than any kingdom. Columns of green light.
I'd go and sit in them for hours. The only place that felt like a home without people in it.
Then one night my crew began to die, one by one, and I buried them in a coral garden.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.dialogue.2: The way is clear. I went down this morning. The ruins remembered me.
The coral garden has grown over them. Pink and orange and alive. I said what I had to say.
My dream: a small window to the sea, here at the harbour. Glass and stone, so anyone can look in.
The shards the guardians leave behind, the blue-green ones, they hold light the way the deep does.
If I line the window with them, it'll glow at night, and the fish will come to see who's looking.
It will be the first thing I've built for the land. For people. In a very long time.
Bring me prismarine shards to line it? Enough for a window to the deep. For the children.
Now the deepest thing. Maybe I didn't hate the land. Maybe I only hated being on it with no one.
I signed my letters 'Nobody' for years. Letters to no one. I threw them into the sea in bottles.
I'm frightened of how much I like this village. The baker's laugh. The children running past my door.
If I love it, the land can take it from me. That's what the land does. It's what I've always believed.
But the sea takes things too. It took my crew. Maybe nothing is safe. Maybe that's not the question.
I watched the children at the harbour yesterday. They were throwing stones, trying to see the bottom.
They'll never see what I've seen. The forests of kelp. The cities under the silt. The whales singing.
Unless someone shows them. Unless someone makes a window, like the one I had on my ship.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.dialogue.3: Now anyone can look into the deep. Keep my helm; you'll go further down than I ever did.
The children press their noses against the glass every morning. The fish press back. It's a stand-off.
I don't hate the land anymore. I don't love it yet, either. I'm learning. It's slow, like a tide.
You brought me shells and shards and cleared my path to the dead. I owe you more than a name.
But I'll give you a name anyway. My real one. Come closer. ...There. Now you're the only one who knows.
If you ever look into deep water and feel it looking back, don't be afraid. That's just the sea saying hello.
Go on, then. Walk your dry roads. I'll be at the window, watching both worlds at once.
The baker brings bread to the window at dawn. She says it tastes better with a view.
I still sign every letter 'Nobody'. But now I address them to people in the village.
The mayor got one yesterday. It was about the drains. He was very moved. I don't know why.
I've opened my books to anyone who wants them. Twelve thousand, less what I lost. The shelves groan.
A girl asked me how the ship worked. I drew it for her on the harbour wall. She understood it all.
Maybe she'll build one someday. I hope she builds it with a window, and a door, and a way home.
Remember the guardians? I still dream of their eye opening in the dark. Now you're in the dream too.
I went down to the coral garden again last month. I left flowers. Land flowers. They floated.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.epilogue: They still sign every letter with a single word: 'Nobody'. But now the letters are addressed to people in the village.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.source: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas — Jules Verne (1870)

hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.stage.0.do: Perfect spirals. The sea knew how to build ships long before we did.

hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.stage.1.do: The way is clear. I went down this morning. The ruins remembered me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.stage.2.as: I want to build a small window to the sea here, at the harbour, for the children. Bring me prismarine shards to line it.

hearthbound.persona.myth_nemo.title: Twenty thousand leagues down
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.bio.0: In the tales, the all-father gave an eye to drink from the well of wisdom. When I was young I gave up my sight in one eye to a fever, and called it a bargain.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.bio.1: I've wandered for years in a grey cloak, asking questions at strangers' fires. I've collected a thousand answers. I'm still missing the one that matters.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.dialogue.0: Sit, sit. The fire is warmer when someone else is looking at it too.
Those two ravens on the roof are with me. The fat one is Thought, the loud one is Memory. Ignore them both.
Lately the answers slip away. Yesterday I forgot the name of a river I crossed forty times.
The ravens noticed. Memory has been sulking on the chimney all week.
If I lose what I've gathered, the eye was paid for nothing. That frightens me more than the dead do.
I've been thinking I should write it all down. Every answer, every fire, before the cup leaks dry.
Would you bring me paper? Sixteen sheets should start it. Wisdom is heavier than it looks.
You wonder about the eye. Everyone does. Ask; I like people who ask.
I've slept by more strangers' fires than I have fingers, toes and grey hairs combined.
Bread tastes different in every village. Here it tastes of patience. I approve.
When I was small a fever took the sight of my left eye. I told my mother it was a bargain.
The old tales say the all-father gave an eye to drink from a well of wisdom. I decided mine had bought something too.
So I put on a grey cloak and started walking, to find out what I'd paid for.
I've asked questions at a hundred hearths. Why the rivers bend. Why the dead walk at night. Why bread rises.
I have a thousand answers in this old head. Yet one question stays empty, like a cup nobody fills.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.dialogue.1: Sixteen pages! My hand aches like after a day of rowing. A good ache.
I began with the big answers and somehow ended up explaining how to boil an egg. It seemed urgent at the time.
There's a doubt that sits with me at night. What if the question I'm missing isn't anywhere I've been?
I've listened at every fire in this valley. I know who snores, who lies, who sings off-key.
There must be someone, somewhere, with a question I've never heard. That's where the missing piece lives.
My legs are old and the dead are many. But you walk far and fast, I've watched you.
Find me a village I've never visited. Somewhere with a new fire, and a new mouth asking something new.
Writing is strange. On paper, my wisdom looks smaller and much more crooked.
Here is a secret: I never truly knew why I left home. I only knew staying felt like closing my good eye too.
My mother cried when I went. I wrote to her from every village, and never once said where I was going.
Because I didn't know. A wanderer who admits that is rare. Most pretend they have a map.
Page nine is about a fisherman who taught me to read clouds. Page ten is about his wife, who taught me to be quiet.
Thought the raven tore a corner off page twelve. I suspect he disagreed with it.
Rereading, I noticed something: every answer came from someone who stopped to talk. Not one came from a book.
Which makes me wonder if the well in the tale was ever water at all.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.dialogue.2: A child asked me why the sky doesn't fall. I had no answer! Do you know how long it's been?
I laughed so hard the ravens flew off. They came back offended, but they came back.
Do you think someone can be looking for something he already had and walked away from?
The ravens think so. Memory keeps landing on your roof instead of mine. Traitor.
There's one last thing I want to try. They say an eye of ender seeks out what is hidden.
If it can find strongholds under the earth, maybe it can find what I was looking for when I gave mine away.
Bring me one, friend. Let the green eye look for me, since mine is tired of looking.
Not knowing felt like the first spring after a long winter. I'd forgotten that feeling.
I'll tell you something I've never told anyone. The fever that took my eye nearly took the rest of me.
I lay for nine days in the dark. My mother sat by me and asked, over and over, if I could hear her.
I could. I couldn't answer. I think I've been answering her questions ever since, to every stranger I meet.
The truth is, I'm afraid of stopping. If I sit still, I'll have to admit the cup is still empty.
My dream is foolish: to find the thing I was looking for, and then, for once, to stay.
The tales say the all-father saw everything from his high seat, and was still lonely. I understand him better every year.
Some nights I hold my hand over the good eye and try to see what the blind one sees. Only darkness, and my mother's voice.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.dialogue.3: The ender eye rose, spun in the air, and pointed straight at you. I nearly fell off my stool.
Of course it did. I spent forty years asking strangers, and the answer was simply someone who sat down and listened.
You never once gave me an answer I expected. That is the highest praise I know.
My blind eye still sees darkness, but these days it's the soft kind, like a room where someone is sleeping.
If you ever feel you're walking without knowing why, come sit here. I know the feeling well.
The fire's warmer with two. I said that the first day, didn't I? I was right, for once.
Go on, the road is waiting for you. I'll be here, listening, with a question saved for when you return.
You kept my glass, I hope. See far for both of us; I've seen quite enough of distances.
I finished the book. Last page says: 'The well was a friend. Drink often.' Too short, but true.
The egg-boiling chapter remains the most popular. People have no respect for philosophy.
I wrote to my mother's grave, back home. I told her, finally, where I'd gone. Here.
The ravens refuse to comment on any of this. Thought says it's beneath him. Memory says she knew all along.
I've unpacked the grey cloak. It hangs by the door, and I don't look at it more than twice a day.
The child from that far village sent me a new question: why do cats sleep so much? I'm working on it.
Sometimes I still ask questions at the fire. Now I wait for you to answer them.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.epilogue: They say at last they know what they were looking for at the well: someone who would sit down and listen. The ravens, jealous, still refuse to comment.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.stage.0.as: I want to write down everything I've learned before I forget it. Bring me paper; wisdom is heavier than it looks.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.stage.0.do: Sixteen pages, and I've only reached the part about how to boil an egg. Wisdom takes its time.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.stage.1.as: I've listened at every fire in this valley. Find me a village I've never visited; there must be someone there with a new question.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.stage.1.do: A child there asked me why the sky doesn't fall. I didn't know. Marvellous!
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.stage.2.as: Bring me an eye of ender: they say it looks for what's hidden. Maybe it will show me what I was looking for when I gave mine away.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.stage.2.do: It pointed at you. Of course. Take my glass; see far for both of us.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.talk.0: Two ravens follow me everywhere. They gossip. Don't tell them anything.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.talk.1: A question is worth more than an answer. Answers end things.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.talk.2: I lost an eye and gained a habit of listening. Not a bad trade.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.talk.3: Every wanderer is looking for something. Most of us forget what it was halfway.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odin.title: An eye for the well
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.bio.0: I left for a war that lasted ten years, then spent ten more trying to get home. Storms, one-eyed giants, a witch who turned my friends into pigs.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.bio.1: Every road I took was the clever one, and every clever road led further from home. I stopped here because I'm ashamed to arrive so late.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.dialog: If a giant ever asks your name, tell him it's 'Nobody'. Works every time. Well, it worked once, and once was enough.
You walk like someone reading the ground. Good. Roads lie, but mud tells the truth.
I was too proud, sailing off. I shouted my real name back at him. His father rules the sea. The sea never forgave me.
Everything looks the same after twenty years of detours. Every coast is the wrong coast. Every harbour looks almost like mine.
I don't even know which direction home lies anymore. I've stopped trusting my own maps. I drew half of them.
Someone out there must know the road. Some village I haven't seen, where traders talk and sailors drink.
Would you go and find a village I haven't visited? Maybe someone there knows the way to my island.
Tie me to the mast if I start humming. Old habit. There's no mast here, so the fence will do.
I keep watch at night because I can't sleep anyway. Twenty years of rocking decks have ruined beds for me.
The village dog followed me home on my first day. Dogs always know who's been away too long.
I left my island for a war. They told us it would be over by the harvest. It lasted ten years.
We won it with a trick. A wooden horse, big as a barn. It was my idea. I've never been sure I'm proud of that.
Then we set sail for home. It should have taken weeks. I've been trying to get back ever since.
Storms, whirlpools, a one-eyed giant who kept us in his cave and ate my men two at a time. I told him my name was Nobody.
When I blinded him and ran, his brothers asked who'd hurt him. 'Nobody!' he shouted. They went back to bed.
They pointed east. They laughed when you told them how long I'd been walking. I laughed too, when you told me. Then I didn't.
East. All this time, and my island is east. I spent three years sailing west because a clever captain said it was faster.
One by one I lost them all. The last ones to a whirlpool and a six-headed thing. I came ashore alone, clinging to a plank.
I've faced monsters without blinking. But I'm afraid to think of my men as they were before: laughing, rowing, alive.
And now I hear the ones who turn men into beasts still brew by the marsh here. Same sweet smell. Same bubbling pots.
The sailors who come up the river vanish sometimes. I know where they go. I've been in one of those pens.
Stop them before they catch more sailors. Three of those witches should end it. Do it for my old crew.
That's my curse, you see. Every road I took was the clever one, and every clever road led further from home.
Once a king of winds gave me a bag with every storm tied inside. We sailed until we saw the smoke of our own chimneys.
I fell asleep. My crew thought the bag held gold and opened it. The winds blew us all the way back to the start.
After that, an island with a witch. She turned half my crew into pigs with a cup of something sweet.
They still had their own eyes, looking out of those pig faces. I'll never forget it. They knew. They knew the whole time.
I got them back, with a herb and a lot of bargaining. But I stayed a year on that island. A year. I told myself I was resting.
Then the singing rocks, where voices call you to your death so beautifully you'd thank them for it. Tied to the mast, I begged.
My crew had wax in their ears. They rowed while I screamed. I was never so grateful to be ignored.
No more pigs with human eyes. My old crew would buy you a drink, if any were left. So I'll buy it for them.
I raised a cup at the marsh's edge last night. One for each name. It took a long time. I remembered every one.
I've faced monsters without blinking. A letter home is the only thing I've ever been unable to write alone.
So I've been writing it for a month. Fourteen drafts. The first thirteen were too clever. This one just says the truth.
The merchant in the next village sails towards my island every spring. He could carry it to her.
If I go myself, I'll get lost again. You know I will. I'll take a clever shortcut and end up at the edge of the world.
Please carry my letter to the next village. The straight road. Don't let me near it, or I'll find a way to make it longer.
Someone has been weaving and unweaving the same cloth for twenty years, waiting for me. My wife.
She promised the suitors at our door she'd choose once the shroud was finished. She unpicks it every night. I know her.
And a son, a baby when I left. He'll be a man now. He might not know my face. I'm not sure he'd want to.
Here's the shame I haven't told anyone: I spent seven years on another island, with a nymph who loved me and wouldn't let me go.
I wept every day on her beach. But I also stayed. Both are true. I've never known how to tell one without the other.
I stopped here because I'm ashamed to arrive so late. What do you say after twenty years? 'Sorry, the wind'?
My fear is that I'll walk into my own hall and find a stranger's life there. That she stopped weaving. That she was right to.
My dream is small: my old dog at the gate, my wife at her loom, and bread on the table that I didn't have to trick anyone for.
The reply came fast, in a hand I'd know anywhere. Just four words. 'The door is open.'
I read it every morning. It hangs by the door. I read it every evening too. It still says the same thing. I check.
When I leave, look after the fence I tied myself to. The children think it's a mast. Let them.
I'll write when I arrive. A real letter. Probably late. Some habits are harder to break than giants.
If you ever sail past a small rocky island with goats and a loom by the window, stop. There'll be bread, and no tricks.
Twenty years of the long way. Maybe it had to be long, so I'd know the short way when I saw it.
Go on, then, friend. The door is open, it says. Yours too, here, whenever you come back.
Did you keep the bow I gave you? Only someone who comes back deserves it. You always come back. That's rarer than cleverness.
I've started packing. Very slowly. A shirt a day. The short way home, the old sailor says, is the one you walk step by step.
The village dog sleeps by my pack now. He knows. Dogs always know when someone's about to go home.
People ask if I'm afraid of the suitors. I tell them I've faced a one-eyed giant. They should be afraid of her, not me.
I realised something: I stopped for so long not because I was lost, but because I was scared of being found.
You found me. Twice, really. Once when you asked about the letter, and once when you carried it without asking why it took so long.
I still say 'Nobody' when a stranger asks my name. But I say it smiling now. Here, somebody knows who I am.
Last night I dreamed of the sea, and for once it wasn't angry. Just grey and calm, like it had finally forgotten my shouting.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.epilog: Now the reply hangs by the door, just four words: 'The door is open.' They've started packing, very slowly, the short way.
Everything looks the same after twenty years of detours. Find a village I haven't seen, maybe someone there knows the road.
They pointed east. They laughed when I said how long I'd been walking. So did I.
The ones who turn men into beasts still brew by the marsh. I lost friends to their pots. Stop them before they catch more sailors.
No more pigs with human eyes. My old crew would buy you a drink, if any were left.
I wrote it. Please carry it to the next village; their merchant sails towards my island. If I go myself, I'll get lost again.
The reply came fast, in a hand I'd know anywhere. Take my bow: only someone who comes back deserves it.

hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.talk.1: Tie me to the mast if I start humming. Old habit.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.talk.2: Someone has been weaving and unweaving the same cloth for twenty years, waiting for me.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.talk.3: I've faced monsters without blinking. A letter home is the only thing I can't write alone.
hearthbound.persona.myth_odysseus.title: Ten years of the long way
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.bio.0: When I sing, the birds go quiet and the rocks lean in to listen. The day the one I loved died of a snakebite, I stopped singing altogether.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.bio.1: The old tales say that a song sad enough can open the gates below. I don't want to believe it. I want it so badly that I've started rehearsing.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.dialogu: Hum with me, it's easy. No? Everyone's shy the first time.
Stones make the best audience. They never leave before the end.
The day of the burial, I closed my lyre in a box. The strings snapped in the cold since then.
My old instruments cracked in the silence. Wood forgets its shape if nobody plays it.
Lately I catch myself tapping rhythms on the table. My hands want to sing, even if my throat doesn't.
I think I have to learn again from nothing. One note. Then two. The way children learn.
Would you bring me note blocks? I'll learn to sing again, one note at a time. I promise to try.
I wrote a verse about you. It's mostly about your muddy boots. It rhymes with 'roots'.
The sparrows on my roof used to go quiet when I sang. Now they sing over me. It's their turn.
People say I had a voice once that made the rocks lean in. People exaggerate. Slightly.
I haven't sung properly in a long time. I hum. Humming doesn't count. Humming is hiding.
There was someone. We married in the spring. The wedding torches smoked and wouldn't catch.
Everyone laughed it off. A bad omen, the old women said. I told them omens are for cowards.
A few days later, walking through the meadow, a snake. A tiny bite on the ankle. That was all.
I carried my love home. By evening there was nobody left to carry.
Listen... it still works. My throat is rusty, but my heart remembered the melody.
I played until midnight. The innkeeper cried. The dog howled. I'll take both as praise.
The road below is dark. Darker than any mine. Nothing lights it but what burns in the red lands.
I've looked into the portal ruins past the hills. The air smells of sulphur and grief.
If I go, I need fire I can carry. Fire that doesn't go out when fear blows on it.
I'm not asking you to come down with me. Only to help me light the way, there and back.
Bring me blaze rods? To light the road down and, if the tales are kind, the road back up.
Now I'll tell you the secret I keep under the humming. Promise not to laugh.
The old tales say a song sad enough can open the gates below. Where the dead go.
I don't want to believe it. I want it so badly that I've started rehearsing.
Every night, a verse. Every verse, sadder. My neighbours think I have a very sad cat.
In the oldest version, a singer went down alive, and the ferryman of the dead let him cross for a song.
The three-headed dog lay down to listen. The wheel of the damned stopped turning, just for a while.
I don't know if that's true. I know that when I sing, something far away holds its breath.
Am I mad? You can say it. I've said it to myself every morning while shaving my hope.
I can feel the heat in my hands. There's no excuse now: the path is lit.
I sat all night with the rods glowing on the table. I didn't sleep. I composed.
If I could hold one of those tears, I'd know my song could reach down there. I'd sing to it.
The weeping ghosts of the red lands cry tears like that. Great white things that sob as they fly.
I know what I'm asking. Their fire is cruel. But you've carried fire for me before.
I don't want the gates to open for me alone. I want to know that love can be heard from below.
Bring me a tear of the weeping ghosts? I'll sing to it until the gates open. Or until I'm answered.
Here is the part of the story nobody wants to hear. The singer in the tale failed.
The lord of the dead let the singer's love go back, on one condition: don't look back.
Walk ahead, trust the footsteps behind you, and never turn around until you reach the sun.
He almost made it. At the very edge of the light, he couldn't bear it, and turned. And lost everything.
That's why I made you promise, remember? If you ever have to come back from somewhere, don't look.
My deepest fear is not the dark below. It's my own neck. I know I'm the kind who turns.
I've been practising. Walking to the well without looking back. The children follow me, giggling.
They say the lord of the dead only wept once, ever, and it was at a song.
I sang, and something sang back from very far away. I didn't look back. I swear I didn't.
Nobody knows what came up that night. I'm not going to tell you. Some songs lose their shine if explained.
Remember the night I burned my fingers on a blaze rod? I composed a very rude song about it.
I keep the ghast tear in a little glass vial on a string. Warm. Not sad anymore. Just full.
If you ever have to go somewhere dark, hum. You don't need a good voice. You need company.
I lost a voice and found two. And a friend who carried fire and tears for a fool with a lyre.
Go on, walk ahead. I won't look back at you either. I'll just sing, and you'll know I'm here.
But I sing in two voices now. The second one you'll never see. Listen closely at dusk.
The innkeeper swears she hears a harmony when I'm alone in the cellar. She's stopped asking.
I walked home that night without turning my head once. My neck hurt for a week. Worth it.
The sparrows are quiet again when I sing. Not out of respect, I think. Out of curiosity.
I've started teaching the children. They're dreadful. They're wonderful. They look back all the time.
I tell them it's fine for them. Looking back is only dangerous when you're carrying something precious.
The stones behind the inn still lean in to listen. I'm almost sure they've moved a hand closer.
I finished that verse about your boots. It's now eleven verses. It's become an epic about mud.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.epilogu: Nobody knows what came up from below that night. But now the song has two voices, and the second one is never seen.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.stage.0: My old instruments cracked in the silence. Bring me note blocks and I'll learn to sing again, one note at a time.
Listen... it still works. My throat is rusty, but my heart remembered the melody.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.stage.1: The road below is lit only by what burns in the red lands. Bring me blaze rods, to light the way there and back.
I can feel the heat in my hands. There's no excuse now: the path is lit.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.stage.2: They say the lord of the dead wept only once, at a song. Bring me a tear of the weeping ghosts, and I'll sing to it until the gates open.
I sang, and something sang back from very far away. I didn't look back. I swear, this time I didn't look back.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.talk.0: Hum with me, it's easy. No? Everyone's shy the first time.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.talk.1: Stones make the best audience. They never leave before the end.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.talk.2: I wrote a verse about you. It's mostly about your muddy boots.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.talk.3: If you ever go somewhere and have to come back, don't look behind you. Promise me that.
hearthbound.persona.myth_orpheus.title: A song for the underworld
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.bio.0: There was a sealed jar in my attic with a note: 'Never open.' Of course I opened it. Things flew out, small and fast and many-legged.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.bio.1: Everyone blames me for every bad night since. But when the jar was empty I heard something still moving at the bottom, very softly. I closed the lid on it.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.dialogu: Oh! You startled me. Come in, but don't touch anything with a lid. Anything. I'm serious.
Curiosity is a terrible landlord and a wonderful friend.
I screamed. The neighbours came. By then the things were gone into the cracks of the world.
Since then the mines have been crawling with little venomous things. Everyone knows where they came from.
The miners say it to my face. 'Your jar.' They're not wrong. I opened it. It's my mess.
I can't go down into the dark myself; I faint at the sight of too many legs. It's embarrassing.
The first things out went down into the mines. Hunt them, please? It's my mess, but I can't clean it alone.
If you find a sealed jar, leave it sealed. Or at least call me first.
I read every letter that isn't mine. I'm working on it. It's been a slow year.
You look curious too. It's in the eyebrows. We'd better keep an eye on each other.
When I moved into this house, the attic was locked. The key hung right next to the lock. Rude, really.
Up there, under a blanket of dust, was a big clay jar. Sealed with wax, and a note tied to it.
'Never open.' Two words. Who writes that and expects it to work? It's practically an invitation.
I held out for a week. Then one night, with a candle and a bread knife, I cut the seal.
Things flew out. Small and fast and many-legged. They ran over my hands and down the stairs.
Fewer legs in the dark. One mess cleaned up. A few hundred left, but still. Thank you.
The miners nodded at me today. Not smiled. Nodded. It's a start. I baked them a cake anyway.
They say I let every sorrow into the world. They forget I kept one thing in.
But there's something else that escaped. The worst one, maybe. The thing that steals sleep.
People lie awake, night after night, worrying. Then the grey wings come down for the sleepless.
I watch them from my window, circling. They're drawn to worry like moths to a lamp.
Clear the night sky of them? The thing that keeps people awake until the grey wings come. Please.
Now I'll tell you the part I don't tell. Everyone blames me for every bad night since that jar.
Sour milk? The jar. A cough? The jar. The baker's burnt loaves? Apparently, also the jar.
There's an old tale of a woman named Pandora, made by the gods and given a jar she mustn't open.
When I first heard it, I laughed. Then I stopped laughing, because it sounded a lot like my attic.
I wonder sometimes if someone left that jar there on purpose. For someone like me. Curious enough.
And here's the secret. When the jar was empty, I heard something still moving at the bottom.
Very softly. Like a bird's heartbeat, or someone breathing in their sleep.
I panicked. I closed the lid on it. I didn't even look. I was too scared of what else might come out.
The village slept well last night. I didn't, but that's my own fault. I was listening to the jar.
The jar still sits on my table. Sometimes I put my ear to it. It's warm.
But whatever's in there is afraid of the dark. I can tell. It shivers when I blow out the candle.
It's been in the dark for so long. It shouldn't come out into more dark. It deserves some light.
The glowing dust from the red lands, the kind that shines without burning. That's what I want.
If I fill a lantern with it, and set it by the lid, whatever comes out will have somewhere bright to go.
Bring me something that glows? I'm going to open the jar again, just a crack. For the thing that stayed.
Warmer each night. And the sound inside has changed. It used to breathe. Now it hums.
I'm afraid. Not of what's in there. Of being wrong again. Of opening a lid and ruining everything twice.
But I've also realised something. I kept it in the dark all this time. In a sealed jar. Alone.
If it's what I think it is, it can't do any good down there. It needs the world. It needs people.
In the old tale, the last thing left in the jar was hope. Just that. The one gift that stayed behind.
I used to think closing the lid was the only good thing I ever did. Now I think it was the worst.
My dream is this: to open something on purpose, for once. Carefully. Gently. For the right reason.
I'm going to open the jar again. Just a crack. I've decided. My hands are shaking just saying it.
It came out slowly and sat in the lantern like a small sun. Keep a little. Everyone needs some.
It doesn't do much. It doesn't cure coughs or fix burnt loaves. It just glows. It's enough.
They always ask which one won. I tell them to come back at night and look at the lantern.
You went into the mines and into the night sky for someone the whole village blamed. I won't forget that.
If you ever find a sealed jar on your road, call me. Not to open it. Just to sit with you while you decide.
The lantern flickers when you leave. I think it likes you. I know I do.
Go on, then. Carry your little piece of light. There's more here whenever you run low.
No more blaming at the well. On the worst nights, people knock on my door to borrow a little light.
The miller came first. His wife was ill. He sat by the lantern for an hour and left looking lighter.
Then the miners. Then the baker. I've started keeping chairs by the door. And cake.
The jar is empty now. Truly empty. I planted a geranium in it. It's very happy.
I still read letters that aren't mine. Only the boring ones, though. The interesting ones I give back.
Remember how I fainted at the spiders? I held one yesterday. A tiny one. For almost a breath.
Curiosity is still a terrible landlord. But I've learned how to be a better tenant.
The children ask me what was in the jar. I tell them: everything bad, and one thing good.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.epilogu: Since then there has been no more blaming at the well. On the worst nights, people knock on that door to borrow a little light.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.stage.0: The first things out were small and many-legged, and they went down into the mines. Hunt them, please; it's my mess.
Fewer legs in the dark. One mess cleaned up. A few hundred left, but still.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.stage.1: Something else got out: the thing that keeps people awake until the grey wings come for them. Clear the night sky.
The village slept well last night. I didn't, but that's my own fault.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.stage.2: I'm going to open the jar again, just a crack. What's left inside is afraid of the dark. Bring me something that glows.
It came out slowly and sat in the lantern like a small sun. Take it with you. Everyone needs some.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.talk.0: If you find a sealed jar, leave it sealed. Or at least call me first.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.talk.1: Curiosity is a terrible landlord and a wonderful friend.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.talk.2: The jar still sits on my table. Sometimes I put my ear to it. It's warm.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.talk.3: They say I let every sorrow into the world. They forget I kept one thing in.
hearthbound.persona.myth_pandora.title: The jar in the attic
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.bio.0: Someone I love sailed away twenty years ago. Suitors crowd my door, so I promised to choose once this cloth is finished. Every night I unpick it.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.bio.1: I'm not waiting because I'm patient. I'm waiting because I'm stubborn, and because the day I finish this cloth I'll have to admit what I believe.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.dialog: Mind the threads, please. Some of them I've woven eleven thousand times. They deserve a little respect.
Sit, if you can find a stool the suitors haven't broken. That one wobbles. So does that one. Stand, perhaps.
I told them I'd choose one when this cloth was finished. A shroud, I said, for an old relative. It was a good lie.
Every day I weave it. Every night, by candlelight, I unpick the day's work. Thread by thread. Row by row.
The trouble is, the cloth has to look like it's growing, or they'll notice. Some of them are sharper than they look. Not many.
My wool is worn thin from being woven and unwoven so often. It's frayed and grey. It looks like what it is: a trick.
Bring me fresh wool, a good armful, so the day's work looks honest. I'll handle the night's work myself.
Patience is just stubbornness with better manners. I've had twenty years to polish mine.
The suitors eat my bread and sing badly. I've started burning the bread on purpose. They haven't noticed yet.
You don't look at the loom the way they do. They look at it like a clock. You look at it like a loom.
Twenty years ago, someone I love sailed away to a war across the sea. Just for a season, they said.
I stood on the harbour wall until the sail was a speck, then a guess, then nothing. I came home and started weaving.
The war ended long ago. Other ships came home. Neighbours hugged at the docks. I brought them bread and went back to my loom.
Some sailors say they saw that ship blown off course. Others say it sank. One swore he'd seen it sail into the sunset on purpose.
After a few years, the suitors came. Men who wanted the house, the fields, and me, in roughly that order.
Beautiful wool. It'll look splendid until about midnight. Then it'll look splendid again tomorrow, by noon.
One of the suitors praised the colour today. He said I'd be finished by spring. I smiled and said, 'Surely.'
Meanwhile, the nights are getting worse. The suitors aren't the only ones knocking at my door after dark.
Pests have grown bold: shambling dead, rattling skeletons, the things that hiss by the woodpile. They've been circling the houses.
The village doesn't sleep. The children cry. The suitors, bless them, have taken to sleeping in my kitchen for safety.
I can't weave at night if I'm listening for scratching at the shutters. And I can't unpick if the suitors are all indoors.
Clear them from around the houses, would you? Stand guard one night, and let the village sleep, and let me work.
You might wonder why I bother. Why not just tell them no? Because they'd take the house anyway. The cloth keeps them polite.
The first year, I unpicked with my teeth set, angry. Now I unpick like breathing. Some nights I hum while I do it.
Sometimes I weave the sea into it. Then I unpick the sea, too. It's easier than waiting.
I've woven faces into it: the one who left, my child as a baby, my old dog. None of them lasted past midnight.
My child is grown now, half at sea himself, looking for news. He comes back each time with a story and no ship.
My maids know about the unpicking. One of them almost told a suitor last month, for a ribbon. I don't blame her. Ribbons are nice.
The truth is, I'm not waiting because I'm patient. I'm waiting because I'm stubborn. I want to be right.
And there's another thing. The day I finish this cloth, I'll have to admit what I believe. I'm not ready to say it.
Quiet at last. Even the suitors went home, frightened by all that noise. A double victory. I unpicked in peace till dawn.
I have a confession. That night, with nobody watching, I didn't unpick straight away. I just looked at the cloth. It's lovely.
I'll announce a test: whoever strings that bow and shoots straight may speak to me about marriage. Just speak.
None of them has the knack. But they're strong fools, and strength might do what skill can't, with a weak string.
So the string must be the best in the land. Tight, strong, perfect. Strong enough that none of them manages it.
If they fail in front of everyone, they'll lose face, and a man who loses face leaves faster than one who loses an argument.
Bring me good strings, eight of them, so I can twist the finest bowstring ever made. And let's watch them struggle.
Twenty years of weaving and unweaving, and my hands have become very good. I'm the best weaver in the land. Nobody knows it.
Here's what I've never said to anyone: I don't know if the one I'm waiting for is alive. I've never known.
Some days I'm certain. Some days I'm certain of the opposite. The loom is the only place I don't have to choose.
My fear is that I've spent my life guarding a door nobody will walk through. And calling it faithfulness.
My other fear is the opposite: that they'll walk through, and I'll have become someone they won't recognise.
My dream is simple. I want to finish something. Anything. To tie the last knot and not pull it undone.
The suitors are growing impatient. One found a pile of unpicked thread under my bench. He didn't understand it. Yet.
So I need a new plan. In the storeroom is an old bow, the one my love used to string with one hand, laughing.
Nobody could string it. Not one. The biggest one turned purple. And I made a decision: that night I didn't unpick the cloth.
I finished it. I tied the last knot at dawn and didn't pull it undone. My hands shook. Then they didn't.
And the bowstring hangs by the door, still unstrung on the bow. I keep it as a reminder: some tests are meant to be failed.
You never asked me why I waited. Everyone else did. You just brought wool. That meant more than I can say.
My child came home last month and saw the sail and cried. Then asked if he could come. I said: bring your own oar.
When I set sail, you'll come to the harbour, won't you? Stand on the wall. Wave until I'm a speck. Then go and live.
Go on, then. Mind the threads on your way out, though there are fewer now. The cloth is finished, and so, at last, is the waiting.
It isn't a shroud. It never was. When I held it up, the whole room saw it: it's a sail. A big white sail with the sea woven in.
I think I knew all along. I was weaving a way to go, not a way to wait. It just took twenty years to admit it.
The loom stands still now. I dust it. I don't miss it. Well, I miss the humming, a little.
There's one more boat in the harbour. My sail is on it. The carpenter built the hull; I told him exactly how I wanted it.
I haven't sailed yet. I'm learning. The fishermen teach me knots. I already know every knot there is, but not the sailor's names.
If the one I love comes home, they'll find the door open and a note. If they don't, I'll go and look. Either way, I'm done waiting.
The suitors have mostly gone. One stayed to help with the boat. He's quite nice when he isn't eating my bread.
Remember the wool you brought me first? The white in the sail is that wool. I didn't unpick that part. Not once.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.epilog: The cloth is finished at last, but it isn't a shroud: it's a sail. Since then, the loom stands still and the harbour has one more boat.
The cloth has to look like it's growing, or they'll notice. Bring me wool so the day's work looks honest.
Beautiful. It'll look splendid until about midnight.
The pests who come knocking at night have grown bold. Clear them from around the houses so the village can sleep.
Quiet at last. Even the suitors went home, frightened by all that noise. A double victory.
I've announced a test: whoever strings the old bow may speak to me. I need good strings, strong enough that none of them manages it.
Nobody could string it. And I've made a decision: tonight I won't unpick the cloth.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.talk.0: Mind the threads, please. Some of them I've woven eleven thousand times.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.talk.1: Patience is just stubbornness with better manners.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.talk.2: The suitors eat my bread and sing badly. I've started burning the bread on purpose.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.talk.3: Sometimes I weave the sea into it. Then I unpick the sea, too. It's easier than waiting.
hearthbound.persona.myth_penelope.title: The cloth that never ends
I went up the mountain to escape my chores. Some odd little men were playing ninepins with a sound like thunder. I shared their drink and fell asleep.
When I woke up my beard reached my belt and my dog was gone. Twenty years had passed. My daughter has grey hair now. I missed all of it.
Morning! Or is it afternoon? I've learned not to trust my own sense of time. Long story. Very long, actually.
Is the old innkeeper still around? Big laugh, bad ale? No? Twenty years... right. I keep forgetting.
I came down to a village I didn't know. New faces, a new sign on the tavern. They laughed at my beard.
Twenty years, they said. I asked after my friends. Dead, gone to war, moved away. My wife, gone too.
My daughter took me in. Her hair is grey now. The last time I saw her she was a child with a doll.
There must be someone left who remembers me. My old friend Derrick moved to the next village, they say.
Would you carry him a letter? Tell him I'm... awake. That's the word. I'm finally awake.
Fine beard, isn't it? I trimmed it last week. It used to reach my belt. Grew it without trying, you might say.
I used to be the laziest soul in the valley. I'd mend anyone's fence but my own. My wife had words for that.
Never drink with strangers who bowl in the mountains. Very specific advice, I know. Take it anyway.
One autumn I took my gun and my dog up the mountain, just to escape the chores. Wolf, the dog was called.
Near the top, someone called my name. A little man in old-fashioned clothes, hauling a keg up the slope.
In a hollow, a whole crowd of them were playing ninepins. Every ball they rolled sounded like thunder.
Nobody spoke. They just drank and bowled with grave faces. I helped myself to their flagon. Several times.
I closed my eyes for a moment. When I opened them, my gun was rusted through and Wolf was nowhere.
An old friend answered! Derrick, the schoolmaster's boy. He thought I'd run off to escape my wife. He's half right.
He doesn't believe the mountain story. Nobody does. But he sent me a pouch of good tobacco, and that's belief enough.
My grandson thinks I'm the best storyteller alive. I just tell him what happened. That's the strange part.
Lately, at night, I hear it again from the mountain. That thunder. A rattling, like dry sticks.
The shepherds say the rattling ones play up there at night, pale things with bows. Not my little men. Worse.
A shepherd boy went up after a lost lamb and came back white as milk. What if he'd stayed? What if he'd slept?
Would you clear the mountain of those rattling things? Eight or so. Nobody else should lose twenty years.
Let me tell you what I never told the village. The little men had beards like mine now, and faces like old stone.
Their clothes were two hundred years old. Doublets, buckled shoes. As if they'd stepped out of a painting.
The drink tasted like the best cider you've ever had, with something cold underneath. Like frost on a grave.
My grandmother used to say an old captain and his crew haunt the mountain, playing at thunder. I laughed at her.
Sometimes I think I only fell asleep because I wanted to. No chores, no scolding. Just a long, quiet nothing.
And I got it. Twenty years of nothing. Be careful what you wish for on a mountain.
My daughter married a good man while I snored. I missed the wedding. I missed my grandson's first word.
I missed a war, too. They asked whose side I was on. I didn't know there were sides.
The mountain's quiet. No thunder, no ninepins. I might even go up for a walk. In daylight. With company.
I'll tell you the part that hurts. When I woke, I whistled for Wolf. Whistled and whistled. Only the wind answered.
My dream is smaller than you'd think. A dog at my feet. Someone who waits for me, even if it's late.
The miller says an old dog lived by the mill for years, always facing the mountain road. Died of old age.
His grandpup lives there now. Same scruffy ears, same crooked tail. I swear it's Wolf's blood.
But he doesn't know me. He barks when I pass. I'm a stranger to him, like I was to everyone.
Would you bring me some bones? Six should do. I want him to trust me. I want to be waited for again.
He was a scruffy thing, afraid of my wife and devoted to me. He sat with me through every scolding.
When I came home, a mangy cur by the gate growled at me. Was it him, too old to know me? I've always wondered.
Then my daughter. She came through the crowd with a baby on her arm and looked right at me without knowing me.
I said her name. She said someone from her family went up the mountain twenty years ago and never came back.
Do you know what it's like to be a ghost at your own door? Everyone polite, nobody sure who you are.
She's grey now, my little girl. Some mornings I catch her looking at me like she's still deciding.
My fear is simple. That I'll close my eyes one night and open them to another twenty years gone.
So I barely sleep. I sit by the window and count the stars until the rooster takes over.
He licked my beard! Twenty years late, and I finally have a dog to go home with. I called him Wolf, of course.
He sleeps across my doorway now. If I ever wander up a mountain again, he'll trip me first.
Strange: the things I ran away from turned out to be what I missed most. Arguments, fences, being needed.
The new innkeeper lets me tell my story on market days. People laugh. The children don't. They check the clocks.
You gave me back three things: a friend, a quiet mountain and a dog. That's more than twenty years gave me.
If you ever find strangers bowling in the hills, walk the other way. And come tell me. I'll know.
Go on, it's getting late, and I don't do late any more. Come by tomorrow; I'll be up. I always am now.
Every morning I wake and count on my fingers. One night. Only one. Then I laugh and get up.
My daughter saw Wolf follow me home and cried. She said I always had a dog at my heels, back then. She said it like she finally knew me.
It took her twenty years and a dog to be sure. I don't blame her one bit.
Derrick came to visit. He looked at my beard, then at the mountain, and said, 'Maybe.' That's progress.
I walked up the mountain last week. In daylight, with Wolf. Just rocks and pines. No kegs anywhere.
Well, there was one hollow with an odd flat patch, like a bowling green. We didn't stay.
My grandson wants to go up at night to see the ninepins. I told him the mountain is closed. Forever.
I've started doing my chores, too. All of them. Even the fence. My wife would faint to see it.
Now they sleep very little and very late, and wake up every morning to count, to be sure, only one night has passed.
Rip Van Winkle — Washington Irving (1819)
There must be someone in the next village who remembers me. Carry this letter; tell them I'm... awake.
An old friend answered! He thought I'd run off. He didn't believe the story. Nobody does.
Anyone who remembers
On the mountain, the rattling ones still play at night, and they're not friendly. Clear them, so no one else loses twenty years.
The mountain's quiet. No thunder, no ninepins. I might even go up for a walk. In daylight.
The bowlers of the mountain
My old dog must have waited for me a long time. His grandpup lives by the mill. Bring me bones; I want him to trust me.
He licked my beard. Twenty years late, I finally have a dog to go home with.
A dog of my own
Is the old innkeeper still around? No? Twenty years... right.
Never drink with strangers who bowl in the mountains. Very specific advice, I know.
Everyone I argued with is gone. I miss the arguments more than I'd have guessed.
My grandson thinks I'm the best storyteller alive. I just tell him what happened.
A nap of twenty years
hearthbound.persona.myth_scheherazade.bi: The old lord of this valley swore to burn a house each week after his son died. I went to his hall and began a story. I stopped at the best part.
He spared the valley one more night to hear the ending. I've never finished a story since. It's been almost three years.
hearthbound.persona.myth_scheherazade.di: Once upon a time... no, no, you'll have to come back tonight for that. Everyone does, sooner or later.
Sit by the fire. My inn has the best chairs in the valley, and the worst soup. People come for the chairs.
So I climbed the hill, knocked on his door, and before he could shout, I started a story.
I stopped right at the best part. He roared. I bowed and said, 'Tomorrow, my lord, if the valley still stands.'
He spared the valley one more night to hear the ending. And the next. And the next. I've been going up that hill ever since.
His hall is dark. Always dark. He sits in shadow, and I tell stories to a pair of eyes and nothing else.
I tell better stories by candlelight. Would you bring me candles? The more the better. Let me give the dark some shapes.
Every story is a door. The trick is to open the next one before the last one closes.
You listen with your whole face. Do you know how rare that is? Most people listen with half an ear and a full mouth.
I read everything: flour sacks, tavern bills, the backs of letters. You never know where a good story is hiding.
Do you see the dark hall up on the hill? An old lord lives there. He hasn't come down in almost three years.
His only son died of a fever one spring. The lord shut his doors, and when he opened them again, he wasn't the same.
He swore that every week, a house in this valley would burn, until the valley grieved as much as he did.
The first week, a barn burned. The second, the miller's shed. Everyone was waiting to see whose roof would be next.
I didn't have a sword or an army. I had a sister who liked my tales, and a mouth that doesn't know when to stop.
Last night the shadows on the wall played the villains. He leaned forward when the candle-thief crept in. He loved it.
Thank you. You've no idea how different a story sounds when you can see the listener's hands clench.
If he notices, the spell breaks. He'll remember that the stories are a trick to stop him burning us.
My memory is fraying like an old rug. I can't keep a thousand tangled threads in my head any longer.
I need to write them down. Every tale I've told, every one I'm planning, so I never repeat myself.
But paper here is scarce, and I need books that stay bound, with room to write, not loose leaves blown away by the wind.
Bring me books to write in, would you? Two. That's enough for a thousand nights, if I write very small.
Now you know what I do each night. Let me tell you what it costs. I've never finished a story since that first one.
Not one. Every tale ends in the middle of another. A merchant meets a spirit, who tells of a fisherman, who finds a jar...
My sister helps. She sits by the lord's chair and says, 'Oh, tell us what happened next.' She's heard them all. She pretends.
The old book of a thousand and one nights has someone like me in it. I've read it. I steal from it shamelessly.
But you can only borrow so much. I'm running out of tales. Some nights I invent them on the walk up the hill.
The walk takes twenty minutes. I've made up a sultan, three thieves and a talking fish in less than that.
What I'm afraid of isn't the lord. It's the night I have nothing left to say.
Worse: last week I began a tale and realised halfway I'd told it before, eight months ago. He didn't notice. I did.
I've already filled a page. It's about a traveller who brings candles. It ends on a cliff, of course.
Don't worry, you survive. Probably. It depends on how he's feeling tomorrow night.
Yes, he has a daughter. She married and left for the next village before the fever. She writes. He never opens her letters.
The truth is the only story I haven't told him. It's also the only one that could end all this, one way or another.
If it goes wrong, the fires begin again. I know that. But I can't keep him asleep forever with fairy tales.
I've written her a letter explaining everything. She should hear it too, and come, if she's willing.
Carry this letter to his daughter in the next village? I'll go up the hill tonight. You're my last page.
I've written down nine hundred and some tales. My hand aches. My head feels lighter than it has in years.
And reading them all at once, I noticed something. Every story I've told him is about someone who lost somebody.
A merchant who lost a brother. A fisherman who lost a son to the sea. A queen who lost her voice. I did it without thinking.
I think I've been telling him his own story for three years, one mask at a time. He hasn't seen it. Or he has.
Here's my deepest secret: I'm not only afraid of running out. I'm tired. I've given him a thousand nights and kept none for me.
I have a dream I never say aloud. To tell a story all the way to 'the end', and then go home and sleep.
The book is nearly full. By my count, tomorrow is the thousand and first night. I have nothing left. Not one tale.
So I'll tell him the truth instead. About his son. About the valley. About the daughter he forgot.
He listened to the truth until dawn, and then he asked for his daughter. I think my story is finally over.
She arrived the next evening. Your letter must have run faster than you did. They didn't speak at first. Then they did.
Children ask me for 'the one with the scary lord'. I tell them there isn't one. Just a sad old man who got better.
Sometimes I still stop at the best part, out of habit. The children throw bread at me until I continue.
Every story is a door, I once told you. It turns out some doors lead home. It just takes a thousand tries.
Come by any evening. Once upon a time... no, you know how it works. Come back tonight and you'll hear the end.
Go on, then. I'll keep your chair warm, and I promise: this time, every story you hear will have an ending.
On the thousand and first night he wept instead of threatening. I'd never seen him cry. I'd told him a thousand sad tales.
He still asks for stories. But now only because he likes them, and he comes down the hill to hear them at my inn.
He sits in that chair by the fire. The one you used. He says it's the best chair in the valley. He's right.
I finished a story last week. Beginning, middle, end. I cried. My sister laughed at me for an hour.
The two books sit on my shelf. One is full of tales, the other of true things I've started writing. Your candles are in it.
The miller's shed has been rebuilt. The lord paid for it himself, and carried the first beam, badly.
I sleep through the night now. The first week, I kept waking at midnight with my mouth open, ready to start a tale.
Do you know what I call the tale of you? 'The traveller who carried the truth'. It has no cliffhanger. It's my favourite.
hearthbound.persona.myth_scheherazade.ep: On the thousand and first night the lord wept instead of threatening, and now he asks for stories only because he likes them.
hearthbound.persona.myth_scheherazade.so: The Thousand and One Nights — Anonymous (c. 9th–14th century)
hearthbound.persona.myth_scheherazade.st: His hall is dark and I tell better stories by candlelight. Bring me candles, the more the better.
Tonight the shadows on the wall will play the villains. He'll love it.
My memory is fraying. Bring me books to write in, so I never tell the same tale twice.
I've already filled a page. It's about a traveller who brings candles. It ends on a cliff, of course.
Tonight I have nothing left. So I'll tell him the truth. Carry this letter to his daughter in the next village; she should hear it too.
He listened to the truth until dawn, and then he asked for his daughter. I think my story is finally over.
hearthbound.persona.myth_scheherazade.ta: Once upon a time... no, no, you'll have to come back tonight for that.
Every story is a door. The trick is to open the next one before the last one closes.
I'm running out of tales, you know. Some nights I invent them on the walk up the hill.
What I'm afraid of isn't the lord. It's the night I have nothing left to say.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.bio.0: I sailed seven times and was shipwrecked seven times. I camped on an island that turned out to be a whale, and a giant bird carried me off by the ankle.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.bio.1: Each time I swore never again, and each time the harbour smelled of salt and I went. I'm not brave. I'm just very bad at staying.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.dialogue: Sit down, traveller. This chair has a story, and so do I. Mine is longer, and has more whales in it.
Tea? It's from a port whose name I've forgotten. The tea remembers, though. Taste the salt at the bottom.
Each time I got home I swore never again. And each time the harbour smelled of salt, and my feet walked me to the docks.
I'm not brave, you understand. I'm just very bad at staying. Brave people know what they're running towards.
Lately I've been wondering what it would be like to stand on ground that doesn't move. Truly solid ground.
I can't go looking myself; if I set out, I'll end up on a ship by the third day. I know myself too well.
Would you go for me? Find me a shore that won't swim away: another village somewhere, with real ground under it.
Never light a fire on an island you haven't met properly. That's the first rule of the sea, and I learned it the wet way.
You have the look of someone who leaves. I know it well. I see it every morning in the washing bowl.
Don't mind the scar on my ankle. A bird did that. A very, very large bird. We'll get to the bird.
I was born to a rich merchant and spent it all by twenty. So I bought goods, boarded a ship, and went to earn it back.
Seven times I sailed. Seven times I was shipwrecked. My friends stopped coming to see me off after the third.
The first voyage we moored beside a green island, lit a fire for supper, and the island began to shake.
It was a whale, asleep so long that trees had grown on its back. Our fire woke it. It dived. So did we, less gracefully.
I floated on a washtub for a day and a night. I still can't look at a washtub without saying thank you.
A real village on real ground! And it didn't sink when you walked in? You'd be amazed how rare that is in my memoirs.
Tell me everything. Did they have a well? Wells are good signs. Islands with wells are almost never whales.
The fifth voyage is the one I don't joke about. There was an old man on a riverbank who asked me to carry him across.
I lifted him onto my shoulders. He wrapped his legs around my neck and never let go. For days. For weeks.
I finally got him drunk on grape juice I'd left to ferment in a gourd, and he slipped off. I didn't look back.
Now his cousins crawl out of the water here, grey and dripping, and grab at the fishermen. I feel it in my shoulders.
Drive them back into the deep for me. Eight of them, say. My neck will thank you, though I wasn't even there.
On my second voyage the ship left without me while I slept under a tree. I woke to an empty beach and a huge white dome.
I walked around the dome for an hour. Then the sky went dark, and I understood it was an egg, and its mother was home.
I tied myself to her ankle with my turban. She flew me over the sea without noticing a passenger. My ankle noticed.
She dropped me in a valley whose floor was all diamonds, and whose walls were full of serpents as long as masts.
I'll tell you how I got out another day. It involves meat. It's not dignified.
On the third voyage, a giant with one eye. On the fourth, a burial I wasn't supposed to walk away from. I walked.
Every time I came home, I told the stories at dinner. People laughed and said 'Sinbad, the teller of tall tales'.
That's the name the old books give me, you know. 'The sailor'. I've never been much of a sailor. I've been mostly a swimmer.
My shoulders feel lighter already, and I stayed in my chair the whole time. That's the best kind of adventure.
The fishermen came by to thank you. They brought me a fish. I told them I prefer fish that don't remind me of anything.
My dream is not to sail again. I think. My dream is for someone to look at me and say: yes, I believe you.
Proof would help. Just a little proof. Diamonds, like the ones in the valley. It wouldn't be the same diamonds, but they'd shine the same.
I'd put them on the mantel above this chair. Every time someone laughed at the valley story, I'd just point.
I know it's silly. An old tale-teller asking for jewels to prove a tale. But it's the only thing I've never had: evidence.
Bring me two diamonds, would you? Two, so the story finally has proof, and I can stop defending it.
I promised the valley of diamonds. So: the merchants there threw slabs of meat from the cliffs, and eagles carried them up with diamonds stuck on.
I tied myself to the biggest slab and waited. An eagle carried me up with the meat. The merchants were very surprised.
I filled my pockets with diamonds on the way. Big ones, like pigeons' eggs. I remember the weight of them exactly.
And then I lost every one. Shipwreck, of course. The sixth one. The diamonds are at the bottom of some sea, with my luggage.
Nobody believes the diamond story. Not one person. Even my own cook rolls his eyes when I get to the part with the meat.
Here's my secret, since you've listened this long: I'm afraid that none of it happened the way I tell it.
Some nights I wonder if I've polished the stories so much that the true ones are gone underneath.
Seven voyages, and not one of them had a friend waiting at the end. So nobody could tell me what was real.
Proof at last! Two diamonds on the mantel. The cook stopped rolling his eyes. Now he just sighs. Progress.
Did you use the rod I gave you? It has fished whales. Well, one whale. Well, it fished near one. Be careful where you cast.
When I'm gone, the chair and the diamonds go to the village. And the stories go to whoever tells them best. Probably you.
Remember that shore you found me, the solid one? I walked there last spring. It didn't move. I nearly cried.
I'm still very bad at staying. But I'm getting better at it. Every evening is a little practice.
Tell me about your travels next time. I'm tired of my own stories; I want one where I only listen.
Go on, the tide's turning somewhere. Come back and sit a while. The chair will wait. So will I.
The children come every evening now. I point at the diamonds and they gasp before I've even got to the eagle.
I've noticed something: I haven't looked at the harbour in weeks. My feet have stopped walking there on their own.
Do you know what they call the latest tale? The eighth voyage. The one where a traveller came here and stayed to listen.
It's the only voyage without a shipwreck. I keep waiting for the storm. It keeps not coming.
Last night I told the whale story and a little girl asked if the whale was all right. Nobody ever asked that. I think it was.
You have the look of someone who leaves, I said once. You do. But you also come back. That's rarer than diamonds.
If you ever need a chair, this one is yours. I'll sit on the barrel. I've sat on worse. Much worse. On a roc.
I still smell the salt when the wind turns. I let myself enjoy it now, like a song you know but don't have to sing.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.epilogue: Now there is an eighth voyage in the tales: the one about a traveller who came to the village and stayed to listen.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.source: The Thousand and One Nights — Anonymous (c. 9th–14th century)
My first voyage ended when the island woke up and dived. Go find me a shore that won't swim away: a new village, solid ground.
A real village on real ground! You'd be amazed how rare that is in my memoirs.
On my fifth voyage an old man climbed on my shoulders and wouldn't get off. His cousins still crawl out of the water. Drive them back.
My shoulders feel lighter already, and I wasn't even there.
The old man of the sea
I once escaped a valley of diamonds tied to a slab of meat. I kept none. Bring me two, so the story finally has proof.
Proof at last! Take my rod, it has fished whales. Well, one whale. Well, it fished near one.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.talk.0: Sit down, traveller. This chair has a story, and so do I. Mine is longer.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.talk.1: Never light a fire on an island you haven't met properly.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.talk.2: You have the look of someone who leaves. I know it well. I see it in every puddle.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.talk.3: Seven voyages, and not one of them had a friend waiting at the end. Until now, perhaps.
hearthbound.persona.myth_sinbad.title: Seven voyages, one chair
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.bio.0: My grandfather's clan of Hrimfell swore our forge-hammer was a copy of the thunder god's. One morning it was gone, and long, thin tracks led away.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.bio.1: In the old tale the god got his hammer back by dressing as a bride. I laughed at that story for years. Now I'm starting to measure myself for a veil.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.dialogue.0: HELLO! Sorry. Loud? Me? This is my indoor voice.
Thunder is just the sky working a forge. I respect that.
One morning, it was gone. The hook empty. The door shut. Nothing else touched. Not even the coins.
And outside, in the frost, tracks. Long and thin, far apart, as if something walked on stilts.
The tracks went ten paces and stopped. Then started again, far away. As if the walker blinked.
Without the hammer the forge is dead. The fire burns, but nothing I make with another hammer rings true.
Bring me iron? I'll make a temporary hammer while I find the real one. The forge needs to breathe.
I ate a whole goat once on a bet. Don't tell my mother.
I'm strong enough to lift anything, except my own pride. That one's heavy.
You've got a good arm for hauling ore. I can tell. Arms are my second favourite thing after hammers.
My grandfather's clan came from Hrimfell, up in the cold north, where the forges never go out.
We had a hammer. Short handle, heavy head, runes worn smooth. Every smith in the clan swung it once.
