The old ones swore it was a copy of the thunder god's own hammer. Made the same night, from the same star.
I don't know about that. I know it rang like a bell and never once missed the anvil.
It came down to me when grandfather died. I hung it over the forge. I polished it every evening.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.dialogue.1: It's no heirloom, but it rings true. The forge breathes again. So do I.
I made the village three hinges, a gate and a very ugly spoon. The spoon was an accident.
I've followed the tracks. They lead to the tall dark ones who carry blocks. Purple eyes. They blink away.
They steal pieces of the world and never put them back. I'm sure one of them took my hammer.
I'm not good at being sneaky. I'm good at hitting things. For once those skills agree.
If I hunt enough of them, one will drop what it took. That's how they work. They drop things.
Hunt the tall thieves with me until one drops what it took? The tracks vanish and reappear. So will we.
Now I can tell you the tale my grandfather told, because I'm starting to think it's about us.
In the old story, the thunder god woke up and his hammer was gone. A giant had stolen it.
The giant buried it eight leagues under the earth and said: send me the goddess of love as my bride.
The goddess refused so loudly the walls shook. So the gods had a very bad idea.
They dressed the thunder god himself as the bride. Veil, dress, necklace, the lot. Beard hidden. Mostly.
At the wedding feast, the bride ate a whole ox and eight salmon. The giant was a little worried.
I laughed at that story for years. Grandfather would do the voices. I'd roll on the floor.
Now look at me. My hammer, stolen by something tall and strange. I'm not laughing so much.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.dialogue.2: One of them was carrying the hammer's leather strap. The rest is in their chief's hall. I know what I have to do.
I sat up all night holding the strap. It still smells of grandfather's forge. Of smoke and pine tar.
You're my clever friend. You don't have to wear anything. Just keep him from lifting the veil too soon.
I need a dress that hides shoulders like mine. That's a lot of dress. A lot of veil. All white.
The tailor has agreed to sew it in secret. She's sworn silence. She laughed for ten minutes first.
I'll need wool. Lots of white wool. I'm going to the wedding. As the bride.
Bring me white wool? Enough for a wedding dress for a very large, very angry bride.
Now I'll tell you the embarrassing part. A message came. Scratched on a stone by my door.
'The hammer for a bride.' That's all. Their chief wants a bride in exchange. Exactly like the old tale.
Nobody in the village will go, of course. I wouldn't let them. It's my hammer. It's my job.
So. I'm starting to measure myself for a veil. Stop laughing. You're laughing. I can hear it.
My deepest fear? Not the chief. Not his hall. It's that someone from the village will see me in the dress.
No, really. My deepest fear is failing grandfather. The hammer is the last of Hrimfell. The last of him.
If I lose it, the clan is just a name on a stone. If I get it back, it rings again, for my children.
In the tale, the god's clever friend went along as bridesmaid and talked the giant out of suspicion.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.dialogue.3: They lifted the veil, I grabbed the hammer, and the rest is a very short story. Keep my old axe as a wedding favour.
The forge rings with the true hammer again. It sounds like grandfather laughing.
I still ate a whole goat at the wedding feast, by the way. Tradition. Don't tell my mother.
Loud? Still loud. Proud? A little less. It's easier to lift now. You helped with that.
If you ever need a very large bride, a very loud guard or a very good hinge, you know where I am.
Every time the hammer rings, I think of you. You'll hear it from the road. Everyone does.
Go on, then. Walk tall. Not too tall, though. We've had enough of the tall ones for a while.
The veil is folded in a chest. Nobody in the village is allowed to mention it. Nobody.
The tailor mentions it. Every day. She says it's her finest work. She's not wrong. I looked lovely.
Remember when the chief tried to kiss the bride? I've never seen anyone teleport that fast.
I told the tale at the inn once. Only once. My version has more lightning and less lace.
I made the tailor a pair of silver scissors as thanks. She uses them to threaten me.
The tall thieves don't come near the village anymore. I think word got around about the bride.
I've started teaching the smith's apprentice to swing the hammer. Once. Like the clan did.
Grandfather would be proud. Then he'd laugh about the dress. Then he'd be proud again.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.epilogue: Now the forge rings with the true hammer again. The veil is folded in a chest, and nobody in the village is allowed to mention it.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.stage.0.as: Without the hammer the forge is dead. Bring me iron; I'll make a temporary one while I find the real one.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.stage.0.do: It's no heirloom, but it rings true. The forge breathes again.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.stage.1.as: The tracks are long and they vanish and reappear. Those tall dark giants who steal blocks! Hunt them until one drops what it took.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.stage.1.do: One of them was carrying the hammer's leather strap. The rest is in their chief's hall. I know what I have to do.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.stage.2.as: Their chief wants a bride in exchange. Bring me wool, lots of white wool. I'm going to the wedding. As the bride.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.stage.2.do: They lifted the veil, I grabbed the hammer, and the rest is a very short story. Take my old axe as a wedding favour.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.talk.0: Loud? Me? This is my indoor voice.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.talk.1: Thunder is just the sky working a forge. I respect that.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.talk.2: I ate a whole goat once on a bet. Don't tell my mother.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.talk.3: I'm strong enough to lift anything, except my own pride. That one's heavy.
hearthbound.persona.myth_thor.title: The stolen hammer
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.bio.0: Someone has to stay awake while the village sleeps. That's been me for eleven years.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.bio.1: I know every sound of the night. The owl, the wind in the mill... and the ones that aren't from this world.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.bio.2: I lost a friend to a creeper that nobody heard coming. Since then I light every corner I can.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.dialogue: Quiet night so far. I don't trust quiet nights. The loud ones at least tell you where the trouble is.
Coffee? No? More for me. It's my fourth pot. Or fifth. The night blurs.
It's good to have someone watching my back for a change. Hollis used to. Nobody has since.
The nights are getting worse. Every dusk, more shapes at the treeline. More than last week. More than last month.
Last night I counted them from the wall: eleven. Eleven against one tired watcher and a bell.
The guards do what they can, but they sleep too, and the dead don't. Sunrise never comes fast enough.
They come every night, and every night there are more. Help me hold the village until dawn. Just one night.
Eleven years on this wall. Someone has to stay awake while the village sleeps. Turns out that someone is me.
I sleep when the sun is up. Don't tell the elder I nap on the wall at noon. The pigeons keep my secret.
Listen. That's the owl on the mill roof. That's wind in the sails. And that scrape? A goat. Probably.
I know every sound of the night. In eleven years you learn which ones belong to this world.
The dead groan. Skeletons rattle. Spiders click. There's always a warning, if you're listening.
Almost always. There's one thing that makes no sound at all. I'll tell you about it another night.
I had a friend once. Hollis. He kept the other half of the watch with me. Told terrible jokes to keep us awake.
The worst was about a chicken and a bell. I still don't get it. He laughed every single time.
Dawn. We made it. You can sleep now; I'll keep watch. Well, I'd keep watch anyway. Sleep.
You fought like someone who's done it before. Twice as many came, and none reached a door. Not one.
Darkness is where they hide. Where light doesn't reach, they appear and wait. I've watched it happen.
I've drawn a map of every dark alley in the village. Thirty-two spots. I've counted them a hundred times.
Behind the well. The gap by the stables. The steps down to the cellar where the cats sleep.
Thirty-two dark corners. Thirty-two places where another Hollis could die tonight. I can't afford that many torches.
Bring me torches, thirty-two of them, and I'll light every alley in this village. Let them try sneaking in then.
Hollis. I promised I'd tell you. A spring night, nine years ago. Warm and quiet. Too quiet.
He went down to check the east gate. Said he'd heard nothing, which is exactly why he went.
I was on the wall with the lantern. I saw him turn the corner by the baker's. The dark there was thick as tar.
Then the flash. And the noise. And then no noise at all, for a very long time.
It was a creeper. It came out of the shadow behind the baker's woodpile. No groan, no rattle. Nothing.
They found his lantern twenty paces away, still burning. Isn't that strange? The lantern survived.
Since then I've been lighting corners. Every corner I can. With my own coin, when there is any.
The baker's corner has four lanterns now. The baker complains. I don't care. Let him complain in the light.
Look at it glow. Every alley, every step. I walked the village last night and my shadow never left my side.
The cats are furious. Their cellar steps are bright now. They glare at me. I glare back.
I've seen three of them skulking in the tall grass past the fields. Green shapes, standing far too still.
I can shoot, but my crossbow is for things that groan and come at you. Creepers don't give you time.
You move fast, and you listen. You'd hear the hiss before it's too late. I trust your ears more than mine now.
If three of them go, the village breathes. And maybe I close my eyes for a few hours without that dream.
Please. Hunt a few before they reach a house. Three would be enough. Three, for Hollis.
Mothers let their children play outside after sunset again. First time in years. I heard laughter at dusk.
I'll tell you a secret. I cried a little, lighting the one by the baker's woodpile. Blame the smoke.
But light doesn't stop everything. The silent ones still come from further out, from the fields and the woods.
The creepers are what I fear most. No groan, no rattle, nothing. You only hear them when it's too late.
Some nights I dream I'm walking toward the baker's corner. I know what's waiting there. My feet keep walking.
Eleven years awake, and not once have I truly rested. I'd like to. Just once. Before my hair turns grey.
My dream is simple: a whole night's sleep, in a bed, window open, and no bell to ring.
Last week one blew up the old shed by the south fence. Empty, thank the stars. Next time it might not be.
Three fewer. Take my crossbow. It reloads faster than any other in the realm, and it's never once failed me.
I slept last night. Four whole hours, in a bed. I woke and didn't know where I was. It was wonderful.
The cats have forgiven me. Mostly. One sleeps on my boots when I'm up on the wall.
I still don't trust quiet nights. But now, when it's quiet, sometimes I think it's just... quiet.
If you ever camp out there in the dark, light your corners. Promise me. I've already lost one friend to shadows.
You watched my back when nobody else did. That's a debt no amount of torches repays.
Go on, the sun's coming up. Your turn to walk into the day, mine to sleep. See you at dusk, maybe.
The young guard, Pell, takes the first half of the watch now. He's good. Tells awful jokes. I like him.
The streets glow at night with your torches. Travellers say our village looks like a lantern from the hills.
I finally got Hollis's joke, the chicken and the bell. It's still terrible. I laughed for an hour.
The baker gave me a free loaf yesterday. First time in eleven years. I think the light won him over.
Coffee? No? Still more for me. Although I only drink two pots a night now. Progress.
I went down to the baker's corner at dusk. Just stood there, in the light. Nothing came. Nothing hid.
Remember that first long night? You kept asking if dawn was near. It's the only thing anyone ever asks me.
I put a lantern on Hollis's grave. It burns all night. I think he'd find that funny. Or fitting.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.epilogue: Thanks to you, the night watch sleeps a few hours more. The village streets glow with the torches you brought.
They come every night, and every night there are more. Help me hold the village until dawn.
Dawn. We made it. You can sleep now; I'll keep watch.
Darkness is where they hide. Bring me torches and I'll light every alley in this village.
Look at it glow. Let them try to sneak in now.
The creepers are what I fear most. No groan, no rattle, nothing. Hunt a few before they reach a house.
Three fewer. Take my crossbow; it reloads faster than any other in the realm.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.talk.0: Quiet night so far. I don't trust quiet nights.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.talk.2: I sleep when the sun is up. Don't tell the elder I nap on the wall.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.talk.3: It's good to have someone watching my back for a change.
hearthbound.persona.night_watch.title: Night Watch
hearthbound.persona.none.bio.0: Just another soul trying to make a living in this village.
hearthbound.persona.none.talk.2: Nice to see a friendly face.
hearthbound.persona.none.title: Settler
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.bio.0: One summer afternoon in my childhood I followed a rabbit in a waistcoat into a hole and fell for what felt like an hour. Nobody believes me.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.bio.1: I grew too tall, then too small, then argued with a queen made of cards. I'd give anything to find that little garden door again.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.dialogue: Have you ever wondered why a raven is like a writing desk? Me neither. Well, once. For a whole afternoon.
If you see a rabbit checking a pocket watch, please don't laugh. Just follow it. And tell me afterwards.
Through it I saw the loveliest garden: bright flowers, cool fountains. I couldn't fit through. I cried a whole pool.
On a glass table there was a little cake with EAT ME spelled on it in currants. So I did.
I grew like a telescope! My feet went so far away I thought I'd have to post them presents at Christmas.
I've tried every cake since, just in case. Nothing. But I have a hunch about cookies. They look mischievous.
Bring me some cookies? I want to see if anything happens. If I shoot up through the roof, don't panic.
Curiouser and curiouser... that's what I said when I first saw you, you know. It's a compliment.
Everyone says it was a dream. But dreams don't leave jam on your sleeve.
I always look under tables. You never know where a little key might be hiding.
It was a hot summer afternoon. I was sitting on a riverbank, bored, while someone read a book with no pictures.
Then a white rabbit ran past, took a watch out of its waistcoat pocket, and said, 'Oh dear! I shall be too late!'
I'd never seen a rabbit with a waistcoat, or a watch. So of course I followed it, straight down a hole under the hedge.
I fell, and fell, and fell. So slowly that I took a jar of marmalade off a shelf on the way down. It was empty.
At the bottom was a long hall full of locked doors, and one tiny door, behind a curtain, no higher than my knee.
Nothing. Not a single inch. Still, they were delicious, and I'll keep trying. Science takes patience.
I measured myself against the doorframe before and after. Identical. I ate three more to be sure.
I'd give anything to find that little garden door again. Sometimes I dream I'm the right size, at last, and it opens.
Before the cake, there was a bottle. It said DRINK ME, and I shrank to the size of a thimble. The key was out of reach.
I've been thinking about what that bottle tasted of. Cherry tart, custard, pineapple, roast turkey, toffee, buttered toast.
Honey is the closest thing I can think of. Sweet and golden and a bit strange. Worth a try, surely?
Bring me honey? A few bottles. If I shrink, please put me in your pocket, gently.
Now listen. After the cake, there was a caterpillar on a mushroom, smoking a hookah, asking 'Who are YOU?'
I honestly didn't know. I'd changed size so many times that morning. That question still follows me around.
One side of his mushroom made you grow, the other made you shrink. I nibbled both until my head went up past the trees.
A pigeon screamed at me that I was a serpent. I said I was a... well, I wasn't sure what I was. That was the trouble.
I met a Duchess with a howling baby that turned into a pig. And her cook threw pepper at everything. Everything.
Then a cat on a branch grinned at me and vanished, bit by bit, until only the grin was left. I think of it on quiet nights.
Nobody believes me. My family says I had sunstroke. The village says I read too many books without pictures.
Sometimes I start to believe them. Then I find something odd in my pocket, a playing card, a crumb of tart, and I know.
I felt small for a moment, but I think it was just humility. Thank you for humouring me. You're very good at it.
I drank it slowly, by the window, the way a scientist would. Or a very silly person. Possibly both.
So I write everything down, every night. The notebooks fill a whole shelf. Nobody reads them. Maybe you will.
My dream is simple: to know the garden is real. Not to go back, necessarily. Just to know it's somewhere.
You travel. You see places I'll never see. Maybe, beyond the hills, there's a village with a garden like that.
Go beyond the hills, find a village you've never seen, and tell me if it has roses painted red. Please.
Even if it doesn't, tell me about it anyway. Every detail. I'll know if you're making it up. Probably.
Here's the part I don't tell everyone. I got into the garden in the end. It was the Queen of Hearts' garden.
Gardeners who were playing cards were painting white roses red, terrified, because they'd planted the wrong colour.
The Queen shouted 'Off with their heads!' at everyone. At the gardeners, at the Duchess, at the Cheshire Cat's head.
We played croquet with flamingos for mallets and hedgehogs for balls. The hedgehogs kept walking away.
Then there was a trial, about stolen tarts. I kept growing, all by myself. At the end I said: 'You're nothing but a pack of cards!'
They flew up at me, all fifty-two, and I woke up on the riverbank with leaves falling on my face.
My fear is that I'll grow old and forget. That one day I'll say 'it was a dream' and mean it.
I'm already forgetting some things. What the Mock Turtle's song was about. The Dormouse's story about the treacle well.
White roses, painted red by nervous gardeners? You're teasing me... and yet you're smiling. Have some cake.
You never said yes and you never said no. That's exactly how things work in Wonderland. I'm delighted.
Sometimes, just before sleep, I hear a far-off voice saying 'Off with her head!' I just laugh now.
If you ever fall down a hole, don't be frightened. Look around. Take the marmalade. Remember everything.
Thank you for going over the hills for me. Whatever you found there, you brought back a little bit of the garden.
Who are YOU? the caterpillar asked me. I think I finally know: someone who never stopped being curious.
Come to the well at dusk sometime. We'll wait for the rabbit together. It's always late, you know.
Now the village children gather at dusk to hear about Wonderland. I do all the voices. The Queen is their favourite.
One of them swears he saw a white rabbit checking its watch by the well. I told him to follow it, carefully.
Remember those cookies that didn't make me grow? I feel taller anyway, since you listened to me.
I've stopped caring if people believe me. The children do. You do, a bit. That's plenty.
I left a little table by the well with a bottle on it. The label says DRINK ME. It's just lemonade. Mostly.
The old baker has started making tarts with hearts on top. She says it's a coincidence. I'm suspicious.
I finally worked out the raven and the writing desk. No, I won't tell you. Some riddles are better unsolved.
My notebooks have readers now. Three children, a goat who eats the corners, and you, I hope.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.epilogue: Now the village children gather at dusk to hear about the Wonderland, and one of them swears he saw a white rabbit checking its watch by the well.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll (1865)
Down there, a little cake said EAT ME and I grew like a telescope. Bring me some cookies; I want to see if anything happens.
Nothing. Not a single inch. Still, they were delicious, and I'll keep trying.
Then there was a bottle that said DRINK ME, and I shrank to the size of a thimble. Honey is the closest thing I can think of.
I felt small for a moment, but I think it was just humility. Thank you for humouring me.
The garden behind the door was the loveliest place I ever saw. Go beyond the hills, find a village you've never seen, and tell me if it has roses painted red.
White roses, painted red by nervous gardeners? You're teasing me... and yet you're smiling. Here, have some cake.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.talk.0: Have you ever wondered why a raven is like a writing desk? Me neither. Well, once.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.talk.1: If you see a rabbit checking a pocket watch, please don't laugh. Just follow it.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.talk.2: Curiouser and curiouser... that's what I said when I first saw you, you know.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.talk.3: Everyone says it was a dream. But dreams don't leave jam on your sleeve.
hearthbound.persona.novel_alice.title: Down the rabbit hole
hearthbound.persona.novel_canterville_gh: My family says I've haunted this old house for three hundred years. I rattle chains at midnight. The new neighbours just oil them and go back to sleep.
The truth? I'm tired. I haven't slept in centuries. There's a garden where the almond blossom grows and nobody wakes; I'd like to lie down there.
Boo. ...No? Not even a little shiver? You people have no respect for tradition.
I've been doing this for three hundred years, you know. Midnight groans, rattling chains, the lot.
Only the daughter, Virginia, never laughed at me. She'd just look at me, very seriously, as if I were sad.
I keep up the haunting anyway. What else would I do? It's the family business. Well, it's my family's business.
But my chains have been oiled so often they don't clank anymore. They go 'shhh'. Like a librarian.
Do you know how humiliating it is to drag a chain down a hall and have it purr? I'd rather be exorcised.
Bring me some proper chains, would you? Four. Good, rusty, honest iron. I have a reputation to keep.
The new neighbours left me a bottle of oil for my chains, with a note. 'For your convenience.' The insult!
Being frightening used to be an art. Costumes, timing, a good echo. Now it's just paperwork.
You're the only one who knocks before entering my room. I appreciate the gesture. Truly.
In my prime I made a duchess faint at a ball. Four footmen and a bishop ran screaming. Glorious nights.
I once played 'the Headless Earl' for a whole winter. My neck ached terribly, but the reviews were superb.
Then this new family moved in, with twin boys who set traps for me. Butter on the stairs. Butter!
They threw pillows at me. At me! A spectre of three centuries, pelted with pillows by children in nightshirts.
Their father offered me a patent stain remover for my famous bloodstain. He meant well. That's the worst part.
CLANK. CLANK. Oh, that's the sound! Someone upstairs just said 'bless you'. Sigh. But still, CLANK.
Let me tell you why I haunt. Three centuries ago, I did something rather bad to my wife. People said I killed her.
Now she says she doesn't mind me using her paints. But she's running out of red. She paints sunsets, you see.
I don't want to take her sunsets from her. That seems... wrong, somehow. Even for me.
I haven't cared whether something was wrong in a very long time. It's an odd feeling. Like a draught in the soul.
If I had my own red, she could keep hers. And I could keep my stain. Everyone happy. Well, happier.
Could you bring me some red dye? Six will last a good while. The fireplace looks naked without it.
Her brothers walled me up and let me starve. I've been walking these halls ever since, with a clanking conscience.
I told myself I haunt because it's my duty. The truth is, I didn't know how to stop.
There's a stain by the fireplace. Blood, supposedly. Hers, the story says. I renew it every single night.
The family scrubs it away each morning, and each night I paint it back. It's become our little ritual.
The trouble is, I don't have real blood anymore. I use paints. Stolen paints, to be precise.
I borrow them from Virginia's paintbox. She knows. She's never once told her parents.
Some nights the stain was green, when the red ran out. Nobody believed a green bloodstain. I lost all credibility.
Once it was bright purple. The twins asked if I'd been eating plums. I haunted them for a week out of spite.
Bright red again. She says she doesn't mind. She's the first person in three hundred years who's ever pitied me.
I'll tell you something I've never told anyone living. I'm tired. Not bored. Tired to the bones I don't have.
She went with me into the dark, and she prayed for me. I heard it. It was the kindest sound I've ever heard.
Now the rest is up to the tree. The old almond is dead. But the prophecy says a blossoming tree, not an old one.
The pink tree from the valleys, the one that flowers like a blush, would do. I'm sure of it. Almost.
I'd plant it where the stain used to be. Or in the garden, where I'd like to rest. You pick.
Bring me a blossoming sapling, please. One is enough. It's all I need to finally go to sleep.
I haven't slept since the year they walled me up. Three hundred winters with my eyes open.
Sleep is the thing I want most in the world. Not revenge, not an audience. Just to lie down and close my eyes.
There's a garden past the pinewood where almond blossom grows. Nobody wakes there. The grass is long and quiet.
I've stood at its gate a thousand nights. I can't go in. Something holds me back, a debt, a door.
There's an old prophecy carved on the library window. The children never read it. Virginia did.
It says: when a golden girl can win a prayer from sinful lips, and the barren almond tree bears, the house will rest.
I told her what it meant: she'd have to weep for my sins, because I had no tears of my own.
She said she wasn't afraid. I was. Terribly. For her. That was the first time I'd been afraid for someone else.
It's planted. I feel... sleepy. Can you imagine? Me, sleepy. Take the chains. I won't need to scare anyone again.
The pink tree bloomed in a single night. Virginia cried, and then laughed, and then cried again. So did I.
I dream now. Mostly about almond blossom and very soft chairs. Once about you, bringing me chains in a wheelbarrow.
Virginia visits every spring with flowers. She's grown, you know. She brought her little boy last time.
He wasn't afraid of me at all. He asked if I wanted to play hide and seek. I'm unbeatable at it, obviously.
When I finally go all the way to sleep, and I will one day, soon, I'll go smiling. You helped with that.
Goodnight, my friend. Three hundred years of haunting, and the best part was the end. Mind the petals on the path.
I lie under it most of the day now. The grass is soft, and nobody asks me to rattle anything.
The neighbours say they hear snoring on quiet nights. That's me. I'm rather proud of the volume.
The twins came to apologise for the butter. I forgave them. Then I said 'boo', gently. They fell over. Still got it.
The stain by the fireplace is gone. I told Virginia to keep her red for sunsets. She painted one for me.
It hangs above my old spot in the hall. When I wake, I look at it and think: that's what red is for.
I used to think haunting was an art. Resting is the real art. I'm just a beginner.
You knocked before entering, every time. It seems so small, but it was the first courtesy I'd had in ages.
If anyone in the village ever needs frightening, a thief, a bully, let me know. For you I'd come out of retirement.
Now a pink tree blooms in the garden of the old house, and on quiet nights, instead of chains, the neighbours hear someone snoring peacefully.
The Canterville Ghost — Oscar Wilde (1887)
My chains have been oiled so often they don't clank anymore. It's humiliating. Bring me proper ones.
CLANK. CLANK. Oh, that's the sound. Someone upstairs just said 'bless you'. Sigh.
New chains to rattle
There's a bloodstain by the fireplace that I renew each night. The girl of the house lends me her paints, but red is running out.
Bright red again. She says she doesn't mind me using her paints. She's the first person who's ever pitied me.
The stain on the floor
The girl said she'd pray for me, and the old prophecy says: when a child weeps for the ghost, the almond tree will bloom. Bring a blossoming sapling to plant.
It's planted. I feel... sleepy. Take these; I won't need to scare anyone again.
The garden of rest
Boo. ...No? Not even a little shiver?
The new neighbours left me a bottle of lubricant for my chains. The insult!
Being frightening used to be an art. Now it's just paperwork.
You're the only one who knocks before entering my room. I appreciate the gesture.
Three hundred years of haunting
hearthbound.persona.novel_captain_hook.b: I was the most feared captain on the seas. A boy who never grew up cut off my hand in a duel and threw it to a crocodile, which liked the taste.
It swallowed a clock, and ever since, the sound of ticking makes me tremble. I left the sea. I never left the fear.
hearthbound.persona.novel_captain_hook.d: Good day. Do wipe your boots. One may have left the sea, but one keeps a tidy deck.
Manners, please. Even in a fight one must show good form. Especially in a fight.
I sold the ship long ago and came inland. Rivers seemed safer than oceans. Mostly.
Something moves in the river at night. Splashes. Groans. I watch it from the bridge with a lantern.
It isn't the crocodile, I know that. Crocodiles don't groan. And they don't carry tridents.
The drowned ones, the villagers call them. Pale, bloated, and far too fond of the dark.
Deal with them, would you? Half a dozen, perhaps. I'd go myself, but water and I have a history.
Did you hear that? ...No? Good. Good. Carry on.
I was educated at a very fine school. I still wonder whether they'd approve of me now.
The hook? An old souvenir. Don't stare; it's bad form. Well, stare a little. It is rather striking.
I once commanded the most feared ship on any sea. Grown sailors wept at the sight of my flag.
There was a boy. A boy who never grew up, cheeky and quick, who crowed like a rooster.
In a duel he cut off my hand. Then he tossed it to a crocodile, as casually as a crust of bread.
The crocodile liked the taste. It followed me for years, from sea to sea, hoping for the rest.
Horrid beast. Patient. Grinning. I'd see its eyes in the water while I ate my supper.
No ticking. Only splashing. I can bear splashing. Thank you, truly.
I stood on the bridge the whole time with my lantern. Moral support. Very important, moral support.
The hook helps, oddly. Lifts baskets, opens doors, picks locks when the baker forgets his key.
But look at it now. Worn down to a nub. It can barely hold a teacup.
Without it I feel like half of myself. And the wrong half: the one from the lagoon.
The smith says he can forge a new one, properly curved and polished, if I bring him the metal.
Bring me iron? Four ingots should do. I'd like to be myself again, in a better edition.
You fought with excellent form. Feet planted, no wasted flourishes. My old bosun would have wept.
I'll tell you the whole of it. That boy and I fought on a rock in a lagoon, with the tide rising.
I had the upper hand. Then I had no hand at all. He was so quick, and so pleased with himself.
The worst wasn't the pain. It was his laughter, as if I were a game he'd grown bored of.
I had the ship's smith fit me a hook. Iron, polished till it shone. I wore it like a medal.
A villain needs a signature, you see. Mine was that hook, and a very good coat.
I'm not proud of the captain I was. Bad form, most of it. Cruelty dressed up as elegance.
Here I try to be... gentler. I guard the market and help the old folk with their baskets.
Sharp and shining. I feel like a captain again, a gentle one this time. See how it catches the sun?
I carried the baker's flour sacks all morning with it. He says no one has ever hauled flour so elegantly.
My dream is embarrassingly small: to sleep one whole night without listening for ticking.
I've been thinking about it the way one thinks about a duel. You can't win by running.
The only way to stop fearing the ticking may be to live with it. Every night. Right beside me.
If it's by my bed, it can't creep up on me. It'll just be a clock. Just a clock.
Bring me a clock. Only one. I'll set it on my nightstand, and we'll see which of us blinks first.
Now, the part I never tell. The crocodile, remember? It swallowed a clock. A whole clock.
And the clock kept ticking inside it. Tick, tock. That's how I always knew it was near.
In the end the ticking was worse than the teeth. I heard it in my sleep, in the rain, in my own pulse.
I left the sea because of that sound. I thought distance would cure me. It didn't.
The miller's clock nearly finished me my first week here. I dropped an entire tray of eggs.
I avoid the stall that sells pocket watches. I walk the long way round the chapel bell.
You're the first person I've let near me with a clock in your pocket. Did you know? I noticed.
My true fear is that I'll die still running from a sound. What a ridiculous ending that would be.
Tick, tock, and I'm still here. Every night. I've named it. Don't laugh: it's called Smee.
I slept until noon yesterday. Noon! The baker thought I'd died and came round with soup.
I write to my old school now and then. They never answer. I've decided your approval is enough.
Remember the eggs I dropped because of the miller's clock? I paid him back in eggs. And a clock; his broke.
If anything ever frightens you so much it follows you from sea to sea, come to me. I know the way through.
Hiding isn't braver. It's only quieter. You taught me that without even trying.
Off you go. Mind your manners, keep your form, and don't be late. I'll know; I have a clock.
You have my old sword now. It's finer in your hands than it ever was in mine.
I passed the watch stall this morning. I bought nothing, but I stopped. I stopped and listened.
The ticking sounds almost friendly now. Like someone counting me into a waltz.
The river's been quiet since you cleared it. I fish from the bridge. Terrible catch. Lovely evenings.
I wonder what became of that crocodile. Asleep somewhere, perhaps, with a clock that finally stopped.
And the boy? I hope he's well. Isn't that absurd? I truly hope he's well.
The children ask me to play the pirate at festivals. I'm rather good. I let them win, with good form.
My new hook is the talk of the market. It opens jars better than any hand.
hearthbound.persona.novel_captain_hook.e: Now there's a clock ticking by the old captain's bed every night, and for the first time in years, they sleep until noon.
hearthbound.persona.novel_captain_hook.s: Peter and Wendy — J. M. Barrie (1911)
Something moves in the river at night. It isn't the crocodile, I know that... but deal with the drowned ones, would you?
No ticking. Only splashing. I can bear splashing.
My iron hook is worn down to a nub. Bring me iron, and I'll have the smith forge me one with proper polish.
Sharp and shining. I feel like a captain again, a gentle one this time.
I think the only way to stop fearing the ticking is to live with it. Bring me a clock. I'll keep it by my bed.
Tick, tock... and I'm still here. Take my old sword; you've shown better form than any gentleman I knew.
hearthbound.persona.novel_captain_hook.t: Did you hear that? ...No? Good. Good.
Manners, please. Even in a fight, one must show good form.
I was educated at a fine school. I still dream of their approval.
You're the first person I've let near me with a clock in your pocket.
I have the loudest roar in the village. Everyone runs from it. What they don't know is that I run too, just in the other direction.
Once I jumped a chasm carrying my friends and fought beasts for them, trembling the whole time. I thought that didn't count because I was afraid.
ROAR! ...Oh, it's you. Good morning. I practise at dawn, when fewer people are awake.
I'm the guard here, technically. I guard mostly from behind the well.
The dead have been shuffling near the fields at night. The farmers look at me as if I'll handle it.
I did handle it, sort of. I roared at them from behind the fence. They didn't notice.
My paws sweat just thinking of going out there. Lions don't even have sweaty paws. Only me.
Five of them, I think. Maybe six. I lost count when I closed my eyes.
Would you... go first? I'll be right behind you, roaring encouragingly. Very encouragingly.
My mane takes an hour to comb. A guard must look fierce, even if the guard isn't.
Did you hear that rustle? No? Probably a leaf. Probably. I'll stand here a little longer.
The farmers give me carrots for keeping watch. I don't tell them I watch with my eyes half shut.
Everyone runs when I roar. I roar, they run, and I run too. Just in the other direction.
Where I come from, everyone expected the lion to be the bravest beast. Imagine the pressure.
I used to lie awake listing the things that could eat me. It was a long list. Some were rabbits.
Once I walked a yellow road with a straw man, a tin one, and a girl with a little dog.
I'll tell you about that road someday. Some parts I'm still not sure happened the way I remember.
You were magnificent out there. I was... audible. Very audible.
The farmers thanked me. I let them. Then I came straight here to thank you properly.
The dogs are howling tonight. The old woman by the mill says it means something big is coming.
Last time the raiders came, I hid in the barn with the goats. The goats were braver.
I've been thinking. I don't want to be the guard behind the barn door anymore.
This time I want to stand at the gate. My knees will shake. I'm telling you now so you won't be surprised.
Stay with me tonight, at the gate? With you beside me, I think my legs will stay where I put them.
A confession: by the third one my eyes were shut. I roared at a pumpkin.
My roar is the loudest in the village. That's the curse of it: everyone expects the rest of me to match.
As a cub I roared at an echo, and the echo roared back. I ran for a whole afternoon.
In the old forest they called me King of Beasts, and they said it with a smirk.
So I learned to roar first, big and loud, so nobody would see how small I felt behind it.
It works on sheep. It works on bandits, sometimes. It never once worked on me.
The girl with the dog slapped my nose once for scaring her friends. I cried. She hugged me afterwards.
Do you think some lions are brave without trying? Or are they all pretending, like me?
I didn't run. Did you see? My tail was shaking so hard it dusted the gate, but I didn't run.
I slept all morning afterwards. Being brave is exhausting. How do you manage it every day?
My dream? To walk into the dark without counting my breaths. Just once, as if it were nothing.
In the old forest a giant spider was eating the animals. They begged me to kill it, and I did.
It was asleep. I leapt on it and struck its head off with one blow. Then I was sick behind a tree.
Spiders crawl around the village at night now, dozens of them. Every time, my claws forget the forest.
Hunt them with me? Ten or so. I want to remember I'm the one who did it, not the one who ran.
The children drew me on the barn wall with an enormous mane. They left out the shaking. Kind of them.
There's something I've never told anyone here. On that old yellow road, I did brave things.
We reached a chasm too wide to cross. I carried my friends over on my back, one by one, jumping.
I was sure I'd fall every time. My heart was a drum. I jumped anyway, because they were counting on me.
Later, beasts with bear bodies and tiger heads chased us. I turned to face them. My teeth were chattering.
I always thought it didn't count, because I was terrified. Real heroes aren't scared, I told myself.
A wizard told me courage is facing danger while afraid. I laughed. Then I stopped laughing.
What I fear now is forgetting. Going back to hiding and calling it good sense.
No shield at my side anymore. It's yours now. My paws feel oddly free, like a cub's.
The wizard's dish of 'courage' was only honey, remember? I've had honey since. Didn't need any.
I tell the children: being afraid is how you know you're about to do something important.
Last week a bandit saw me yawn and fled. I was only sleepy. I let him believe what he liked.
If you're ever afraid, come to the gate. I'll stand beside you and roar encouragingly. It works.
My knees still shake on cold nights. Just the cold, surely. And if it isn't, that's fine too.
Go and have your adventures. The gate is guarded, by a lion. A real one, it turns out.
I still get scared. Now I just say it out loud, 'I'm scared', and then I go anyway.
The spiders keep away from the gate now. I think they talk to each other. I think they've heard.
I've decided to roar only once a year, at the harvest feast. It'll be an occasion.
The children asked me to teach them to roar. We practise behind the barn. The goats are unimpressed.
Last night I walked the whole wall in the dark. I counted nothing. Well, stars. Stars are allowed.
Remember the pumpkin? The farmers put a little crown on one this year. Very funny. Very funny.
The old woman by the mill brings me pie now. She says a brave guard needs feeding.
I wrote to the straw man and the tin one. They say they always knew. I wish someone had told me.
Now the guard at the gate roars only once a year, at the harvest feast, and the children cheer instead of running.
The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum (1900)
There are dead things near the fields. I'm supposed to deal with them. Would you... go first? I'll roar encouragingly.
I roared the whole time. I think it helped. Did it help?
You go first
Something big is coming tonight. I want to stand at the gate this time, not hide in the barn. Stay with me.
I didn't run. My tail was shaking, but I didn't run.
The night of the siege
In the old forest I once killed a giant spider that ate the animals. Here they crawl in the dark. This time I want to remember I can do it.
The wizard gave me a dish of 'courage' to drink. It was only honey. Take this shield; I don't need to hide behind it anymore.
The great spider
ROAR! ...Sorry. Did I startle you? I startled myself.
My knees shake at night. Just the cold, surely.
A wizard told me courage is facing danger while afraid. Then I've been brave for years without noticing.
With you beside me, my roar almost sounds real.
A roar without courage
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorian_gray.bi: A painter once made my portrait, and I wished aloud that it would age instead of me. Years have passed. Look at me: not a single line.
The portrait is locked in my attic. Every cruel thing I've done appears on its face, not mine. I haven't dared look at it in a long time.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorian_gray.di: Welcome, welcome. Silks, perfumes, pretty trifles. Everything here is lovely. I make sure of it.
People say I look exactly as I did twenty years ago. They mean it as a compliment. I take it as one.
I read a little yellow book once that ruined me. Be careful what you read. And more careful what you wish.
I keep the portrait in my attic, behind a locked door. I haven't looked at it in a very long time.
A few nights ago I heard a crack from up there. Sharp, like ice on a pond. I think the frame split.
I don't want to go up. But I also can't stand the thought of that door, bare and waiting, every morning.
Bring me a couple of frames, would you? I'll hang something pretty over the attic door. Flowers, perhaps.
Beauty is a wonderful thing. It's also a very heavy one. Nobody warns you about the weight.
I don't keep mirrors in the shop. Too many customers staring at themselves instead of the goods.
Do you ever feel that time is looking at you? No? You're lucky. It's only looking away from me.
When I was young, a painter asked to paint me. He said my face had changed how he saw everything.
He worked for weeks. I sat in his studio with the lilacs outside and a clever friend of his talking to me.
That friend said youth was the only thing worth having. I believed every word. I was very young.
When the portrait was done, I looked at it and wept. It would stay beautiful, and I would grow old.
I said aloud that I'd give anything for it to be the other way round. Anything. My soul, I said. Idly.
Pretty frames, pretty flowers. No one will guess what lies behind them. You have excellent taste.
Now you've helped me hide it, I'll tell you what it is. Every cruel thing I've done appears on its face.
But I've been thinking. If I never look at it, it wins. It carries my sins and I carry nothing. Not even the truth.
I've decided to look at it. Not today. But one day soon, with the door wide open.
The attic has no window. It's dark as a shut eye. I'll need light, a lot of light.
I can't bear half-shadows up there. In half-shadow the face seems to move. It's better seen whole.
Bring me candles, would you? Six of them. Enough to see every line I've earned.
Not mine. Its. I stay smooth and fresh, and it takes the lines, the sneer, the cruelty around the mouth.
The first time I noticed, it was after I broke a young actress's heart. The portrait had a new curve of spite.
She had played Juliet so beautifully. Then one night she played badly, because she was in love with me.
I told her she'd killed my love. She died that night. The portrait smiled a little crueller in the morning.
After that I lived as if nothing counted. Nothing did count, not on my face. That's a dangerous freedom.
You look at me as if you saw what's upstairs. And you stay anyway. I don't know what to make of that.
The painter came to see me once, years later. He wanted to see his masterpiece. I showed him.
I won't tell you what happened then. Not yet. Some doors stay closed even in a confession.
I opened the door a finger's width. Then I closed it. Tomorrow. I keep saying tomorrow.
I smelled the dust and the old oil paint, and I heard my own breathing. It sounded like someone else's.
There are witches in the marsh here. At night I hear them. The same laugh. The very same.
I think they came for a bargain that's still being paid. Every cruelty, a coin in their pocket.
I want that laughter gone before I face the portrait. I can't climb those stairs with it in my ears.
I'm no fighter. I've never lifted anything heavier than a wine glass. You know that about me.
Silence them for me. Three will do. Then I'll go up to the attic with all the candles lit. I swear it.
The painter, since you'll ask. He saw the portrait and was horrified. He begged me to pray. I didn't.
I did something that night I can never undo. He never left the attic. That's all I'll ever say.
You're still here. After that. I don't understand you. I think I'm starting to rely on you.
My deepest fear isn't that the portrait is ugly. It's that it's honest, and I'll recognise myself.
My dream? To have one grey hair. One wrinkle. Some small proof that time touched me like everyone else.
I never told you who really granted my wish. It wasn't the painter. He never knew anything about magic.
The day I said those words, an old woman passed the studio window, dressed in purple, laughing.
I heard that laughter again the night the actress died. And again the night the painter came.
I went up. It's hideous, and it's mine. I stood there until the candles burned down, and I didn't look away.
Keep those crystals. I used to adore my reflection in them. Now I'd rather see yours.
I've burned the little yellow book. It went up so quickly. Some poisons are very thin.
You're the only one who ever looked at me and saw more than my face. You saw upstairs, and you stayed.
In twenty years I'll be wrinkled and grey like everyone else. I can't wait. Save me a bench by the well.
If anyone ever asks you what the secret to eternal youth is, tell them: don't. It isn't worth it.
Come back soon. I'll have a new grey hair to show you. I'm counting them now, the way I once counted compliments.
Guess what I found this morning. A grey hair! Right here, at the temple. Look! Isn't it magnificent?
I've shown it to everyone. The baker, the smith, a very confused goat. I may have it framed.
The portrait is still in the attic. I've left the door open. It doesn't hide anything now, and neither do I.
I think its face softened a little, after. Not beautiful. But less cruel. Or maybe I'm finally seeing clearly.
I've started apologising to people. It's exhausting and terrifying and I recommend it to nobody but myself.
I sell fewer mirrors and more candles now. People think it's a fashion. I let them think so.
Beauty is still heavy. But I've put some of it down. My shoulders are grateful, and so is my conscience.
The marsh is quiet. When the frogs sing, that's all it is: frogs. No laughing. I listen every night.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorian_gray.ep: Since the attic door was opened, the eternally young face in the village has gained one grey hair, and its owner shows it to everyone, delighted.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorian_gray.so: The Picture of Dorian Gray — Oscar Wilde (1890)
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorian_gray.st: The frame of the portrait cracked; I heard it at night. Bring me frames, so I can hang something pretty over the attic door.
Pretty frames, pretty flowers. No one will guess what lies behind them.
I've decided to look at it. Not today. But I'll need light, a lot of light. Bring candles.
I opened the door a finger's width. Then I closed it. Tomorrow.
The painter never knew; the wish was answered by a witch who laughed. They still gather in the marsh. I want that laughter gone before I face the portrait.
I went up. It's hideous, and it's mine. Take these crystals: I used to adore my reflection in them.
The one who sold the wish
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorian_gray.ta: People say I look exactly as I did twenty years ago. They mean it as a compliment.
Beauty is a wonderful thing. It's also a very heavy one.
I read a little yellow book once that ruined me. Be careful what you read.
You look at me as if you saw what's upstairs. And you stay anyway.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.bio.0: I grew up on a grey farm on a grey prairie with a grey aunt and uncle. Then a cyclone picked up the whole house, with me and my dog inside.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.bio.1: It dropped us in a land of colour, right on top of a wicked witch. Everyone called me a heroine. All I wanted was to go home.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.dialog: Hello! Sorry, I keep staring at your fields. Where I grew up, even the wheat looked tired and grey.
My dog hid under the bed again last night. Thunder. He has good reasons to hate the wind, believe me.
On that road I found a straw man, a tin man and a lion. We walked together for a long time.
Everybody kept saying one man in a green city could send me home. The wizard. I still haven't met him.
I've walked so far that I've lost count of the villages. Each one is lovely. None of them is Kansas.
I can't leave the farm long enough to look properly. The cows, the dog, the harvest... you understand.
Would you walk the road ahead for me? Find a village I haven't seen. Maybe the wizard is there.
Do you like my shoes? They're silver. They pinch a little, but I can't bring myself to take them off.
I milk the cows at dawn out of habit. Uncle Henry always said the cows don't care where you've been.
I sing to the chickens. They're a tough audience, but kinder than the crows I met on the road.
Aunt Em never smiled. The sun had baked it out of her. I used to laugh just to see her jump.
There was a cellar under our house for cyclones. That day I ran back for my dog and missed the door.
The house spun for hours. I fell asleep inside a storm, can you imagine? I woke up somewhere full of colour.
The house landed on a wicked witch. People cheered as if I'd planned it. I only wanted to cry.
Little people in blue gave me her silver shoes and pointed to a yellow road. Follow it, they said.
You found another village! No wizard, but it felt good to hear there's more road ahead. Thank you.
Can I tell you a secret? The wizard in the green city was just a little man behind a curtain.
Then she sent winged monkeys, and they carried me off. I scrubbed her floors for weeks.
She tried to steal my shoe. I was so angry I threw a bucket of water at her. She melted. Just like that.
I still dream of that sound, a sort of hiss and a wail. And then there's the cackling.
There are witches here too, in the marsh. I hear them at night, laughing just like she did.
I can't throw another bucket. I just can't. Could you deal with them for me, please?
He had a big voice and a bigger head made of paper. He was a humbug. A kind humbug, though.
He gave my friends a heart of silk, brains of bran and courage from a bottle. They were so happy.
And me? He had nothing for me. He tried to fly me home in a balloon and floated off without me.
I think that's why I walked here. If nobody could send me home, maybe I could find somewhere new.
Before the balloon, he sent me after the witch of the West. That was the price of his help.
She had one eye, but it saw like a telescope. She watched us cross the whole land.
She sent wolves first. The Tin Woodman stood in front of me and swung his axe until morning.
Then crows, then black bees. The Scarecrow hid us under his straw so the bees broke their stings on tin.
The marsh is quiet. I slept all night, and my dog did too. You're braver than a lion, you know.
Speaking of lions, mine was so scared he trembled at a squirrel. Then he fought a monster spider for us.
And then in the dream I don't know if I'm happy or sad to be back. That's the scariest part.
I think I don't need the shoes. I need to know someone is waiting. Then I can walk home myself.
I've written a letter to Aunt Em. It took me four tries. The first three were mostly crying.
It says I'm alive, that I'm well, that I miss her, and that I'm on my way. That's all.
Would you carry it to her? The shoes can stay on the shelf. I'd rather it reached her by a friend.
I've learned that about people. They're usually already what they wish they were. They just don't know it.
Here's what the Good Witch of the South told me at the very end. It's a little embarrassing.
The silver shoes could have taken me home from the first day. Three knocks of the heels, and a wish.
All that walking. All those wolves and monkeys. And the way home was on my feet the whole time.
I was furious for a day. Then I thought: without the road, I'd never have known my friends.
So why am I still here? Because I'm afraid. What if I click my heels and home isn't grey anymore?
What if Aunt Em has given up on me? What if the farm is gone, blown away by another storm?
I dream of it: the grey door, Uncle Henry at the gate, Aunt Em running out with her apron flapping.
You gave her my letter! What did she do? Did she smile? Tell me she smiled, even a little.
I don't need the shoes to find the way anymore. I hope they carry you somewhere wonderful.
You walked ahead of me when I couldn't. Nobody else did that for me, not even the wizard.
Whenever the wind rises, I don't hide in the cellar anymore. I stand at the green door and listen.
Aunt Em wrote back. Three lines. The last one says: we kept your room. I've read it a hundred times.
Someday I'll walk to her. Not today; the cows need me. But the road is there, and I know it's mine.
There's no place like home, and you helped me find mine. Come for supper whenever you like.
I painted the farmhouse door bright green, like the city of the wizard. Uncle Henry would hate it.
My dog barks at the wind now, but it's a happy bark. He knows storms can bring you somewhere good.
I've decided home isn't one place. It's wherever someone is expecting you for supper.
Sometimes I still hear a cackle at dusk. Then I remember you went to the marsh, and it's just a heron.
The children ask me about the wizard. I tell them the truth: he was a humbug, but a useful one.
I told the Scarecrow's story to the farmer next door. He tapped his head and swore it was full of bran.
If you see a straw man, a tin man or a lion on the road, say hello. Tell them I got where I was going.
I planted marigolds along the path. It isn't yellow brick, but it's the brightest road in the valley.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.epilog: Now that farm has a door painted bright green, and whenever the wind rises, the whole village swears it hears a little dog barking with joy.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum (1900)
They told me: follow the yellow brick road and you'll find someone who can send you home. Walk ahead of me, find a village I haven't seen.
Another village, and still no wizard. But the road goes on, and so do we.
A witch sent wolves, crows and bees after me. In the end a bucket of water finished her. Here there are witches in the marsh; please, deal with them.
Melted? Oh, I'd rather not look. Thank you. I can sleep without the sound of cackling.
The silver shoes could have taken me home all along; I just had to click my heels. Carry a letter to my aunt; tell her I'm on my way.
You gave her my letter. Now I don't need the shoes to find the way. Take them: they've walked enough.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.talk.0: Where I come from, even the grass is grey. Isn't this place bright?
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.talk.1: My dog barks at every storm. I don't blame him.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.talk.2: I made friends on that road: one without brains, one without a heart, one without courage. They had plenty of all three.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.talk.3: There's no place like home. I've just started to wonder where home is.
hearthbound.persona.novel_dorothy.title: A road of yellow brick
hearthbound.persona.novel_frankenstein_c: I was put together from pieces by someone who ran away the moment I opened my eyes. People scream at my face before I can say hello.
I learned to speak by listening at the wall of a poor family's cottage. I left them firewood every night. They never knew it was me.
Don't be afraid. I'm only big. That's all it is.
I like fire. I learned that it warms before I learned that it burns.
There's a family at the end of the lane. The father coughs all night. Their chimney barely smokes.
I've seen the children gathering twigs in the snow. Twigs don't heat a house.
I've been leaving wood by their door before dawn. They think a neighbour does it. I let them.
But I fell trees slowly, and winter is quick. I need more than my two mismatched hands can cut.
Help me? Bring logs, sixteen or so, and don't tell them where they came from. Please.
I walk at dawn, when the paths are empty. It spares people the trouble of screaming.
The birds don't mind me. Birds are sensible. They judge you by what you do with your hands.
You looked at me the first day and didn't step back. I remember that. I always will.
I woke on a table in a room full of jars. The one who made me looked once, and ran.
I didn't know what running meant. I thought it might be a game, and that I should follow.
I'm made of many people, I think. My hands don't match. The left one is gentler.
The first village I found, I walked into smiling. They threw stones. I didn't know what a smile looked like on me.
I have read about gods and heroes since. None of them had to ask to be loved.
They found the pile and called it a miracle from the woods. I'll let them keep their miracle.
The father's cough is softer. The smoke from their chimney is thick and grey. It's beautiful.
Letters were like doors. Each one opened onto somewhere I hadn't been allowed to go.
Then I found a satchel in the woods: three books, dropped by some traveller.
A book of lives, a book about a war in heaven, a book of a young man's sorrows. They taught me what a soul is.
I've read them so often the pages are soft as cloth. I want more words. I want to know what else I am.
Would you bring me books? Three would do. I'll read slowly, to make them last.
I've done this before, you know. Long ago, for another family, in another forest.
After the stones, I hid in a hovel built against the wall of a poor cottage. There was a crack I could see through.
An old man, a young man, a young woman. They were gentle with one another. I had never seen gentleness.
I learned to speak by listening to them. Bread. Fire. Father. I whispered each word to the dark.
They were poor and hungry, so I stopped taking from their store. I ate berries and roots instead.
At night I cut their wood and stacked it by the door. They said a good spirit was helping them.
A good spirit. I held that name close for a whole winter. It was the first name I ever had.
One day a stranger came to stay, and they taught her their language. I learned alongside her, through the wall.
I read until the candle died. Now I have words for what I feel. That is better, and worse.
There's a word, 'lonely'. I'd carried it for years without knowing it had a name.
For years I followed the old man's road, afraid to find him, afraid not to. He came here, at the end.
He's buried behind the chapel. No flowers. Nobody here remembers who he was.
My fear is that I'll forget his voice. It was the only kind voice I had, until yours.
My dream? To stand at his grave without being chased away, and say thank you where he can hear.
Bring flowers for him? A dozen small ones, the kind that grow wild. He would have liked wild ones.
And a word, 'friend'. I've been practising it. I said it to a cow. She didn't object.
I'll tell you how the cottage story ended. I've never told anyone.
One day the young ones went out, and only the old father stayed home. He was blind.
I knocked. I spoke. He couldn't see my face, only hear my voice. He called me friend.
We talked for an hour. The best hour of my life. I still have every word of it.
Then the others came home and found me kneeling at his feet. The son struck me with a stick.
I could have broken him in two. I didn't. I ran. By morning the family had left the cottage for good.
They never knew who had cut their wood. They only knew what my face looked like.
He would have liked those. I planted a few roots too, so they come back each spring.
My coat is yours now. I stitched it from scraps, like myself. It kept me whole; let it keep you.
Remember the cow I called friend? She follows me everywhere now. I think she believed me.
I've thought about the one who made me. I don't hate him. I only wish he'd stayed one minute longer.
You stayed. From the very first day. I've written that down, so even if I forget, the page won't.
If anyone ever runs from you, come and sit on my step. There's usually soup.
Go on, friend. I've practised that word so much it doesn't frighten me anymore.
Someone leaves a bowl of soup on my doorstep now, every evening. I don't know who. I let it be a miracle.
A child sat on my step yesterday and asked me to read to her. She didn't look at my face. She looked at the book.
I read her the book of lives. She fell asleep on page nine. I didn't move until her mother came.
Her mother didn't scream. She said 'thank you' and carried the child home. I sat there a long while.
The family at the end of the lane asked me to supper. They'd worked out who brought the wood.
The father said, 'So you're the miracle.' I said I was only big. He laughed until he coughed.
I have more books now. People bring the ones they've finished. My shelf is crooked. I built it.
I still walk at dawn. Now it's because I like the light, not because I'm hiding.
Now the villagers leave a bowl of soup on the doorstep of the patched-up giant, and some mornings, a child sits there to be read to.
Frankenstein — Mary Shelley (1818)
There's a family in the village struggling to keep warm. I leave them wood before dawn. Help me: bring logs, and don't tell them.
They found the pile and called it a miracle from the woods. I'll let them.
Wood by the door
I found three books in a satchel once, and they taught me what a soul is. I want more. Would you bring me books?
I read until the candle died. Now I have words for what I feel. That is better, and worse.
Learning to read
The only one who ever spoke kindly to me was an old blind man who couldn't see my face. He's buried here. Bring flowers for his grave.
He would have liked these. Take my coat; I stitched it from scraps, like myself, and it has kept me whole.
Flowers for the blind elder
Don't be afraid. I'm only big. That's all.
I like fire. I learned that it warms before I learned it burns.
I have read about gods and heroes. None of them had to ask to be loved.
You looked at me the first day and didn't step back. I remember that.
Stitched together
hearthbound.persona.novel_happy_prince.b: I grew up in a palace where sorrow wasn't allowed in. Everyone called me happy. Only when I lost it all did I see how much misery lay outside the walls.
Now I give away what I have left, piece by piece. I can't carry it myself, so I need a messenger, like the swallow in the old tale.
hearthbound.persona.novel_happy_prince.d: Hello, hello. Sit down; the step is warm. They used to call me happy. I'm happier now, and much poorer.
Do you like the sparrows? I feed them crumbs at noon. They argue like merchants over every one.
A little bird once stayed with a statue all winter, just to be kind. It froze. I think of that tale often.
The statue was a prince covered in gold leaf, with sapphire eyes and a ruby on his sword. He gave it all away.
I'm no statue. But I have a few things left from the palace, and I'd like to give them away too, piece by piece.
There's a seamstress in the next village. She embroiders passion flowers on a lady's gown while her child burns with fever.
I've folded a ruby into a letter for her. Would you carry it? I can't walk that far anymore. You'd be my swallow.
My coat was gold-trimmed once. Look, you can still see where the buttons were. I like the little holes.
I've a habit of counting chimneys without smoke. Each one is a cold family. It's a bad habit, but I keep it.
Have you seen the seamstress by the river? Her boy has a fever. I think about him when the wind blows.
I grew up in a palace called the Garden of No Sorrow. Sorrow wasn't allowed in. Neither were beggars.
I played in the garden by day and danced in the great hall by night. There was a high wall around everything.
I never asked what lay beyond the wall. Everything inside was so beautiful. Everyone called me happy.
When I lost it all, and I did, very suddenly, I found myself outside that wall for the first time.
The misery out there was enormous. I'd lived a whole life a street away from it and never heard a thing.
She cried, you say? Good tears, I hope. The child will have medicine. I slept better than I have in years.
You're my swallow, you know. Don't you dare freeze on me. I'm serious. It's the one condition.
But I still see too much. There's a little girl in the square who sells matches. No coat, no shoes, no hat.
Yesterday she dropped her matches in the gutter. They're ruined. She's afraid to go home without money.
Her father will beat her. I heard her tell the pigeons. She thought nobody was listening.
I have nothing left but my coat's lining. I've already ripped it out once. It's mostly thread now.
Could you bring bread? Sixteen loaves. Enough for her and every child on the church steps. I'll pay you in thanks.
I should tell you how I lost the palace. There was no war, no thief. A debt, and pride, and a hard winter.
My advisors had kept the gold flowing for years by squeezing the villages. I never read the accounts.
When the villages had nothing left to give, everything collapsed at once. And the villagers remembered my face.
They didn't hate me. That was the worst of it. They just looked at me as if I'd never been real.
I wandered for a long time. An old priest let me sleep in his church. He said: your eyes are open now. Use them.
So I began to give. A sapphire went to a young writer freezing in an attic. Another to a girl in the square.
I sold my silver, then my brass, then the good boots. You'd be amazed how much one pair of boots can feed.
Now I have almost nothing. And a strange thing: I'm happy. Not palace-happy. Real happy. Sore-feet happy.
She ate on the steps of the church. I sold my last gold button to pay you back; it was worth it.
Sit closer. The sun's going and I want to tell you something. I'm afraid, sometimes, of how little I have left.
Every morning I look under the eaves, terrified, the way you look at someone you love when they're ill.
In the tale, the swallow died at the statue's feet, and the statue's lead heart cracked in two.
I won't let that happen. Not to this bird. The nights are getting colder, and its nest is just mud and straw.
If I had wool, I'd line the nest, pad it thick and warm, so the cold can't reach it until spring.
Bring wool, please. Eight bundles. So it doesn't freeze like the one in the tale. So we get a different ending.
Not for me. For them. When the last button is gone, who will I give to? What will I be, then?
The priest says love isn't counted in buttons. I believe him on Sundays. On Tuesdays I'm not so sure.
My deepest fear is being useless. For so long I was only decoration. Gold and smiles and nothing behind them.
And my dream, well. My dream is a winter in which nobody in this valley goes to bed hungry.
A small dream, you'd say. It's as high as the palace wall ever was. Higher.
Something happened last autumn. A swallow built a nest under my eaves. A real one, blue-backed and quick.
It should have flown south with the others weeks ago. It stayed. It's been helping me feed my sparrows.
I swear it's true. It carries crumbs from my windowsill to the chicks in the hedge. Like a little messenger.
Warm and fluffy. It will live to see spring. Keep the gold flakes; they're the last, but honestly given.
The swallow made it through the winter! It sat on my shoulder the first warm morning and sang right in my ear.
Some nights I dream of the old palace. It's empty and full of gold. I walk out of it smiling every time.
When people ask me if I'm sorry I lost it all, I say: I found everything else instead.
I've started teaching the children to count. We count chimneys with smoke now. The number goes up every winter.
In spring the swallow will come back. I'm sure of it. I've kept the wool in the nest, just in case.
Sit with me when it returns. We'll watch it land, and we'll both pretend we aren't crying. Deal?
It flew south in March, late and cheeky, and I cried like a fool. Then I laughed. Then I fed the sparrows.
Someone painted a heart on my doorstep. A red heart, smudged. I think it was the match girl. I never wash it.
She sells bread now, not matches. The baker took her on. She slips me a crust when he isn't looking.
The seamstress's boy is walking again. He came to thank me. I said: thank the swallow. He looked at you.
The priest says my eyes are brighter than any sapphire. I told him to stop flattering the poor. He laughed.
I have nothing left to give now. Nothing. And do you know, people keep leaving things at my door.
Bread, eggs, a scarf someone knitted badly. I give most of it away again. It's a lovely game.
You were my swallow. You carried rubies and bread and wool, and you never froze. You kept the one condition.
hearthbound.persona.novel_happy_prince.e: Now there's a heart-shaped mark on the doorstep of that humble house, and every spring a swallow returns to nest above it, singing.
hearthbound.persona.novel_happy_prince.s: There's a seamstress in the next village with a sick child and no money. Carry this letter to her; there's a ruby folded inside.
She cried, you say? Good tears, I hope. The child will have medicine.
A child sells matches in the square. She dropped them in the gutter and fears going home. I have nothing left but my coat's lining. Bring bread.
She ate on the steps of the church. I sold my last gold button; it was worth it.
Bread for the little match seller
A real swallow nests under my eaves; it stayed too late helping me feed my sparrows. Bring wool, so it doesn't freeze like the one in the tale.
Warm and fluffy. It will live to see spring. Take the last of my gold: flakes, but honestly given.
hearthbound.persona.novel_happy_prince.t: They used to call me happy. I'm happier now, and much poorer.
Have you seen the seamstress by the river? Her boy has a fever.
A little bird once stayed with a statue all winter, just to be kind. It froze. I think of it often.
You're my swallow, you know. Don't you dare freeze on me.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.bio.0: Everyone here knows me as a kind, respectable sage. I once brewed a draught to split my good self from my worst, and it worked too well.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.bio.1: The other one came out at night, small and cruel and free, and I envied him. Now he comes without the draught. I don't know how long I'll stay me.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.dialogu: Good evening. Or is it? I lose track of evenings. The candles tell me more than the sky does.
Come in, come in. People bring me their headaches and their quarrels. I'm told I give sensible advice.
If you ever find me not myself, don't follow me. Promise. I'll explain one day. Maybe.
Since I came here I've tried to live as simply as I can. Herbs, tinctures, a garden. Honest work.
But there's a room behind my house full of broken glass. I won't let anyone clean it. I did that to it.
I want to make something there again. The reverse of what I once made. A cure, if such a thing exists.
For that I need clean bottles, eight of them. Would you bring them? I can't face the glassblower's questions.
I keep my hands very clean. Wash them twice before tea. A physician's habit, and something more.
Every person holds two. Most never meet the other. Consider yourself lucky if you haven't met yours.
I like your boots. Honest mud on them. I used to walk the whole city at night, once. Not in these shoes.
I was a doctor in a great grey city, with a fine house and a laboratory behind it, down a crooked lane.
Everyone praised my charity. Dinners, donations, a good word for everyone. It was all true. It wasn't all of me.
There was a part of me that wanted to be cruel and careless and never answer for it. I kept him on a leash.
I thought: what if a draught could split the two? The good self free of the bad, and the bad free of me.
My old friend, a lawyer, warned me that my experiments sounded like a fairy tale. He was very nearly right.
Rows of clean bottles. For a moment, filling them felt like the honest work I used to do. Thank you.
You've earned the truth. The draught worked. I drank it one night and became someone else. Smaller. Younger.
When it ran out, I sent for more. The new salt was pure, and it did nothing. Nothing at all.
So the change must have come from some impurity in the first batch. A flaw no one could name.
If I found another salt like it, I could make the reverse draught. Put him back where he came from.
The Nether has white crystals in its walls. Quartz, strange and unclean, from a place that burns.
Would you bring me eight of those crystals? Perhaps... Perhaps. I won't promise more than perhaps.
He had my memories but none of my shame. He walked out into the fog and felt, for the first time, entirely free.
I named him Hyde. I rented rooms for him, opened a bank account for him. I treated him like a guest.
He trampled a child in the street once and paid the family off with my cheque. I told myself it was an accident.
Then he did worse. Much worse. An old gentleman, a cane broken in two. I don't sleep on that night.
I swore off the draught. I lasted two months. Can you imagine missing being wicked? I did. I envied him.
And then, one morning, I woke with his hand on the blanket. No draught. He'd come on his own.
Your visits keep me in my own skin. I mean that exactly. When you're here, he stays very quiet.
I've been reading my old notebooks. The first batch used a white salt I bought from a chemist.
It's no use. This is pure, and purity doesn't work. It was the flaw that did it. It always was.
Don't look so sorry. You brought exactly what I asked for. The failure is mine, as it has always been.
Then I'll seal it, and put it on the village shelf, marked so no one mistakes it for a cookery book.
And I'll burn the recipe. Not the confession. The confession stays. People need to read what it costs.
Writing it will be like opening that door in the lane again. But this time I'll be the one holding the key.
If he comes while I'm writing, keep me at the desk. Talk to me. Say my name. The good one.
Bring me a book to write in, with a quill. One will be enough. I have a long story, and not much time.
I'll tell you what frightens me most. It isn't him. It's how much I enjoyed being him.
Last week I woke in the orchard, barefoot, with scratches on my hands. I don't know whose apples I stole.
He's getting stronger. Each time, it's harder to come back. My hands look smaller in the morning.
In the old city, it ended badly. My lawyer friend broke down the door and found only one of us.
I got away from that ending. I came here, to a quiet village, to a different name. He followed.
My dream is foolish. I want one ordinary evening: supper, a book, bed, and to wake as myself.
Since there's no cure, I'll do the next best thing. I'll make sure no one else ever tries what I did.
I want to write it all down. The pride, the recipe, the envy, the child in the street. Every page.
It's written. Every page. I burned the recipe; I kept the confession. The ash smelled of nothing at all.
For once, only one of us slept here that night. I woke at dawn and counted my own fingers. All mine.
If ever you want to be someone else for a night, come here instead. We'll play cards. Badly.
My lawyer friend would have liked you. He was dry as dust and loyal as a dog, and so are you. Well, less dusty.
I walk the lanes at night now just to walk them. The fog is only fog. It doesn't know me anymore.
You kept me in my own skin when I couldn't. Every time you visited, you said my name, the good one.
Good evening, my friend. And yes, it is an evening. I know exactly which one. Isn't that wonderful?
There's a sealed book on the village shelf now, marked 'Do not brew'. The children dare each other to touch it.
I haven't had a bad night since. Not one. I keep a tally on the wall like a prisoner, but in reverse.
The broken glass is swept. I use the old laboratory to dry herbs now. It smells of mint and lavender.
My hands stay the right size. I check them less every week. Yesterday I forgot entirely. Imagine.
I still believe every person holds two. But I think now the other one can simply be ignored, like a draught.
Forgive the pun. It's the first one I've made in twenty years. You bring out the silly in me.
The quartz you brought is on my windowsill. Pure and useless. I've grown fond of it, like an honest failure.
