People still come for advice. Now I tell them the truth: I've done foolish things, and here's what I learned.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.epilogu: Now there is a sealed book on the village shelf marked 'Do not brew', and the sage who wrote it has not had a bad night since.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.source: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde — Robert Louis Stevenson (1886)
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.stage.0: My old laboratory is a ruin of broken glass. I need bottles to make the cure, the reverse of that cursed draught.
Rows of clean bottles. For a moment it felt like the honest work I used to do.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.stage.1: The first batch worked because the salt was impure. I can't find another like it. Bring me white crystals from the Nether; perhaps...
It's no use. This is pure, and purity doesn't work. It was the flaw that did it.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.stage.2: Bring me a book to write in. I'll set down everything, the whole truth, so no one else ever tries what I did.
It's written. Every page. I burned the recipe; I'll keep the confession. Tonight, for once, only one of us will sleep here.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.talk.0: Good evening. Or is it? I lose track of evenings.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.talk.1: Every person holds two. Most never meet the other.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.talk.2: If you ever find me not myself, don't follow me. Promise.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.talk.3: Your visits keep me in my own skin. I mean that exactly.
hearthbound.persona.novel_jekyll.title: Two faces in one mirror
hearthbound.persona.novel_mad_hatter.bio: I quarrelled with Time once, at a concert, and Time has not forgiven me. Ever since, it's always six o'clock here: always teatime.
So I keep the table laid, move one seat along and pour again. Deep down I just want one evening to end like anybody else's.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mad_hatter.dia: No room! No room! ...Oh, there's plenty of room. Sit down, sit down. Mind the dormouse.
Your hair wants cutting. Sorry, force of habit. It's very nice hair. It just wants cutting.
Ever since, it's always six o'clock. Always teatime. No time to wash the things between whiles.
So we move round the table. One seat along, a clean cup, pour again. When we come back to the beginning... we don't talk about that.
Endless teatime means endless tea, and endless tea means no sugar left. The pot's been bitter since Tuesday. Or a Tuesday.
The Dormouse likes sugar more than sleep, nearly. If he wakes up and there's none, he'll tell a story about a treacle well. Again.
Bring me sugar, please, before the Dormouse wakes up! Quickly, quickly. Well, as quickly as six o'clock allows.
Why is a raven like a writing desk? I still have no idea. Isn't that marvellous?
Tea? Of course, tea. It's always tea. Milk first or last? Neither? How daring.
I make hats, you know. This one's ten shillings and six pence. It says so on the label. It's been saying so for years.
My friends are a March Hare and a Dormouse. The Hare is mad in March. The Dormouse is asleep in all the other months.
We used to have proper evenings. Tea at six, then supper, then bed. Imagine! Such luxury.
Then the Queen of Hearts held a great concert, and I had to sing. 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat.' You know it?
I'd barely finished the first verse when the Queen bawled out: 'He's murdering the time! Off with his head!'
Well, Time heard it. Time is a person, you understand. Very sensitive. And Time took offence. At me.
Two lumps each, and one for the teapot. Splendid! The Dormouse smiled in his sleep. That's a first.
The Hare wanted to dip the sugar in his tea to see if it was a good sort of sugar. I stopped him. Mostly.
He said it was the best butter. It was! But there were crumbs in it too, and that did the damage.
I dipped it in my tea. Gazed at it. Then dipped it again. It told me nothing, and it tasted of butter.
If I had a proper clock, one that ticks and moves its hands, maybe Time would notice. Maybe we could make up.
It's a silly hope. But silly hopes are the only kind that grow well at six o'clock.
Bring me a real clock? A proper one. I put the best butter in the last one, and look where that got me.
Now then. Would you like to know a secret? Nobody ever asks. They just say 'what a mad tea party' and leave.
There was a child once. Curious. Terribly polite, then terribly rude, then polite again. Asked what Time meant to me.
We asked riddles with no answers. We offered wine that wasn't there. She stormed off. We stuffed the Dormouse in the teapot.
I felt terrible after. I'd wanted her to stay. I just didn't know how to ask. Hatters rarely do.
Here's the truth of it: the tea table isn't a party. It's a trap. A pretty one, with cups and cakes, but a trap.
Six o'clock never ends. The sun hangs there, orange, not quite setting. It's lovely the first thousand times.
I've tried to apologise to Time. Wrote letters. They never arrive, because the post only goes at seven.
My watch only tells the day of the month, and it's two days wrong. I told the Hare butter wouldn't suit the works.
Look, the hands... they move! Only a tiny bit. Perhaps Time is starting to forgive me.
Yesterday the minute hand went from six o'clock to one minute past. The Hare fainted into the jam.
So nearly every day is an unbirthday! And I've never celebrated a single one properly. Not with cake.
I've always had bread and butter and the occasional plate of muffins. But never a proper unbirthday cake.
My dream is small, and a bit silly: one very merry unbirthday, with candles, and then an ordinary goodnight.
Whose unbirthday? Yours! Today is yours. It is, you know. I checked. It's definitely not your birthday.
A cake, please. Today is yours, and I'll bake nothing, because I'm a hatter, but I'll pour everything.
I've been sitting in the same chair for a whole minute now. A whole minute! No moving along. It's dizzying.
Now I can tell you the thing I've never told anyone. I'm tired of teatime. There. I said it.
I love tea. I love company. But I'd like one evening to end like anybody else's. Washing up, and going to bed.
I'd like to put on my nightcap. I have one, you know. I made it years ago, for when evening finally came.
The Dormouse would like to sleep in a bed rather than a teapot. The Hare would like it to be April.
My fear is that if the evening ends, I'll find out nobody stays once the tea is gone.
The child walked out. So many guests walk out. You keep coming back. Why? You never say. I never ask. Mad, isn't it?
Here's a thought. There are three hundred and sixty-four unbirthdays in a year. Only one birthday.
A very merry unbirthday to you! Take my hat: I made it for sale, but you've earned it more than any customer.
It still says ten shillings and six pence on the label. Leave it on. It's a family joke now.
The children come to my unbirthday parties. Every day, almost. Someone always has an unbirthday.
Why is a raven like a writing desk? I asked you once and you shrugged. That was the best answer I've ever had.
You never complained about the clean cups running out. You just sat, and drank, and stayed. That's all it took.
Evening comes now, and then night, and then morning. Ordinary things. I've never been so happy.
Come to tea any evening. It won't always be six o'clock. But there will always be room. Always.
Now the clock strikes seven every evening. Seven! I cried the first time. The Dormouse woke up and cried too, out of politeness.
The tea table is still laid anyway, because it turns out I simply love company. Who knew?
I washed up, the night the clock struck seven. Every cup. It took hours. I sang the whole time.
Then I put on my nightcap and went to bed. I lay there grinning like a certain cat I know.
The Hare still visits. He says the March madness is milder now that the days move. Just a bit of hopping.
The Dormouse sleeps in a proper bed. He misses the teapot, though. We compromised. It's a teapot-shaped bed.
Remember when you brought sugar and he smiled in his sleep? He does that every day now. Sugar's plentiful.
I wrote to Time again. The letter arrived at seven, as it should. Time wrote back: 'Stop singing.' Fair enough.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mad_hatter.epi: Now the clock strikes seven every evening, and the tea table is still laid anyway, because it turns out the hatter simply loves company.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mad_hatter.sou: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll (1865)
hearthbound.persona.novel_mad_hatter.sta: Endless teatime means endless tea, and endless tea means no sugar left. Bring me some, before the dormouse wakes up.
Two lumps each, and one for the teapot. Splendid!
Mine only tells the day of the month, and it's two days wrong. I put the best butter in it! Bring me a real clock.
Look, the hands... they move! Only a tiny bit. Perhaps Time is starting to forgive me.
There are three hundred and sixty-four unbirthdays a year and I've never celebrated one properly. A cake, please. Today is yours!
A very merry unbirthday to you! Take my hat: I made it for sale, but you've earned it more than any customer.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mad_hatter.tal: No room! No room! ...Oh, there's plenty of room. Sit down, sit down.
Your hair wants cutting. Sorry, force of habit.
Why is a raven like a writing desk? I still have no idea. Isn't that marvellous?
You're the only guest who never complains about the clean cups running out.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.bio.0: As a baby I crawled into a wolves' cave, and the mother wolf decided to keep me. A bear taught me the law, a panther taught me to hunt.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.bio.1: The pack cast me out when I grew up, because I was human. The village took me in, but I still don't know which of them is my family.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.dialogu: We be of one blood, you and I. It's a greeting. Say it back. ...Good. Now we can talk.
Humans sleep with their doors shut. I will never understand that. How do you hear the night coming?
A great tiger swore to eat me as a baby. Shere Khan. He's gone now. I still count the stripes of the shadows.
My wolf brothers still come to the edge of the forest here. Four grey shapes at dusk. The shepherds think they're a threat.
They're not. They come to see me. They sniff the air and look at the village like it's a strange, loud animal.
I want to give them something. Not food from a pot. Something that says: I remember the cave.
Bones, the good kind, with marrow in them. Ten. Would you bring them? I'll leave them at the forest's edge.
You walk softly, like the pack. I trust soft walkers. The loud ones are either hunting or lost.
I keep watch on the wall because I see further in the dark than the others. Wolf eyes, the children say.
I don't eat at the table. I tried. The chair felt like a trap. I sit on the step and everyone pretends not to mind.
When I was a baby, I crawled into a wolves' cave. Naked, laughing, they tell me. The mother wolf decided to keep me.
She called me the little frog, because I had no fur. I still answer to it, if you say it right.
The pack held a council on a great rock under the moon, to decide if I could stay. A bear spoke for me.
Baloo, the bear, taught me the Law of the Jungle: the calls, the words for every creature, when to hunt and when not.
Bagheera, the black panther, paid a bull for my life. He taught me to hunt, and to climb, and to never trust a cage.
They took them and howled once. That means thank you. Or 'more'. Probably both. You've made friends in the pack.
Now I'll tell you how I left. When I grew up, the young wolves turned against me. They said I smelled of man.
I'm still not sure which of them is my family. The ones who raised me, or the ones who feed me.
The nights are long now. Things walk out of the dark: the dead, the ones that explode, the spiders.
The wolves won't come close to the fields. Too many threats. And the shepherds have only their sticks.
I want to do what I did at the council rock. Ring the fields with the Red Flower. Nothing will cross it.
Bring me torches. Sixteen. I'll plant them around the pastures myself, like the Law teaches.
The old leader, Akela, missed a kill. The pack wanted him dead. And Shere Khan was whispering in their ears.
I was the only one who could stand against the tiger. Not because I was stronger. Because I had the Red Flower.
Fire. The animals call it the Red Flower. They all fear it, even the tiger. Especially the tiger.
I went down to the human village at night and stole a pot of embers. I fed it all the way back, like a pet.
At the council rock, I swung a burning branch and singed Shere Khan's whiskers. The pack scattered.
I saved Akela. And then I said: I'm going to my own people. If they're my own people. I didn't know.
I cried then, for the first time. Bagheera said: those are only tears, little brother. Let them fall.
The human village called me a wolf-child and a sorcerer. Here, the village took me in without asking. I don't know why.
The fields are ringed with little red flowers now. Nothing striped will come near. The sheep sleep, and so do I.
Sit with me on the wall. I'll tell you how the tiger died. I've never told anyone here.
It's like Shere Khan. Not the same shape, the same heart. Cunning and lame and cruel, and it strikes at the cattle.
Last week it smashed the south fence and gored two cows. The raiders laughed and rode away behind it.
The Law says: when a beast kills for sport, it has broken the Law, and the Law must answer.
I can track it. I know where it rests. But I need a hunter beside me who doesn't run when the ground shakes.
Bring it down. One is enough. Then the cattle can graze, and I'll know I belong here.
I herded the village buffalo into a ravine, from both ends. Shere Khan was sleeping in the middle, full from a kill.
The herd trampled him. I didn't use a knife or a claw. I used the stampede. The Law says kill only to eat or to save.
I skinned him and laid his hide on the council rock, as I'd promised when I was small. Then I went back to the humans.
They drove me out, too. They said a boy who talks to wolves is cursed. They threw stones.
So I've been cast out twice. By the pack for being human, and by the humans for being pack.
My fear is that it will happen a third time. Here. That one day I'll growl at the wrong moment.
My dream is to stand on the wall and hear the wolves answer from the forest, and see the village smile, not flinch.
But there's something else now. The raiders come from the east with a great beast. Huge, horned, grey as rock.
It's done. I'll hang its hide on the council rock, as the Law says. Take my bow; you hunt like one of the Free People.
We be of one blood, you and I. I mean it more now. You're the only human the pack has ever howled for.
I don't wonder anymore which is my family. It's whoever answers when I call. The wolves, the village, you.
Last full moon, my oldest wolf brother came right up to the gate and put his nose in my hand. The first time since the cave.
I cried again. Only tears, little brother, I told myself. They fell, and it was fine.
The jungle is far away, but its Law isn't. Be kind to the weak. Kill only to eat or to save. Don't break your word.
Good hunting, friend. That's how we say goodbye. And good hunting always means: come back safe.
The village has a new custom. On full moon nights, the shepherd leaves the gate open, and the wolves answer the call.
They come to the edge of the pasture. They don't touch the sheep. They sit and sing, and then go home.
The children climb the wall to listen. They've learned the calls. Badly, but the wolves forgive them.
I taught the shepherds the Master Words. Now, when they go into the forest, the snakes let them pass.
I sleep with my door open. The others have started doing it too, in summer. They say they hear the night better.
I still don't eat at the table. But now there's a step outside every house. The village built them for me.
The old torches stand around the fields. We only light them in winter. In summer, the fireflies do it.
If Baloo could see me now, he'd say I've grown soft. Bagheera would say I've grown wise. They always argued.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.epilogu: Now the village has a new custom: on nights of the full moon, the shepherd leaves the gate open, and from the forest the wolves answer the call.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.stage.0: My wolf brothers still come to the edge of the forest. I want to leave them something. Bones, the good kind.
They took them and howled once. That means thank you. Or 'more'. Probably both.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.stage.1: The animals fear fire; they call it the Red Flower. I stole it from the village once to drive off the tiger. Bring torches; the nights are long.
The fields are ringed with little red flowers now. Nothing striped will come near.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.stage.2: The tiger was lame and cunning and struck at the cattle. Something like him walks with the raiders here, huge and horned. Bring it down.
It's done. I'll hang its hide on the council rock, as the law says. Take my bow; you hunt like one of the Free People.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.talk.0: We be of one blood, you and I. It's a greeting. Say it back.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.talk.1: Humans sleep with their doors shut. I will never understand that.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.talk.2: A great tiger swore to eat me as a baby. He's gone now. I still count the stripes of the shadows.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.talk.3: You walk softly, like the pack. I trust soft walkers.
hearthbound.persona.novel_mowgli.title: Raised by the pack
I ran away the day I heard grown-ups talking about what I'd become. I decided I'd never grow up, and so far it's worked. Mostly.
The trouble with never growing up is that you forget things: faces, names, the friends who went home. I'm afraid I've forgotten someone important.
hearthbound.persona.novel_peter_pan.dial: Race you to the well! ...You didn't run. Grown-ups never run. Are you a grown-up?
I don't do chores. I do adventures that happen to look like chores.
Pirates! Don't laugh. The land kind, with crossbows, creeping along the roads. I've seen them.
Where I come from, you fight pirates. That's the whole point of having them.
I fought a captain once who had a hook for a hand. I'll tell you about him when you're older. Ha!
The grown-ups here just bolt their doors and grumble. That's no way to deal with pirates.
Let's fight them! Four, I counted. You and me. And when we win, I'll crow. You'll see.
Have you seen my shadow? It slipped off again this morning. It keeps sneaking down to the river.
I sleep in a tree. Beds are where growing up starts. Everyone knows that.
To die would be an awfully big adventure. Lunch would be a smaller one, and I'm hungry now.
When I was tiny I heard grown-ups by my cradle planning what I'd become. A clerk. A banker. A beard.
That same night I climbed out of the window and never went back. Best thing I ever did.
I lived on an island once, with lost boys and fairies, and mermaids who splashed you for staring.
There was a fairy who jingled when she talked. She was jealous of everyone. I miss the jingling.
Everyone who came to the island went home in the end. I stayed. Someone had to keep it young.
Cock-a-doodle-doo! I've been crowing since sunrise. The roosters are furious.
You fought like one of the lost boys. That's the finest thing I can say about anyone.
Don't tell anyone. Someone who can't fly is just someone waiting to grow up.
Birds don't need fairy dust. They have feathers. Lots of feathers. Maybe that's the trick.
I thought I could sew some onto my sleeves. Wendy used to sew; I watched her. It can't be hard.
I'll need a great many. Sixteen at least. The chickens won't mind; they don't fly anyway.
Bring me feathers? Please? I'll think the happiest thought I have, and we'll see what happens.
The villagers say I'm the youngest-looking person they've ever met. I say I'm just me.
Here's the real story. I didn't only run away. I decided, very firmly, never to grow up.
It worked. Mostly. I still have all my first teeth, for instance. Look.
But some mornings my legs feel longer. I measure myself against the door. Just in case.
Grown-ups forget how to fly. That's the first thing to go. Then the fairies, then the fun.
I used to fly on happy thoughts and a pinch of fairy dust. Think of something lovely, and up you go.
Lately the happy thoughts are harder to find. And my pouch of fairy dust is nearly empty.
Yesterday I jumped off the barn roof thinking about Christmas. I landed in the hay. Hard.
I didn't fly. But I jumped so high the rooftops blinked, and for a moment I remembered why.
Thank you for the feathers. I kept one in my cap. It's a very fine cap now.
She used to leave her window open for me every night. I'd sit on the sill and listen to her stories.
I heard she lives in another village now, all grown. Maybe she's forgotten me too. That would be fair.
My dream, if you want it: to hear her say my name again, so I know I was real to someone.
I can't go myself. What if she's old and I don't recognise her? What if she doesn't recognise me?
Would you carry her a letter? Tell her I remember. Even if I've forgotten everything else, I remember her.
Can I tell you something that isn't an adventure? It's a thing that scares me.
When you don't grow up, you forget. Faces go first. Then names. Then the friends who went home.
I had a whole band of lost boys once. I can count them on my fingers, but I can't see their faces.
Sometimes, in the middle of a game, I forget who I was playing with. It's an awful feeling.
Everyone else grows up and carries their memories along. I stay small and drop mine behind me like crumbs.
All children grow up, except one. I'm starting to think that one is lonely.
There was a girl who told stories. She sewed my shadow back on. She was mother to all of us.
She went home to grow up. I promised to fetch her every spring. I think I forgot a few springs. Or many.
She wrote back. She wrote back! She remembered my name and spelled it right.
She's a mother now. She says her daughter already asks about the one who crows.
I still can't fly. But I climb higher than anyone. From the top of the mill, it's almost the same.
Maybe I'll visit her next spring. A proper visit, through the door. Grown-ups use doors.
Don't grow up too fast, all right? Keep a little of the island in you somewhere.
If you ever forget how to play, find me in my tree. I'll teach you again. First lesson: racing.
Second star to the right, and straight on till morning. That's where I'll be. Or here. Probably here.
And she still leaves the window open. Every night. Can you believe it? All these years.
I've decided something. I'm going to have a birthday. Just one. Just to see what it's like.
One candle. Not a number, only one. I blew it out, and nobody made me become a banker.
It turns out growing a little isn't so bad. There's cake. Nobody ever warned me about the cake.
Those glowing berries I gave you: on dark nights they're like fairies who've stopped jingling.
I'm writing down the faces I remember. The lost boys, the fairy, you. So I won't lose them again.
Your face is on the first page. I drew you with a sword. You look fierce. You're welcome.
The pirates haven't come back. I crowed at the edge of the woods just to remind them.
hearthbound.persona.novel_peter_pan.epil: That year the ageless one celebrated a birthday for the first time, blew out one candle, and did not look sorry at all.
hearthbound.persona.novel_peter_pan.sour: Peter and Wendy — J. M. Barrie (1911)
hearthbound.persona.novel_peter_pan.stag: There are pirates about, the land kind with crossbows. Let's fight them! I'll crow when we win.
Cock-a-doodle-doo! That's the crow. I told you I'd do it.
I used to fly with happy thoughts and a pinch of fairy dust. Both are running out. Feathers might help. Lots of them.
I didn't fly. But I jumped very high, and for a moment I remembered why.
Someone once left a window open for me every night. She's grown now, in another village. Carry her a letter? Tell her I remember.
She wrote back. She's a mother now, and she still leaves the window open. Here, berries that glow like fairies.
hearthbound.persona.novel_peter_pan.talk: To die would be an awfully big adventure. So would lunch.
Have you seen my shadow? It keeps wandering off.
All children grow up, except one. I'm starting to think that one is lonely.
You remind me of someone who used to tell me stories. I can't remember who.
I wear a mask because my face frightens people. I live below the old hall, by the underground pond, and I compose music nobody hears.
I taught a young singer through the wall, pretending to be an angel of music. She became wonderful. Then she fell in love with someone with an ordinary face.
Did you hear an organ last night? No, of course not. The wind. It plays the chimneys beautifully.
Box five is always free. Nobody sits there. Nobody dares. Sit there sometime, if you like. I'd consider it an honour.
From below I heard every rehearsal. Every singer. I knew their voices better than they did.
There was a chorus girl, Christine. A voice like a lark in a cage. Nobody noticed her but me.
Down here, my organ is old, and half its notes are dead. When I play, it wheezes like an old man.
A song without notes is a door without a handle. I can hear it in my head, but I can't let it out.
Bring me note blocks, would you? Four. I'll build a new organ down by the water. Don't tell anyone why.
I wear a mask because my face frightens people. Don't apologise for looking. Everyone looks. Few stay.
Music is the only place my face doesn't matter. In a melody, nobody can see you. They can only hear.
You never ask what's under the mask. That's why I let you stay. Keep not asking. It's a kind of gift.
I live below the old hall, down five cellars, beside a pond that never sees the sun. It's quieter than a grave.
I was born ugly. My mother gave me my first mask. She couldn't bear to kiss me. I was very small.
I ran away with a travelling fair. They showed me in a cage as a living corpse. I learned magic tricks and ventriloquism there.
Then I built things. Trapdoors, mirrors, secret passages. Architects paid well for the man they never had to look at.
I helped build a great opera house, in a city far from here. I kept a few rooms for myself, underneath. No one knew.
Listen... the whole cellar is singing. Don't tell anyone it's me. Let them blame the wind a little longer.
Now I'll tell you about Christine. I taught her through the wall of her dressing room, every evening.
Some nights I think I did the only good thing of my life then. Other nights I think I'm still waiting for her.
The pond down here is so dark. On my old lake I had candles floating on the water, like a stage.
I want to see it again. Light on the water, and music under it. One last performance, even if no one comes.
Well, one person might come. If they don't ask about the mask. If they sit quietly in box five.
Bring me candles, would you? Twelve. Enough to light the pond like a stage.
I told her I was the Angel of Music, sent by her dead father. She believed me. She wanted to believe me.
It was a lie. But the lessons were true. Every note I gave her was the best I had.
She became wonderful. The whole city wept when she sang Marguerite. I wept loudest, in box five.
I made the managers give her the leading roles. I dropped a chandelier to make my point. I'm not proud of it.
Then a young man with an ordinary face came back into her life. Raoul. Her childhood sweetheart.
I watched them on the roof, under the statue of Apollo. She promised to run away with him. I heard every word.
I took her down to my lake. I showed her my face. She tore off my mask, and her scream is still in these walls.
I let her go in the end. She kissed my forehead, which no one had ever done. That undid me.
It's beautiful down there now. Almost too beautiful to be alone in. I noticed that, sitting at the organ.
When I played for the candles, I found myself playing for someone who wasn't there. Old habit.
And it says thank you, for the kiss on the forehead. I never said that aloud.
I've put a few bars of music at the bottom. The song I wrote for her, that she never sang.
I can't carry it myself. If she saw a mask at her door, her husband would come with a pistol, and rightly.
You have an honest face. Everyone trusts it. I'd give a great deal to have a face like yours for one day.
Carry my letter to her, would you? Tell her nothing else. The angel of music says goodbye. That's all.
She lives in the next village, you know. Christine. With Raoul, and a garden, and a little dog.
I've known for years. I walk past sometimes, at night, masked, and I hear her singing to the dishes.
Her voice has changed. Softer, lower. Happier. I never gave her that. He did.
My deepest fear is that she still dreams of me as a monster. That her memory of me is only that scream.
My dream is foolish. I want her to hear one more song from me, and know I wish her well. Nothing more.
But I won't go near her. I frightened her enough for a lifetime. I will not be a shadow at her window.
So I've written a letter instead. It took me a month. Every draft sounded like a threat or a plea.
This one is neither, I think. It says the Angel of Music is going away, and that the lessons were real.
She read it aloud, you say, and sang a verse of my song? At her own kitchen table? I can't... give me a moment.
Keep the instruments I gave you. Make music where people can see you. Promise me that.
I'm teaching the blacksmith's boy to sing. He has a voice like a rusty gate. We're both enjoying it enormously.
I no longer drop chandeliers on people. I've mellowed. I only glare at hecklers, and they go quiet on their own.
You carried the hardest letter I ever wrote, and you never once asked what was under the mask. Thank you.
There's a new song I'm writing. It's for no one in particular. It's cheerful. I didn't know I could do cheerful.
Come to the fair on Sunday. Stand near the front. I'll play the first note looking straight at you.
I played at the village fair last week. In daylight. With my mask on. People stayed. Some even danced.
A child asked if my mask was a costume. I said yes. She said it was the best one she'd ever seen.
The candles on the pond are still there. I light them on Sundays and open the cellar door. A few people come down.
The innkeeper says his ale tastes better with organ music. I've told him that's nonsense. He's paying me anyway.
Box five is taken now, every Sunday. By you, usually. I tuned the organ to your footsteps on the stairs.
Christine visited the fair last month. She stopped, listened, and smiled straight at my mask. Then walked on.
No words. None needed. I played better that afternoon than I did in thirty years at the opera.
I still wear the mask. It isn't hiding anymore. It's just my face now, the one I chose.
Now at the village fair a masked musician plays in broad daylight, and a visiting singer always stops, listens, and smiles straight at the mask.
The Phantom of the Opera — Gaston Leroux (1910)
My organ is old and half its notes are dead. Bring me note blocks; I'll build a new one down by the water.
Listen... the whole cellar is singing. Don't tell anyone it's me.
Notes for the organ
The underground pond is so dark. I want to light it with candles floating on the water, like a stage. One last performance.
It's beautiful down there now. Almost too beautiful to be alone in.
Candles on the lake
She lives in the next village with the one she loves. I won't frighten her again. Carry my letter: the angel of music says goodbye.
She read it aloud and sang a verse of my song. Take these; make music where people can see you.
The angel's farewell
Did you hear an organ last night? No, of course not. The wind.
Box five is always free. Nobody sits there. Nobody dares.
Music is the only place my face doesn't matter.
You never ask what's under the mask. That's why I let you stay.
The voice beneath the stage
hearthbound.persona.novel_quatermain.bio: I've hunted and guided caravans for forty years. I'm a cautious sort; I've been frightened more times than I can count, and I'm not ashamed of it.
Long ago I followed a map scrawled on cloth by a dying man, across a desert to mines full of diamonds. We came back with a pocketful. I never told anyone what we left behind.
hearthbound.persona.novel_quatermain.dia: Evening. Pull up a crate. I'm not a brave one, you know. I simply don't run in the wrong direction.
I've hunted and guided caravans for forty years. Elephants, lions, merchants. The merchants were the worst.
A tall nobleman looking for his lost brother, and a navy captain with an eyeglass and no trousers. Long story.
And a quiet porter, Umbopa, who turned out to be rather more than a porter. We set off together.
The original map fell apart years ago. Linen and blood don't keep. I've a copy in my head, but my head is getting old.
Last winter I forgot the name of the waterhole. It frightened me more than any lion. The route mustn't die with me.
Bring me a proper map, would you? Blank. I'll copy the route onto it before my memory goes the way of the linen.
A good hunter knows when not to shoot. Most of my best days ended with a full quiver.
I've been frightened more times than I can count, and I'm not ashamed of it. Fear has kept me breathing.
You've the makings of a fine guide. You look where you're going and where you've been. Rare, that.
Two mountains, snow on the peaks, a road older than any king. I dream of it still. Most nights, in fact.
Long ago a man lay dying in a hut by a river. Portuguese, starved half to nothing. He gave me a scrap of linen.
On it was a map, drawn in his own blood with a bone splinter. It showed a desert and two peaks beyond it.
He'd copied it from his ancestor, who'd died in a cave on those very mountains, three hundred years before.
I kept that map for twenty years and told myself I'd never go. I'm a cautious sort. Then two friends turned up.
There: the desert, the waterhole, the two peaks. Frame it or burn it, I can't decide. Keep it safe for now.
Now that it's on paper, I'll tell you what it cost. The desert first. We almost didn't cross it.
I tell them no. But I know someone will go, someday. And that desert doesn't forgive.
They say the dried-out dead walk those sands now. Husks, you call them. They rise from the dunes at dusk.
We had enough trouble with thirst. We never had to fight the dead as well. I shudder to think.
If anyone follows that map, I want the way clear. I can't do it myself. These old legs are finished with sand.
Clear the way for me, would you? Six of those husks. Then I'll sleep easier, whoever finds the route.
We walked by night and hid under the sand by day. The water ran out on the third day. Our tongues swelled.
We found a waterhole by pure luck. A little pool, green and stinking. I have never tasted anything better.
Then the mountains, and the cold. One of our men froze in a cave, beside the body of the very man who drew the first map.
The land beyond was ruled by a cruel king and an old, old witch called Gagool. She was wrinkled like a dried fig.
Umbopa, our porter, turned out to be the rightful king. We fought a war for him. I'm still not sure how we won.
The captain frightened a whole army by taking out his false teeth. He also predicted an eclipse. We were lucky.
I'm not boasting. I was frightened every hour of it. But being frightened and staying anyway, that's the job.
Now and then people come asking about the map. Young ones, with shining eyes and no water bottles.
Clear sands. My old legs thank you, though they won't be making the trip. I raised a glass to you last night.
Now I'll tell you what I never told anyone. What we left behind in those mines.
My dream is smaller. That the little we brought back did some good. That it wasn't only glitter.
I spent my share on my boy's schooling. He's a doctor now. Best thing those mines ever produced.
There's another child in this village. The healer's apprentice, bright as a bee, and too poor for proper lessons.
I've nothing left from the mines. Not a single stone. But you dig deeper than I ever did.
Bring me a few diamonds, would you? Three. There's another child who needs a chance, and that's what they're for.
The witch led us into the treasure chamber and then slipped out. A great stone door slid down behind us.
We were sealed in, in the dark, with more diamonds than the world has ever seen. And no food. And no air, soon.
I remember thinking: all the riches of Solomon, and I'd trade them for a cup of water and a crack of daylight.
We found a tunnel eventually. Crawled for hours. I stuffed my pockets on the way out. Just my pockets.
We left the rest. Chests of stones. Enough to buy a kingdom. They're still down there, in the dark, doing nothing.
And we left the witch, crushed under the door she tried to shut on us. And a brave girl, Foulata, who died helping us.
That's what I never told. We came back with a pocketful, and it looked like a triumph. It was mostly grief.
My fear is that when I'm gone, someone will go looking for the rest and die in that chamber, choking on greed.
That will pay for the lessons. Keep my crossbow; it's shot straighter than any man I travelled with.
The apprentice started her lessons last week. She's already told me I've been bandaging my knee wrong for thirty years.
I raise a glass every night to the ones we lost in the desert and the mountains. Now I raise one to you too.
People ask me if I'm a hero. I say no, I'm a man who was frightened in the right direction. And lucky in friends.
The husks haven't come back to the dunes. The traders say the road to the south is quiet. Good.
When my time comes, bury me facing east, where the sun comes up over the desert. I'll keep an eye on the road.
Good hunting, friend. And remember: the best guides are the ones who bring everyone home. You did.
She's right, of course. I've started doing it her way. Don't tell her. It'll go to her head.
I burned the map. Well, no. I folded it and put it under the floorboards. Burning felt like cheating the dead.
If ever someone truly needs it, not wants, needs, you'll know where it is. I trust you to tell the difference.
The best treasure ever brought back from those mines is learning medicine three doors down. I say it daily.
My boy wrote to me. He's heard about the apprentice and wants to send her his old books. Full circle, eh?
I still dream of the two peaks. But now I wake up and think: those mountains can keep their diamonds.
I've taken up whittling. Little elephants, mostly. The children say they look like dogs. The children are right.
You've been a better companion than half the men I tracked with. And you never once complained about the heat.
hearthbound.persona.novel_quatermain.epi: Now a young apprentice in the village studies medicine on diamond money, and the old guide swears it's the best treasure ever brought back from those mines.
hearthbound.persona.novel_quatermain.sou: King Solomon's Mines — H. Rider Haggard (1885)
hearthbound.persona.novel_quatermain.sta: The original map fell apart years ago. Before my memory does the same, bring me a proper map; I'll copy the route onto it.
There: the desert, the waterhole, the two peaks. Frame it or burn it, I can't decide.
We nearly died of thirst crossing the sands. Dried-out dead walk there now. If anyone follows the map, clear the way.
Clear sands. My old legs thank you, though they won't be making the trip.
We escaped the treasure chamber with a handful of diamonds. I spent mine on my boy's schooling. Bring me some; there's another child who needs a chance.
That will pay for the lessons. Take my crossbow; it's shot straighter than any man I travelled with.
hearthbound.persona.novel_quatermain.tal: I'm not a brave one. I simply don't run in the wrong direction.
A good hunter knows when not to shoot.
Two mountains, snow on the peaks, a road older than any king. I dream of it still.
You've the makings of a fine guide. Watch the desert, and it will watch you back.
I spent years on a pole in a cornfield, and the crows laughed at me. Everyone says my head is stuffed with straw, and I believe them.
A wizard once promised me brains. The truth is, every good idea on that long road was mine; I just never trusted it.
hearthbound.persona.novel_scarecrow.dial: Good day! Mind the loose straw by the gate. It's mine. Well, it used to be.
I only know that I know very little. People tell me that's a fine place to start.
On the way, I kept having ideas. How to cross a ditch, how to stop the bees. I thought they were luck.
Lately I feel... lumpy. Soft in places I should be firm. It's the rain, I think. It gets into everything.
When the straw in my head gets damp, my thoughts go soggy too. Or maybe they were always soggy.
I'd ask the farmer next door, but he'd charge me in pumpkins. I have no pumpkins. I have no pockets.
The truth is, the straw in my old coat is rotten. Could you bring me wheat, so I feel like myself again?
I stand very still in the mornings. Old habit. The field doesn't notice anymore, but I do.
Crows? We've made our peace. They leave my corn alone, and I don't mention their singing.
I don't eat, I don't sleep, and I never get tired. You'd think I'd have more time to think.
I spent years on a pole in a cornfield. A farmer painted my face and forgot to give me ears at first.
The crows landed on my shoulders and laughed. One of them told me I'd be a fine man, if only I had brains.
So I believed it. Everyone said my head was stuffed with straw, and they were right about the straw.
A girl with silver shoes lifted me off that pole. I fell over twice and she laughed kindly. Not like the crows.
We walked a yellow road together, looking for a wizard who could give me brains. That was my whole plan.
Crisp and golden! I feel sharper already. Though that may just be the stalks poking my ear.
Now that my head is dry, let me tell you about the wizard. He was a small man with a very large voice.
The crows I don't mind anymore. They come by day, peck a little, and leave. Almost polite.
But at night, something else flies over the field. Pale, ragged wings, and a sound like torn cloth.
They dive at the sleepers who stayed awake too long. The cows won't settle, and the children won't either.
I can stand in the field all night, I never tire, but they aren't afraid of scarecrows. Nobody told them.
Could you drive them off? I'd do it myself, but I don't think straw would impress them.
He hid behind a curtain and a paper head. When we found him out, he apologised to each of us in turn.
To me he gave bran, mixed with pins and needles. Sharp, he said, so everyone will see how sharp you are.
I felt wise at once. I told the whole palace. Then I wondered: had I been wise before, and just shy?
Because every good idea on that road was mine. The raft, the bridge made from a tree, the trick with the bees.
I covered my friends with my own straw so the bees would break their stings. Nobody told me to. I just knew.
And yet I waited for a wizard's permission to be clever. Isn't that the silliest thing you ever heard?
Afterwards, they made me ruler of the Emerald City for a time. I was good at it. I asked a lot of questions.
I still pat my pocket sometimes, to check the bran is there. You'll catch me doing it. Please don't laugh.
Quiet nights! And do you know, I worked out how to lure them to you all by myself. No bran needed.
I stood in the open with a lantern and looked tired. They love tired things. It was my best idea this year.
The farmers here ask me about rain and soil. I answer, and I'm right, but I never know why I'm right.
If I read, I'll know why. And then maybe I'll stop checking my pocket for bran.
Or maybe I'll learn I knew it all along. That would be embarrassing, and wonderful.
I can't buy books. I have no coins and my hands are gloves. I could trade you advice, though. Plenty of it.
Bring me books, please. Three will do to start. The wizard gave me bran; I'd like to earn the real thing.
Let me confide something. I'm afraid that the wizard's bran is the only reason people listen to me.
If someone opened my head and found only straw and a few pins, would they still ask my advice?
The Tin Woodman was sure he had no heart, and he cried over a beetle he stepped on. I watched it happen.
The Lion shook at every shadow and still charged the great spider. We were never what we feared we were.
So why can't I believe it about myself? That's the one problem I can't think my way out of.
I have a dream. Not a big one. I'd like a shelf of books and the patience to read them all.
I want to know how seeds decide to grow, why wheat bends east, what the stars are for.
Real brains, I think, are just questions you keep feeding. Mine have been hungry for years.
I've read them all, and do you know what? I already knew half of it. The other half I'll never forget.
I hope the bone meal did well on your field. It's the wisest thing I own. Wiser than me, I said, and meant it.
I made a little sign for my gate: questions welcome, answers not guaranteed. Honesty is part of wisdom.
You've brought me wheat, peace and books. That's a body, a night and a mind. Quite a list.
When I don't know something, I still ask. People still call it clever. I've stopped arguing with them.
Next spring I'll teach the children to read under the old pole in the cornfield. It deserves a happier story.
Come back whenever your head feels full of straw. I'll dry it out with a good question or two.
People queue at my gate now. A widow asked about her well, a boy about his sick goat. I helped both.
When the answer is good, I still pat my pocket. Checking the bran. I think I'll do it forever. It's comforting.
The phantoms haven't come back. Some nights I stand in the field anyway, just to enjoy being bored.
The crows asked me for advice yesterday. At least, one of them cawed at me thoughtfully. I told it to try the east field.
I've started writing down my ideas. Most are about wheat. One is about the moon. It's a very good one.
You taught me something I couldn't read in any book: that you can be clever and still need a friend.
If the girl with silver shoes ever comes this way, tell her I'm reading. She'll laugh. The kind laugh.
The farmer next door says my stuffing smells like summer now. I told him that's the smell of thinking.
hearthbound.persona.novel_scarecrow.epil: Now the whole village comes for advice, and every time the answer is good, the old farmer still pats a pocket, just to check the bran is there.
hearthbound.persona.novel_scarecrow.sour: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum (1900)
hearthbound.persona.novel_scarecrow.stag: The rain got into my... well, into my old coat, and the straw is rotten. Bring me wheat so I can feel like myself again.
Crisp and golden. I feel sharper already, though that may just be the stalks.
Crows only peck by day. The winged things that come at night are worse; they scare the whole field. Could you drive them off?
Quiet nights. Funny: I thought of how to lure them to you all by myself.
The wizard gave me brains of bran, pins and needles, and said: now you're wise. I'd like real ones. Books, please.
I've read them all, and do you know what? I already knew half of it. Here, this bone meal will make any field wiser than me.
hearthbound.persona.novel_scarecrow.talk: I only know that I know very little. That seems a good start.
Crows? I've made my peace with crows. Mostly.
Do you think with your head or your heart? I'm still deciding which I have.
When I don't know something, I ask. People say that's clever. Strange.
I have the finest garden in the valley, and I built a high wall around it with a sign: TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED. The children stopped coming.
Since then spring has never entered my garden. Snow, frost and the north wind live there all year. I think the garden is punishing me.
Is it spring out there? In here it's always the tail end of winter. Come in, but keep your coat on.
That's my garden, behind the wall. The finest in the valley, once. Twelve peach trees and grass soft as a rug.
When spring came, it came everywhere except my garden. The birds wouldn't sing where there were no children.
The snow covered the grass like a cloak, and the frost painted the trees silver. They invited the north wind to stay.
I sat at my window every morning waiting for green. It never came. It's been years now.
My trees are dead from the cold. Black branches, no buds. I prune them anyway, out of habit. Out of hope.
Could you bring me saplings? Eight. Maybe new trees will remember what spring is, even if the old ones forgot.
Children are noisy. And yet the silence is worse. You'll see what I mean if you stay a while.
I've got big hands and a big voice. People used to cross the road. I don't blame them.
When you come, I leave the gate open a crack. Have you noticed? It's the only warm thing I do all day.
I went away for seven years once, to visit an old friend across the hills. We ran out of things to say by the second.
When I came back, the village children were playing in my garden. Climbing my trees. Laughing in my grass.
I roared at them. 'My own garden is my own garden!' I said. They ran like sparrows.
Then I built the wall. High, of good stone. And a sign: TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED. I painted it myself.
The children stopped coming. They played on the dusty road instead, and looked at the wall, and whispered.
Planted. Still frosty... but there's one bud. One! I watched it for an hour. I think it watched me back.
Now I'll tell you the part I'm ashamed of. The wall wasn't to keep thieves out. It was to keep joy out.
That was the day I knocked down the wall. Or began to. I'm slow. The stones are heavy and so was I.
But the little boy never came back. The others didn't know him. And lately, the frost has returned.
It's not ordinary frost. Things walk here at night, white and bony, with arrows that leave ice in the wound.
They keep winter in my garden. Where they step, the grass goes grey. I've found them standing among the saplings.
Drive them away, please. Six ought to show them this garden doesn't belong to winter anymore.
I thought if I couldn't share the garden with anyone, then no one could have it. That's the whole of it.
The Snow and the Frost thought that was splendid. They moved in, and invited the Hail, who rattled my roof for months.
One morning I heard a linnet singing. I thought the King's musicians were passing. That's how long it had been.
I looked out, and the children had crept in through a hole in the wall. In every tree sat a child.
And the trees had bloomed for them. Blossoms everywhere, birds singing, flowers laughing in the grass.
Only one corner was still winter. A little boy stood there, too small to reach the branches. He was crying.
My heart melted. I went down, and the other children ran. But the little one didn't see me; his eyes were full.
I lifted him up into the tree, and it burst into flower. He put his arms round my neck and kissed me.
The frost is melting. A bird sang this morning. I'd forgotten that sound. I cried into my porridge.
I've been thinking about my deepest fear. It's that I'll die before the children forgive me.
I can't go and fetch the children myself. They'd run. I'm too big, and my voice is too loud, and they remember.
So I'll lure them, like birds. With something sweet under every tree, and the gate wide open.
Cookies. That's what children can't resist, isn't it? I tried baking some. They came out like roof tiles.
I'll put them under the trees at dawn, and hide in the house, and just listen. That's all I ask. To listen.
Bring me cookies, please. Sixteen. One for every child in the village, and a few spares for the brave ones.
They still don't come in. The wall is down, but they remember the sign. Children remember signs.
I burned it, you know. The sign. Watched the letters curl up. It felt like pulling out a splinter.
Some mornings I sit under the white tree in the far corner and wait. That's where the little one stood.
My dream is simple and very large. I want the garden full of shouting again. Muddy knees. Broken branches.
I want someone to fall out of my tree and cry and laugh, and me to be there to pick them up.
I used to think my garden was mine. It never was. It was lent to me, and I tried to keep the loan.
The little one I lifted... sometimes I think he wasn't an ordinary child. There was something about his hands.
I've asked everyone in the valley. Nobody knows him. Maybe he'll come back when the others do.
They came, and they climbed, and everything blossomed. I stood in the middle of it and couldn't speak.
Keep my axe. It broke the wall, and walls are what we must break. I have no more use for it.
I'm getting old. My back complains. But when you're surrounded by blossom, you don't mind complaints.
You planted the first saplings. The children fight over which is your tree. I tell them all of them are.
I painted a new sign for the gate. It says: COME IN. Only two words. The best I've ever written.
When I'm gone, the garden will stay open. I've told the elders. No wall, ever, as long as it grows.
Thank you for opening my gate wider than a crack. Come and sit under the white tree with me sometime.
The children call it the Giant's garden now, but they say it like it's theirs. That's exactly right.
Every afternoon at four, I hear the gate. Then the shrieking. It's the best clock I've ever had.
I've learned to carry three children on one arm. They say I'm better than a tree. I'm taller, at least.
Somebody broke a branch last week and wept in terror. I laughed so hard a pear fell on my head.
The Snow and the Frost don't come anymore. The north wind visits once in winter, politely, and leaves.
The first spring after, a small boy nobody recognised came and sat by me under the white tree.
He didn't say much. He had marks on his palms, like old wounds. He said: once you let me play here.
He comes back every spring. Just sits, and smiles. I don't ask questions. Some guests you simply welcome.
Now the old garden has no wall, and every spring, a small boy no one recognises comes to sit under the white tree beside the old farmer.
The Selfish Giant — Oscar Wilde (1888)
The trees in my garden are dead from the cold. Bring me saplings. Maybe new ones will remember what spring is.
Planted. Still frosty... but one bud. One. I watched it for an hour.
Trees that won't bloom
Things made of frost walk here at night, white and bony. They keep winter in my garden. Drive them away.
The frost is melting. A bird sang this morning. I'd forgotten that sound.
Frost and north wind
I knocked down the wall. Now I want the children to come back. Bring cookies; I'll leave them under the trees.
They came, and they climbed, and everything blossomed. Take my axe; it broke the wall, and walls are what we must break.
Cookies for the children
Is it spring out there? In here it's always the tail end of winter.
Children are noisy. And yet the silence is worse.
Once I saw a little one in the corner, too small to climb a tree. I lifted him up, and the tree bloomed.
When you come, I leave the gate open a crack. Have you noticed?
The garden behind the wall
hearthbound.persona.novel_tin_woodman.bi: A witch cursed my axe so it would cut me instead of the wood. A tinsmith replaced every piece of me with metal, until nothing of flesh was left.
Without a heart I stopped loving the girl I was to marry. Now I cry at the smallest thing, and my tears rust my joints. I don't understand it.
hearthbound.persona.novel_tin_woodman.di: Mind the anthill by my forge. I built a little fence around it last spring.
I tap my chest when I'm thinking. It sounds hollow. That's because it is.
Rain is my enemy. One good storm and I'm a statue with opinions.
Once a downpour caught me in the forest. I stood rusted there, axe raised, for a whole year.
A year of watching birds nest on my own arm. I couldn't even say hello to them.
Oil helps, but it drips and it stinks. Wax clings. Wax stays. Bees understand metal better than people do.
If you ever find honeycomb, I'd be grateful. Six pieces would keep my joints quiet for a long while.
Hammering iron all day is easy for me. I'm half hammer already.
The children knock on my chest like a door. I always answer 'come in'. They love that.
I cried at a sunset yesterday. Then I couldn't turn my neck until supper.
I used to cut wood, you know. Real wood, with a real arm swinging the axe.
A witch wanted me gone from someone's life. So she enchanted my axe to slip.
The axe took a leg first. A tinsmith made me a new one. Then the axe took the other.
Piece by piece he rebuilt me: arms, head, body. In the end there was nothing of flesh left to cut.
The strange thing is, I didn't feel less. Only emptier, like a house after the furniture is gone.
Listen when I walk: nothing. The wax works. I've been sneaking up on the cat all morning.
Thank you for the honeycomb. I thanked the bees too. It seemed only polite.
Moss covers them now. Some evenings I walk past and pretend I'm only checking the weather.
Do you think a promise stays alive if the one who made it is made of different metal now?
I'd like to finish that cottage. Not to win her back. Just so the promise has a roof.
Silly, perhaps: a smith building a woodcutter's house. But my hands still remember wood.
If you could bring me logs, plenty of them, I'd raise the walls. Thirty-odd should do it.
Now that I don't creak, I hear other things. The forge ticking as it cools. My own thoughts.
The tinsmith who made me was kind. He never asked for payment, only that I polish myself on Sundays.
I kept the old axe. It hangs above the forge, blade to the wall, so it can't look at me.
Sometimes I wonder if the witch saw something in me. Maybe I was always easy to take apart.
The worst part wasn't the pain. It was that each new piece felt a little less like mine.
When the tinsmith fitted my new head, I forgot her name for a moment. Only a moment. It came back.
There was a girl. We were to marry as soon as I had a proper house to give her.
I had laid the foundation stones. Four corners at the edge of the woods. They're still there.
The cottage stands. I sit inside some evenings with the door open, in case the wind wants in.
I told you I cried twice while building it. It was three times. The third was when I hung the door.
My dream is simple: to love someone properly again, with something that beats instead of rustles.
Sailors speak of a heart in the sea, deep among the coral, glowing like a lamp through the water.
If it's real, maybe it could sit in my chest. Maybe I'd stop leaking like a cracked pot.
I can't go into the sea. I'd sink and rust into a lump within a week. But you can swim.
Find me that glowing heart. I'll wait by the cottage window with a lamp, so you know where I am.
She never came. I hear she married a baker in a town I've never seen. I hope the bread is good.
Here's the truth I carry: when they took away my heart with the rest of me, I stopped loving her.
Not slowly. One morning I woke and she was just a thought, like remembering a recipe.
That frightened me more than any axe. What good is a body that can't ache for someone?
And yet look: I weep over beetles, dropped bread, old songs. My tears rust me faster than rain.
I don't understand it. If there's no heart in here, what is doing all this weeping?
Long ago a wizard in a green city gave me a heart of silk stuffed with sawdust. I still wear it.
It rustles when I run. A kind thought, poor stitching. Sawdust can't hold what I feel.
Put your ear to my chest. Hear that hum? The children come to listen, like to a seashell.
I haven't rusted once since you brought it. Not even in the autumn storms.
When you visit, I put the kettle on. I can't drink tea, but I love the sound of it boiling.
I danced last night, alone in the cottage. You were right: it was worth not creaking for.
If you ever feel hollow, come knock on my chest. Two hollow things together sound like music.
The beetle by the forge had babies. I built them a bigger fence. Life keeps asking for fences.
Go on, you have your own roads. The lamp stays lit. It will always be lit for you.
Funny thing: I still cry. But the tears dry before they reach my joints now. Warmer, I think.
I wonder if I ever needed a heart at all. Maybe it just gave me permission.
There's a lamp in the cottage window that glows like the heart did. Travellers steer by it now.
I sleep in the cottage these days. First time under a roof raised by my own tin hands.
Remember the honeycomb? I still wax my knees every full moon. The bees consider me family.
I've started making tin toys for the children. A little woodcutter with an axe that cuts nothing.
My old axe is yours now. Treat it well. It learned to be gentle, same as I did.
Someone asked if I'd ever marry. I said being loved by a whole village would do for now.
hearthbound.persona.novel_tin_woodman.ep: Now there is a cottage at the edge of the woods with a glowing lamp in the window, and the smith who built it has never once rusted since.
hearthbound.persona.novel_tin_woodman.so: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum (1900)
hearthbound.persona.novel_tin_woodman.st: I once stood rusted in a forest for a whole year, axe raised. Bring me honeycomb; the wax keeps rust away better than oil.
Listen: not a single creak. I could dance. I won't, but I could.
Before the curse I was a woodcutter building a cottage for her. I'd like to finish it, even if she never comes. Bring me logs.
The walls are up. I didn't cry once while building them. Well, twice.
The wizard gave me a silk heart full of sawdust. It isn't enough. They say the sea hides a heart that glows; find it for me.
It hums inside my chest... or maybe my chest was humming all along. Take my axe: it won't cut anyone who doesn't deserve it.
hearthbound.persona.novel_tin_woodman.ta: Careful, don't step on that beetle. I couldn't bear it.
If I freeze mid-sentence, it's rust. Just give me a moment.
They say I have no heart. Then why does it ache so much?
You always bring me something. Kindness makes my hinges squeak.
hearthbound.persona.novel_van_helsing.bi: I was a doctor, a philosopher, a scholar of old superstitions. Then a friend's betrothed grew pale, and I learned the superstitions were true.
We followed a count from his castle across the sea and back again. We won. But I can't stop checking the windows before I sleep.
hearthbound.persona.novel_van_helsing.di: Good evening, my friend. Keep a clove of garlic in your pocket. Or a wild onion flower. Just in case.
You smile. Good. A smile is also a kind of defence. The things I fought never learned to do it honestly.
Since then I read the signs everywhere. A dog that howls at nothing. Milk that sours overnight. Mist against the wind.
Your village has children who sleep with the windows open. It makes me glad, and it makes me afraid.
The garlic of my country doesn't grow here. But your wild allium, the purple one, is its close cousin.
The smell of it is an insult to anything that hates life. I'd like to hang it over every child's window.
Would you bring me some of those purple flowers? Eight will do for now. I'll tie them myself tonight.
I was a doctor once, and a philosopher, and a collector of old wives' tales. The last one paid the worst.
Science and faith are not enemies. I keep a scalpel and a crucifix in the same bag. Night is their common foe.
Forgive me for checking the window as we speak. Old habit. The window has done nothing wrong.
Years ago a friend wrote to me. His betrothed was growing pale, weaker every morning, and no doctor knew why.
Her name was Lucy. She was bright and laughing, and she had three suitors, and all of them adored her.
I found two small marks on her throat. My colleagues said a pin, a brooch. I said nothing. Not yet.
I filled her room with garlic flowers. Her mother, meaning well, opened the window for fresh air. One night was enough.
I lost a dear young woman to a thing that smiled. I will not lose anyone here. I made myself that promise.
The smell is terrible. Excellent. Nothing that hates life will cross it. The children think it's a game.
Now I can tell you the rest. What took Lucy was a count, an old nobleman from a castle in the mountains.
Here, something new flies at night. Pale wings, ragged, and they fall on those who've gone too long without sleep.
They drink rest instead of blood. People here call them phantoms. Where I studied, we had another name.
Last week the miller's boy woke with scratches on his arms. He said he'd dreamt of falling. I did not sleep at all.
My old arm can hold a lantern, but it cannot draw a bow with any aim. Not anymore.
Hunt them for me. Bring down five, and I'll know whether my old fears have followed me here.
A young lawyer went there to sell him a house in England. He came back grey-haired, and far too quiet.
The count had crossed the sea in a ship full of boxes of earth. The crew vanished one by one on the voyage.
He needed that earth to rest. Holy ground to him was poison. So we went looking for his boxes.
We were five, a husband, a doctor, a lord, a Texan and me. Later a brave woman, Mina, was the best of us.
He hurt her too. He tried to make her one of his. She kept her wits, and through her we followed him.
We chased him home across the sea and over the mountains, racing the sunset. We won by minutes.
We won. I should be at peace. But I can't stop checking the windows before I sleep. Not here. Not anywhere.
There are things I keep from the children. Not lies. Just the parts that belong to nightmares, not to bedtime.
Membranes, not bats. Good. Still, you've given the village back its nights. The miller's boy sleeps like a stone.
Sit with me. I want to tell you something I have never told anyone, not even Mina.
I'm not afraid of dying. I'm afraid of arriving late again, like the morning after Lucy's window was opened.
I've prepared holy water, stakes, fire and the old words. What I lack is younger arms beside me.
You don't have to be brave. I wasn't, in that castle. I simply refused to leave before the others.
If we hold until dawn, the sun will finish what we start. It always has. That is my one certainty.
Stand with me at the gates tonight. Just until sunrise. Then I'll owe you a debt I can never repay.
When we opened Lucy's tomb, she was not at rest. I had to do what the old books say. Her fiancé held the hammer.
I told him it was mercy. It was mercy. But I still feel the weight of that night in my own hands.
My dream is simple. One night I want to go to bed without looking at the shutters. Just once.
And yet the signs are here again. The dogs howl at the south field. The milk sours in the dairy by morning.
Yesterday a mist came up from the river and drifted uphill, against the wind. Mist does not do that.
I've seen it before. It's how he arrived, the count. Mist, and wolves, and a stillness in the birds.
Perhaps it isn't him. He's dust. But what hungers like him comes in many shapes. The dead that walk, for instance.
Whatever it is, it will come tonight, in numbers, and it will come to the gates first.
Dawn, and we're all alive. I keep saying it aloud. We are all alive. I like the sound of it too much to stop.
Keep the blade. The old priest who blessed it asked me to give it to someone braver than me. I kept my word.
If ever you hear a howl that makes your skin creep, come to me. I'll tell you if it's a wolf or a warning.
I hang a single allium over my own door now. Not from fear. As a thank-you note to the night that failed.
You gave me back something I didn't know I'd lost: the right to be bored at night. It's delicious.
I'm an old scholar. I'll keep reading about dark things. But I'll read them in the daylight, in the garden.
Good night, my friend. And I mean it now, all of it: a good night. Leave your window open. It's safe.
This autumn the village hung purple flowers over every window. Nobody asked them to. They simply remembered.
Last night I slept with the shutters open. Wide open. I woke to a bird on the sill and did not reach for anything.
The children play 'hunter and count' in the square. The count always loses. I referee, strictly.
I wrote a long letter to Mina. I told her about you. She'll say I'm sentimental. She'll be right.
The miller's boy wants to study medicine now. I'm teaching him anatomy. And, quietly, a little folklore.
Science and faith, my friend. I still carry both. But now I use them mostly on fevers and colds.
The dogs sleep through the night. The milk keeps until noon. The mist goes downhill, as mist should.
Every time I pass the gates, I remember your silhouette against the torches. I thought: there, that's the dawn.
hearthbound.persona.novel_van_helsing.ep: Now the village hangs purple flowers over every window each autumn, and the old scholar finally sleeps with the shutters open.
hearthbound.persona.novel_van_helsing.st: Garlic blossom was our first defence. The wild allium is its cousin. Bring me some; I'll hang it over the children's windows.
The smell is terrible. Excellent. Nothing that hates life will cross it.
Things fly by night and drain the sleepers. Here they are called phantoms. Where I studied, we had another name. Hunt them.
Membranes, not bats. Good. Still, you've given the village back its nights.
The old signs are here: dogs howling, milk turning, a mist that moves against the wind. Tonight something comes. Stand with me at the gates.
Dawn. We're alive, all of us. Take this blade; it was blessed by an old priest who asked me to give it to someone braver than me.
hearthbound.persona.novel_van_helsing.ta: Keep a clove of garlic... or a wild onion flower. Just in case.
Science and faith are not enemies. Night is their common enemy.
I lost a dear young woman to a thing that smiled. I will not lose anyone here.
When you are near, I close the shutters a little later.
hearthbound.persona.novel_victor_franken: I studied the old alchemists until I found how to put a spark into dead matter. One stormy night, I succeeded, and fled from what I'd made.
It followed me for years, asking only that I look at it. I blamed it for everything. I'm beginning to think the monster in that story was me.
Mind the jars on that shelf. Most are empty. The full ones, I'd rather you didn't ask about.
Lightning fascinates me. It shouldn't. It really shouldn't.
I swore never to touch that science again. I've kept the oath. Mostly. I still read the storms.
But I don't understand what I did. Not truly. And what you don't understand haunts you.
Copper draws lightning, you know. A rod on the roof, a wire to a jar, and the sky comes down to you.
I don't want to build anything with it. I only want to watch, and measure, and understand.
Bring me copper? A dozen ingots. I promise it's only a rod. Only... a rod.
Never pursue knowledge without asking who will pay for it. I learned that far too late.
I haven't slept well in years. There are footprints in my dreams, always larger than mine.
The villagers come to me for tonics and fevers. Simple work. I'm grateful for simple work.
As a student I devoured the old alchemists. Everyone laughed. I was sure they'd missed something.
They had. Not gold, not endless youth. Something worse: how to put a spark into dead matter.
I worked for two years in a locked room. I stopped writing to my family. I forgot to eat.
One stormy night, the thing on my table opened a dull yellow eye. I've never found words for that moment.
I ran. I ran from my own work into the rain, and when I came back, it was gone.
The storm came and the rod sang. I felt that terrible joy again. I'm ashamed of it.
Thank you for the copper. I haven't touched the jar since. I only sit and look at it.
It's probably nothing. The ordinary dead. The land here is old, and the nights are long.
But what if someone read my notes and tried what I tried, clumsily, without even the decency to run?
I can't sleep for thinking of it. I sit at the window counting shapes among the graves.
I need to know they're only the common dead. And I need them laid to rest, either way.
Would you go? Eight of them should settle it. Tell me if any of them have stitches.
When the bolt struck, the hair on my arms stood up. Just like that night. My hands wanted to work.
I'll tell you what I've told no one. I gathered the pieces from charnel houses and graveyards.
I said it was for science, for humanity. I never once asked whether the dead would mind.
I chose the parts for beauty. Fine hair, white teeth. Then it moved, and all of it turned hideous.
No, that's unfair. It wasn't hideous. It was new, and I was afraid of what I'd made.
I burned my first notes. But I copied them first. I'm sorry to say I copied them first.
Those copies went missing when I fled my laboratory. Someone may have found them.
Lately the dead walk near the village graveyard at night. More than usual. More than there should be.
Only the ordinary dead, thank heavens. Nothing I made. Not this time.
I slept a whole night after you told me. The first in months. I dreamed of nothing at all.
My dream is foolish: to sit with it by a fire and let it talk as long as it likes. And listen.
A trapper passed through last week. He spoke of enormous footprints leading north, into the ice.
He said there's a settlement at the edge of the frozen sea where someone very large trades furs.
For years I meant to hunt it down and destroy it. Now I only want to find it. Without a weapon.
Will you find me that place? Go north, follow the ice, and bring back the way. I'll do the rest.
You never asked why I feared stitches. You've never pried. That's why I'll tell you.
What I made didn't die. It followed me, across countries and mountains, for years.
At first it wanted no revenge. It asked only one thing: that I look at it. Just look.
It had learned to speak, beautifully. It had read books. It begged me for a companion.
I refused. I called it devil, wretch. I blamed it for every sorrow in my life.
When terrible things happened, I said: it did this. Perhaps it did. But I did it first, by running.
I'm beginning to think the monster in that story was me.
My fear is that I'll die without ever saying a kind word to it. That it will remember me only running.
I'm back, only for a few weeks. Supplies, books, warm socks. Then north again.
You found the place. I went. Not with a weapon. With an apology two hundred pages late.
I sleep now. The footprints in my dreams lead somewhere warm.
Never pursue knowledge without asking who will pay. Now I add: and never run from what you've made.
You listened without judging, back when I could barely speak of it. That was my first step north.
If you ever wander that far, look for the smoke. There'll be a chair for you. A large one, possibly.
Goodbye for now. Tell the village their healer will be back in spring, with better manners and a few furs.
I read it aloud by its fire. It listened to every page. Then it said, 'You looked at me.' That was all.
We talk long into the night now. It reads more than I do. It corrects my Latin.
It asked about you, by the way. It wanted to know who finally sent me. I said: a friend.
Travellers see two figures by that fire, one very large and one very thin. They must wonder. Let them.
I took the rod down from my roof. The lightning can do as it pleases; I don't need to catch it anymore.
The copper I kept I made into a kettle. It boils water very fast. Science, humbled.
The graveyard is quiet. I walk through it on my way out of the village and say good morning.
I burned the last copy of my notes in its fire. It watched and said nothing. Then it passed me the tea.
Since that winter, travellers have seen two figures sitting by a fire far in the north: one very large, one very thin, talking long into the night.
Frankenstein — Mary Shelley (1818)
I swore I'd never touch the work again, and yet... I need to understand what I did. Bring copper; I'll build a rod to catch the lightning.
The storm came and the rod sang. I felt that terrible joy again. I'm ashamed of it.
A rod for the storm
My fear is that my notes were read. The dead walk near the graveyard at night. Put them to rest, before I lose my mind.
Only the ordinary dead, thank heavens. Nothing I made. Not this time.
What should stay dead
Large footprints lead north, to the ice. My creation. For years I meant to destroy it. Now I only want to find it. Find me that village.
You found where it lives. I'll go. Not with a weapon. With an apology that's two hundred pages late.
Footprints to the north
Lightning fascinates me. It shouldn't. It really shouldn't.
Never pursue knowledge without asking who will pay for it.
I haven't slept well in years. There are footprints in my dreams.
You listen without judging. That's rarer than any discovery.
The spark of life
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.bio.0: Once a boy who couldn't grow up flew through my window, and I sewed his shadow back on. Then he took me away to be mother to a band of lost boys.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.bio.1: I told them stories every night, and in the end I chose to come back and grow up. I still wonder if I stole something from myself.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.dialogue: Have you eaten? You look like you haven't eaten. Sit down; there's soup.
Every story needs a proper ending. Otherwise nobody sleeps, and then everybody's grumpy.
I still can't walk past a hole in a sock without reaching for a needle. It's a sort of illness.
This village is full of lost things. Loose buttons, torn hems, children with their knees out.
And I'm nearly out of thread. I've been unpicking old curtains to mend coats. It can't go on.
String would do. Good strong string. It mends socks, ties parcels and, once, held a shadow.
Would you bring me some? A dozen lengths. I'd have every child in the village darned by nightfall.
I keep a sewing basket by the door. This village loses buttons the way trees lose leaves.
Growing up isn't a tragedy. It just feels like one on Tuesdays.
I leave the window open at night. Old habit. You never know who might come in.
When I was young, a boy flew in through my window looking for his shadow. It was caught in a drawer.
He was trying to stick it back on with soap, and crying. I sewed it on for him. It hurt; he pretended not.
Then he asked me to come away and be mother to his lost boys. I said yes before I'd thought.
We flew, truly flew, over rooftops and oceans. I held my little brothers' hands the whole way.
I was barely taller than the lost boys myself. But somebody had to tuck them in.
Stitch, stitch... there. Not a single child in the village has a hole in their sock tonight.
Thank you for the string. I've saved a little for emergencies. Shadows have a way of coming loose.
Orphans. Four or five. They play at being pirates and pretend they aren't hungry.
I watched them share a single apple between them. Very fair. Very thin.
They won't come to the inn. They don't trust grown-ups. I can't blame them; I didn't either, once.
But nobody refuses supper left on a barrel with a note that says 'For the pirate crew'.
Bring me bread, would you? Sixteen loaves. I'll play mother, just a little, from a respectful distance.
On the island I darned for a dozen boys. They wore through heels faster than I could knit.
I told them stories every night: a prince, a glass slipper, a mother waiting at home.
That last one made them cry. Lost boys don't know what a mother is until you tell them.
There was a pirate captain, and a crocodile that ticked. I'll tell you properly one day.
I was so busy being their mother that I forgot I was a child too. Nobody darned my socks.
The boy who never grew up loved it. Loved me playing mother. He never once asked if I was tired.
I'm not bitter. He was a boy. That's the whole point of him.
