Here, I've noticed something. There are children sleeping in the barn by the mill.
They ate everything and then asked for a story. That's how you know they're really children.
I told them about the crocodile with the clock inside. The smallest one hid in the hay, delighted.
The orphans will grow. Other children will come. Who'll tell them about mermaids and pirates then?
I've told the same tales so often they've gone smooth as pebbles. I want to catch them before they wear away.
Every one of them: the shadow, the island, the jingling fairy, the pirate with the hook.
I'll need a proper book to write in. Not a printed one; one with blank pages waiting.
Will you bring me one? I'll put every story down, and draw the pictures badly, which children prefer.
They call me 'Mother' now, when they think I can't hear. I pretend I can't hear.
Here's something I rarely say. In the end I chose to leave the island and come home to grow up.
The boy begged me to stay. He said I'd get old and dull and forget how to fly. He was right about some of it.
I brought the lost boys back with me. They grew up too: clerks, farmers, one judge. All of them forgot.
Sometimes I wonder if I stole something from myself. A girl who'd still be flying, somewhere.
Then I watch the orphans eating bread and think: no. This is what the flying was for.
He promised to fetch me for spring cleaning every year. He came a few times. Then he forgot. I didn't.
My fear is simple. I won't be here forever, and stories die if nobody writes them down.
It's finished. Pirates, mermaids, the crocodile with a clock inside. All of it, in ink.
I bound it in blue cloth from an old dress. It already looks worn. Good; books should.
I still leave the window open. These days it's mostly for the cat. Mostly.
The smallest orphan asked if she could mother the others one day. I said only if she wants to.
If you ever need a sock darned or a story told, the inn door is open, and so is the window.
You've been a sort of lost child to me, you know. Not so lost now. Neither am I.
Go on. Every story needs a proper ending, but yours isn't finished yet. Come back and tell me the next part.
The orphans read it by turns. The eldest does the pirate voices. He's far too good at them.
Did you enjoy the cookies? And remember: tell the stories wrong on purpose sometimes. It keeps children sharp.
Someone wrote on the last page, in a clumsy hand: 'the window is still open'. It wasn't me.
I suspect a certain someone with a feather in their cap. I haven't asked. Some mysteries are better kept.
Two of the orphans sleep at the inn now. The rest still prefer the barn. Pirates need their ship.
I've started a new chapter at the back, about a traveller who brought string and bread. Guess who.
In it you have a sword and a very good hat. I took liberties. Stories are allowed to.
Growing up turned out well, I think. I only had to decide what to keep from before.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.epilogue: Now the village children have a book with a worn blue cover, and on the last page someone has written, in a clumsy hand: 'the window is still open'.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.source: Peter and Wendy — J. M. Barrie (1911)
There's always a sock to darn and a shadow to sew back on. Bring me string, please; this village is full of lost things.
Stitch, stitch... there. Not a single child in the village has a hole in their sock tonight.
Some orphans sleep in the barn by the mill. They pretend to be pirates and forget to eat. Bring bread; I'll play mother.
They ate everything and then asked for a story. That's how you know they're really children.
When I'm gone, who'll tell them the stories? Bring me a book I can write in. I'll put every one of them down.
It's all there: pirates, mermaids, the crocodile with a clock inside. Take some cookies; tell it wrong on purpose sometimes.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.talk.0: Every story needs a proper ending. Otherwise the children won't sleep.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.talk.1: Have you eaten? You look like you haven't eaten.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.talk.2: Growing up isn't a tragedy. It just feels like one on Tuesdays.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.talk.3: I leave the window open at night. Old habit. You never know who might come in.
hearthbound.persona.novel_wendy.title: Stories for lost children
hearthbound.persona.novel_white_rabbit.b: I'm late. I've been late all my life: to my own christening, to my first job, to every appointment with the Duchess. Oh dear, oh dear.
I once served a queen who shouted 'off with their heads' at anyone who was late. The fear never left me. I dream of arriving early, just once.
hearthbound.persona.novel_white_rabbit.d: Oh my ears and whiskers, is that the time? No, don't tell me. Yes, tell me. No!
No time to say hello, goodbye! ...Well, perhaps a moment. A very small one. There. Hello.
I carried a pocket watch everywhere. A lovely silver thing. I'd look at it and run faster, and it never helped.
And now I've lost it! Somewhere between the well and the bakery. Or the bakery and the chapel. Or...
Without it I don't know how late I am, which is somehow worse. I could be a minute late. Or a week!
I keep reaching for my waistcoat pocket and finding nothing. My paw goes cold every time.
Bring me a clock, quickly! Any clock! Well, a good clock. But quickly!
You never seem to be in a hurry. How do you do it? Is it a trick? Can it be learned?
Sometimes I stop running and look at the clouds. Then I panic, of course. Clouds take ages.
I've worn a path in the grass between my house and the square. It's very straight. I never have time for curves.
I'm late. I've been late all my life. I was late to my own christening. The priest had already gone home.
I was late for my first job, my first dance, my first proper hat fitting. The hatter was very rude about it.
My mother used to say I was born running, and still arrived a day after I was due.
I once served in a very grand household, in a land under the ground. The Duchess employed me. Oh, the Duchess.
She would wait at her door, fanning herself, and every time I arrived she'd say: 'Late again.' Every single time.
Tick, tick... oh, I'm only slightly late. What a relief! Slightly late is practically on time, for me.
I've hung it by my bed. I wake up, look at it, and gasp. Then I remember it's only slightly. Lovely.
I threw pebbles through the window and they turned into little cakes. It was a very strange afternoon.
Speaking of gloves: I dropped my white kid gloves somewhere and the Duchess will be furious. Still, after all these years.
I know, I know, she isn't here. But I hear her voice every time I look at my bare paws. 'Late, and gloveless!'
A proper person should have proper gloves. White, soft, buttoned at the wrist. I feel undressed without them.
Bring me leather so I can have new ones made? Please. Before she notices. Before anyone notices.
Now, since you've been so kind, I'll tell you about the Queen. The Queen of Hearts. Please lower your voice.
After the Duchess, I served at the Queen's court. I was the herald. I blew the trumpet and read the charges.
She shouted 'Off with their heads!' at anyone who was late. Anyone who was early. Anyone at all, really.
Nobody was actually beheaded, I think. The King quietly pardoned them all afterwards. But one never knew.
Every morning I'd run to the palace with my heart in my throat. Every evening I'd run home counting my ears.
The fear never left me. Even here, where there are no queens, I flinch when someone shouts 'Off!'. Even 'off to market'.
There was a girl once, down there. She chased me all the way through that land. I never stopped to talk to her.
I mistook her for my housemaid and sent her for my gloves and fan. How embarrassing. She grew enormous in my house.
Proper gloves again. I feel almost dignified. Almost. I only dropped them twice today.
The tailor asked if I wanted them white. I said yes, of course, white, like before. Then I said: no, brown. Brown doesn't show dirt.
I've tried to take such messages before. I get there with the moon up and everyone asleep. Every time.
The elder there must have it today. If not, they'll miss the carts, and the grain will spoil. Oh dear, oh dear.
My legs are quick, but my head is always behind. I stop to check the time, I panic, I take the wrong turn.
You never hurry, and you always arrive. That's a kind of magic I don't have. Well, it's not magic. It's calm.
Would you carry it for me, just this once? Before sunset. Please. I'll watch the sun from the gate.
That's the first decision I've made without imagining the Duchess's face. I felt dizzy. In a nice way.
Here's my secret, the deep one: I'm not really afraid of being late. I'm afraid of being in trouble.
Down there, trouble came with a shout and a crown. Up here, nobody shouts. And still, my heart races.
Some nights I dream the Queen is at the foot of my bed, holding a flamingo. I wake up with my ears flat.
I dream of arriving early, just once. Early! Imagine walking in, and waiting for others, and being calm.
I'd sit down. I'd fold my gloves in my lap. Someone would come in late and I'd say: 'No matter. Take your time.'
I've never said 'take your time' to anyone. I've never had any to give.
Now there's a message that must be delivered to the next village before sunset. It's important. Harvest business.
Delivered early? EARLY? I'll have to sit down. Take those boots: in them I've fallen down holes and never broken a thing.
The elder sent a note back: 'Arrived with daylight to spare.' I read it eleven times. Then I framed it.
The Queen visits my dreams less often. When she does, I tell her: 'I'm early.' She has no idea what to say.
If you ever fall down a hole, don't worry. The boots I gave you know the way out. They've done it before.
Thank you for being calm when I couldn't be. You lent me some. I'm still using it.
I've even started taking the long way home. The one with curves. It's full of flowers I'd never seen.
Come by any time. Any time at all. For once, I have plenty of it, and I'd like to spend some with you.
Since then a village clock has been set five minutes fast, just for me. Did you arrange that? Someone did.
And now I arrive, for the first time, on time. Sometimes even a minute early. I stand there and don't know what to do.
Yesterday I was early to the market. I sat on a bench. I watched a cloud. I didn't panic. The cloud was lovely.
The children laugh when I say 'Oh my ears and whiskers!' So I say it on purpose now. Why not?
I still wear the brown gloves. They show nothing. They're perfect. The Duchess would hate them.
Remember how I panicked over the lost watch? I found it, in the end. In the bread bin. It had stopped.
I didn't wind it again. I put it on the shelf, next to the clock you brought. The past and the present, side by side.
When someone arrives late at my door, I say 'No matter, take your time.' It feels like giving a present.
hearthbound.persona.novel_white_rabbit.e: Since then a village clock has been set five minutes fast, just for the rabbit-hearted neighbour, who now arrives, for the first time, on time.
hearthbound.persona.novel_white_rabbit.s: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll (1865)
I've lost my watch! Without it I don't know how late I am, which is somehow worse. Bring me a clock, quickly!
Tick, tick... oh, I'm only slightly late. What a relief!
I dropped my white kid gloves somewhere and the Duchess will be furious. Bring me leather so I can have new ones made.
Proper gloves again. I feel almost dignified. Almost.
I must deliver a message to the next village before sunset, and I never arrive before sunset. Would you carry it for me, just this once?
Delivered early? EARLY? I'll have to sit down. Take these boots: in them I've fallen down holes and never broken a thing.
hearthbound.persona.novel_white_rabbit.t: Oh my ears and whiskers, is that the time?
No time to say hello, goodbye! ...Well, perhaps a moment.
You never seem to be in a hurry. How do you do it?
Sometimes I stop running and look at the clouds. Then I panic, of course.
People bow to me as the great sage of the village. Truth is, I was a balloonist at a travelling fair until the wind carried me off.
I never had any power, only tricks, green spectacles and a big voice behind a curtain. I'm tired of pretending, and terrified of being found out.
Ah, a visitor. Do come in. Mind the curtain; it's... structural.
People bring me their troubles and I nod gravely. Nodding gravely is half of wisdom.
I kept up the act there for years. And here too, I'm afraid. Habits travel well.
Do you know why that city looked so green? Everyone wore spectacles of green glass. My rule.
Emeralds everywhere, they said. Glass, mostly. People see what they're told to see.
I'd like to show the village that trick, just once, as a game. A street of 'emeralds' for a day.
Bring me green glass, sixteen panes or so. Let me be wonderful one more time, and laugh about it after.
I once sold a lion a bowl of courage. Very popular item. Limited stock.
My voice carries wonderfully in a large hall. In a small room I just sound like a cough.
Do you like my spectacles? Green lenses. The world is kinder in green.
Before I was a sage I had other trades. Ventriloquist. Balloonist. Mostly balloonist.
I went up at country fairs in a painted balloon, waving at the crowds. Best job I ever had.
One day the rope snapped and the wind took me. For days I floated over lands I'd never seen.
I came down in a green city. People saw someone fall from the sky and decided I was a wizard.
I didn't correct them. Would you have? They'd built me a throne before I'd finished landing.
Did you see their faces on the emerald street? I haven't laughed like that since the fair.
Thank you for the glass. Half the village still thinks the street turned to emerald overnight.
Here I've been doing the same: good advice wrapped in fog. The advice is sound. The fog is a lie.
Every time someone bows to me, the curtain feels a little heavier.
I think I must confess. Publicly. Before someone finds the tube and the mask on their own.
I'll write it plainly: 'I am no wizard, only a humbug.' And pin it to every door in the village.
Bring me paper, sixteen sheets, quickly, before I lose my nerve and write a riddle instead.
Wicked and happy at once, that's how I felt. I'm afraid it's always been my favourite mixture.
At the fair I earned a copper a flight. Children threw me flowers. Nobody bowed.
I miss that. Being admired for going up, not for pretending to know things.
The wind that carried me off was no magic. Just a storm. I cried my first night up there.
When I landed, a crowd was kneeling. I was still clutching a sandbag. I said, 'Rise, my people.' Ridiculous.
I built a curtain, a big voice behind it, and a papier-mâché head that spoke through a tube.
Once a girl and her friends came asking for brains, a heart, courage and a way home. I gave them props.
Bran for brains, a silk heart, a dish of honey. They left happy. It still keeps me awake at night.
They read it, every door. And this morning there was a queue outside my house as usual. I don't understand people.
A farmer asked if his cow was cursed. I said, 'No, she's old.' He thanked me as if I'd worked a miracle.
The old basket is in my shed. The silk rotted long ago. Mice have been living in it for years.
The new skin needs to be light and tough, something that won't tear in a gust. Silk won't do.
Phantom wings, perhaps. They carry those horrid things across the night sky; they could carry me.
Don't tell anyone yet. If I go, I'd rather they remember the posters than a sad goodbye.
Bring me four phantom membranes. Whether I fly or not, I want the choice to be a real one.
Thank you for the paper. I wrote the first draft with flourishes. The second without. The second was better.
So now you know the deepest part: I never had any power. Not a spark. Only tricks and a very good voice.
Green spectacles, a curtain, a trumpet to boom through. That's the whole of my art.
For years I lived in terror of a pulled curtain. I'd wake at night sure the crowd was at my door.
Oddly, now that it's pulled, I'm still frightened. Of being useful without the mask.
Deep down I'm a showman. And a showman with no show... what is that, exactly?
I keep dreaming of the basket. Wind in my face, the fairground shrinking below, nobody expecting anything.
I came in a balloon, and I always meant to leave in one. Perhaps it's time.
The balloon went up without me one windy morning. I untied it myself. It seemed happier that way.
Half the village watched it drift over the hills and waved. I waved too, from the ground. Strange feeling.
I wonder where the balloon came down. I hope nobody took it for a sign and built it a throne.
You saw me without the curtain before anyone else, and you didn't laugh. I won't forget that.
I'm learning real things now. Herbs, from the healer. It's slow. Real things usually are.
If a stranger ever calls you great and terrible, look behind them for a curtain. Then smile anyway.
Off you go. Come back with problems; you'll get my honest best, and a biscuit.
Those emeralds I gave you are real. I had them checked twice. Old habits.
I'm still the village sage. Honest now. People say my advice sounds better without the echo.
I burned the curtain for kindling. It kept me warm through a whole frosty night. Useful at last.
The children play 'wizard' now: one hides behind a blanket and the others shout 'Humbug!' Delightful.
Do you know what I tell people now? 'I don't know, but let's find out.' It's astonishingly popular.
I kept one pair of green spectacles. On gloomy days I put them on. A small lie, just for me.
Remember the emerald street? That glass is in the chapel window now. On Sundays the light is green.
Someone left flowers on my step with a note: 'For the humbug.' I've never been so moved.
The balloon floated off one windy morning with no one in it, and the village kept its sage: honest now, and oddly more respected than before.
The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum (1900)
The city was only green because everyone wore green spectacles. I want to show the village that trick. Bring me green glass.
Look at them, marvelling at the 'emerald' street. I feel wicked and happy at once.
Emerald spectacles
I'm going to confess. On paper, pinned to every door: 'I am no wizard, only a humbug.' Bring me paper, before I change my mind.
They read it... and they're still bringing me their problems. I don't understand people.
Posters for a humbug
I came in a balloon and I meant to leave in one. Its skin needs something light and tough. Phantom wings, perhaps?
It's ready. But I don't think I'll go. Take these emeralds: they're real, unlike everything else I've ever sold.
A new balloon
Pay no attention to the person behind the... never mind.
Everything looks greener through the right glass. Everything.
I once gave a scarecrow bran for brains. It worked. People mostly need to be believed in.
You're the only one who's seen me without the curtain. You didn't laugh. Thank you.
Behind the curtain
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.bio.0: Sixty winters by the water. The fish know me by name. Well, they know my rod.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.bio.1: I don't see as well as I used to, and my hands shake when the line pulls. The lake is patient with me.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.bio.2: There's a fish that has escaped me for forty years. Round, spiny, mocking. I want to see it once more before I go.
Shh. Speak softly. The fish are listening, and they gossip.
The best conversations are the silent ones, by the water. Sit. Say nothing. Perfect.
There's a fish that's escaped me for forty years. Round, spiny, mocking. You'll hear about that one.
Lately my basket comes home near empty. The tavern cook doesn't say anything. That's worse.
Friday is fish day in this village. Always has been. I'd hate to be the one who ended it.
I've never asked for help on this jetty. Not once in sixty years. Pride's a heavy tackle box.
My eyes won't let me fish like before, and the village counts on my catch. Would you bring me some cod?
Want to learn? Patience first. Rod second. Bait third. Talking, never.
Sixty winters by this lake. The fish know me by name. Well, they know my rod.
See that ripple by the reeds? Perch. Old one. We've been ignoring each other for years.
I built this jetty with my father when I was a sprat. Half the planks are still his.
Mornings, I used to row out before the mist lifted. The lake was mine until the birds woke.
Every family in the village has eaten my fish. Some of them three generations over.
My eyes aren't what they were. The float's a blur now. I strike late, or too early.
And my hands shake when the line pulls. The lake is patient with me. Kinder than I deserve.
Good fish. Firm, bright-eyed. The village won't go hungry this week. Thank you.
The tavern cook asked who caught them. I said 'a friend'. First time I've shared credit.
My mother taught me. Three days of smoke, turning them at dawn and dusk.
The village keeps them for winter. When snow blocks the roads, smoked salmon is what keeps folk going.
I can't wade the rapids anymore. One slip and they'd be fishing me out instead.
The run's happening now. Hear the water? It's louder. That's them, climbing.
Bring me a few salmon from upriver? I'll smoke them the old way and teach you while I'm at it.
Now then. Let me tell you about the mocking fish. You've been patient enough.
Forty years ago I hooked something that fought like a mule. I hauled it up and it puffed out like a ball.
Spines everywhere. Little round eyes. And I swear on this jetty, it looked at me and laughed.
I was so startled I let go. Splash. Gone. My brother laughed for a week. He was worse than the fish.
Since then I've seen them now and then, deep in warm water, never here. Mocking me from afar.
My brother's gone now. I think of him whenever I think of that fish. Funny, the tackle memory keeps.
But first, there's another tradition I can't keep up alone. The smokehouse behind my hut.
Every autumn, the salmon run up the river, and I smoke them the old way. Alder wood, salt, patience.
Smell that? Sixty years of smoke and salt. Every family will have salmon on the shelf this winter.
You turned them well at dawn. Mother would have said you have smoker's hands. Good hands.
I've even kept a special bucket for it. Painted blue. Been waiting forty years, empty.
Sometimes I dream I catch it and it speaks. It says 'took you long enough'.
When I'm gone, someone should keep an eye on this lake. I've been thinking it might be you.
But that's later. First, the rascal. I'd like to have a laugh with an old enemy.
Bring me those round, spiny ones, the ones that puff up. I want to see that face one last time and laugh.
I've been thinking about my years. How many winters are left. You think about that, at my age.
I'm not afraid of the end. The lake will still be here. The fish don't mind who holds the rod.
What I'm afraid of is leaving with a knot untied. A story with no ending.
That mocking fish. Forty years. I want to see that face once more before I go. Just once.
Not to win. I've made peace with losing to it. I just want to laugh back this time.
My brother and I used to imitate its face. Cheeks puffed, eyes crossed. Mother despaired.
Only warm seas have them, I hear. Far from here. My legs won't take me that far anymore.
They're poisonous, careful. Don't eat one. Don't let the tavern cook get clever with one either.
Ha! I still laugh every time I look in the blue bucket. There it is, the rascal!
It puffed up at me. I puffed my cheeks back. The whole jetty watched. Best day in forty years.
Maybe it'll tell its children about the old fisher who finally laughed back.
I told my brother about it. At his stone, by the hill. I think he laughed too.
The lake is patient. I'm learning to be patient with myself. It only took sixty winters.
When I'm gone, the lake's yours to watch. No rush. I plan to be very slow about going.
Shh, now. Sit a while. Say nothing. That's the best thanks I know how to give.
Is the rod treating you well? It's caught everything in this lake. And now that one too. Through you.
I don't fish much anymore. I sit by the water and just watch. It turns out I love that best.
When you fish nearby, I'll tell you where the big ones are. Left of the reeds, early. Trust me.
The perch by the reeds still ignores me. We're old friends now, I think. Equally stubborn.
The children come down to the jetty. I teach them knots. They don't listen. Neither did I.
Friday's still fish day. The village didn't miss one. That's thanks to you, in part.
The smokehouse is going strong. The young baker's apprentice helps now. Terrible at turning, good at eating.
I set the rascal free, after a week. It gave me one last look. I swear it winked.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.epilogue: The old fisher now sits by the water just to watch. When you fish nearby, they tell you where the big ones are.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.stage.0.a: My eyes won't let me fish like before, and the village counts on my catch. Would you bring me some cod?
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.stage.0.d: Good fish. The village won't go hungry this week.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.stage.1.a: The salmon run upriver this season. Bring me a few and I'll smoke them the old way.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.stage.1.d: Smell that? Sixty years of smoke and salt.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.stage.2.a: Bring me those round, spiny ones, the ones that puff up. I want to see that face one last time and laugh.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.stage.2.d: Ha! There it is, the rascal! Take my rod. It's caught everything in this lake... except that one. Until today.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.talk.0: Shh. Speak softly, the fish are listening.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.talk.1: The best conversations are the silent ones, by the water.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.talk.2: Want to learn? Patience first. Rod second.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.talk.3: When I'm gone, someone should keep an eye on this lake. Maybe you.
hearthbound.persona.old_fisher.title: Old Fisher
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.bio.0: My fields have fed this village for three generations. Three! And now the earth refuses to give.
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.bio.1: The crops rot from the roots, and at night things walk among the furrows. I've seen them.
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.bio.2: They tell me to plant somewhere else. This is where my grandparents are buried. I'm not leaving.
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.dialo: Mind the furrows. Walk between them, not across. The soil remembers every boot.
Rain, sun, rain. That's all a farmer asks. That, and to be left in peace.
I'm not leaving. This is where they are. This is where I'll be, when my time comes.
And then there's the other thing. The thing I don't say at the tavern, because they'd laugh.
At night, things walk among the furrows. Slow, dragging. I've seen them from the window. More each week.
They trample the seedlings and leave the ground torn up like a battlefield. I can't guard it alone.
Stand watch with me in the village tonight? Help me drive them off. Please.
You have calluses on your hands. Good. Honest hands. You can stay and talk.
Look at this wheat. Grey. Brittle. It snaps like old bones. It breaks my heart.
When the pumpkins grow again, I'll carve the biggest one for the festival. You'll see.
These fields have fed this village for three generations. Three! Grandfather broke this ground with an ox.
Grandmother planted the apple tree by the gate. It still gives, even when nothing else does.
They're both buried under it. I talk to them while I weed. They're better company than most.
Two summers ago, the roots started rotting. First one row, then half a field. Nobody knows why.
The elder says plant somewhere else. Leave the old fields. As if I could pack my grandparents in a cart.
The furrows are still standing. First time this month. I walked every row at dawn just to check.
Thank you for standing with me. I haven't slept that well since the rot began.
Next spring her beans were taller than the fence. Nobody laughed after that.
I've been thinking of her trick. Bone, ground fine, worked into the furrows. Wake the soil up.
The walkers you drove off leave bones behind sometimes. Poetic, isn't it? What harms the field can heal it.
But I'd need a lot. Sacks and sacks. More than I can grind with these old hands.
The earth is exhausted. Bone meal will bring it back to life. Bring me plenty?
You fought like someone with something to protect. I noticed. I won't forget it.
Now I can tell you the truth: the walkers weren't the worst of it. They just made it visible.
The soil itself is tired. Two generations of wheat, wheat, wheat. Grandfather never let a field rest.
He did it to feed the village in the hungry years. Nobody blames him. The earth might.
I pick up a handful and it runs through my fingers like ash. No worms. No smell of rain.
My neighbours whisper that the field is cursed, and that I'm cursed with it for staying.
Maybe I'm just stubborn. Grandmother said stubbornness was the family crop. It never fails.
Once, after a dry year, she fed the garden with crushed bones from the stew pot. People laughed.
Look! Green shoots! The field is breathing again. I knelt down and cried like a child.
Grandmother's trick worked. I told the apple tree first. I think it rustled.
The tavern cook said nothing, just gave me an extra bowl. Kindness can hurt more than laughter.
The new shoots won't bear pumpkins in time. The field is waking, but it's still weak.
I don't want the tradition to end with me. Three generations, and I'd be the one who dropped it.
If I had a few big ones, I could carve them, and plant the seeds for next year's crop.
For the festival I always brought the biggest pumpkins. Help me not break the tradition?
The neighbours came by to look. One asked for a handful of the bone meal. I gave two.
Can I tell you something? I was more afraid than I let on. Afraid I'd kill the field by staying.
What if the elder was right, and I was just too stubborn to see it dying?
Some nights I lay awake making lists of places we could go. I tore up every list.
Roots are roots. You can move a tree once, if you're lucky. Move it twice and it dies.
Now there's a new worry. The harvest festival. Every year, for three generations, we brought the pumpkins.
Grandfather started it. The biggest pumpkin on the table, carved with a grin, a candle inside.
Children wait all year to see it. Last year I had none. I came with empty hands. I hid at the back.
The fields are golden again. I stand at the gate every sunset just to look. Golden!
The festival was saved. The children screamed when I lit the big pumpkin. Best sound I know.
The elder came by and said, 'You were right to stay.' I've waited years for that sentence.
I saved seeds from the festival pumpkins. A whole jar. That's the next three generations, right there.
If you ever want a patch of land, there's a corner by the gate. Good soil now. For honest hands.
Rain, sun, rain. And a friend passing by now and then. That's all a farmer asks.
Off you go. And walk between the furrows, not across. The soil remembers you kindly.
How's grandfather's hoe? Sixty years in these fields. Now it gets to see the world, with you.
I named the best pumpkin of this harvest after you. It was enormous. Very handsome. Like you, a bit.
Don't make that face. It's an honour. Next year's will have your name too. And the year after.
The walkers still come sometimes, but the guards take turns now. They learned from watching you.
The soil smells like rain again. Worms everywhere. I've never been so glad to see worms.
The neighbours stopped whispering about curses. Now they ask me for advice. Funny how that goes.
I let the east field rest this year. Clover and sheep only. Grandfather would grumble. Grandmother would nod.
I told them all about you, under the apple tree. I think they approve.
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.epilo: The fields are golden again. The farmer names the best pumpkin of each harvest after you.
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.stage: Something tramples my fields every night. Stand watch with me in the village and drive them off.
The furrows are still standing. First time this month.
The earth is exhausted. Bone meal will bring it back to life. Bring me plenty.
Look! Green shoots! The field is breathing again.
For the harvest festival I always brought the biggest pumpkins. This year I have none... help me not break the tradition.
The festival is saved! Take my grandfather's hoe. It's worked these fields for sixty years.
Look at this wheat. Sad. Grey. It breaks my heart.
Rain, sun, rain. That's all a farmer asks. And to be left in peace.
You have calluses on your hands. Good. Honest hands.
When the pumpkins grow again, I'll carve the biggest one for the festival.
hearthbound.persona.plagued_farmer.title: Stubborn Farmer
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.bio.0: My grandfather forged the gates of this village. My father, the tools that raised it. And me? Horseshoes.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.bio.1: The capital's guild rejected me. "Too provincial", they said. I still have the letter nailed above the forge.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.bio.2: I want to make one masterpiece. Just one. Something they'll talk about in the capital.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.dialogue: Mind the anvil. It's older than both of us and has a worse temper than mine.
Listen to that hammer. Clean strike, clean ring. The day it sounds dull, I'll know I've gone soft.
I keep that letter where the smoke hits it every morning. It reminds me why I get up early.
Lately the fire won't hold heat. I stoke it and stoke it and it just sulks.
A forge without fuel is a cold stone box. And a smith without a forge is just a loud neighbour.
I've an idea brewing, a big one. But nothing starts until this fire roars again.
Coal. That's what I need, and plenty. Help me feed the beast and I'll show you real work.
You're staring at the gates. Yes, they're good. No, I didn't make them.
I shoe horses, mend hinges, sharpen the farmers' sickles. Honest work. Small work.
Your boots have loose nails. I can hear them from here. Sit down before you trip.
My grandfather forged those gates in one winter. People still stop to touch the scrollwork.
My father made every plough and axe that cleared these fields. His mark is on half the village.
And me? I make horseshoes. Very good horseshoes. Nobody writes songs about horseshoes.
See that paper nailed above the forge? Don't read it. Everyone reads it. Fine, read it.
The capital's guild. I walked nine days to show them my best blade. They called it provincial.
Hear that? That's a forge with a full belly. It hasn't sung like that since my father's day.
Thanks for the coal. You carried it without complaint, which is more than my last apprentice did.
Something with a spine of good iron and an edge that makes the guild masters stutter.
But the iron the merchants bring is rubbish. Full of slag. It cracks when it cools, like a coward.
Good iron sings. You know that by now. I need iron that sings a whole song.
I won't start the heart of the work with bad metal. I'd rather not start at all.
Bring me proper ingots, clean and heavy. Then I'll finally begin the piece I've been dreaming of.
Now that the fire's alive, I'll tell you the rest. That letter wasn't the first rejection. It was the third.
The first time, they said my work lacked finesse. The second, that it lacked ambition.
The third time, they didn't even unwrap the blade. Just looked at my boots and said 'provincial'.
I came home and made horseshoes for a year. Out of spite, I think. Or shame.
My father never said a word about it. He just left his best tongs on my bench one morning.
Grandfather used to say the gates weren't his. They belonged to whoever walked through them.
I think about that a lot. Who would walk through something I made?
I've been sketching at night. Charcoal on the back of old orders. A blade. No, more than a blade.
These ingots are beautiful. I tested every one. Not a single complaint from any of them.
The core is forged. I worked it three nights straight. The neighbours think I've gone mad.
I've never worked it before. Nobody in this village has. Diamond doesn't forgive mistakes.
But if I don't try now, I'll spend the rest of my life making horseshoes and telling myself it's fine.
You've already done more than anyone. I hate asking. I'm not good at asking.
It's a lot. I know it's a lot. Deep down, dangerous, hard to find.
Diamonds. Only diamonds will hold the edge I see in my head. Will you bring them?
Maybe I have. But it's the good kind, the kind my grandfather had when he made the gates.
Want to know a secret? I'm frightened. Every strike could be the one that ruins it.
If this fails, the guild was right. Just a provincial smith with big ideas and small hands.
Some nights I take the letter down and hold it over the fire. I never let go.
I don't want to burn it. I want to be able to laugh at it. There's a difference.
My father's tongs, grandfather's hammer, my fire. Three generations in one piece. That's the dream.
I've imagined the edge a thousand times. Thin as a whisper, and it never dulls.
Iron can't hold that. Gold is too soft. There's only one thing hard enough.
There it hangs. My masterpiece. I still walk past it three times before breakfast.
Look closely at the hilt. Three little marks: grandfather's, father's, mine. Side by side.
Maybe I'll take an apprentice. Someone who'll make horseshoes first and dream second. Like I did.
Remember when you brought the coal and I barely said thank you? I say it now. Thank you.
The forge sings every day. It's the happiest sound in this village, and you helped tune it.
My grandfather made the gates. My father, the tools. Me? A blade. And a friend.
Go on, off with you. And fix those loose boot nails, or I'll do it myself while you sleep.
And right next to it, the guild's letter. I read it now and laugh. Out loud. Every morning.
A merchant from the capital saw it last week. Went pale. Asked who taught me. I said, 'this village'.
Rumour says the guild wants to send someone to look. Let them walk nine days. It'll do them good.
How's the one I made you? With the leftovers, remember. Don't tell anyone it's better than theirs.
If you ever notch it, bring it back. I'll scold you and fix it, in that order.
I still make horseshoes, you know. But now I make them like they matter. Because they do.
The farmer's horse wears my shoes, and it hasn't limped once all season. I'm oddly proud of that.
Children come to watch me work now. I let them pump the bellows. One of them has good hands.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.epilogue: Their masterpiece hangs over the forge, next to the guild's rejection letter, which now makes them laugh.
The forge is starving. Bring me coal and I'll show you real work.
Hear that roar? That's a happy forge.
The iron the merchants sell is garbage. Bring me good ingots, and I'll start the piece I've been dreaming of.
Now we're talking. This will be the heart of the work.
It needs diamonds. Only diamonds hold an edge like the one I imagine. I know it's a lot to ask.
It's done. It's... beautiful. And I made you one too, with the leftovers. Don't tell the guild.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.talk.0: Don't touch that, it's still hot. No, the other one's hot too.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.talk.1: Good iron sings when you strike it. Bad iron complains.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.talk.2: Your gear is a disgrace. Leave it with me sometime.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.talk.3: One day my name will be engraved on a blade in the king's hall. You'll see.
hearthbound.persona.proud_smith.title: Proud Smith
hearthbound.persona.restless_builder.bio: Every house in this village has a bit of me in it. I know which beam creaks and which chimney smokes.
I've drawn a hundred plans nobody asked for: bridges, towers, a library with a glass dome.
The elder says we don't need a library. I say a village without a library is just a camp with walls.
hearthbound.persona.restless_builder.dia: Careful where you step, that plank's loose. I put it there. On purpose. Mostly.
That roof over there is three degrees off. Nobody else notices. I notice every morning.
My favourite has a glass dome. You'd sit inside and read with the whole sky above you.
Look at the plaza. Mud when it rains, dust when it doesn't. It's the heart of the village, and it's tired.
If I'm ever going to build my own thing, it starts here, with a proper floor under it.
Cobble cracks, dirt washes away. Stone bricks are square and honest. They stay.
Bring me a good load of stone bricks and I'll rebuild the plaza. Then you'll see what I mean.
Stone is patient, wood is generous. Glass? Glass sulks if you look at it wrong.
I've seen the things you put up around here. Not bad at all. A bit crooked on the left.
I carry a folding rule everywhere. I've measured the elder's chair. Don't tell the elder.
Every house in this village has a bit of me in it. A beam, a hinge, a stubborn chimney.
I know which floor creaks in the tavern and which chimney smokes when the wind blows east.
But I've only ever repaired. Patched. Propped up. I've never built something that was my idea.
At night I draw. Bridges over the river, a bell tower, a gallery for the harvest fair.
I've got a hundred plans rolled up under my bed. Nobody asked for a single one.
Walk across it. Go on, stamp. Solid, square, honest. That's a plaza now.
Thank you. You hauled every brick like it mattered. It did.
I've started the frame already. Just oak and a few stubborn nails. It's small. It's mine.
The problem is light. A reading room without light is just a cupboard with chairs.
Candles are no good near books. Walls of windows, that's what I want. Sun in every corner.
Glass is temperamental, I've told you. It cracks from cold, from heat, from a bad look.
Bring me glass, plenty of it, and please, please don't break it on the way.
Want to know why I really wanted the plaza done? It's the foundation. For something else.
There's a spot on the north side, right where the sun lands longest. I measured it for years.
That's where my library goes. The one with the dome. I've dreamed it down to the nails.
The elder says we don't need a library. We need fences and wells, the elder says.
I say a village without a library is just a camp with walls. We argued. Loudly. Twice.
My old master built barns all his life. Said dreamers make crooked walls.
He wasn't wrong. My first bridge fell into the river. The ducks were very pleased.
But the second one held. It's still there, by the mill. Nobody knows I built it.
Look how the sun comes through. Perfect. I stood inside for an hour doing nothing.
Children have started sitting on the steps already, even with no books on the shelves.
People here work until dusk. If they can only read by day, they'll never read at all.
I tried torches. Smoke on the pages, soot on the glass. The scholar nearly wept.
Lanterns are clean and steady. Hang a few from the beams and the room glows like a hearth.
It's the last detail. The very last. After that, it's finished. My first building. Mine.
Bring me lanterns, so people can read at night. Then my library will be done.
The elder walked past yesterday. Stopped. Looked up. Said nothing. That's a good sign, I think.
Can I tell you what scares me? That I'll finish it and people will just walk past.
A building nobody uses is a gravestone for an idea. I've seen a few of those.
I'm getting older. My hands shake a little on the high beams. I don't let anyone see.
All I've ever wanted is to build something that outlives me. That's it. Just one thing.
When I'm dust, I'd like some child to read a story under that dome and never know my name.
The scholar promised to lend books. The tavern cook wants a shelf for recipes. It's catching.
But when the sun goes down, the whole room goes blind. All that glass, black as a well.
The library stands. I still wake up and have to check it hasn't been a dream.
Every evening the lanterns come on, and the dome glows over the plaza like a second moon.
I still hear which beams creak. Now I hear the pages turning too. Better music.
The scholar reads aloud on market days. Half the village comes. The other half pretends not to.
Remember the glass? You didn't break a single pane. I've told everyone. Twice.
Stone, glass, light. And a friend who carried them. That's what the library is made of.
Come by tomorrow. I want your opinion on the bell tower. And bring your appetite for arguments.
The elder borrowed a book last week. Returned it late. I charged no fine. This time.
How's my old axe treating you? I expect great things. Crooked on the left is forgivable.
I meant it, you know. You'll build greater things than I. I'd like to see them.
The ducks by the mill came to the opening. I suspect they were hoping the bridge would fall.
I've got new plans already. A bell tower. Maybe a bridge that actually looks like a bridge.
Here, look at this one. Be honest. No, more honest. Hmm. You're right about the stairs.
Children draw houses now in the plaza dust. Some of them put domes on top. That's my doing.
The roof that's three degrees off? I fixed it. Took an afternoon. Couldn't sleep better.
hearthbound.persona.restless_builder.epi: The little library stands in the plaza. The architect already has new plans... and wants to know what you think of them.
hearthbound.persona.restless_builder.sta: I want to rebuild the plaza with proper stone bricks. Bring me some and you'll see what I mean.
Solid, square, honest. Just like I like them.
My library needs light. Lots of light. Bring me glass, and don't break it on the way!
Look how the sun comes through. Perfect.
The last detail: lanterns, so people can read at night. Then my library will be finished.
It's finished. The first building that was my own idea. Take my axe; you'll build greater things than I.
hearthbound.persona.restless_builder.tal: See that roof? Three degrees off. It keeps me up at night.
Stone is patient. Wood is generous. Glass is... temperamental.
You build too, don't you? I've seen what you make around here. Not bad!
One day I'll build something that outlives me. That's all I want.
Twenty years in the border companies. Now I sharpen hoes and teach the kids to hold a stick like a sword.
My shield-brother Aldric fell at the Grey Ford. Pillagers. I carried him three days to bury him at home.
I swore I'd never lift a blade again. But I keep my old sword wrapped in oilcloth under the bed. Just in case.
hearthbound.persona.retired_warrior.dial: Your stance is terrible. Feet apart, weight low. Again. No, again. Better. Barely.
My knee aches. Rain before nightfall, mark my words. This knee has never lost a bet.
At night I hear rattling out on the far fields. Bones clattering, looking for something to shoot.
The skeletons have grown bold lately. Last week they shot the miller's mule. Poor beast.
You want to learn from me? Fine. But I teach no one I haven't seen fight. Words are wind.
Talk is cheap. I've heard every boast a tavern can hold, and I've buried most of the boasters.
So show me. Go and put ten of those rattling skeletons back in the ground. Then we'll talk.
Twenty years in the border companies. Now I sharpen hoes and teach children to hold a stick like a sword.
The children think I'm a grumpy old dog. They're right. But they come back every morning for another lesson.
I've seen many young ones like you set off down that road. Most don't come back. You do. I like that.
We held the eastern fords, the worst posts in the realm. Mud, fog, and pillagers who came like wolves at dusk.
I had a shield-brother. Aldric. Laughed at everything, snored like a bear, never missed a parry in twenty years.
He always said the brave ones are those who come back. The fools are those who stay to be admired.
There's a place called the Grey Ford. I don't talk about it. Not yet. Pour me some water, will you?
I barely sleep. The companies teach you to unlearn it. Every creak on the stairs sounds like boots.
Not bad. Not bad at all. Sit, have a drink with this old dog. You've earned the good cup.
Now I'll tell you about the Grey Ford, since you've earned that too. Fog so thick you could lean on it.
Travellers talk in the tavern. They say the band with the grey banner is raiding the south road again.
Grey banner, black crows painted on it. Same band. The ones from the ford. Twenty years, and still riding.
I don't know what I'll do. But I have a feeling I'll need that sword, and I want it ready when I decide.
The smith here is proud but good. With decent iron that blade could sing again. Not with the cheap stuff.
Bring me good iron, six ingots, and I'll have it reforged. Call it an old fool's precaution.
Pillagers came across the water at dawn. Crossbows first, then axes. We were twelve. They were forty.
Aldric took a bolt meant for me. Shoved me aside and laughed, even then. 'You owe me a drink,' he said.
He didn't die right away. That's the part I never tell. He held on until nightfall, talking about his mother's plums.
I carried him home. Three days on my back, through the hills. Nobody asked me to. Nobody could have stopped me.
We buried him under his mother's plum tree. That same week I hung up my sword and swore never again.
Some nights I still owe him that drink. I pour two cups and drink both. Don't tell anyone.
The sword is under my bed, wrapped in oilcloth. I hadn't unwrapped it in years. Yesterday I did.
It's chipped and rusted. Like my knees. A blade left alone forgets what it was made for.
Listen to it sing. Twenty years since I heard that sound. My hands shook on the hilt like a recruit's.
The smith shed a tear working it. Said it was the finest steel ever to cross that anvil. Proud as a rooster, that one.
Last week they hit a farm two valleys over. A family escaped with only their cows. The cows were lucky.
If no one stops them, they'll come here in the end. They always drift toward the next easy village.
I'm not asking for revenge. Well... not only revenge. I'm asking for that road to be safe again.
I can't go. You can. I hate that it's that simple, and I hate asking it of you.
Hunt them down, five of their raiders at least, so the band breaks. Do it for him. For Aldric.
I swung it at dawn in the yard. The children gathered round to watch and forgot to breathe.
And then I had to sit down. My knee, my shoulder, my wind. Twenty years don't forgive a single morning.
Here's the truth I've been dodging: I'm too old to chase them. I'd last a day on the road. Two, perhaps.
I dream of the ford every week. The fog. His laugh. The crows on that banner lifting into the air.
I'm not afraid of dying. I'm afraid of dying having done nothing, while they still ride laughing down the same road.
You fight the way we fought in the companies. Low, patient, never wasting a step. Someone taught you well. Or life did.
I watch you walk off every morning and think: that's what Aldric looked like at the start.
I've heard the band camps near the crossroads south of here. They raid carts and burn what they can't carry.
It's done, then. I never thought I'd live to hear those words. Sit. Tonight we both have that drink.
The blade is yours now. It was never meant to rust under a bed. Carry it well and keep it oiled.
I still pour two cups sometimes. Now I pour three. The third is yours, whether you're here or not.
The south road is busy again. Carts, pilgrims, a travelling puppet show. Aldric would have loved the puppets.
If anyone ever troubles you, send word. I've got years on me, but I'm still standing, and I remember which end is sharp.
Twenty years I carried that ford on my back. You helped me set it down. I won't forget it.
Off you go. Come back, like you always do. That's the only order I'll ever give you.
Yesterday I went to the plum tree and told him. I swear the branches moved, and there wasn't a breath of wind.
I sleep at night now. Whole nights. I'd forgotten what it's like to wake without reaching for a weapon.
My knee still predicts the rain, mind you. Some things not even peace can fix.
I've taken up teaching in the training yard again. Real teaching. No sticks: wooden swords, shields, drills.
I teach them to fight like you. Low stance, patient eyes, not one wasted step. I call it 'the traveller's guard'.
One of the girls asked who you were. I said: someone who comes back. It's the highest praise I have.
Remember that first day, when I said your stance was terrible? It was. It's fine now. Mostly.
Last night I dreamt of the ford, but there was no fog. Just water, and Aldric fishing, laughing at me.
hearthbound.persona.retired_warrior.epil: The old warrior sleeps at night now. Sometimes you find them at the training yard, teaching the young ones how you fight.
hearthbound.persona.retired_warrior.stag: You want my respect? Talk is cheap. Go and put ten of those rattling skeletons back in the ground.
Not bad. Not bad at all. Sit, have a drink with this old dog.
My sword is chipped and rusted. Bring me good iron and I'll have it reforged. I have a feeling I'll need it.
Listen to it sing. It's been twenty years since I heard that sound.
The band that killed Aldric still raids the roads. I'm too old to chase them. You aren't. Do it for him.
It's done, then. Take my blade. It was never meant to rust under a bed. Carry it well.
hearthbound.persona.retired_warrior.talk: Your stance is terrible. Feet apart, weight low. Again.
My knee aches. Rain is coming, mark my words.
I've seen many young ones like you. Most don't come back. You do. I like that.
Aldric would have liked you. He always said the brave ones are the ones who come back.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.bio.0: I tend the shrine: I sweep, I light the candles, I listen. Mostly I listen.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.bio.1: People come to tell me what they can't tell anyone else. I keep a lot of secrets.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.bio.2: The old keeper made me promise to restore the shrine's crystal window. It shattered the night she died.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.dialog: Peace be with you, traveller. You look like the road has been leaning on you.
The candles never go out here. That's my only rule. Everything else is negotiable.
It shattered the night she died. A crack like thunder. People say it grieved with us.
Before she went, she held my hand and made me promise. Keep the candles lit. Restore the window.
I've kept the first promise every single night. The second... one step at a time.
But the candle box is nearly empty. The chandler moved away, and I've been rationing stubs.
The shrine's candles are running out, and I promised they'd never go out. Would you bring me some?
Everyone carries something heavy. What's yours? You don't have to answer today.
I sweep, I light the candles, I listen. Mostly I listen. The broom does most of the talking.
Sit on the bench by the door if you like. It's warm from all the people who sat there before.
People come here to tell me what they can't tell anyone else. I keep a lot of secrets.
Don't worry. I've never told one. Not even to the candles. Well, maybe once, to the candles.
I wasn't always the keeper. The old keeper found me asleep on these steps one winter and gave me soup.
She taught me that silence can be a kind of kindness. That a candle is a promise you can see.
See that boarded window above the altar? Once it was crystal. It filled the plaza with colours at sunset.
The light stays. Thank you, friend. I lit every one of them last night, just to see the room glow.
You brought them so quickly. I think the old keeper would have called that a small miracle.
The baker hasn't slept in four nights. The children are afraid to close their eyes.
I've prayed. I've lit more candles. But candles don't frighten things that hunt in the dark sky.
The old keeper used to say rest is a gift we give each other. Right now nobody can give it.
I'm a keeper, not a fighter. I've never held a sword. You have. I've seen your hands.
Winged shadows come down on those who don't rest. Please, drive them off, so people can sleep again.
Now that the light is safe, let me tell you about her. She laughed loudly. Nobody expects that of a keeper.
She hummed while sweeping, burnt the soup, and forgave everyone. Everyone. Even the ones who didn't ask.
When I came here, I was running from something I'd done. I never told her. She never asked.
She just handed me a broom and said, 'The floor doesn't care who you were.'
I've carried that sentence for years. It's the lightest thing I own and the most precious.
Lately, though, something's wrong. People come to me not with secrets, but with exhaustion.
They say they can't sleep. When they try to stay up late, something shrieks above the rooftops.
Winged shadows. Pale, ragged, with eyes like cold lanterns. They come for those who haven't rested.
People are sleeping again. It's the best prayer I know. The baker snored through the morning bell.
The children leave little drawings on the altar now. Most of them are of you, fighting the shadows.
Amethyst. She said it holds light the way a friend holds a secret: gently, and then gives it back as colour.
Any other glass would be a patch. I don't want a patch. I want her window.
I know it's deep and dark down there. I'd go myself, but I'd get lost after the first turn.
It would mean everything to me. To her, too, wherever she's listening.
For the window I need amethyst, the stone she used. Will you bring me some?
Thank you. I didn't realise how afraid I was until I heard the village breathing quietly at night.
Can I share a secret of my own? I don't know if I'm worthy of this shrine.
She chose me because I needed a home. Not because I was holy. I'm not holy. I burn soup too.
Some nights I stand before the boarded window and feel like a guest in someone else's house.
If I could restore the window, maybe I'd feel I've earned my place. Maybe I'd finally feel forgiven.
I kept one shard of the old glass. Look, it's still violet at the edge. I carry it everywhere.
She made the window herself, when she was young. She climbed into the deep caves for the crystals.
She told me about a cave that sang when the wind passed through. Full of purple stone.
Look how the light breaks into colours. Just like she said. Every sunset, the plaza turns into a painting.
People stop in the middle of the street to watch. Even the guards. Even the grumpy ones.
I finally told someone what I'd been running from. I told the window. It glowed. I'll take that.
If you ever carry something heavy again, come here. I'll listen. That's what I do best.
The shadows haven't come back. People sleep. That's a peace you gave us, and I'll remember it.
Peace be with you, friend. Truly, this time. You look lighter too.
Go on. And whenever you see colours on the stones at sunset, know that one candle is yours.
How does the circlet sit? She would have wanted a hero to have it. I'm sure she's pleased.
I light one extra candle every evening now. It's for you. It burns on the left side of the altar.
Don't argue. It's my only rule, remember? The candles never go out. Especially that one.
The children lie on the plaza stones at sunset and try to catch the colours in their hands.
Last week I stood under the window and, for the first time, I didn't feel like a guest.
I set her old shard into the corner of the new window. You have to know where to look.
The baker brought me bread as thanks. Burnt at the edges. We laughed about it for a long time.
People still bring me their secrets. Now they also bring me flowers. The shrine smells of spring.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.epilog: The shrine's window paints the plaza in colours every sunset. The keeper lights one extra candle, for you.
The shrine's candles are running out and I promised they'd never go out. Would you bring me some?
The light stays. Thank you, friend.
Winged shadows come down at night on those who don't rest. The villagers are afraid to close their eyes. Please.
People are sleeping again. It's the best prayer I know.
For the window I need amethyst. It's what she used, the old keeper. It would mean everything to me.
Look how the light breaks into colours... just like she said. Wear this circlet; she would have wanted a hero to have it.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.talk.0: Peace be with you, traveller. You look tired.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.talk.1: The candles never go out here. That's my only rule.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.talk.2: Everyone carries something heavy. What's yours?
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.talk.3: When the window shines again, the whole plaza will be painted with colours.
hearthbound.persona.shrine_keeper.title: Shrine Keeper
hearthbound.persona.tale_breadcrumb_path: When famine came, our father left my sibling and me in the forest. Birds ate our breadcrumbs. We found a house of gingerbread, and a witch with an oven.
We pushed her in and came home with her jewels. Father wept. I forgave him, but I still keep pebbles in my pockets, never crumbs.
Hello there. Hungry? Everyone who comes to my door gets asked that first. Old habit.
Pebbles shine in moonlight. Bread doesn't. Remember that, if you ever walk the woods at night.
I don't like to talk about the house yet. Just know it's why I bake for hungry children now.
Children still get lost in these woods. Last month the carpenter's boy wandered off for a whole night.
They found him at dawn, shivering, three steps from the path. Three steps, and he couldn't see it.
I lay awake thinking: if there'd been a light, just one, he'd have walked home for supper.
Bring me torches, will you? Sixteen. I'll mark the way home through the trees. Light beats breadcrumbs.
I've got a pocketful of white pebbles. Always. Don't laugh; they've saved my life before.
Gingerbread? No, thank you. Cookies, though... cookies I trust. They're honest about being small.
My sibling runs the mill across the river. We visit every Sunday. Always by the path, never through the trees.
When I was small, a famine came. The pantry was empty and the grown-ups whispered at night.
Our father led my sibling and me deep into the forest one morning. He said he'd be back by dark.
The first time, I'd dropped pebbles all the way. We followed them home by moonlight.
The second time, all I had was bread. I left a trail of crumbs. The birds ate every one.
We walked for three days. Then we smelled something sweet, and found a house made of gingerbread.
A line of little suns through the trees. No bird can eat those. I walked it twice just to be sure.
The carpenter's boy walked it too, proud as a knight. His mother held my hands and couldn't speak.
We came home with her jewels in our pockets. Father wept on the doorstep. Our stepmother was gone.
I forgave him. Truly. But I keep pebbles in my pockets, never crumbs. Forgiving isn't the same as forgetting.
And now there's news that turns my stomach. A cottage with sweets on the roof, deep in the forest.
A woodcutter saw it last week. Sugar tiles, candy on the sills. He almost went in, the fool.
I know what lives in those houses. Please, find them and end it. Three of them, if that's what's there.
All right. I promised you the gingerbread house. Sit down; it's better sitting down.
The walls were cake, the windows spun sugar. We were so hungry we ate the gutter before we saw the door.
An old woman came out, sweet as syrup. She fed us pancakes and gave us white beds. We thought we were saved.
In the morning she locked my sibling in a cage and set me to cooking. She wanted a plump child for her oven.
Every day she felt his finger to see if he was fat enough. He held out a little bone instead. Her eyes were poor.
Weeks of that. I scrubbed her pots and planned, and cried where she couldn't hear.
Then one day she asked me to climb into the oven to check the heat. I said I didn't know how. Show me.
She leaned in. I pushed. I shut the door. I still hear it, sometimes, when I close my own oven.
No more sugar roofs. My hands have stopped shaking. I didn't know they'd been shaking for years.
You walked where I couldn't. I've never been back inside those trees, not even with a torch.
I want every child in this village to taste sweets from a kind oven. Just once, to know what that's like.
Sweetness shouldn't be bait. It should be a gift, given at a door with the door left open.
I've already asked the farmers' families. They'll bring the little ones on Sunday. They think it's a festival.
It is, in a way. The festival of the oven that only ever makes good things.
Bring me cookies, plenty of them. Twenty-four. Enough for every hungry child, and one for the brave woodcutter.
Here's my deepest secret. I sometimes wonder if I'm the one who should be feared. I pushed an old woman into fire.
I know what she was. I know what she'd have done. But I was a child, and I did it, and I carry it.
My sibling says I saved us both. He says it every Sunday, like a prayer. I think he knows I need to hear it.
The other thing I carry is hunger. Not mine anymore. Other children's. I can smell it on them.
When the farmers have a bad year, I know which children are going without. They look at bread too long.
My fear is that one day a child will be hungry enough to walk into the woods looking for a sweet house.
The tales they tell across the mountains say the children came home and lived happily. They skip the nightmares.
My dream is to make sure no child ever needs a witch's house. Not one, not ever.
They ate them on my doorstep, laughing, crumbs everywhere. The birds came, and for once I didn't mind.
Keep the cake I gave you. An oven should only ever make things like that. Mine finally does.
If you're ever hungry, and I mean any kind of hungry, you know my door. It opens outward.
The woodcutter got his cookie. He blushed. He's promised to never go near a sugar roof again.
Life smells different now. Less like smoke, more like cinnamon.
There's a new batch in the oven. I'll save you the ones shaped like pebbles. They're my favourite.
Go on, follow the torches home. And come back Sunday; the children want to meet the one who lit the woods.
The children come every Sunday now. They know which door smells of cookies.
My sibling brought flour from the mill and stayed to help. We burned the first batch. We laughed until we wept.
The line of torches still shines through the forest. I relight them every week. A lamplighter, of sorts.
No child has spent a night lost in the woods since. The carpenter's boy guides the younger ones now.
I closed my oven yesterday and didn't hear that old sound. Just the fire, humming. Just bread.
Father visited. He's very old. He ate a cookie and said, 'You were always the brave one.' I let him say it.
I still keep pebbles in my pockets. But I've started giving them away, to the children, for luck.
You went where I couldn't and came back with the woods a little safer. I don't forget things like that.
Now a line of torches leads out of the forest, and every hungry child knows which door smells of cookies.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
Children still get lost in the woods. Bring me torches and I'll mark the way home. Light beats breadcrumbs.
A line of little suns through the trees. No bird can eat those.
Lights on the forest path
Someone has seen a cottage with sweets on the roof, deep in the forest. I know what lives in those. Please, end it.
No more sugar roofs. My hands have stopped shaking.
Houses in the woods
I want every child in the village to taste sweets from a kind oven. Bring me cookies, plenty of them.
They ate them on my doorstep, laughing. Here, take this cake: an oven should only ever make things like this.
Sweets for every child
Pebbles shine in moonlight. Bread doesn't. Remember that.
Gingerbread? No, thank you. Cookies, though... cookies I trust.
My sibling runs the mill across the river. We visit every Sunday. Always by the path.
I bake for hungry children now. No child should ever need a witch's house.
Breadcrumbs and a sweet house
hearthbound.persona.tale_cat_and_boots.b: My father left the mill to my eldest brother, the donkey to the next, and me only a cat. The cat asked for boots and a sack. I laughed, and gave them.
That cat made me a marquis with lies and rabbits. I have lands now. But I know who earned them, and it wasn't me.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cat_and_boots.d: Hello! Don't sit in that chair, please. The cat sleeps in the best chair. It's his chair, really.
The Marquis of what? Never heard of the place. Neither had I, until a cat invented it.
What happened next is a long, ridiculous story. I'll tell it bit by bit, if you keep visiting.
Those were his first boots. He's worn out many pairs since. He walks miles, even now, patrolling the lane.
The latest pair are worn through. Holes at both toes. He sits by the door and glares at the rain.
He won't set a paw outside without them. Says a gentleman must be properly dressed. He means himself.
Bring me leather? Eight pieces. I'll have the cobbler make new boots, small, soft, and very fashionable.
Never mock what someone asks for first. Boots, for instance. You'll understand one day.
I'm learning to deserve my own luck. Slowly. The cat thinks I'm far too slow.
He's asleep now. When he wakes, bow slightly. He likes that. He'll pretend not to notice.
My father was a miller with three children and not much else. When he died, we split what was left.
My eldest brother got the mill. My middle brother got the donkey. I got the cat.
I sat on the step and complained aloud. 'I can eat the cat and make gloves of his fur, and then I'll have nothing.'
The cat heard me. He looked up and said, very calmly: 'Give me a pair of boots and a sack. You won't regret it.'
A talking cat! I laughed. But I'd nothing to lose, so I spent my last coins on boots and a sack.
He's strutting up and down the lane. Tail high, whiskers forward. I think that's a thank-you.
The cobbler says it's the strangest commission of his life. He made a matching hat, unasked. The cat accepted it.
And every day since, I've wondered if a single thing I own is truly mine.
The rabbits bother me most. That's how it began: a sack of rabbits for the king, who already had everything.
Here in the village, the old folk have hardly anything. Some of them haven't had meat in a month.
I want to do it again, but the right way round. Rabbits for the old folk, not for a king.
Bring me rabbits? Six. Plump ones. The cat says he's retired from hunting, and I've never been any good.
All right. The story. With his new boots and sack, the cat went into the woods and caught a rabbit.
He didn't eat it. He took it to the king and said: 'A gift from my master, the Marquis of Carabas.'
The king had never heard of any Marquis of Carabas. Neither had I. The cat made up the name on the spot.
He did it again and again. Rabbits, partridges, all 'from the Marquis'. The king began to wonder who I was.
Then, one day, the cat told me to bathe in the river. While I was in, he hid my ragged clothes under a rock.
The king's carriage came by. The cat shouted: 'Help! Robbers have stolen my master's clothes!'
The king sent for fine clothes. I climbed out of the river a peasant and into the carriage a lord.
Nothing about it was honest. I knew it even then. I sat beside the princess and sweated through the silk.
The old folk are cooking stew. The whole street smells of it. The cat looks very proud of himself, as usual.
He did nothing. He supervised. But he accepts all credit with great dignity.
And now he's old. Very old, for a cat. He sleeps most of the day. His whiskers are white.
My fear is that he'll go before I've paid him back. Before I've proved I was worth all his scheming.
The tales from over the border say he became a great lord and only chased mice for fun afterwards. That's true, actually.
My dream is to give him a pension. A cat's pension. Nothing to do but sleep in the sun and eat fish.
He's done enough scheming for a lifetime. Bring me cod? Sixteen. Fish for him every day, as long as he lives.
Let me tell you the end of the old story. There was an ogre with a castle and all the land around it.
The cat went to the castle alone. He flattered the ogre: 'They say you can turn into anything. Even a lion?'
The ogre became a lion, to show off. The cat nearly fell off the roof. Then he said: 'But surely not a mouse?'
The ogre became a mouse. The cat ate him. Just like that. And the castle had no owner.
When the king's carriage arrived, the cat was waiting at the gate: 'Welcome to the castle of the Marquis of Carabas!'
That's how I got my lands. A cat, a lie, and a very foolish ogre. Not a single drop of my own sweat.
Here's my secret: I have lands now. But I know who earned them, and it wasn't me.
I've never thanked him properly. How do you thank someone who gave you your whole life?
He purred! He never purrs. He says it's undignified. I nearly wept into the fish.
Keep those gifts I gave you. Half of everything I have is his, and he insisted on paying you from his half.
My brothers visited. The mill's thriving, the donkey's retired. We laughed about who got the best inheritance. I won.
I'm still learning to deserve my luck. But I think I'm getting there. The cat thinks so too; he told me. Once.
When he's gone, I'll keep his chair empty. And the boots on the mantel. And fish on the step, for any cat who needs it.
Life goes on in the sun on the doorstep. Slowly, warmly. Exactly how he likes it.
Go on, then. Bow slightly to the cat on your way out. He'll pretend not to notice. He'll notice.
Now a very old cat in very small boots sleeps in the sun on the doorstep, and I sweep the step around him.
Some call me the Marquis. I don't mind. I know what it means now: the one the cat chose.
The old folk still get rabbits every month. I've learned to snare them myself. Badly, but I've learned.
The cat watches me set snares and sighs. It's the sigh of a teacher who has given up but loves you anyway.
I've started working my own fields. The crops are small. They're mine. I've never been prouder of turnips.
He's taken to wearing only one boot. Says it's the new fashion. I think his back leg is stiff. I say nothing.
You brought leather, rabbits and fish for a cat who once conquered a castle. He'll remember you. Cats do.
If anyone ever asks you for something odd first, like boots, give it. You never know what it's for.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cat_and_boots.e: Now a very old cat in very small boots sleeps in the sun on the doorstep, and the Marquis sweeps the step around him.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cat_and_boots.s: Histoires ou contes du temps passé — Charles Perrault (1697)
The old boots are worn through, and he won't set a paw outside without them. Bring me leather.
He's strutting up and down the lane. I think that's a thank-you.
That's how it began: a sack of rabbits for the king. I want to send some to the old folk here instead. Bring me rabbits.
The old folk are cooking stew. The cat looks very proud of himself, as usual.
My cat is old now, and he's done enough scheming for a lifetime. I want fish for him every day. Bring me cod.
He purred, which he never does. Take these; half of everything I have is his, and he insists on paying you.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cat_and_boots.t: The cat sleeps in the best chair. It's his chair, really.
The Marquis of what? Never heard of the place. Neither had I.
I'm learning to deserve my own luck. Slowly.
Never mock what someone asks for first. Boots, for instance.
A cat, a sack and boots
hearthbound.persona.tale_cinder_hearth.b: Years ago I slept among the ashes of my stepmother's hearth. Then came a ball, a borrowed carriage, and a glass slipper that fit one foot only: mine.
The palace was cold and full of people who never swept. I left it. I'd rather keep an honest hearth than a golden one.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cinder_hearth.d: Welcome in. Mind the hearth, I've just swept it. I always have just swept it.
Pumpkins are underrated, you know. Soup, pie, lanterns. Once, even a carriage, or so the story goes.
Every year, on the night of the ball, I feel restless. Like the clock is still counting somewhere.
I have a small ritual for it. A candle inside a pumpkin, glowing on the doorstep until morning.
It reminds me the magic was real, but so was the ride home in the dark.
This year my garden gave me nothing. Not one pumpkin. The night of the ball is almost here.
Could you bring me a few pumpkins? Six would fill the doorstep. It's a small thing, but it's mine.
I keep the kettle on all day. A warm drink costs nothing and buys a lot of friendship.
Midnight still makes me jumpy. When the bell tolls twelve I check my shoes. Silly habit.
You have kind hands. Callused. People who work never look down on people who sweep.
When I was young, I slept by my stepmother's hearth, in the ashes. It was the only warm spot they left me.
My stepsisters called me Cinder-girl. I let the name stick. Ashes wash off; spite doesn't.
There was a ball once. A borrowed carriage, borrowed silk, and a clock that ran out much too fast.
I lost a glass slipper on the palace stairs. It fit one foot in the whole kingdom: mine.
The palace came after that. Everyone thinks that's the happy part. It wasn't, quite.
Look how they glow! Not a carriage, but they'll do. Honestly, they're friendlier than the carriage was.
The neighbours' children came to stare at the lanterns. One asked if they turn into anything at midnight. I said only soup.
Some nights I wonder if I was ungrateful. The fairy godmother gave me everything, and I walked away from it.
Then I remember: she gave me one night, and I chose what to do with the rest.
There's one thing I still envy from my childhood. In the old house, only my stepsisters had windows.
I slept where light never reached. Even now, I can't bear a dark room at noon.
I want this home full of light. Would you bring me glass? Sixteen panes, and I'll never sweep in the dark again.
I promised you the truth about the palace. It was cold. Enormous rooms, and nobody ever swept them.
Well, servants swept. But no one who lived there ever held a broom. They didn't know what a floor feels like.
The prince was kind, in his way. He loved the girl on the stairs. He never met the one from the ashes.
I tried for a while. Silk every day, smiles every hour. My feet ached more than they ever did from work.
One morning I found myself sweeping the throne room at dawn, just to feel like myself. A lady screamed.
That was the day I understood. I'd rather keep an honest hearth than a golden one.
So I left. Quietly, with the slipper in my apron. No carriage, no bell, just a long walk.
People here think I'm a simple innkeeper. That suits me. Simple is a luxury, believe me.
Sunlight on the floor I used to sweep in the dark. I sat and watched it move for an hour. Thank you.
The dust dances in the light now. Before, I only knew it by touch.
I've drafted a letter of peace. Nine times. The ninth is short: 'Come eat with me. I've forgiven more than you think.'
I can't carry it. My feet would turn around halfway, I know them too well.
They live in the next village over. It isn't far. It's only far for me.
You've got steady feet and no grudge in them. They'd open the door to you.
Would you carry my letter to the next village? And if they ask about me, tell them the hearth is clean.
Can I tell you something heavier? My stepsisters wrote to me last winter.
I didn't answer. The letter is still in the drawer, under the slipper. I read it more often than I admit.
They weren't monsters. They were young, and frightened of their mother, and they took it out on me.
One of them used to leave a crust of bread by the hearth when no one watched. I'd forgotten that until the letter.
