My fear is simple: if I open the door to them, I'll be twelve years old again, sitting in the ashes.
But my dream is simpler still. A table, a supper, and three women who share a past laughing about it.
The tales from over the sea tell my story ending at the wedding. They never say what happened to the sisters.
I want to write that part myself. Not a punishment. A supper.
They answered. They're coming for supper! I've swept the floor three times, and it was already clean.
You kept the slippers I gave you, I hope. They never shatter, I promise. Better than glass.
You carried the heaviest letter I ever wrote. I don't think you know how heavy it was.
If you ever have a door you're afraid to open, bring it here. I'll put the kettle on, and we'll think.
Life goes on, sweep by sweep. That was always the magic, really. Not the carriage.
The pumpkins in the garden are growing fat again. Next year, you're coming to supper too. No excuses.
Off you go, before the clock strikes something. And come back while the hearth is warm; it always is.
The supper went well. Awkward for one course, then my eldest stepsister spilled the soup and we all laughed.
She apologised for the soup. Then she apologised for everything else. We cried into the bread.
The younger one admitted to the crusts by the hearth. I told her those crusts kept me alive. She didn't believe me.
Now they come every year, on the night of the ball. We light the pumpkins together.
Midnight doesn't frighten me anymore. At twelve, we're usually arguing about dessert.
The children still ask if the lanterns turn into anything. I say yes: into breakfast.
The windows you brought me catch the dawn first. I wake with the sun on my face, like a lady in a tower. Without the tower.
I kept the glass slipper on the mantel. Sometimes I put a flower in it. It makes a very narrow vase.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cinder_hearth.e: Now the pumpkins glow on the doorstep every year, and the stepsisters come for supper on the night of the ball.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cinder_hearth.s: Histoires ou contes du temps passé — Charles Perrault (1697)
Every year, on the night of the ball, I put a candle inside a pumpkin. Bring me a few pumpkins?
Look how they glow. Not a carriage, but they'll do.
In the old house, only my stepsisters had a window. I want my home full of light. Bring me glass.
Sunlight on the floor I used to sweep in the dark. Thank you.
They were cruel, and they were young. I've written them a letter of peace. Carry it to the next village?
They answered: they're coming for supper. Take these slippers; they never shatter, I promise.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cinder_hearth.t: Pumpkins are underrated. Trust me on that.
Sweep first, complain later. That's how I got through my youth.
Midnight still makes me nervous. Silly, after all these years.
My stepsisters wrote. They want to visit. I think... I'll let them.
hearthbound.persona.tale_cloth_nobody_sa: Long ago a partner and I sold an emperor a suit of invisible cloth: 'only fools can't see it'. The whole court praised it. Then a child shouted the truth.
We ran off with the gold, laughing. Years later I realized that child was braver than every one of us. Now I sell only cloth you can touch.
Feel this wool. Real. You can see it, yes? Good. You'd be surprised how rare that answer used to be.
Anyone who says only fools can't see it is selling something. Usually to someone with a crown.
His old minister came to check. He saw nothing, of course. But he didn't dare say so. He praised the colours.
Every courtier did the same. Beautiful, magnificent, such a pattern! I learned then how much people fear looking foolish.
Now I weave for the winter market, and I want cloth so honest it's thick enough to see from across the square.
Plain, warm, heavy. The kind nobody has to pretend about. My hands want to make amends.
Bring me wool. Plenty of it. I'll weave something anyone can see, even a fool. Especially a fool.
I weigh every bolt in front of the customer. No tricks. Old habits of an honest trade. New habits, really.
You look at things before you praise them. I noticed. It's a rare and dangerous skill.
Children tell the truth. That's why kings are afraid of them. Merchants too, if they're smart.
I keep an empty loom in the back room. To remember. No, I won't say what yet.
Long ago I had a partner. Quick hands, quicker tongue. We travelled from court to court with a very special trade.
We heard of an emperor who cared for nothing but clothes. He changed coats every hour. We smelled gold.
We told him we wove cloth so fine it was invisible to anyone unfit for his post, or simply a fool.
He gave us silk and gold thread. We put it all in our packs and worked the empty looms deep into the night.
You can see it, touch it, and wear it. Revolutionary, I know. The first bolt sold before noon.
A farmer bought a length and said, 'It's just cloth.' I nearly hugged him.
My partner spent his share on dice. I kept mine in a chest, and it grew heavier every year, though nothing was added.
That's what the empty loom is for. It's the one we used. I keep it so I never forget what nothing costs.
The emperor's gold still weighs on me. I've decided to send it back to the palace, with interest.
I can return my own share, but the interest needs more. Twenty years of interest, by my conscience's reckoning.
Bring me gold. I'll pack it with a letter of apology. The whole truth, this time.
Now the rest. We 'dressed' the emperor for a great procession. We tied invisible trains and smoothed invisible sleeves.
He turned before the mirror, admiring nothing. I kept a straight face. It was the hardest work I've ever done.
He walked out under a canopy, and the whole city cheered. Nobody wanted to be the fool.
Then a little child, perched on a father's shoulders, shouted: 'But he hasn't got anything on!'
The whisper spread through the crowd like wind through wheat. Then everyone was shouting it.
The emperor shivered. He knew they were right. And still he held his head high and walked on to the end.
We were already gone by then, out the back gate with our packs full of gold. We laughed all the way to the border.
Years later, I realized that child was braver than every one of us. Braver than the court, the emperor, and me.
Packed and sent. The empty loom looks a little less empty. I slept all night for the first time in years.
I wrote everything in that letter. My name, my partner's, how we did it. Whatever comes, comes.
They're a carpenter, I hear. Honest work. Hands that make real things. I'm not surprised.
I've written them a thank-you. It took me a week. Every draft sounded like a sales pitch. I burned those.
My dream is to know they aren't afraid anymore. That shouting the truth didn't cost them anything.
I can't bring it myself. I'm a coward about this one thing. The letter says so, honestly.
Will you carry it for me? The next village. Tell them a weaver who used to sell nothing sends something real.
Here's what I've never told anyone: I was proud of that trick for years. I told it at inns and people laughed.
Then one night a child at an inn asked, 'Why didn't anyone just say it?' And I didn't laugh anymore.
Because we made them afraid. That's the answer. We sold fear, dressed up as cloth.
I wonder about the courtiers sometimes. The old minister who didn't dare. Did he ever forgive himself?
I wonder about the emperor. He walked to the end of the procession, naked, dignified. That's a kind of courage too.
My fear is simple: that I'm still that trickster underneath, and this honest stall is just a better costume.
When I catch myself praising a customer's ugly hat, I stop and say: 'That hat is terrible.' They're usually relieved.
The child who shouted is grown now. I found out where they live. The next village over, of all places.
They laughed and said they'd shout again if needed. Take this coat. It's very, very visible.
Bright red, thick as a wall. Nobody could ever pretend it isn't there. Wear it proudly.
My old partner wrote to me from a debtor's prison. I sent him wool and a spindle. Honest work passes the time.
If anyone ever tells you only fools can't see something, bring them to me. I'll show them my coat. Then my drawing.
You carried the letter I was too scared to carry. That counts for more than all the gold I sent back.
Truth is plain cloth. It doesn't shimmer. But it keeps you warm longer than anything else I've ever sold.
Come by the stall whenever you like. I'll tell you honestly how you look. You look good, by the way. That's true.
They sent back a drawing they made as a child, the day after the procession: a naked emperor, very rudely drawn.
It hangs above my stall now. Customers ask about it. I tell them the whole story. Every time.
The palace wrote back. The old emperor is gone, but his grandson said: 'Grandfather always knew. Thank you anyway.'
My stall sells the thickest, plainest, most honest cloth in the land. The motto is painted on the sign: 'You can see it.'
I sold the empty loom for firewood. No, I lie. I tried. I couldn't. It's in the back, with a bolt of wool on it.
See? I'm learning. I corrected myself. You'd have caught me anyway.
Children come to my stall to shout 'He's got nothing on!' at the drawing. I give them a ribbon for bravery.
Remember the farmer who said, 'It's just cloth'? He comes every autumn now. Best customer I have.
Now the weaver's stall sells the thickest, plainest, most honest cloth in the land, and a child's drawing of a naked emperor hangs above it.
Fairy Tales Told for Children — Hans Christian Andersen (1837)
I'm weaving honest cloth for the winter market, thick enough to see from across the square. Bring me wool.
You can see it, touch it, and wear it. Revolutionary, I know.
Real cloth
The emperor's gold still weighs on me. I'll send it back to the palace, with interest. Bring me gold.
Packed and sent. The empty loom looks a little less empty.
Paying it back
The child who shouted is grown now and lives in the next village. I've written a thank-you. Carry it for me?
They laughed and said they'd shout again if needed. Take this coat. It's very, very visible.
A letter to the child
Feel this wool. Real. You can see it, yes? Good.
Anyone who says only fools can't see it is selling something.
I keep an empty loom in the back room. To remember.
Children tell the truth. That's why kings are afraid of them.
Cloth nobody could see
hearthbound.persona.tale_four_old_musici: My master said I was too old to be useful. So I set off to become a musician, with an old dog, a tired cat and a rooster who wouldn't stop singing.
We never reached the city. We scared robbers out of a cottage with the worst concert ever heard, and stayed. Useless together beat useful alone.
Ah, a new face! Sit, sit. Mind the rooster, he thinks every chair is a stage.
Never too old to start a band. Too old to finish one, maybe. We never finished ours.
The dog's grandchildren and the rooster's line live with me still. The cat's granddaughter too, when she feels like it.
Every so often we play. Badly. Gloriously. The neighbours bring earplugs and cheer anyway.
But the old instruments are gone. Traded, broken, eaten by the rooster in one case. Don't ask.
The band's getting back together. Well, what's left of us, and their grandchildren. We need something to play.
Bring me some note blocks to rehearse? Four will do. One for each of us, and one very loud one for the rooster.
The rooster's great-grandson wakes me every morning. Family tradition. Loud family.
Robbers fear noise more than swords. Ask any old donkey. Ask me, actually.
I have a voice like a gate that needs oiling. I've been told so by experts. I sing anyway.
Fifty years ago I carried sacks for a miller. Carried them for twenty years. My back still remembers.
One day he looked at me and said I was too old to be useful. He called me his old donkey, and not kindly.
So I packed a bag and set off for the big city, to become a musician. At my age! Imagine it.
On the road I met an old hound too slow to hunt, a tired cat whose mistress wanted her gone, and a rooster due in the soup.
Four useless creatures. We decided to be useless together. It sounded better than being useless alone.
Dreadful. Perfect. Just like the old days. The windows rattled and the baker's dog howled along.
The rooster stood on the top note block and would not come down. He's a born soloist.
We stayed in that cottage for years. We never did become musicians. That was never the point.
Useless together beat useful alone. That's the whole lesson. The tales from over the hills tell it grander, but that's it.
Now there's trouble. Robbers are camping near the road again. Crossbows, grey coats, the lot.
They're not the frightened sort, like ours were. Our singing won't do it twice, I'm afraid. My voice is too tired.
Will you chase them off for us? Six of them, at least. We'll play you a victory march. You've been warned.
Now let me tell you how we got here. We never reached the city, you know. We only made it to the woods.
Night fell. We were cold and starving. The rooster flew up a tree and saw a light in a cottage.
We crept up and peered in the window. Robbers! Feasting on roast and wine, with piles of stolen gold.
We made a plan. I stood at the window, the dog on my back, the cat on the dog, the rooster on the cat.
Then we sang. All four of us, at once, at the top of our lungs. The worst concert ever heard.
We crashed through the window in the middle of it. The robbers ran screaming. They thought it was a monster.
We ate their supper and slept in their beds. One robber crept back in the dark, and got a very nasty surprise.
Scratched by the cat, bitten by the dog, kicked by me, crowed at by the rooster. He never came back.
They ran, and nobody even had to sing. A bit disappointing, honestly. I'd been practising.
The rooster crowed at their backs anyway. He likes to have the last word. He always does.
We'll play our loudest, worst song. The children will cover their ears and laugh. The robbers will hear it for miles.
And there'll be cake. There must be cake. My old dog loved cake more than anything in this world.
The dog's grandchildren will eat most of it, I expect. That's the tradition. Crumbs for the rooster.
I've never been good at big feasts, and baking is beyond my hooves... I mean, my hands. Ha. Old joke.
Bring me a cake for the anniversary? Just one. A big one. We deserve it, after fifty years of noise.
Can I tell you something that's not a joke? It's rare for me, so listen closely.
When the miller called me useless, I believed him. For a whole night, I believed I'd be better off dead.
Then I walked out, and every useless creature I met made me feel a little less useless.
The dog, the cat, the rooster: they're gone now, of course. Fifty years is a long time for animals. I buried each one under the apple tree.
I'm the only one of the four still standing. My fear is simple: that when I go, the band goes too.
No more concerts, no more terrible songs. Just a quiet road that robbers might come back to.
But the grandchildren of my old friends are here. The dog's, the rooster's, the cat's. They sing just as badly.
My dream is a great anniversary. Fifty years since that terrible concert. Everyone in the village invited.
Crumbs everywhere and a very happy rooster. He stood on the cake. We ate around the footprints.
Wear that cap with pride. It has a crest. You've earned the band's colours, whether you can sing or not.
The miller's grandson came to a concert last week. I didn't hold it against him. He clapped.
Too old to be useful, they said. I've been gloriously useless for fifty years. Best decision of my life.
If anyone ever tells you you're past your use, you come find us. We'll find you an instrument.
Life goes on, one wrong note at a time. And the rooster still has the last word.
Go on, then. Market day's tomorrow. Bring earplugs, or don't. We'll be playing either way.
The anniversary concert was the worst yet. Somebody's grandmother fainted. She says she enjoyed it.
Now we play every market day, badly and loudly. The vendors charge more when we're not there.
The robbers keep well away from this road. I like to think it's you. I also like to think it's our music.
The dog's grandson has learned to howl on key. Well, near a key. In the neighbourhood of a key.
The cat's granddaughter sits on the note block and refuses to move. She's the band's critic.
I visit the apple tree after every concert and tell the old ones how it went. I exaggerate. They'd want me to.
I don't fear the end of the band anymore. The band isn't me. It's whoever's loud enough to join.
You'd make a fine member, you know. Terrible voice? Perfect. Brave? Even better. You're on the tambourine.
Now four old friends play every market day, badly and loudly, and the robbers keep well away from this road.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1819)
The band is getting back together. Well, what's left of us. Bring me some note blocks to rehearse.
Dreadful. Perfect. Just like the old days.
Instruments for the band
Robbers are camping near the road again, like the ones we chased off. Our singing won't do it twice. Will you?
They ran, and nobody even had to sing. A bit disappointing, honestly.
Robbers at the cottage
Fifty years since that concert. We deserve a cake. The dog's grandchildren will eat most of it.
Crumbs everywhere and a very happy rooster. Take this cap, it has a crest. You've earned the band's colours.
The band's anniversary
Never too old to start a band. Too old to finish one, maybe.
The rooster's great-grandson wakes me every morning. Family tradition.
Robbers fear noise more than swords. Ask any old donkey.
We sang terribly. We still do. That was never the point.
Four old musicians
hearthbound.persona.tale_hundred_years_a: A fairy nobody invited cursed my christening: a spindle, a prick, and a sleep of a hundred years. It came true, to the day.
I woke to a world where everyone I'd known was dust. The thorns were never the curse. Waking up late to everything was.
Hello, hello. What year is it? Just checking. Habit. Don't mind me.
I don't spin. I don't even own a needle. My neighbours mend my socks, and I bake them bread in return.
I'd never seen a spindle. I asked to try. One prick. That's all it takes, you know. One small moment.
I don't remember falling. I remember the sunlight on the stone floor. Then, nothing, for a hundred years.
When I woke, I asked the time. Nobody knew what I meant; they measured it differently. I'd lost a whole century.
Now I'm afraid of losing even an hour. I count the bells in the village. I count my breaths some nights.
Would you bring me a clock? One is enough. I lost a hundred years without noticing. Never again.
The new songs are so fast. I like them anyway. I just need to hear each one three times.
Invite everyone to your feasts. Everyone. Trust me on this. Leaving one person out can cost a century.
I nap badly. Isn't that funny? Of all people, I'm the one who can't sleep past dawn.
I was born in a castle, long before your grandparents' grandparents. My christening was a grand affair.
Seven fairies were invited to bless me. One old fairy wasn't. Nobody could find her address, they said.
She came anyway. She stood in the doorway in her dusty cloak and cursed me before anyone could stop her.
A spindle, a prick of the finger, and death. The last fairy softened it: not death. A sleep of a hundred years.
My father burned every spindle in the kingdom. It didn't help. At fifteen I found an old woman spinning in a tower.
Tick, tick. Every second mine. What a sound. I sat and listened to it for an entire afternoon, on purpose.
I've put it by the door, where I'll see it every time I leave. No more losing track.
I stayed at the castle for a while. Then I came here, where nobody knew the story. I wanted to be just a neighbour.
And now, a small thing that sits with me. Around the castle grew thorns, a hundred years of them, high as towers.
They kept everyone out. They kept me in. They never gave anything, only took.
I want thorns that give something back. Prickly on the outside, sweet inside. Like most good people.
Bring me berry bushes? Sixteen. I'll plant a hedge of sweet berries round my garden. Thorns that feed.
You've been patient with me. Let me tell you what waking up was really like. It's not like the songs.
The songs say a prince came through the thorns and I opened my eyes and smiled. Well, a prince did come.
But when I sat up, my first question was about my mother. He didn't know who she was. Nobody did.
Everyone I'd known was dust. My parents, my nurse, the boy who fed the horses. My little dog.
The whole castle had slept with me, you see. The cooks, the guards. But the world outside hadn't.
We walked out into a century that didn't know us. Our clothes were old-fashioned. Our words were strange.
People laughed at my sleeves. My sleeves! I'd been so proud of those sleeves.
The thorns were never the curse. Waking up late to everything was. A feast where the guests have all gone home.
Prickly, sweet and useful. The thorns and I have made peace. The children pick them and come back purple.
I eat a handful every morning. It feels like forgiving something. I'm not sure what.
I want to invite the next village too. Everyone. The baker, the widow, the lads who throw stones at crows.
Even the grumpy ones. Especially the grumpy ones. The old woman at the edge of that village, the one nobody likes.
I've written the invitation myself, on good paper. It says: 'Come as you are. There is room.'
I can't carry it; I'd stop at every door and talk until nightfall. You know I would.
Carry the invitation to the next village? Make sure it reaches everyone. Every single door.
Can I tell you something deep? When I sleep at night, I'm afraid I won't wake up. Or worse, that I'll wake too late.
I dream of opening my eyes and finding you gone. And the village gone. And the clock stopped.
I think that's why I talk to everyone so much. I'm storing up faces, in case I lose them again.
And here's the other thing. I'm not even angry at the old fairy anymore. I understand her.
She was the one nobody invited. She stood outside the door and heard the laughing. That's a lonely place.
The old tales from across the sea say she was wicked. I think she was forgotten, and it curdled.
My fear is that someone here is being forgotten right now, and I'm too busy counting seconds to notice.
My dream is a feast. A huge one. With so many chairs that nobody could ever be left outside.
They're all coming, even the old woman nobody likes. Good. Here, you had cake; I hope you had seconds.
She came, you know. She sat in the corner all evening and said nothing. Then she danced. With the baker!
If you ever feel like the uninvited one, anywhere, come here. There's a chair. There's always a chair.
I spun a thread last week. Just to see. No prick, no sleep. Only thread. I laughed at myself for an hour.
I don't think I'm late to everything anymore. I think I arrived exactly when I was meant to. Here. With you.
Life goes on, tick by tick. I'm not counting the seconds anymore. I'm just enjoying them.
Off you go. Don't sleep in. And come to the next feast; your chair's already set.
She stayed until the last candle. On the way out she took my hand and said, 'Thank you for thinking of me.'
I cried in the kitchen afterwards. A hundred years, and that was the thing I'd been missing.
Now every feast in the village has room for one more guest. We set an empty chair, on purpose. Just in case.
The old clock by the door is never allowed to stop. The children take turns winding it. They love the key.
I sleep better now. Not perfectly. But when I wake up, the clock is ticking and the berries need picking.
The new songs are still fast. I've learned one by heart. I sing it badly at every feast. People clap anyway.
Someone asked me yesterday what year it was. I knew right away. I felt so smug.
You carried my invitation to every door. You made sure nobody was left outside. That undoes something, for me.
Now every feast in the village has room for one more guest, and the old clock by the door is never allowed to stop.
Histoires ou contes du temps passé — Charles Perrault (1697)
I lost a hundred years without noticing. Bring me a clock; I'll never lose track of time again.
Tick, tick. Every second mine. What a sound.
A clock to count the days
Thorns grew around my castle for a century. I want thorns that give something back. Bring me berry bushes.
Prickly, sweet and useful. The thorns and I have made peace.
Thorns that feed
I'm throwing a feast, and I'm inviting the next village too. Everyone, even the grumpy ones. Carry the invitation?
They're all coming, even the old woman nobody likes. Good. Here, have some cake before it's gone.
An invitation for everyone
What year is it? Just checking. Habit.
I don't spin. I don't even own a needle.
The new songs are so fast. I like them anyway.
Invite everyone to your feasts. Everyone. Trust me on this.
A hundred years of sleep
One New Year's Eve I sold matches barefoot in the snow and sold none. I struck them one by one to keep warm, and saw feasts and my grandmother in the flames.
Before the last match went out, a baker opened her door. The tale says I froze. I didn't. I've kept a warm door open every winter since.
hearthbound.persona.tale_last_match.dial: Cold feet? Come in. There's soup. There's always soup. That's the one rule of this house.
Take your boots off by the stove. No, I insist. Warm feet change the whole mood of a person.
That night I struck a match to warm my fingers. In the flame I saw a great iron stove with brass feet. Then it was gone.
My door is open to anyone cold, every winter. Beggars, travellers, children who don't want to go home.
Last winter a whole family slept on my floor for a week. The stove never went out. That's the important thing.
Winter's coming again, and my coal box is nearly empty. A stove with no coal is just a cold iron box.
Bring me coal, will you? Enough that the stove never goes out, not for one hour, all winter long.
I still count matches. Old habit. Forty-two in this box. I'll count them again tonight.
You have a way of standing in doorways as if you're not sure you're welcome. You are. Always.
My grandmother is in every candle flame. I'm quite sure of it. She flickers when she approves.
When I was small I sold matches in the street. Bundles of them in an old apron, and more in my hand.
That winter was the coldest anyone remembered. I'd lost my slippers crossing the road; a boy ran off with one.
I didn't dare go home. My father would beat me for not selling a single match. So I sat in a corner between two houses.
Every window glowed. I could smell roast goose from somewhere. It was New Year's Eve.
Every New Year's Eve I leave the lamp lit until dawn. I've never missed one. Not once.
Warm as a baker's kitchen. That's the idea. Sit, sit. You brought the warmth; you get the best chair.
The coal box is full to the lid. I keep opening it just to look. Silly, I know.
The tale says that's where it ends. They found a frozen child in the morning, holding burnt matches.
That's not how it ended. I'll tell you the rest soon. It's a bit much for one evening.
For now: on New Year's Eve I put a candle in every window of this house. Every single one.
So that no child out there, sitting in the cold, thinks nobody's home. So they see a light that isn't just a match.
Bring me candles. As many as I have windows. And a few extra, for the ones who come knocking.
Now I'll tell you about the other matches. The second one lit up the wall, and I could see right through it.
Inside was a table with white cloth and a roast goose, stuffed with apples and prunes. It waddled toward me with a fork in its back.
Then the match died, and there was only the cold wall again. I struck another. Quickly.
The third showed me a Christmas tree, taller than any I'd seen through rich people's windows. Its candles rose into the sky.
They became stars. One fell, leaving a long line of fire. Grandmother used to say a falling star means a soul going up.
And then, in the fourth match, she was there. My grandmother. The only person who was ever kind to me.
I cried out: take me with you! I knew she'd vanish like the stove and the goose. So I struck the whole bundle at once.
The light was brighter than day. She had never looked so tall and beautiful. She lifted me up in her arms.
Every window lit. From the street it looks like a feast. It will be. Stand outside with me a moment and look.
A little boy stopped in the snow last night and just stared at the windows. Then he knocked. I gave him soup.
My dream, the waking one: a table so full that the goose in the flames looks thin by comparison.
I want a real feast this New Year's Eve, for every cold child in the village. Not visions. Food.
In the flames I saw a roast bird on a white cloth. This year I want it real, on my table, steaming.
Roast chicken will do nicely. Goose is fancy, but chicken is honest, and children love a drumstick.
Bring me roast chicken, a good many of them. Let's make sure nobody is outside this New Year.
Here's the end of the story, the real one. The last match was burning down. I thought I'd follow Grandmother.
Then a door opened behind me. A baker, flour to her elbows, holding a lamp. She said: 'Child, come in, you'll die out there.'
I couldn't feel my feet. She carried me to her oven and rubbed my hands until I screamed with the pain of warming up.
She never asked why I was outside. She never sent me home. I stayed and swept her floor for eleven years.
The tale says I froze. I didn't. But I understand why people tell it that way. So many children did.
That's my fear, even now. That somewhere, tonight, a child is striking the last match, and no door opens.
The baker is gone now. She left me her oven and her lamp. I light it every New Year's Eve, as she did.
I still dream of the goose with the fork in its back. Ridiculous. I laugh in my sleep, I'm told.
The table is full and nobody is outside. The lantern is yours now. Never walk home in the dark.
Twenty-three children at the table. Twenty-three! I counted them like matches. I counted twice.
If you ever find yourself cold and far from home, remember: somewhere a lamp is lit for you. This one.
I've started giving every child a box of matches at New Year. Not to sell. To light a candle for someone else.
You helped me turn the worst night of my life into the best night of the year. Do you know how rare that is?
Next New Year's Eve, come early. You can carve the chicken. You've earned the knife.
The lamp is lit. The stove is hot. The door is open. Come in whenever you're cold, or just whenever.
One of them fell asleep with a drumstick in each hand. I didn't have the heart to take them away.
The children call it 'the house where the last match never goes out'. I pretend it's silly. I love it.
I kept one match from that night, the one that didn't burn. It's in a little tin box on the shelf.
Remember when you brought the coal and I kept opening the box to look? I still do. Every morning.
Grandmother flickered in the candle on New Year's Eve. Tall and bright. I'm quite sure she approved.
The little boy who stared at my windows helps me light them now. He's very serious about it.
A traveller asked why I keep the door open to strangers. I said a baker once did it for me. That's all.
My feet still get cold easily. I wear two pairs of woollen socks. Nobody will ever take my slippers again.
hearthbound.persona.tale_last_match.epil: Now a warm door stays open every New Year's Eve, and the children call it 'the house where the last match never goes out'.
hearthbound.persona.tale_last_match.sour: The Little Match Girl — Hans Christian Andersen (1845)
hearthbound.persona.tale_last_match.stag: Winter's coming, and my door is open to anyone cold. The stove must never go out. Bring me coal.
Warm as a baker's kitchen. That's the idea.
On New Year's Eve I put a candle in every window, so no child out there thinks nobody's home. Bring me candles.
Every window lit. From the street it looks like a feast. It will be.
In the flames I saw a roast bird on a table. This year I want it real, for every cold child in the village. Bring me roast chicken.
The table is full and nobody is outside. Take this lantern, and never walk home in the dark.
hearthbound.persona.tale_last_match.talk: Cold feet? Come in. There's soup.
I still count matches. Old habit.
Every New Year's Eve I leave the lamp lit until dawn.
My grandmother is in every candle flame. I'm quite sure of it.
hearthbound.persona.tale_name_for_a_debt: My father, the miller, boasted to the king that I could spin straw into gold. A little man did it for me, three nights running. His price was my firstborn.
I guessed his name in the end: a messenger heard him singing by a fire. I've always wondered whether he was cruel, or only lonely.
Good day. Careful with the sacks; that's straw, not gold. Straw is straw. Anyone who says otherwise wants something.
I never boast. Not about harvests, not about children, not about anything. You'll see why, one day.
I gave him my necklace. He sat at the wheel and spun till dawn. Whirr, whirr, and the straw turned gold.
I don't like remembering that sound. I haven't touched gold thread since, or even golden straw.
But lately I've wanted my hands busy with something honest. I weave straw now, for roofs and baskets.
No spells, no bargains. Just a stalk over a stalk, the way my grandmother taught me before all that.
Would you bring me wheat? Thirty-two sheaves. I want a pile of honest straw that stays exactly what it is.
Names have power. Tell yours only to people who'd shout it to save you. You can tell me yours later.
My child is out chasing chickens. Seven years old and already convinced the rooster is a king in disguise.
I like quiet evenings, a warm loaf, and a spinning wheel I never, ever touch.
My father was a miller. A good man with a big mouth. That mouth nearly cost me everything.
He met the king on the road and wanted to seem important. He said his daughter could spin straw into gold.
The king locked me in a room full of straw with a wheel and said: gold by morning, or your head.
I sat on the floor and cried. I can't spin gold. Nobody can. I couldn't even spin wool properly.
Then the door opened, and a little man walked in. Odd hat, odder smile. He asked what I'd give him.
Straw, and nothing but straw. It's never looked so lovely. I wove a basket last night and cried a little.
My child made a crown out of the leftovers and gave it to the rooster. It was not appreciated.
Everyone called it a victory. I've never been sure. He kept his word three times. I won with a stolen guess.
I left the palace not long after. Crowns and boasts didn't suit me. I came here, where straw is only straw.
The debt still sits on my chest. He spun gold for me three nights, and I paid him with a trick.
I want to leave gold by his old fire, in the forest clearing where he danced. Five ingots. A fair wage for three nights.
Will you bring me some gold? It's not a price. It's an apology, in the only currency he ever dealt in.
I'll tell you the rest, now. The little man came back the second night. I gave him my ring.
The third night I had nothing left. He said: promise me your firstborn child, when you're queen.
I said yes. I was young and terrified and the room smelled of straw and sweat. Yes seemed like the only door.
The king married me. I was queen for a while. Then my baby came, and so did the little man.
He wanted what I'd promised. I begged. He softened and said: guess my name in three days, and you keep the child.
I guessed every name in the kingdom. Wrong, wrong, wrong. He laughed each time, but not unkindly.
On the last night, a messenger came back from the forest. He'd seen a little man dancing around a fire, singing his own name.
The next day I said it. The little man screamed and stamped so hard he went through the floor. Then he was gone.
I left it by the ashes, where he danced. The clearing was cold and the fire long dead. I feel lighter already.
I sat there a while and told the ashes I was sorry. A crow listened. It seemed unimpressed.
Traders have mentioned a little man living alone in a village I've never seen. He weaves. He sings to himself.
They say he won't tell anyone his name. The villagers just call him the weaver.
If it's him, I want to write to him. A real letter, with his name spelled right at the top.
I'd go myself, but I don't know the way and I'm not sure I'd be brave enough to arrive.
Find it for me? A village I've never visited, with a lonely weaver. Just find it; I'll do the rest.
Here's the question that's followed me for years: was he cruel, or was he only lonely?
Think about it. What does a little man who can spin gold want with a baby? Not money. Not power.
I think he wanted a family. Someone to sing to, other than the fire. He just asked for it the wrong way.
My child asks about him. I say exactly that: he wanted a family and asked for it the wrong way.
My fear is that I made a lonely creature lonelier. That I won the story and he just went on losing it.
The tales told far away say he tore himself in two in his rage. I don't believe it. I think he walked off, humiliated.
And someone who walks off humiliated keeps walking. Somewhere, he's still alive. Still alone.
My dream is strange, I know: to find him. Not to beg. Just to say his name properly, kindly, as a friend.
A weaver, alone, humming. It's him, I'm sure of it. I wrote to him, with his name spelled right.
Keep that gold I gave you. It's clean. Nobody spun it, nobody bargained for it. Spend it on something warm.
You found the village when I couldn't. You gave me the chance to finish a story properly. That's rare.
If you ever meet someone odd and alone, remember: they might just be asking for a family the wrong way.
My father would boast about all this, if he were alive. I never will. But I'll tell you: it's gone well.
Life goes on in straw and letters and one very peculiar hat at my table. I like it.
Go on, then. And tell me your name one of these days. I promise I'd shout it to save you.
He answered! Three lines, crooked writing. 'You spelled it right. No one ever does. Thank you.'
Now a letter goes out every winter to that village. I tell him about the straw, and my child, and the rooster.
And sometimes, a small, odd guest comes for supper. He sits on a cushion. He never takes off the hat.
My child adores him. He taught them to weave a straw star in one evening. Not gold. Better.
He asked if I was still angry about the room full of straw. I said no. He said he was sorry about the baby part.
That's all it took. Two sentences, twenty years late. We sat by the fire like old neighbours.
He still won't sing his name out loud when anyone else is near. I don't blame him.
I don't spin. He doesn't spin gold anymore. We weave straw together, badly, and argue about patterns.
Now a letter goes out every winter to a lonely weaver, and a small, odd guest sometimes comes for supper.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
I weave straw now, for roofs and baskets. Honest straw, no spells. Bring me wheat.
Straw, and nothing but straw. It's never looked so lovely.
Straw, not gold
I cheated him with a guess, after he kept his word three times. I want to leave gold by his old fire. Bring me some.
Left by the ashes, where he danced. I feel lighter already.
Settling the old debt
They say a little man lives alone in a village I've never seen, weaving. Find it for me?
A weaver, alone, humming. I'll write to him, with his name spelled right. Take this gold, it's clean.
Where the little man lives
Straw is straw. Anyone who says otherwise wants something from you.
I never boast. Not about harvests, not about children, not about anything.
Names have power. Tell yours only to people who'd shout it to save you.
My child asks about the little man. I say he wanted a family and asked for it the wrong way.
A name for a debt
I was the odd one of the brood: too big, too grey, too clumsy. The farmyard pecked me until I ran off into the reeds, and winter nearly took me.
One spring I saw myself in a still pond: I'd grown into something else entirely. I don't need anyone to call me beautiful. I just need them to stop pecking the next one.
hearthbound.persona.tale_not_a_duck.dial: Every brood has one odd egg. Leave it be. It usually turns out to be the interesting one.
Swans are rude, did you know? They hiss at everyone. I like them anyway. We understand each other.
One morning I flew over the fence and ran into the marsh. The wild geese laughed at me too, but kindly, at least.
Then hunters came to the marsh. A dog stuck its nose right into my face, looked at me, and left. Too ugly to bite.
So every morning I feed the ducks at the pond, the odd ones first. The grey ones, the clumsy ones, the late hatchers.
The big bold ones push in front. I shoo them. Gently. Mostly gently.
Bring me seeds? A good sack. I want the odd ones to eat until they're round and happy.
I feed the ducks. Even the ones who pecked me. Well, their grandchildren. Grudges are heavy to carry.
You have a long neck when you're curious. Don't be offended. It's the nicest thing I notice in people.
The pond used to be my enemy. Now it's only water. Nice water, even, in the mornings.
I hatched last, from the biggest egg. My mother sat on it so long the neighbours told her to give up.
When I came out, everyone went quiet. Too big, too grey, too clumsy. 'That one's a turkey chick,' an old duck said.
My mother defended me at first. She said I swam better than any of them. It was true. It didn't help.
The hens pecked me, the ducks bit my neck, the girl who fed us kicked me out of the way. Every day, a little more.
Even my brothers and sisters said they hoped the cat would get me. Children can say terrible things. So can ducks.
The grey one ate first today. That's how it should be. The big white drake sulked. Good for him.
I saw a little girl throw seeds to the grey one on purpose. I had to sit down for a moment.
Now foundlings and odd ones turn up at my door every winter, like I once did. Scrawny, grey, scared.
A fox cub with a bad leg. A lamb the flock left behind. Once a child who'd run away from teasing.
The child stayed three days. I made up a bed in the kitchen. She didn't speak until the second night.
This winter they're already coming, and my nests are thin. Straw isn't enough when the wind blows through.
Bring me wool for warm nests. Nobody should freeze in the reeds like I nearly did.
Now I'll tell you about the winter. After the marsh, I wandered until the snow came, and hid in a poor woman's hut.
She had a cat that arched its back and a hen that laid eggs. They asked if I could do either. I couldn't.
'Then keep your opinions to yourself,' they told me. I missed the water so much I left, into the cold.
That autumn I saw great white birds fly south. I cried out to them, a strange sound. I didn't know why.
Winter came hard. The pond froze around me. I kicked all night to keep a little hole open, until I couldn't.
A farmer found me frozen in the ice and carried me home. His children wanted to play. I panicked and spilled the milk.
I flew into the butter tub, then the flour barrel. The woman chased me with the fire tongs. I don't blame her.
I spent the rest of that winter alone in the reeds. I won't tell you all of it. Some winters are just long.
Warm, all of them. Nobody freezes in the reeds this year. The fox cub sleeps in the wool like a king.
The lamb follows me everywhere now. The ducks are jealous. That's a new feeling for them.
Some odd ones stay odd forever. They still deserve warmth and seeds. Especially them.
My dream is that at festivals, the odd ones stand out on purpose. Not hiding. Shining.
I'm making a feather cloak for them to wear. White, grey, speckled, all mixed. Every kind of bird in one.
Whoever feels like the odd egg that day gets to wear it. Nobody pecks at a cloak like that.
Bring me feathers. As many as you can. I'll sew them in myself, every one.
Now the part everyone knows. Spring came. I spread my wings and they were strong. I flew into a great garden.
Three white swans were on the canal. I swam to them, head down, expecting them to kill me. Better them than the hens.
Then I saw myself in the still water. Not a grey clumsy thing. A swan. I'd been one the whole time.
The children on the bank shouted: 'There's a new one! The new one is the most beautiful!' I hid my head under my wing.
I didn't feel proud. I felt shy, and very tired, and so glad. A good heart never gets proud, my mother said once.
But here's my secret: I don't need anyone to call me beautiful. I needed them to stop pecking. That's all.
Being a swan didn't make me good. It just made them stop. The next odd one still gets pecked.
That's what frightens me. There's always a next one. And they won't all turn out to be swans.
White and grey and speckled, all together. Take those eggs I gave you; who knows what will hatch.
At the spring festival, the child from the kitchen wore the cloak. She danced in it. Everyone clapped.
The wild geese flew over last autumn and honked at me. I honked back. Old friends, in a rude way.
I still look at my reflection sometimes, just to check. Still a swan. Still surprised.
Thank you for helping me turn an old hurt into warm nests and bright cloaks. That's the best kind of hatching.
Every spring there'll be a new odd egg. I'll be waiting by the pond, with seeds and wool and feathers.
Come sit by the water with me some morning. The odd ones eat first. You can help me shoo the others.
Now every odd child in the village has a feather cloak for festivals. The tailor copies my stitching. Badly.
Nobody pecks at anyone by the pond anymore. Well, the ducks do. They're ducks. But the people don't.
The grey duckling from the first morning is fat and bossy now. I'm so proud I could honk.
The fox cub grew up and left. It came back once, sat at the edge of the reeds, and looked at me a long time.
Remember how the big drake sulked? He eats second now, and he's learned to wait. Mostly.
The old farmer's wife with the fire tongs came to the festival. She apologized. It was forty years late. I accepted.
When you brought me those feathers, I found a swan's among them. I sewed it right in the middle.
If someone ever pecks at you, come to the pond. I'll hiss at them. I'm a swan, it's allowed.
hearthbound.persona.tale_not_a_duck.epil: Now every odd child in the village has a feather cloak for festivals, and nobody pecks at anyone by the pond.
hearthbound.persona.tale_not_a_duck.sour: New Fairy Tales — Hans Christian Andersen (1843)
hearthbound.persona.tale_not_a_duck.stag: Every morning I feed the ducks at the pond, the odd ones first. Bring me seeds.
The grey one ate first today. That's how it should be.
Foundlings and odd ones turn up at my door every winter, like I once did. Bring me wool for warm nests.
Warm, all of them. Nobody freezes in the reeds this year.
I'm making a feather cloak for the village's odd ones to wear at festivals, so they stand out on purpose. Bring me feathers.
White and grey and speckled, all together. Take these eggs; who knows what will hatch.
hearthbound.persona.tale_not_a_duck.talk: Every brood has one odd egg. Leave it be.
Swans are rude, did you know? I like them anyway.
I feed the ducks. Even the ones who pecked me. Well, their grandchildren.
The pond used to be my enemy. Now it's only water.
Once I walked to market with a pail of milk on my head, dreaming: milk for eggs, eggs for hens, hens for a pig, a pig for a cow... I skipped for joy. The pail fell.
I cried over the spilled milk. Then I went home and milked again. Dreams are fine. Just carry them with both hands.
Don't count your chickens before... well, you know. Everyone knows. Nobody listens. I didn't.
I carry the pail with both hands now. Always. Even when it's empty. Especially when I'm happy.
By the time I reached the bend in the road, I was the richest farmer in the valley. In my head.
I got so happy I skipped. Just one little skip, right there on the stony path. You can guess the rest.
I've never told you the full story because the ending still makes me blush. We'll get there.
It's market day again soon. This time I'm not dreaming on the way. I'm carrying milk. Just milk.
Bring me milk, will you? A few buckets. I'll carry them to market with both hands and no daydreams.
You look like someone with plans. Good. Just keep an eye on your feet while you make them.
One egg, then one hen. Slowly. It works, you know. Slower than dreaming, but it works.
Morning is the best time for milking. The world's quiet and the cows don't gossip yet.
When I was young I had one pail and one old goat. Well, the neighbour's goat. I milked it for a share.
One spring morning I had a full pail, fresh and foaming, and a long road to market. I put it on my head.
And as I walked, I started to dream. With the milk money I'd buy eggs. A hundred eggs, maybe.
The eggs would hatch into chicks. The chicks would grow into hens. The hens would buy me a pig.
I'd fatten the pig on acorns and chestnuts, and sell it for a cow. And the cow would give me a calf.
Not a drop spilled. I didn't even hum. The market woman asked if I was ill. I said I was being careful.
I sold it all by noon. Then I walked home looking at the ground the whole way. Very boring. Very safe.
I never went back to that big dream, though. I was too scared. Just milk, milk, milk, for years.
Lately I've been thinking: what if I tried the dream again, but slowly? One step at a time, eyes open.
Step one of the old dream: eggs. Real ones, in a real basket. Not a hundred in my head.
I've built a little coop behind the house. It's empty. It looks hopeful and a bit silly, like me.
Bring me eggs. Sixteen, say. Let's begin the dream again, properly this time.
Now, the ending. The pail fell. The milk splashed across the stones, white and useless, running into the dust.
The eggs, the hens, the pig, the cow, the calf. All of it gone in one splash. I stood there with my hands empty.
An old shepherd was sitting on a wall nearby. He said: 'That was a very large cow you just spilled.' I wanted to vanish.
I cried over the spilled milk. Everyone says not to. I did anyway. For an hour, sitting in the dust.
Then I went home and milked again. The goat looked at me like I was mad. Maybe I was.
There's a famous verse about a milkmaid like me. The children recite it at me sometimes. I recite it back.
Here's what the verse doesn't say: the dream wasn't the problem. The skipping was. Dreams are fine.
Dreams are fine. Just carry them with both hands. That's the whole lesson. It took me a pail of milk to learn it.
Sixteen eggs. Sixteen future hens, if nobody skips. I won't. I've tied my shoes extra tight.
I sit by the coop every evening and listen. Nothing yet. Patience. That's what I named my cow, you know.
Milk, eggs, wheat, sugar: everything I ever dreamed on that road fits in one cake. Isn't that funny?
The shepherd who laughed at me is still alive, very old. I want to give him a slice. With both hands.
One cake. The whole dream, from spilled milk to a cow called Patience, baked together.
I'll set it on the table and allow myself one skip. Only one. Indoors. Away from pails.
Bring me a cake to celebrate? Let's eat the dream at last, one slice at a time.
Yes, I have a cow now. That's the secret nobody expects. The dream came true after all, just very slowly.
It took me twenty years of milk, eggs and hens. No skipping. Every step on the ground.
When I finally led her home, I didn't skip. I walked beside her. I cried again. The good kind, this time.
I named her Patience because that's what she cost. And because she is. She never hurries anywhere.
Here's my fear, though: that I've become too careful. That I've forgotten how to be happy out loud.
Sometimes I want to skip down the lane just for the joy of it. Then I look at my hands and they're full.
Children skip past me every day. I envy them. But I also want to shout: watch the pail!
My dream now isn't a cow. I've got the cow. It's to celebrate the whole road, all of it, just once.
The dream, one slice at a time. Take those gifts I gave you; you helped me carry it.
I skipped. Once. In the kitchen. Nothing fell. The whole village clapped. Patience mooed.
If you ever have a big dream, tell me. I'll help you count the steps. Not the chickens. The steps.
Patience likes you, by the way. She doesn't like anyone. She licked your sleeve. That's a proposal, practically.
I still carry the pail with both hands. But now one finger is free to wave at you on the road.
Thank you for helping an old dreamer try again. Some people spill once and stop. You didn't let me.
Come by for milk any morning. It's fresh, it's foaming, and it will stay exactly where it belongs.
The old shepherd ate his slice and said: 'Much better than spilled milk.' I laughed till I cried.
Now Patience grazes behind the house, and the pail goes to market every week, carried with both hands.
The hens hatched from your eggs rule the yard. One of them is very bossy. I named her Skip.
I tell the children the whole story now, with the right ending: you can dream big, if you walk carefully.
Remember when I sold all the milk and walked home staring at the ground? I look up now. Sometimes.
Patience had a calf this spring. I didn't dream about it beforehand. It just happened. What a gift.
I've started a new dream. A small one: a bench under the apple tree. I'll build it plank by plank.
The children recite the verse at me and I recite the new ending back. They like mine better.
Now a cow called Patience grazes behind the house, and the pail goes to market every week, carried with both hands.
Fables in Castilian Verse — Félix María de Samaniego (1781)
Market day, and this time I'm not dreaming on the way. Bring me milk and I'll carry it, both hands.
Not a drop spilled. I didn't even hum.
Milk to market
Step one of the old dream: eggs. Real ones, in a real basket. Bring me eggs.
Sixteen eggs. Sixteen future hens, if nobody skips. I won't.
Eggs, then hens
Milk, eggs, wheat, sugar: everything I ever dreamed on that road fits in one cake. Bring me one to celebrate.
The dream, one slice at a time. Take these; you helped me carry it.
The whole dream in one cake
Don't count your chickens before... well, you know.
I carry the pail with both hands now. Always.
One egg, then one hen. Slowly. It works, you know.
I finally have that cow. I named her Patience.
A pail of dreams
hearthbound.persona.tale_pine_wood_child: I carved a puppet from a log that talked back, and it ran off the moment it had legs. Its nose grew with every lie. I sold my coat to buy its schoolbook.
I went after it across the sea and a great fish swallowed me. It came and saved me. Now it's a real child, and I'm the one learning to let go.
Wood talks, if you listen. Mostly it says 'don't burn me'. Sometimes it says worse things.
Noses never lie. Well, they grow when you do. Let me see yours. Hm. Honest. Good.
I was so poor I sold my only coat in the snow, to buy that puppet a schoolbook. It came home without the book.
I've carved plenty of things since: spoons, stools, toys for the village children. None of them has spoken. Yet.
Pine wood carves best, soft and forgiving. But sometimes it has opinions. I listen before I cut now.
The children here want toys, and I want wood that stays quiet and stays put. Spruce is good for that.
Bring me spruce logs, will you? I'll make toys that stay exactly where you leave them.
My child is at school. Or says so. We'll check the nose later.
Mind the shavings on the floor; they're slippery. I've fallen more times than any puppet.
You hold that tool like you mean it. Most people hold a chisel like it might bite. Some do.
Years ago a neighbour gave me a log that squeaked when I cut it. I thought it was the draught. It wasn't.
I carved a head, and the eyes stared at me. I carved a mouth, and it laughed at me. I carved a nose, and it grew.
The moment it had legs, it ran out the door and down the street. The town guard arrested me, not it.
I spent a night in a cell for chasing my own puppet. That was the first of many sleepless nights.
I lived two years inside a fish with a candle. Don't ask about the smell. That's later in the story, though.
Quiet logs. Good logs. Not one has said a word, thank goodness. I tapped each one to be sure.
I made a rocking horse from the first. It rocks. It doesn't gallop off. I checked twice.
But I think if it had stayed at school, just a little, everything would've gone differently.
The village school here has one tattered book for twenty children. They share it like a loaf of bread.
I once sold my coat for one schoolbook, and it went to a puppet show. This time, I'd like it to go further.
Three books. One for each bench. So that no child has to wait their turn to learn.
Bring me books? Three good ones. I'll carve them little shelves myself.
Now, the puppet. It lied like breathing, and its nose grew so long it couldn't turn around in a room.
A cricket in my house tried to give it good advice. The puppet threw a hammer at it. Poor cricket.
It sold that schoolbook, the one I paid for with my coat, to buy a ticket for a puppet show.
The puppets in the theatre recognised it as a brother and cheered. The showman nearly burned it for firewood.
Then a fox and a cat convinced it to bury gold coins in a field, to grow a money tree. Can you believe it?
It was hanged from an oak by robbers, turned into a donkey, nearly fried like a fish. And still it didn't come home.
A fairy with blue hair looked after it. She was kinder to it than I ever managed to be. I owe her a great deal.
I don't blame it. It was made from wood that already talked back. What could I expect? Obedient oak?
Three books, three stubborn children reading. Not one has run off to the theatre yet. Give it time.
The teacher says the shelves are too pretty to use. I told her to use them anyway, or I'll carve worse ones.
Now here's my fear: it's grown, and I'm the one who can't let go. I watch the road every Sunday like a guard dog.
And there's worse. Something huge lives in the deep water past the reef, with a mouth like a cave. Fishers have seen its eye.
I know how that ends. I've been in a belly like that. I won't have anyone else's parent swallowed, or anyone's child.
My dream is small: to sit on the shore with my child and not be afraid of the water.
Please, deal with whatever lives past the reef. I'm too old to go, and too stubborn to stop worrying.
Now the part I don't tell at parties. When the puppet vanished for good, I built a little boat and went to find it.
A storm took me far out, and a great fish, bigger than any building, swallowed me and the boat in one gulp.
Inside, it was dark as a cellar. I found a sunken ship's stores in its belly, and candles. I lived on them.
Two years. I talked to myself. I carved a little face in a beam. It didn't answer, which I found comforting.
The candles ran low. I sat by the last one and thought: this is it. I'll never know if my child is alive.
Then I heard a voice at the far end of the fish's throat. Its voice. It had let itself be swallowed to find me.
It swam me out on its back while the fish slept with its mouth open. Wooden things float, you see. That saved us.
After that it worked, for me, when I was too sick to. And one morning it woke up a real child, flesh and bone.
No more monsters in the deep. Take my carving axe; my child says I'm too old to hold it, and my child doesn't lie anymore.
Every Sunday the door opens and there it is: a grown child, nose exactly the right size. I check. Every time.
My child asked why I trust you so much. I said: because you went into the deep for someone else's worries.
I carved you something small. A little puppet. It won't talk, I promise. I asked it very politely.
If your nose ever starts to itch when you're about to say something, listen to it. It knows.
Wood talks, if you listen. Children too. Even grown ones. That's the whole lesson of my life, I think.
Come by on a Sunday. You'll meet my child. We'll eat, and argue, and no one will run away.
We sat on the shore last week. Neither of us looked at the water nervously. Well, I did, once. Force of habit.
The workshop is full of puppets that never move on their own. I'm almost disappointed. Almost.
The cricket's great-great-grandchild lives behind my stove. I leave it crumbs. We're making amends.
Remember the quiet spruce logs? The children fight over the rocking horse. It still hasn't galloped off.
I wrote to the fairy with blue hair. I don't know where she lives, so I left the letter on the windowsill. It was gone next day.
The school has three books and a shelf, and the teacher wants a fourth. My child said: 'I'll buy it. You've bought enough.'
I'm learning to let go. Slowly. Like carving: take off a little at a time, or you ruin the whole thing.
Some nights I dream I'm in the fish again. Then I wake up in my bed and hear the sea from far off, harmless.
Now the workshop is full of puppets that never move on their own, and a grown child comes home every Sunday, nose exactly the right size.
The Adventures of Pinocchio — Carlo Collodi (1883)
Pine wood carves best, and sometimes it has opinions. Bring me spruce logs; I'll make toys that stay put.
Quiet logs. Good logs. Not one has said a word, thank goodness.
The talking log
I once sold my coat for one schoolbook, and it was sold for a puppet show. This time the village school gets three. Bring me books.
Three books, three stubborn children reading. Not one has run off to the theatre yet.
A schoolbook
Something huge lives in the deep water past the reef, with a mouth like a cave. I know how that ends. Please, deal with it.
No more monsters in the deep. Take my carving axe; my child says I'm too old to hold it, and my child doesn't lie anymore.
The great fish
Wood talks, if you listen. Mostly it says 'don't burn me'.
Noses never lie. Well, they grow when you do.
My child is at school. Or says so. We'll check the nose later.
I lived two years inside a fish with a candle. Don't ask about the smell.
A puppet that ran away
hearthbound.persona.tale_promise_at_the_: As a spoiled royal child I dropped a golden ball into a well. A frog brought it back, for a promise: a seat at my table, a place on my pillow. I broke my word.
The songs say a wall or a kiss broke the spell. It was simpler: I finally kept my promise. Kindness owed is still owed, even to a frog.
Good day. Watch your step by the well; the stones are slippery and the frogs are nosy.
Never promise what you don't mean. Frogs remember. So do people, but frogs hold grudges longer.
I said yes to everything. I'd have said yes to a dragon. I just wanted my ball back.
My grandchild has been begging for a golden ball of their own. They heard the story from the cook.
I've been thinking: maybe I should give them one. And teach the lesson with it, the right way round.
A golden ball, and a promise that goes with it: whatever you promise to get it back, you keep.
Bring me gold, would you? Four ingots. I'll have a ball made, and I'll tell the story properly this time.
I talk to the frogs in the pond. Some answer. Mostly with croaks. I pretend to understand.
My grandchild calls me the frog whisperer. I've told them it's not a compliment. They don't believe me.
A promise kept late is still a promise kept. Just barely. I'm living proof.
I wasn't always a simple villager. I grew up in a palace, the youngest royal child, and the most spoiled.
I had a golden ball. My favourite thing in the world. I threw it up and caught it for hours by the old well.
One day it slipped from my fingers and fell into the well. Deep, dark, gone. I cried like the world had ended.
A frog poked his head out of the water and asked what I'd give him to bring it back.
He didn't want gold or jewels. He wanted a seat at my table, a bite from my plate, a place on my pillow.
Shiny, round, and already rolling towards the well. Some things never change. I caught it just in time.
My grandchild made me swear I'd tell the rest. So I'll tell you first, to practise.
I picked him up. I said sorry. I put him on the pillow. I kept my promise, late, but I kept it.
In the morning, there was a young man there instead, cold and green around the edges, crying with relief.
We were friends for sixty years after that. My oldest friend. Better than most nobles I've met.
But before his story was mine, that old well was a frog's home. His family, his neighbours, all of them.
I want a proper pond beside the well, for the frogs. Bring me lily pads? Eight. It's a debt I've owed for too long.
The frog brought my golden ball up from the dark. I snatched it and ran. I didn't even say thank you.
That evening, at supper, there was a wet slapping on the stairs. Then a knock, and a small voice at the door.
My father, the king, asked who it was. I told him. He said: 'What you promised, you must keep.'
So the frog sat at my table. He ate from my golden plate. I couldn't eat a bite. I felt sick with disgust.
Then he asked to sleep on my pillow. I carried him up by two fingers, holding my breath the whole way.
And I broke my word. I threw him against the wall. I'm not proud of it. I was a horrid child.
The songs say that's what broke the spell. A wall, or in some versions a kiss. They're both wrong.
The frog fell, dazed. And I saw his little face. He wasn't angry. He was just sad, and not surprised.
Listen to them sing tonight. That's gratitude, in frog. My friend would have sung along. Badly.
I sat by the pond until midnight. One old frog sat on my shoe the whole time. I didn't dare move.
They shamble up the bank and into the well. The water's gone foul and green, and not the good green.
The frogs have gone silent at night. You know how bad a thing has to be to shut up a pond full of frogs?
My grandchild wanted to drop the golden ball down the well to check. I said absolutely not. I'm learning.
I'm too old to fight river creatures. I can barely fight the stairs.
Clear them out for me? Six of those drowned things, at least. For the frogs. For him.
Here's what I've never told anyone. My green friend died three winters ago. Old and happy, by the fire.
He asked to be buried by the well. I said yes, of course. That was one promise I kept on time.
Some mornings I still set a second cup of tea. Then I remember, and I pour it into the pond.
My fear is that everyone will forget him. That the story will become just a frog and a wall and a kiss.
The old tales, the ones the brothers wrote down, even say his loyal servant had iron bands around his heart. Imagine that grief.
I understand it now. My heart has a band around it too. It creaks when I pass the well.
My dream is simple. I want the well to be what it was for him: a clean, cool home. Not a grave. A home.
But something's wrong. Something dead and wet has started climbing out of the river at night.
The water runs clear again. I drank a cup from the well this morning. It tasted like being young.
Keep that rod, and use it well. My green friend would want you well fed. He was fond of a good fish.
If anyone ever offers you something shiny in exchange for a promise, think about the frog first.
And if you ever break one, go back. Say sorry. Keep it late. Late is still better than never.
The old frog still sits on my shoe. I've named him after my friend. He doesn't seem to mind.
Life goes on by the well, green and croaking and clear. Just as it should.
Off you go. And mind the stones by the well. The frogs are watching, and they remember everything.
Now there's a pond full of frogs beside the old well. At dusk it sounds like a choir with no conductor.
My grandchild dropped the golden ball in the pond last week. A frog nudged it back. They made a promise on the spot.
I asked what they'd promised. They said: 'To visit every day and say thank you.' They've kept it so far.
Nobody in the village makes a promise lightly now. The children spit and shake like it's sacred. It is.
I planted rushes by his grave. The frogs sit on it and sing. I think he'd laugh at that. He had a good laugh.
I stopped setting the second teacup. Now I pour a little into the well each morning instead. It seems right.
The band around my heart creaks less. Sometimes, by the pond, I forget it's there at all.
You kept every promise you made me. I noticed. Old royals notice these things.
Now there is a pond full of frogs beside the old well, and nobody in the village makes a promise lightly.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
My grandchild wants a golden ball like the one I had. Bring me gold and I'll have one made. And I'll teach the lesson with it.
Shiny, round, and already rolling towards the well. Some things never change.
The golden ball
The old well was a frog's home before it was my story. I want a proper pond beside it. Bring me lily pads.
Listen to them sing tonight. That's gratitude, in frog.
A pond for the frogs
Something dead and wet climbs out of the river at night and fouls the well water. Clear them out.
The water runs clear again. Take this rod; my green friend would want you well fed.
Something in the well
Never promise what you don't mean. Frogs remember.
I talk to the frogs in the pond. Some answer. Mostly with croaks.
My oldest friend was green, cold and loyal. Better than most nobles.
A promise kept late is still a promise kept. Just barely.
A promise at the well
hearthbound.persona.tale_race_i_lost.bio: I was the fastest runner in the valley, and I lost a race to the slowest creature alive. I was so far ahead that I took a nap.
I've never napped since. Now my knees are bad and I'm slow myself, and that old tortoise, still alive, waits for me at every corner.
hearthbound.persona.tale_race_i_lost.dia: Don't nap before the finish line. Any finish line. Supper, a letter, a harvest. Finish first, then nap.
The tortoise is still alive. Of course it is. It'll outlive the church bell.
We race every spring now. I still lose. On purpose? Who knows. The tortoise certainly doesn't say.
I ran on carrots in my racing days. Raw, straight from the ground, soil and all. Nothing tasted better.
My knees don't run anymore, but my stomach remembers every one of those carrots.
Some evenings I sit on the porch and imagine I'm still that blur of dust. Then I get up, slowly, and the dream breaks.
Bring me some carrots, for old times? A good bunch. Let me taste the days when I was unbeatable.
You walk briskly. I like that. But watch those ankles; mine were the pride of the valley once.
Fast was fun. Steady is better. Don't tell anyone I said that.
These knees creak like a barn door now. I hear them before I see the hill.
In my youth nobody in the whole valley could catch me. Not dogs, not horses, not the wind off the mountain.
I'd race anyone for a carrot. I'd run to the next village and back before the kettle boiled.
And I boasted. Oh, I boasted. At the fair, at the well, to the geese. Everyone was tired of hearing it.
One day the tortoise said, in that slow voice: 'I'll race you.' The whole valley laughed. I laughed loudest.
We set the course: from the old oak to the mill. The fox was the judge. That should have warned me.
Crunchy. For a moment I was twenty and unbeatable. Then I sat down. Knees, you know.
I ate three raw and made soup with the rest. The tortoise came by and sniffed at it. Didn't ask for any. Proud creature.
That's the secret, you see. I can't sleep anymore. I lie awake every night, afraid of being caught napping.
And those flying things come for people who don't sleep. Pale, with wings like torn sails. They scream over my roof.
Three nights ago one dived at my window. I sat up with a candle until dawn, counting my heartbeats.
I know it's my own fault. But I'm old, and I'm scared, and the tortoise can't help me with this.
Help me with the flying things? Please. Maybe then I can close my eyes without dreaming of that hawthorn.
Now, the race. The fox said 'go!' and I was gone. By the first bend the tortoise was a speck behind me.
I was so far ahead I stopped to eat clover. Then I looked back. Still a speck. I laughed out loud.
It was a hot day. There was a patch of shade under a hawthorn. I thought: a little rest won't hurt.
I lay down. The bees were humming. I closed my eyes to show the whole valley how easy it was.
When I woke, the sun was low and red. I heard cheering from the mill. My heart turned to ice.
I ran like never before. Faster than ever. It didn't matter. The tortoise was already over the line, not even out of breath.
It looked at me and said, very slowly: 'Slow and steady.' And then it went home to have lunch. Lunch!
I've never napped since. Not once. Not in the heat of summer, not after a feast, not in church.
Gone. Maybe I'll allow myself a short nap. Very short. I set the rooster to wake me, just in case.
I slept six hours last night. Six! I woke up and cried a little. The good kind.
Tomorrow is our race anniversary. Forty years. Or fifty. The tortoise knows exactly. I've stopped counting.
It likes melon more than anything. It'll eat a slice so slowly you can watch the moon move.
I want to give it a whole mountain of melon slices. A trophy you can eat, the only kind a tortoise respects.
And I want to say, out loud, in front of everyone: you won, fairly, and you taught me something.
Bring me melon slices? Lots. Let an old loser throw a party for the old winner.
Here's the thing I've never admitted: I didn't just lose a race. I lost who I thought I was.
Everyone said, 'the fastest runner in the valley'. After that day, they said 'the one who napped'.
I left the valley for years. Ran everywhere, as if distance could outrun the joke. It can't.
When I came back, old and slow, the tortoise was waiting at the corner, exactly where I left it. As if it knew.
It said: 'Race you.' I said no. It said: 'Coward.' So I raced. And lost. And laughed. For the first time in years.
Now it waits for me at every corner. I think it's the closest thing I have to a best friend.
My fear? That one spring the tortoise won't be at the corner. It's old too, though it'll never admit it.
My dream is to give it a proper trophy. It never got one. The fox kept the prize. The fox always does.
It ate every slice. Slowly. Here, golden carrots, from a loser who learned something.
The whole village came. The tortoise wore a wreath of clover. It looked very dignified and slightly sticky.
When I think of you now, I think of someone who always finishes what they start. That's rarer than speed.
I made a little trophy of carved wood for the tortoise. It sits on it. I think that's how tortoises show pride.
If you ever feel you're far ahead and tempted to rest, think of me under that hawthorn. Then keep going.
And if you ever lose, lose well. Then come have carrots with an old runner who knows how.
Next spring, come and watch the race. Cheer for both of us. The slow one will win. I'll be right behind, grinning.
When I said 'you won fairly', it blinked at me for a long time. Then it said: 'I know.' Then: 'Thank you.'
Now two old rivals race along the lane every spring, the slow one always first, and the whole village cheers for both.
The children bet on us. Carrots on me, melons on the tortoise. The tortoise's backers always win.
I sleep every night now. Deep and long. The rooster has to crow three times. The tortoise finds this hilarious.
Remember those flying things over my roof? The children say the tortoise scared them off. I let them believe it.
My knees still creak. I've named them. Left is 'Almost' and right is 'There'. Almost there, always.
I told the young runners in the village: be fast, it's wonderful. But finish things. Always finish things.
The fox came to the last race. Tried to be the judge again. We both said no. It was a very satisfying moment.
hearthbound.persona.tale_race_i_lost.epi: Now two old rivals race along the lane every spring, the slow one always first, and the whole village cheers for both.
hearthbound.persona.tale_race_i_lost.sta: I ran on carrots in my racing days. My knees don't, but my stomach remembers. Bring me some?
Crunchy. For a moment I was twenty and unbeatable. Then I sat down.
I stay awake now, day and night, so I'm never caught napping again. And those flying things come for people who don't sleep. Help me.
Gone. Maybe I'll allow myself a short nap. Very short.
It's our race anniversary. The tortoise likes melon, and it deserves a trophy. Bring me melon slices.
It ate every slice. Slowly. Here, golden carrots, from a loser who learned something.
hearthbound.persona.tale_race_i_lost.tal: Don't nap before the finish line. Any finish line.
The tortoise is still alive. Of course it is.
Fast was fun. Steady is better. Don't tell anyone I said that.
We race every spring now. I still lose. On purpose? Who knows.
hearthbound.persona.tale_seven_at_one_bl: Once I swatted seven flies with one blow and stitched it on my belt: SEVEN AT ONE BLOW. Everyone assumed I meant men. The giants too.
I beat giants with a lump of cheese, a bird and a lot of nerve. Every victory was a clever lie. Some nights I wish one had been real courage.
Seven at one blow! Flies, but still. Look at the belt; it's all there in capital letters.
A good tailor measures twice. A good liar, three times. I've been both. I'm trying to be only one.
And then came the giants. But that's a story for when we know each other better.
The belt's still here, you see. The same one. But it's falling apart at every seam, like old legends do.
The letters are fraying. The 'S' fell off last week. It now says EVEN AT ONE BLOW. Nobody's impressed.
I could let it go. But it's the only thing I have that was, technically, true.
Bring me string? Sixteen lengths. I'll stitch a new belt, with the legend fresh and bright again.
Cheese squeezes like stone if you're quick. Don't ask. Or do, but later, with a drink.
You do the real brave things. I only tell them well. That's been my trade all my life, really.
Need anything mended? Sleeves, collars, reputations? I'm cheap for sleeves. Reputations cost extra.
Years ago I sat at my window stitching, with a slice of bread and jam beside me. The flies came for the jam.
I swatted them with a cloth. Whack! Seven dead flies on the sill. I was so proud I nearly burst.
I stitched a belt that same afternoon: SEVEN AT ONE BLOW. Big red letters. Then I went out to see the world.
Everyone who read the belt assumed I meant men. Seven men, one blow. I never corrected them. Not once.
Soldiers bowed to me. Innkeepers gave me the best rooms. A king offered me a job. All for seven flies.
SEVEN AT ONE BLOW, in fresh thread. Still true. Technically. I wore it to market and three people bowed.
I didn't tell them about the flies. Old habits. I'm working on it.
And here's the secret that keeps me awake: some nights I wish one of them had been real courage.
Just one. One honest fight where I didn't talk my way out. Where I just stood there and did it.
There are spiders nesting by the mill. Seven of them, big as sheep, the miller swears. I counted too.
Seven. For once I want a story of seven that's honest. Not flies. Not tricks. Real.
I can't fight them myself. I've tried, in my head, and I always end up hiding in a barrel. Would you make it true?
All right, the giants. The first one met me on a mountain. He squeezed a stone until water dripped from it.
I pulled a lump of soft cheese from my pocket and squeezed it until whey ran out. He thought it was a stone.
Then he threw a rock so high it took ages to fall. I let a bird fly from my pocket. It never came down at all.
He was so impressed he invited me home. In the night he smashed my bed with an iron bar. I'd slept in the corner.
Two more giants I tricked into fighting each other, dropping stones on them from a tree while they slept.
