The king gave me half his kingdom and his daughter's hand. All for cheese, a bird, and a lot of nerve.
People think I'm brave. I'm not. I'm quick, and I'm good at making others think I'm brave.
Every victory was a clever lie. The giants, the unicorn, the wild boar. Tricks, all of them.
Seven at, well, several blows. Honest ones. I'll stitch your name next to mine. You earned the belt more than I did.
The miller's grinding again and the children are playing in the mill yard. That's real. That's yours.
The children say tall shadows walk the fields at night. Taller than a door. Eyes like purple coals.
Giants, if you ask the children. They don't look at you if you're lucky, and you mustn't look at them.
I could try tricking them. Cheese, a bird, a clever word. But I'll not trick them. I'm done with tricks.
I want this one to be real, done by someone with real courage. Someone like you.
You fight them. Three at least. I'll hold the lantern and tell the truth about it afterwards, every word.
May I tell you something I've never admitted? I'm not a king anymore. I left the kingdom years ago.
The princess found out about the flies. She heard me talking in my sleep: 'Boy, stitch that seam or I'll hit you.'
She laughed. But she never looked at me the same. The court whispered: a tailor, just a tailor.
I don't blame her. I'd built a castle on seven flies. It was bound to wobble.
So I came here, where I'm only a tailor. It's a relief, honestly. Tailors don't have to fight anything.
But I still wear the belt. And some nights I'm afraid that's all I'll ever be: a good story with nothing inside.
My dream is simple. I want to stop telling stories about myself and start telling true stories about others.
Your story, for instance. That's worth stitching. That's worth a belt of its own.
Real giants, really beaten. I watched from behind the fence. I didn't hide in a barrel. Well, not the whole time.
Keep that blade. It was always meant for someone braver than a tailor. It looks right in your hand.
You gave an old liar a story to be proud of, and it wasn't even his. That's a strange, generous gift.
If you ever need a sleeve mended, it's free. Forever. Reputations too, but yours doesn't need it.
I think courage is just doing it without the belt. I'm learning. You taught me by showing.
Life goes on, stitch by stitch, one true story at a time. It's quieter. I like it better.
Go on, hero. The real kind. I'll be here, telling everyone exactly what you did. No more, no less.
I've stitched a new belt. SEVEN AT ONE BLOW on one side. Your name on the other. Big red letters.
When people ask about the belt, I turn it round and tell them about you. Every word true.
I only tell true stories now. It's harder. People don't bow as much. But they listen longer.
The children asked me to tell the fly story. I told it honestly. They laughed so hard one fell off the bench.
Turns out the truth is funnier than the legend. I wish someone had told me thirty years ago.
I still squeeze cheese sometimes, to amuse the little ones. I tell them it's cheese first.
The miller brought me a sack of flour for the spider story. The honest version. I've never been paid for truth before.
I sleep better. No more dreams about giants finding out. There's nothing left for them to find.
Now the tailor's belt says SEVEN AT ONE BLOW on one side and your name on the other, and the tailor tells only true stories.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
My old belt is falling apart, and the legend with it. Bring me string and I'll stitch a new one.
SEVEN AT ONE BLOW, in fresh thread. Still true. Technically.
Thread for the belt
Seven spiders nest by the mill. For once I want a story of seven that's honest. Would you make it so?
Seven at, well, several blows. Honest ones. I'll stitch your name next to mine.
Seven, for real
Tall shadows walk the fields at night. Giants, if you ask the children. I'll not trick them. You fight them.
Real giants, really beaten. Take this blade; it was always meant for someone braver than a tailor.
The tall ones
Seven at one blow! Flies, but still.
Cheese squeezes like stone if you're quick. Don't ask.
A good tailor measures twice. A good liar, three times.
You do the real brave things. I only tell them well.
Seven at one blow
hearthbound.persona.tale_seven_league_bo: I was the smallest of seven, and the only one awake when our parents planned to lose us. I dropped pebbles, then breadcrumbs. Then we met an ogre.
I stole the sleeping ogre's seven-league boots and carried messages for kings. Now the magic's worn out and I walk like anyone. Slowly is lovely.
Small people hear what big people whisper. Remember that, and no village meeting will ever surprise you.
You walk like someone going somewhere. I like that. Most folk just wander between the well and the bread oven.
These legs once crossed seven leagues in a single stride. Now they grumble climbing up to the chapel.
Some mornings my feet itch for the road so badly I can't sit still. Then my knees remind me of my age.
I used to carry messages for kings. Sealed letters, urgent news, love notes too, though I never read them. Much.
There's a letter on my table that must go to the next village. I keep staring at it like an old friend.
Would you carry it for me? I'd go myself, but it would take me all week, and it deserves to arrive warm.
I was the smallest of seven brothers. They said I could fit in a boot. Well, almost.
I don't talk much, but I listen to everything. Old habit from a crowded house with thin walls.
Have you noticed how every road smells different? This one smells of hay and a little of rain.
Our parents were woodcutters, and poor. One hungry winter night I heard them whisper about the forest. I didn't sleep.
At dawn I filled my pockets with white pebbles from the stream. They shone under the moon like a trail of little stars.
The second time I only had breadcrumbs. The birds ate every one. Lesson learned: never trust a path made of food.
Lost in the forest, we saw a light and knocked. The woman who opened whispered: 'Run. My husband eats children.'
The ogre came home sniffing the air. I've never felt so small in my life, and that's saying something.
You delivered it! Tell me, did they read it at once, or put it on a shelf? I always wondered that.
That feeling of handing over a letter, the little bow, the door closing. It never gets old.
I carried battle reports, peace treaties, a proposal of marriage. All delivered before breakfast.
My brothers went home and grew tall and ordinary. I sent gold to our parents. They never asked where it came from.
Then one morning the boots only took five leagues. Then two. Then one. Magic wears out like leather.
Now they sit under my bed, dusty and soft. Some nights I still put them on, just to feel them try.
I want ordinary boots now, for ordinary walks. Bring me good leather and I'll have a cobbler make them properly.
Now I'll tell you about the boots. The ogre slept in them, fat as a haystack, snoring like a storm.
Seven-league boots shrink or stretch to fit whoever wears them. On me they became tiny. I crept close and pulled.
First stride, I cleared a whole valley. I screamed. A shepherd down below crossed himself three times.
Before that, though, there was the night of the caps. I'm not proud of it.
The ogre's seven daughters slept in golden crowns. My brothers and I wore nightcaps. In the dark, I swapped them.
The ogre came with his knife and felt for the caps. He chose wrong. Clever, not kind. I still think about it.
They were ogres, yes. But they were also girls asleep in a bed. The tale never lingers there. I do.
With the boots I went to the king's court. Nobody hires a small person, until the small person arrives before the news.
They fit! They don't fly. The left one squeaks a little. They're perfect.
I walked to the mill yesterday and noticed it has a blue door. In forty years I'd never seen it.
Smoke from its chimneys, a bell tower, maybe someone waving. Then gone, seven leagues behind me.
I'm afraid I've lived a life of arrivals and not a single journey. Does that make sense to you?
My dream is small, like me: to walk into a village I've never seen, and have someone say good morning.
My new boots are ready for it. My knees are... negotiating.
Find me a village I've never seen, somewhere past the hills. Tell me the way, and everything in between.
Slowly is lovely. I say it like a joke, but I mean it with my whole heart.
Here's something I never told anyone: I miss being needed. A courier with slow feet is just a person.
In the old days kings waited for me. Now I wait for the kettle. Both have their charm.
Sometimes I dream the ogre is chasing me and my boots won't stride. I wake up kicking the blanket.
I still think about his daughters. I never learned their names. I'd have liked to say sorry to somebody.
My brothers write to me. The eldest has grandchildren now, all tiny, all clever. I worry about them.
Here's my shame: with the boots I skipped everything in between. Villages, fields, people. Just blurs under my feet.
There was one village I always leapt over, at the edge of every route. I only ever saw its roofs from the sky.
So that's what was between the strides. Fields, crooked fences, a dog that follows you for a mile.
I walked it after you, slowly. Three days. I stopped at every well and every bench.
Remember coming back from that first delivery, breathless and proud? I saw myself at twenty.
My squeaky left boot is broken in now. It sounds like a little bird on the cobbles.
I sleep late these days. No kings, no ogres, no urgent letters. Just the rooster, who is always late himself.
Whenever you pass through, knock. I'll have tea, and a new village to tell you about.
The road is long and I'm finally in no hurry. Walk with me a while, whenever you like.
A woman there gave me soup and asked where I came from. I said: from just over there. For once it was true.
The old boots are yours now. There's a little stride left in them. Use it wisely, or for fun.
If you jump too far in them, don't blame me. They have opinions about puddles.
I wrote to my brothers about the walk. The eldest wrote back: 'Finally, you're one of us, the slow ones.'
I've planned another walk. And another. Every village the giant strides skipped. It's a long list.
I lit a candle at the chapel for the ogre's daughters. Small, I know. Small people do small, true things.
Children follow me to the gate asking for the ogre story. I tell it, but I stop at the part with the caps.
Then I tell them: be clever, but be kind too. Clever is quick. Kind lasts longer.
Now the smallest of seven walks the roads slowly, stopping at every village the giant strides once skipped.
Histoires ou contes du temps passé — Charles Perrault (1697)
My legs itch for the road, but they're old legs. Carry this letter to the next village for me, as I once would have.
Delivered! Not in one stride, I bet, but delivered. That feeling never gets old.
One more message
The magic boots are dust. I want ordinary ones, good for ordinary walks. Bring me leather.
They fit. They don't fly. They're perfect.
Ordinary boots
In all my giant strides there was one village I always skipped. Find me one I've never seen.
So that's what was between the strides. Take the old boots; there's a little stride left in them, for you.
A place I never reached
Small people hear what big people whisper.
Seven leagues a stride. My knees still remember.
I swapped our caps for the ogre's daughters' crowns in the dark. Clever, not kind. I still think about it.
My brothers all grew taller. I grew wiser. Fair trade.
Seven-league boots
hearthbound.persona.tale_seven_small_cha: A jealous queen once wanted me dead for being fairer than her. I hid in a cottage with seven miners and learned to cook for a whole mine.
I never eat red apples. Not from fear: from respect. One bite taught me that being praised for beauty is a dangerous thing.
Come in, but don't sit on the little chairs. They're spoken for, all seven of them.
Mirrors? I keep none. They talk too much, and never about anything useful.
They taught me to cook for a whole mine. Potatoes, mostly. Mountains of baked potatoes.
They're old now, and they still come down from the mountain once a year to eat at my table.
They sit in the small chairs and complain about my stew. It's their way of saying they love me.
Tonight is the night. They'll be here after dark, hungry as bears, and my cellar is nearly empty.
Would you bring me baked potatoes? Lots of them. Sixteen at least, or there'll be a riot.
Seven miners, one broom. Guess who held the broom. Go on, guess.
I can cook for thirty without blinking. Cooking for one still feels strange.
If someone offers you a gift too perfect, look at it twice. Then look at the hands holding it.
I grew up in a castle with a stepmother who asked her mirror every morning who was fairest.
One day the mirror gave the wrong answer. Wrong for me, anyway. She wanted me dead by nightfall.
A huntsman was sent to take me into the woods. He let me run instead. I still light a candle for him.
I found a cottage with seven small beds and seven small chairs. I fell asleep across three of the beds.
Seven miners came home, grumbling, and found a stranger snoring. They let me stay if I kept house.
Seven empty plates and seven happy snores. Just like old times. Thank you, truly.
The grumpiest one said my potatoes were acceptable. From him, that's a sonnet.
Sometimes I wonder if I'd have woken at all, if the miners hadn't kept watch every single night.
Now I hear something that makes my hands shake. A woman with a basket of shiny apples, near the woods.
She's been seen offering them to children. The children say she laughs strangely. Like broken glass.
It isn't my stepmother; she's long gone. But there are witches in the woods, and they know that trick.
Please, chase them off. Three of them, at least. I can't bear the thought of a child taking that bite.
The shy one left a little carved bird on my windowsill. He never says anything; he carves.
I'll tell you why I never eat red apples. Not from fear. From respect.
My stepmother found me, even at the cottage. She came three times, in three disguises.
The last time, she was an old woman with a basket of apples, the reddest you ever saw.
She praised my face, my hair, my hands. I was so hungry for kindness that I took a bite.
I fell into a sleep so deep they thought I'd died. The miners built me a glass coffin.
That's the lesson I carry: being praised for beauty is a dangerous thing. Praise can be bait.
People think I was saved by a prince. I was saved by a stumble. The piece of apple came loose.
No more baskets in the woods. The children went berry-picking this morning. I cried into the dough.
You don't know what that meant to me. I've kept the woods in my nightmares for years.
The miners laughed when I told them. Then the grumpy one said, 'About time.' Then he blew his nose loudly.
They'll come for the pie. All seven. They insist on being there, in case I fall asleep again.
I told them I won't. I think I believe it. Mostly.
I can't pick the apples myself. My hands won't do it yet. That's where you come in.
Bring me apples, sixteen of them. I'll bake a pie for the whole village and take the first bite myself.
Here's the deepest thing I carry: sometimes, in the glass coffin, I think I was awake.
I couldn't move. I heard the miners weeping. I heard the seasons change outside. I heard everything.
When I close my eyes too long, I'm afraid I'll go back there. I sleep with a candle burning.
And the apples. Every autumn the trees fill up with them, red and beautiful, and I walk the long way round.
I'm tired of walking the long way round. Fear has taken enough mornings from me.
My dream is foolish, maybe: to bake an apple pie. A plain, honest pie, and to eat the first slice.
In the old tales from beyond the mountains, the girl marries and the story ends. Mine didn't end. It went on, scared.
I want my story to go on, not scared. Sweet. With cinnamon, if I can find some.
Sweet, and nothing more. Nothing more! I laughed so hard I had to sit on one of the little chairs.
You have the pick, I hope. The miners forged it for me long ago. It should dig again, in braver hands.
If anyone ever offers you a gift too perfect, you remember me. Then come have a real one: pie.
The children call me the pie lady. Better than any title a castle ever gave me.
Someday the miners won't come down the mountain anymore. I'll keep the chairs anyway. Chairs remember.
Life goes on here, apple by apple. Slow and sweet. I didn't know it could.
Go on, before the grumpy one arrives and eats your slice. Sunday, don't forget. Pie waits for no one.
The whole village came. Even the old baker, who never admits anyone else's pie is good.
The grumpy miner had three slices and then said it was too sweet. He's keeping the dish.
Now I bake an apple pie every Sunday. It cools on the windowsill and the children pretend not to smell it.
I walk under the apple trees now. I even talk to them. They're much better company than mirrors.
I blew out the night candle last week. Slept till dawn. Woke up and remembered every dream, and they were nice.
The shy miner carved an apple for me. Wooden, red paint. It sits where a mirror would be.
Seven small chairs, always set around the table. I added an eighth, a bit bigger. That one's yours.
You chased the baskets out of the woods and the fear out of my kitchen. Not a small job.
Now an apple pie cools on the windowsill every Sunday, and seven small chairs are always set around the table.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
The seven miners come down from the mountain tonight, hungry as bears. Bring me baked potatoes, lots of them.
Seven empty plates and seven happy snores. Just like old times.
Supper for seven
A woman with a basket of shiny apples has been seen by the woods, offering them to children. Witches. Chase them off.
No more baskets in the woods. The children can go berry-picking again.
The woman with the basket
It's time I stopped fearing apples. Bring me some; I'll bake a pie for the whole village and take the first bite.
Sweet, and nothing more. The miners forged this pick for me long ago. It should dig again.
An apple pie
Mirrors? I keep none. They talk too much.
Seven miners, one broom. Guess who held the broom.
The old miners still visit. They sit in the small chairs and complain about my stew.
If someone offers you a gift too perfect, look at it twice.
Seven small chairs
hearthbound.persona.tale_singing_all_sum: I sang all summer while the ants stored grain. When winter came I knocked on their door. 'You sang? Then dance now,' they said, and shut it.
I survived, barely. Now I work in summer, and I still sing while I work. The ants next door have started to hum along.
Sing while you work. Doubles the joy, halves the pain. Try it. Even humming counts.
Winter's coming. It always is. That's no reason to stop singing.
The fields emptied. The flies vanished. I went looking for crumbs and found nothing. Not even a worm.
I remember my stomach making a sound like a sad cello. I tried to sing over it. It didn't work.
That's all behind me, mostly. This summer I sing AND store. Both. For the first time in my life.
The granary behind my house is empty and echoing. It has perfect acoustics, but I'd rather it had grain.
Bring me wheat for the granary, a good pile. I'll provide the music while we fill it.
You've got a good walking rhythm. Left, right, left. I could write a song to it. I might.
The old ant next door taps her foot to my songs. I've seen it. She denies it, of course.
My fiddle's strings are made from horsehair and stubbornness. Mostly stubbornness.
When I was young, summer felt endless. Warm grass, long evenings, and a song for every one of them.
The ants worked from dawn to dusk hauling grain. I sang to them. I thought I was helping. I thought it was a gift.
They'd pass under my branch with their loads and say: 'Winter is coming.' I'd answer with another verse.
I never stored a single seed. Why would I? The fields were full. The world was full.
Then the first frost came, one morning in autumn. The grass went white and my fiddle went out of tune.
A full granary and a new song about it. Both, for once. It goes 'wheat, wheat, beautiful wheat'. Work in progress.
The old ant came to look at the granary. She said nothing. She nodded once. I nearly fell off my stool.
I don't hate the ants. They were right, in a hard way. But a shut door isn't the only way to be right.
Hungry neighbours will knock this winter, like I once did. Somebody always does. Somebody always will.
I want bread ready for every one of them. Stacked, crusty, warm. No questions about what they did all summer.
Grain alone isn't enough. A starving person can't wait for milling and baking. I know. I tried to eat raw wheat once.
Bring me bread. Plenty. Nobody gets told to dance at my door.
Now I'll tell you the rest. When I was starving, I knocked on the ants' door. It was warm inside, I could smell bread.
I asked for a few grains, only until spring. I promised to pay back with interest. My word as a musician.
The ant looked at me for a long time. 'What were you doing all summer?' she asked.
'Singing, day and night, for everyone,' I said. I thought it would soften her. I was proud of it.
'You sang? Then dance now,' she said, and shut the door. I stood in the snow, listening to the latch click.
I didn't dance. I cried, then I walked. I don't remember much of that winter. Cold, and hunger, and the sound of doors.
An old miller finally let me sleep in the flour loft. I played for him every night. He fed me porridge. We were both happy.
I survived, barely. Now I work in summer. Every day. And I still sing while I work.
Stacked to the rafters. No door shuts on anyone this year. The whole house smells of crust.
A young traveller knocked last night. I gave him a loaf and a song. He cried at the song, not the bread. Artists.
I want to throw a concert in the granary. The whole village. Ants included. Especially the ants.
There must be pie. Songs are food for the soul, but the soul lives in a body, and bodies want pie.
Pumpkin pie, with spice. The miller made one for me my first winter. I've never tasted anything warmer.
I'm writing a new song for the concert. It's about a door. It opens at the end. It took me thirty years to write the ending.
Bring me pumpkin pie, enough for the whole village. Let's fill the darkest night with singing and crumbs.
Here's what I've never said aloud: I'm afraid I haven't really changed. That I only work because I'm afraid of the cold.
If fear is the reason, is it still virtue? I lie awake with that one. Then I get up and hum until it passes.
The ants next door have started to hum along. Faintly. At work. I hear them through the wall.
Last week the old ant knocked on MY door. She'd hurt her leg and couldn't carry her grain. I carried it. I sang the whole way.
She didn't say thank you. She said: 'Your second verse is too long.' That's thank you, in ant.
Her grandchildren sneak over to hear me play. She scolds them. Then she stands at the window, pretending to dust.
My dream is simple: one night where everybody sings together. The ants, the travellers, the old miller, me.
Midwinter is the darkest night, the hungriest, the coldest. That's exactly when we need music most.
The ants danced. I swear they danced. Take this honey; sweet things are for sharing.
The old ant danced with the miller. Stiffly. Beautifully. I nearly dropped my bow.
You helped me fill a granary, a pantry and a concert hall. That's a whole symphony, friend.
I wrote you a verse. It's in the midwinter song now. The children know it by heart. You'll blush.
Work hard, sing loud, and never shut the door on anyone. That's the whole song, really.
Winter's coming. It always is. But now I look forward to it. Who'd have guessed?
Come to the granary next midwinter. Bring your voice, however it sounds. Every voice is welcome.
Now every midwinter the whole village sings in the granary. People bring pies, fiddles, spoons to bang on pots.
The ants dance too, a little stiffly. They practise in secret all autumn. I pretend not to know.
The door song was a success. When I sang the last line, 'and the door swung open', everyone cheered.
Remember that empty, echoing granary? Now it's full every autumn, and it still has perfect acoustics.
I teach the children to sing while they work. Their chores go twice as fast and three times as loud.
The old ant gave me a jar of her own honey this spring. With a note: 'Second verse still too long.' I've kept it that way on purpose.
When travellers knock in winter now, I don't wait for them to ask. The bread's by the door before the knock ends.
I still hear that latch clicking some nights. Then I hear the ants humming through the wall, and I go back to sleep.
Now every midwinter the whole village sings in the granary, and the ants dance too, a little stiffly.
Fables — Jean de La Fontaine (1668)
This summer I sing AND store. Bring me wheat for the granary; I'll provide the music.
A full granary and a new song about it. Both, for once.
Grain for the granary
Hungry neighbours will knock this winter, like I once did. I want bread ready for every one of them.
Stacked to the rafters. No door shuts on anyone this year.
Bread for winter
Midwinter, and I'm throwing a concert for the whole village, ants included. We need pies. Bring me pumpkin pie.
The ants danced. I swear they danced. Take this honey; sweet things are for sharing.
A winter concert
Sing while you work. Doubles the joy, halves the pain.
Winter's coming. It always is. That's no reason to stop singing.
The old ant next door taps her foot to my songs. I've seen it.
Next winter nobody knocks in vain. My granary door is open.
Singing all summer
hearthbound.persona.tale_small_golden_ke: I married a rich lord with a blue beard. He gave me every key and forbade one small door. I opened it. The key bled, and would not wash clean.
My brothers rode in just in time. I kept his fortune and spent it opening other doors: debts, cells, cages. Curiosity saved my life.
Come in, the door's open. It's always open. I don't own a single lock. Not one.
Some doors should be opened. Especially the forbidden ones. Don't look so shocked; I'm only half joking.
'Except the small room at the end of the lower hall. That little golden key, never use it.'
I'll tell you what happened next, but not today. Today I want to talk about keys that do some good.
In this village, the landlord holds the keys to half the houses. He can lock a family out on a whim.
No one should ever hold all the keys again. Not him, not anyone. Every family should hold its own.
Bring me iron? Eight ingots. I'll have keys forged for every family's own door. And none for mine.
Sister Anne, sister Anne, do you see anyone coming? ...An old joke. A sad one. I'll explain someday.
If anyone ever forbids you a door, ask why. Then ask again. Then, perhaps, open it anyway.
I have a small golden key on a nail by the hearth. It opens nothing here. I keep it for remembering.
When I was young, a rich lord came to court me. He had castles, horses, silver plates. And a beard that was blue.
Not dark. Blue. Like a bruise, like a deep lake. My sister shuddered. I told her I didn't mind.
He'd been married before. Several times. Nobody knew what became of the others. I didn't ask. I should have.
We married. For a month he was charming. Feasts, dancing, gifts. Then he said he had to travel.
He gave me a great ring of keys. Every room, every chest, every cellar. 'Open anything you like,' he said.
A key for each house, and none for mine. That's how I like it. The landlord is furious. Good.
The blacksmith's widow wept when I gave her the key. She'd been locked out once, in winter, with a baby.
I ran to the top of the tower where my sister Anne was staying. 'Sister Anne, do you see anyone coming?'
She watched the road. 'Only the sun and the dust.' Again. 'Only a flock of sheep.' He was shouting from below.
That's the old joke, you see. Sister Anne on the tower, watching for rescue. It's not funny. But I laugh anyway.
My sister still lives in the next village. She still watches the road for me, every evening. Out of habit.
Carry her my letter? Tell her I'm well, and there's no need to watch anymore. Let her rest her eyes.
Now I'll tell you about the small room. I lasted three days. On the fourth, I couldn't bear it.
I ran down the lower hall so fast I nearly fell. My hands shook so badly I dropped the key twice.
I opened the door. The floor was dark and sticky. And along the wall... his other wives. All of them.
I dropped the little key. It fell into the blood. I snatched it up, locked the door and fled.
I scrubbed that key with sand, with soap, with ash. The stain wouldn't come out. It was an enchanted key.
As soon as I cleaned one side, the blood came back on the other. The key knew. The key would tell him.
He came home early. Of course he did. He asked for the keys. He looked at the little golden one. He smiled.
'You will join them,' he said. I begged for a few minutes to pray. He gave me a quarter of an hour.
She wrote back one line: 'I see someone coming. It's you.' I laughed until I cried. That's her all over.
She's been watching that road for thirty years. She says she'll stop now. I don't believe her.
My fear is that there are still men like him, with rooms like that, and nobody curious enough to look.
And there are. Brutes in grey coats, with axes. They hold captives in their mansions, deep in the dark forest.
Travellers vanish on the forest road. Some come back months later, thin and silent. Some never come back.
My dream is simple: to open every one of those doors. I have the gold for it. I don't have the arm.
Break their hold, for me? Four of them, at least. Let whoever is locked in those mansions see the sun.
I'll finish the story. Just as he raised his sword, Anne cried out: 'Two riders! Our brothers!'
My brothers rode in just in time. A soldier and a musketeer. They didn't ask questions. He didn't survive them.
I inherited everything. His castles, his gold, his horses. I sold almost all of it.
I spent his fortune opening other doors. Debts paid off. Prisoners freed. Cages opened, birds and people both.
Curiosity saved my life. Everyone says it's a sin. It's what showed me the truth before it was too late.
But here's what I've never said aloud. I still dream of that room. Of being one of the women on the wall.
I wonder what they'd have said if they'd opened the door sooner. If they'd been curious enough.
The old French tale ends with a warning to curious wives. I think it should warn husbands with forbidden rooms.
Doors opened, people freed. You've done what my brothers did for me, for strangers. I have no words for that.
Keep that gold I gave you. It was his, and now it's done some good. That's the best thing it's ever done.
You opened doors for me that I couldn't open. With iron, with a letter, with your own two hands.
If anyone ever forbids you a door and won't say why, come and tell me. I'll ask why for you. Twice.
Curiosity isn't a sin. It's a lantern. Carry yours high, and don't let anyone tell you to put it out.
Life goes on here, doors open, windows open, neighbours wandering in for tea without knocking. I love it.
Off you go. No need to knock when you come back. There's nothing here to knock on.
One of the freed travellers came to thank me. She'd been in that mansion two years. She asked for my recipe for bread.
She's staying in the village now. She sleeps with the door open. I understand completely.
No door in the village is locked now. The landlord moved away. He said we were all mad. We are, a bit.
The old golden key hangs on the nail by the hearth. I looked at it this morning. The stain is gone.
I don't know when it happened. Maybe when the last cage opened. Maybe it just got tired of remembering.
Anne came to visit. She climbed the old watchtower out of habit, looked at the road, and said: 'Nothing. Lovely.'
We sat at the top all afternoon, watching nothing come. It was the most peaceful day of my life.
My brothers are old now. They visit at harvest. They still ride in too fast and scare the chickens.
Now no door in the village is locked, and the old golden key hangs on a nail, clean at last.
Histoires ou contes du temps passé — Charles Perrault (1697)
I'll forge keys for every family's own door, so no one ever holds all the keys again. Bring me iron.
A key for each house, and none for mine. That's how I like it.
A key for every family
My sister still lives in the next village and still watches the road for me. Carry my letter so she can rest her eyes.
She wrote back one line: 'I see someone coming. It's you.' I laughed until I cried.
Riders for sister Anne
Brutes in grey coats hold captives in their mansions, like he did. Break their hold.
Doors opened, people freed. Take this gold; it was his, and now it's done some good.
Men like him
Some doors should be opened. Especially the forbidden ones.
I don't own a single lock. Not one.
Sister Anne, sister Anne, do you see anyone coming? ...An old joke. A sad one.
If anyone ever forbids you a door, ask why. Then ask again.
The small golden key
hearthbound.persona.tale_splinter_of_mir: My dearest friend got a splinter of a troll's mirror in his eye. Everything turned ugly to him, and the Snow Queen carried him north. I followed, barefoot.
I found him in a palace of ice, spelling words with frozen shards. My tears melted the splinter. We came home grown up, and the roses had waited.
Roses in the window boxes. Every house should have them. Don't you think a lane looks sad without them?
Crows gave me directions once. I still feed them. That big one on the fence is a regular.
He became clever and cruel. He mocked Grandmother's walk. He only liked snowflakes, because they were perfect and cold.
Then one winter he tied his sled to a great white sleigh, and it carried him north. He never came home that spring.
I went looking for him, barefoot, when the roses bloomed again. I gave my red shoes to the river for news of him.
Now I live here, and the lane has only bare window boxes. It frightens me more than it should.
Would you bring me rose bushes? Enough so that every window here has some. Ice doesn't reach where roses grow.
You have warm eyes. I notice eyes. Cold ones see only faults. Warm ones see the rest.
He still shivers in winter. I knit him scarves. He complains. He wears them.
Winter here is gentle, mostly. I keep watching the north sky anyway. Old habit.
When we were small, he and I lived in two attics facing each other, with a gutter between our windows.
Our parents put a wooden box across the gap and planted roses in it. We sat under them all summer.
Grandmother told us about the Snow Queen, who flies in the snowflakes and looks in at windows. We laughed. Then we didn't.
One day he cried out: something in my eye, something in my heart. After that, he laughed at the roses. Called them worm-eaten.
It was a splinter of a troll's mirror, a mirror that made everything good look ugly. It broke into a thousand pieces over the world.
The whole lane smells of summer. The ice can't reach us here. Thank you, truly.
Old Mother Hebbel across the lane cried when she saw them. Her window box had been empty for twenty years.
I held him and cried. My tears ran into his heart and melted the splinter. He cried too, and the one in his eye washed out.
We came home in spring and climbed to our attics. The roses were blooming. We were grown up, and still children.
But lately the pale archers walk down from the frozen lands. Their arrows leave frost on the doorsteps.
I think the Snow Queen hasn't forgotten us. Or it's just winter. I've learned not to trust cold things.
Please stop them before they reach the roses. I couldn't bear to see this lane go grey again.
Now the rest of the story. I walked and walked. An old woman with a garden of flowers made me forget, for a while.
She combed my hair with a golden comb and hid all her roses underground, so I wouldn't remember him.
But one rose was painted on her hat. I saw it, and wept, and my tears woke the buried roses. They told me he wasn't dead.
A crow led me to a palace. It wasn't him there, only a prince who looked a bit like him. They gave me a coach and boots.
Robbers stopped the coach in a dark forest. A robber girl, wild as a wolf cub, claimed me as her playmate.
She slept with a knife and kept a reindeer tied up. She threatened me all night. Then, at dawn, she set me free.
She gave me her reindeer, her mother's big mittens, and her own bread. I had nothing. She didn't care.
At the Snow Queen's palace I found him, blue with cold, trying to spell a word with shards of ice. 'Eternity'.
No more frost on the doorsteps. The north can keep its cold. I planted a new rose by the gate to celebrate.
He came out to thank you himself, wearing three of my scarves. That's affection, in his language.
The Lapp woman and the Finn woman helped me too. They wrote their messages on dried fish. I kept one. It still smells.
My dream is that nobody here ever walks north alone, barefoot, with only tears for a weapon. Like I did.
And I'd like to see her face when she hears the barefoot child made it home, and grew up, and planted roses.
The letter is finished. Fourth try. I didn't tear it. I even drew a reindeer on the corner, badly.
Take my thanks to her in the next village, will you? Tell her the mittens were worn out with love.
Can I tell you my fear? That the splinter isn't all gone. Sometimes he looks at something and frowns, and I hold my breath.
Then he says something kind about it, and I breathe again. It's been years. I still hold my breath.
Grandmother died while we were away. She waited as long as she could. I think about that every winter.
The robber girl is the one I owe the most, and I've never thanked her properly. She'd laugh at me for trying.
She said she'd go out and see the world. She did, riding a stolen horse. Now she lives in the next village, respectable.
Respectable! The girl who kept a knife under her pillow and tickled her reindeer's neck with it.
I heard she has a family, and a bakery. I imagine her scolding the bread for rising too slowly.
I've written her a letter three times and torn it up. Words feel too small next to reindeer and mittens.
She sent back her old coat with a note: 'You need it more.' I'm giving it to you. She'd approve.
Did she really laugh when you mentioned the reindeer? I can hear it. She always laughed like a door slamming.
Grandmother's chair by the window has a rose beside it now. I talk to it sometimes. It doesn't answer, but it blooms.
Cold eyes see only faults. You looked at this lane and saw what it could be. That's warmth.
If you ever feel a splinter in your heart, come to me. I have roses, scarves and plenty of tears to spare.
Summer smells best between two windows. Come sit under the roses any afternoon you like.
The winter will come again, and we'll be ready, with our roses and our scarves. And with you, I hope.
Wear that coat in the frozen lands. It has walked through worse, I promise you.
Roses bloom between every pair of windows in the lane now. Even the priest asked for a box.
The Snow Queen's winters pass us by. Maybe it's the roses. Maybe it's you. I think both.
He reads to the children in the evenings now. His favourite word is still 'eternity'. He says it warmly now.
The crows bring me shiny things. A button, a buckle, once a ring. I return them to their owners, mostly.
I keep one of the mirror's shards in a box, the one that fell from his eye. It's harmless now. Just glass.
Remember the pale archers at the doorsteps? The children built snowmen there this winter. Friendly ones.
The robber girl says she's coming for a visit in spring. I'm already worried about the bread.
Now roses bloom between every pair of windows in the lane, and the Snow Queen's winters pass this village by.
The Snow Queen — Hans Christian Andersen (1844)
Our roses grew in a box between two windows, his and mine. Bring me rose bushes so every window here has some.
The whole lane smells of summer. The ice can't reach us here.
Roses in the window
Pale archers walk down from the frozen lands, as if someone had sent them. Stop them before they reach the roses.
No more frost on the doorsteps. The north can keep its cold.
Frozen things from the north
A robber girl gave me her reindeer and her gloves when I had nothing. She lives in the next village now. Take her my thanks.
She sent back her old coat with a note: 'You need it more.' Now I'm giving it to you. She'd approve.
Thanks to the robber girl
Roses in the window boxes. Every house should have them.
Crows gave me directions once. I still feed them.
Cold eyes see only faults. Warm ones see the rest.
He still shivers in winter. I knit him scarves. He complains. He wears them.
A splinter of mirror
hearthbound.persona.tale_steady_on_one_l: I came back from the wars on one leg and a wooden stump. Then I saw a dancer who balanced on one foot, and thought: there's someone like me.
Gutters, rats, a flood, even the belly of a river pike: I went through all of it without flinching. The fever took her. What's left of me is small, and shaped like a heart.
Stand steady. Even on one leg. Especially on one leg. That's the only advice I give for free.
You shift your weight when you talk. Plant your feet. The world pushes less when you don't wobble.
I keep a little tin spangle in my pocket. It was hers. I'll tell you how I got it, some day.
Now I cast little tin soldiers for the children here. It keeps my hands busy and my head quiet.
Every soldier I ever cast had two legs, except the first one. Children always ask why that one's different.
I've decided: this winter, a whole new regiment, every one of them standing on two good legs.
Bring me iron, will you? Enough for a regiment. The children deserve soldiers who don't wobble.
Paper boats sink. I rode one once. Long story. Maybe I'll tell it when I know you better.
This stump is oak. The leg I lost was mine. I prefer the oak on rainy days; it doesn't ache.
Children knock on my stump for luck. I let them. Nobody else gets to.
I was one of twenty-five brothers-in-arms, all cast from the same old spoon, as the saying went. The metal ran short on me.
I came back from the wars on one leg. Nobody stared at the others. Everybody stared at me.
Then, in a town square, I saw a dancer on a painted stage, balanced on one foot, arms raised like a swan.
I thought: there's someone like me. I didn't know yet that she had two legs. She just kept one hidden under her skirt.
I stood by that stage every evening. Never spoke. A soldier doesn't flinch, but he doesn't talk much either.
A whole regiment, all on two legs. Well... I kept one on one leg. For luck. Don't tell the children.
The little ones lined them up on the windowsills. The whole lane looks like a parade.
She looked at me. I looked at her. Nobody said a word. We both stood very still, which is our kind of talking.
I never told her I loved her. I thought there'd be time. Flinching never saved anyone. Neither did waiting.
Now I stand at the gate most nights. Monsters test our walls: the dead, the bone archers, sometimes worse.
I'll stand there, steady as always. But one leg is one leg short. I need someone beside me.
Stand with me tonight? Not one step back. That's all I ask.
Here's the long story. A goblin, some said, or just a gust of wind. I fell from a high window onto the street.
Two boys found me, folded a boat from newspaper, and set me sailing down the gutter in the rain.
The gutter went under a bridge, into the dark. A big water rat stood up and demanded my passport. I didn't flinch.
The boat went soft. The water rose to my neck. I thought of the dancer, and stood straight.
Then the paper tore, and a great river pike swallowed me whole. Inside it was darker than any trench.
The fish was caught, sold at market, and cut open in a kitchen. And there I was, in the same house I'd fallen from.
The cook screamed. Then she laughed. Then she put me back on the table, right in front of the dancer's stage.
Everyone called it a miracle. I called it standing steady. Some things come back to you if you don't let go.
Not one step back, either of us. She'd have been proud. I think she saw it, somehow.
You fought well. You didn't flinch once. I watched, the way I watch the gate.
My dream is gentler: that every child here looks at a window and sees a dancer who never falls.
She had a castle of card with little trees and a mirror-lake. Her dancer stood at the door, forever on one toe.
I want to cut paper dancers like that for the children's windows. Hundreds of them, all balanced, all brave.
My hands are good with tin, clumsy with scissors. I'll learn. I learned to walk again, didn't I?
Bring me paper. A good stack. I'll cut the first one tonight, and she'll be looking over my shoulder.
Now the rest, which I tell nobody. The fever came to town that winter. She danced through it until she couldn't.
I sat by her bed. She said I was the steadiest thing she'd ever seen. I didn't know what to answer. I stood.
She died in the night. The next day they burned her things in the stove, and a boy tossed me in too, for no reason.
I stood in the flames. Hot, bright, still standing. Then a draft blew her paper costume in beside me.
It flared once and was gone. When they cleaned the stove, all they found of me was a little lump, shaped like a heart.
And her spangle, burnt black as coal. That's the one in my pocket. The tale ends there. I didn't.
They say I melted. I say I got smaller and truer. What's left of me fits in the palm of a hand.
My fear is the day my stump breaks and I can't stand at the gate. Then who holds the line?
A whole troupe, all on one toe. The shield is yours now. It has never flinched either.
Look at the windows at dusk. Every lamp throws a little dancer's shadow on the street.
When my oak stump cracked last month, three people brought me new wood the same day. I nearly flinched. From joy.
If you ever feel you're standing on one leg, come by. I'll show you how to lean on something.
Steady isn't the same as still. You taught me that. You never stop moving, but you never waver either.
When I'm gone, keep one paper dancer in your window. That's all the monument I need.
Now go on. I've got the gate. I always have. But come back and stand with me sometimes.
The children stand on one foot to copy them. They wobble. I tell them wobbling is how you learn.
I still stand at the gate. But now I have company some nights, and it's you, and it's good.
The little one-legged soldier sits on my windowsill, next to a paper dancer. They look happy. Don't laugh.
Remember the night we held the line? The blacksmith says it's already a song. A terrible song. I like it.
I told the children about the water rat and the passport. They made me do the rat's voice twice.
The spangle in my pocket feels warmer lately. Maybe from my hand. Maybe not.
I cut a new dancer every Sunday. My scissors are almost as steady as my feet now.
Someone asked if I'm lonely. I said I have a regiment, a troupe, a gate and a friend. Plenty.
Now paper dancers balance in every window of the village, and a guard on one leg stands at the gate, steady as ever.
Fairy Tales Told for Children — Hans Christian Andersen (1838)
I cast little soldiers for the children, and this time every one gets both legs. Bring me iron.
A whole regiment, all on two legs. Well... I kept one on one leg. For luck.
Tin for new soldiers
Monsters test our walls every night. I'll stand at the gate, steady as always. Stand with me.
Not one step back, either of us. She'd have been proud.
Hold the line
I want to cut paper dancers for the children's windows, like the one in her castle of card. Bring me paper.
A whole troupe, all on one toe. Take this shield; it has never flinched either.
Paper dancers
Stand steady. Even on one leg.
Paper boats sink. I rode one once. Long story.
I keep a little tin spangle in my pocket. It was hers.
Flinching never saved anyone. Standing still, sometimes, did.
Steady on one leg
hearthbound.persona.tale_tower_without_d: I grew up in a tower with no door. A witch climbed my braid every evening, until a stranger learned the call and climbed it too.
She cut my hair and cast me into the wilderness. My tears gave my stranger his sight back. Now I build towers with doors. Many doors.
Mind the step. And notice the door. Every house needs a door. You'd be surprised how many people forget.
I build things. Walls, roofs, stairs. Mostly doors, if I'm honest. I have a weakness for hinges.
There's an old watchtower at the edge of this village. I can see it from my window. It has no ladders.
The children dare each other to climb it. Last week one got halfway up the stones and froze.
I heard her crying for help, and for a moment I was back at that window, waiting for someone to climb.
Nobody should ever need someone's hair to climb. Or luck. Or courage they don't have yet.
Bring me ladders for the old watchtower? Sixteen. Enough to go up and, more importantly, come down.
I cut my hair every spring. Short. Always. The barber thinks I'm in mourning. I'm not.
See the greens in my garden? Rampion. A stolen salad started it all. I grow it now, out of spite.
From a tower you see everything and touch nothing. Down here is better. Down here you get mud on your boots.
My mother craved that rampion when she carried me. My father climbed a witch's wall to steal it.
The witch caught him. The price for the salad was me. I was handed over as a baby, like a basket.
She raised me in a tower in the woods. No stairs. No door. One window, very high.
Every evening she stood below and called up for me to let down my hair. I'd lower my braid, and she'd climb it.
I thought that was what love felt like. A weight on your scalp, and someone arriving.
Anyone can go up now, and come down whenever they like. That's the whole point. I tested every rung.
The girl who froze went up yesterday. She waved from the top. Then she climbed down, just because she could.
She cast me out into a wilderness, with nothing. Then she waited in the tower, with my hair tied to the hook.
He climbed, and found her there. He leapt from the window into the thorns. They took his sight.
The tales stop being tidy there. It took us years to find each other again. I don't talk about those years.
Now, at dusk, witches circle the old tower. Three of them, flying low, as if waiting for a braid.
Please, drive them away for good. I can't watch that tower and see them waiting. Not again.
I promised you the rest of my story. It gets stranger. A stranger, in fact.
One evening a young man heard the witch's call from the trees, and watched my braid come down.
The next night, after she'd gone, he called up the same words. I let down my hair, and he climbed.
I'd never seen anyone but her. He was the most frightening thing I'd ever met. Then he made me laugh.
He came every night. We made plans. Every visit he brought silk thread so I could weave a ladder out.
A ladder. You see why I care so much about them. I was making one, thread by thread, in secret.
Then I made a silly slip. I asked the witch why she was so much heavier to pull up than him.
She cut my braid with two snips. The sound of it... like shears through wet grass. I still flinch at shears.
The dusk is empty. I slept with the window open for the first time in years. I'd forgotten how night smells.
You don't know how long I've slept with shutters barred. Thank you, from the bottom of my chest.
Imagine a tower with a bell at the top. Rung at festivals, at weddings, at danger. Heard in every home.
A tower that says 'come here' instead of 'stay there'. It would undo something in me. I'm sure of it.
He says I should ring it myself, the first time. I told him he could hold the ladder.
I've already built the frame at the top. It's just waiting for the bell, like a nest waiting for its bird.
Bring me a bell to hang at the top? One is enough. One voice, loud enough for the whole valley.
Here's what I rarely say. When I found him again, in the wilderness, he was blind and thin and singing to himself.
I knew his voice. I held him and cried, and two of my tears fell into his eyes. And he could see again.
The old tales make it sound like magic. I think it was just that, for the first time, someone cried for him.
He lives with me now, of course. He's the one who taught me carpentry. He can't stand heights anymore.
My fear, the one I keep in a locked drawer, is that I'll build walls instead of doors, without noticing.
The witch wasn't a monster at first. She loved me like a thing she owned. I'm afraid I could love like that too.
So I make myself build open things. Doors. Ladders. Porches where anyone can sit.
My dream is that old tower. I want it to call people in, not hide anyone away.
Hear it? That's a tower saying 'come in'. I rang it until my arms ached. He cried. I pretended not to notice.
You have my spyglass, I hope. I've looked out long enough. Now I'd rather look at people, up close.
You made my ugliest tower into the prettiest place in the valley. That's a builder's dream, you know.
If you ever feel shut in, anywhere, ring that bell. I'll hear it. I'll bring a ladder.
The shears don't scare me as much now. I trimmed the rampion with them yesterday. Small victories.
Life goes on down here, muddy and noisy and full of doors. I wouldn't trade one for a tower of gold.
Go on, the sun's setting. Climb up and watch it with the children. And come down whenever you like.
The old tower has a door now, a bell and a ladder. The children climb it to watch the sunset.
They call up to each other from the top: 'Let down your ladder!' I didn't teach them that. I laughed anyway.
The rampion's doing well this year. I gave a basket to a woman who's expecting. For free. No price, no tower.
I cut my hair again this spring. Short. But this time it felt like a choice, not a scar.
I've built four doors this month. One for the baker, two for the stables, one for a shed nobody needed. I got carried away.
He's learning to climb again. Only the first few rungs of the ladder. He says the view is already excellent.
When the bell rings at dusk, the whole village looks up. Nobody looks at the tower and feels trapped anymore.
Sometimes I think of the witch. Alone at the top, with my braid tied to a hook. I hope she found a door too.
Now the old tower has a door, a bell and a ladder, and the children climb it to watch the sunset.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
Nobody should ever need someone's hair to climb. Bring me ladders for the old watchtower.
Anyone can go up now, and come down whenever they like. That's the whole point.
Ladders, not braids
Witches still circle the old tower at dusk, as if waiting for a braid. Drive them away for good.
The dusk is empty. I slept with the window open for the first time in years.
The witch's sisters
I want the tower to call everyone, not hide anyone. Bring me a bell to hang at the top.
Hear it? That's a tower saying 'come in'. Take my spyglass; I've looked out long enough.
A bell for the tower
Every house needs a door. You'd be surprised how many people forget.
I cut my hair every spring. Short. Always.
A stolen salad started it all. I grow those greens in my garden now, out of spite.
From a tower you see everything and touch nothing. Down here is better.
A tower without a door
hearthbound.persona.tale_unpaid_tune.bio: When I was small, a piper led every child of my town into a mountain. I limped, and fell behind. The door in the rock closed before I reached it.
The town had refused to pay him for clearing the rats. I've spent my life paying every debt twice over, hoping the mountain is listening.
hearthbound.persona.tale_unpaid_tune.dia: Come in, slowly if you like. I do everything slowly. This leg of mine sets the pace.
Always pay the musician. Always. If you learn one thing from me, learn that.
I'm not ready to tell you what he played next. Let me find the words. Some days they limp too.
Anyway. There's something wrong in my cellar. Little grey things crawling out between the stones.
They eat the paper, the flour, the wool. At night I hear them scratching, like tiny feet on the stairs.
Everyone says: get a piper! No. Never. I won't call a piper this time. I won't ever make that bargain.
Would you deal with them for me? Eight or so. And I'll pay you, in full, whether you like it or not.
Rats? No. I keep cats. Three of them. Very well paid, in cream and compliments.
I still hear a tune some nights. Nobody else does. Don't worry, it's a pretty one.
I've paid the baker twice this week. She keeps giving the coins back. I keep leaving them on the counter.
I grew up in a town by a wide river, far from here. The rats there were so bold they ate the soup from the ladle.
One day a stranger came, tall and thin, in a coat of every colour. He said he could pipe the rats away.
The council promised him a thousand coins. He played, and every rat in town followed him into the river.
Then the council laughed and offered him fifty. I remember the mayor's belly shaking. I was very small.
The piper didn't argue. He just smiled a quiet smile, and walked into the street with his pipe.
Gone, and paid for in full. Here, take it, and don't argue. I've had a lifetime of practice not being argued with.
The cats are offended you did their job. Whiskers has turned her back on me all morning.
Here's my secret: I don't know if I was lucky or left out. I've never known. I've asked for seventy years.
Ever since, I pay every debt twice over. The baker, the smith, the musicians. Hoping the mountain is listening.
And now, in this village, the same thing. A travelling musician played at our harvest feast. Lovely music.
The council paid him only half. Said the second half was 'not in the budget'. I nearly fainted on the spot.
Not in my village. Bring me emeralds for the rest, five of them. Let's pay him before he picks up his pipe.
Now I'll finish the story. After the council refused him, the piper played a new tune. Sweeter than any bird.
Every child in the town came running. Out of kitchens, schoolrooms, cradles. I came running too.
We followed him through the streets, laughing, dancing. The grown-ups stood frozen, like statues.
He led us out of the gate, towards the mountain. And the mountain opened, like a door in the rock.
But I limp. I've always limped. I fell behind, and behind, and behind.
By the time I reached the mountain, the door was closing. I saw the last bright coat go in. Then stone.
I stood there alone, the only child left in a town of weeping grown-ups. I was seven.
There's a poem about it, from a distant land. They say the lame child spent a life missing the country behind the door.
The musician wept when I paid. Said nobody ever pays the second half. They should. They must.
He played me a song for free, afterwards. My leg tapped along. It hasn't done that in years.
It can't be him. He'd be two hundred years old, or not a man at all. I know that. I know it.
But I wrote a letter anyway. Late at night, with the cats watching. I wrote it as the child who limped.
I asked him if they're happy. I told him I paid every debt I ever had. I told him I'm sorry for my town.
I can't walk that far. I can't bear to arrive and find a stranger. And I can't bear not to send it.
Carry my letter to the next village? Give it to the piper, whoever he is. Even if he's only a man with a pipe.
I'll tell you what I think about when I can't sleep. The other children. My friends. Where are they?
There was Greta, who stole plums. Little Hans with the big ears. My own sister, who held my hand every morning.
She let go of my hand to run after the music. I've wondered all my life if she looked back for me.
I think the other children were happy, wherever he took them. I have to think that. The alternative is unbearable.
My fear is that the mountain was a punishment, and I'm the only proof it happened.
My dream is foolish: to hear, just once, that they're all right. That the piper was kind to them, in the end.
The tune I hear at night might be him. Or it might be an old ear playing tricks. I've never decided.
Then, last week, a peddler said a piper in motley was seen in the next village. Coloured coat, silver pipe.
He read it and smiled, they say. Then he played a tune about a child who limps. I'll take that.
Did you hear it? You did. I can see it on your face. Tell me it was pretty. It was, wasn't it?
If you ever owe something to someone, pay it quickly. And if someone owes you, forgive them slowly and kindly.
Whiskers has forgiven you, by the way. She sat in your spot on the bench yesterday. Highest honour.
I'm not left out anymore. I think I'm just left here. Here is a good place to be left.
Life goes on, one tune at a time. Mostly in tune, too, if you don't count my humming.
Off with you. Go slowly if you like. And always, always pay the musician.
I haven't heard the night tune since. I think it said what it needed to say. The mountain is quiet.
Now the village always pays its musicians in full. I made the council swear it. On cream. The cats witnessed.
The travelling musician comes back every harvest now. He calls this the only honest town on the road.
I've stopped paying the baker twice. Well, mostly. Once a month, for old times' sake.
On quiet nights, someone by the well hums a very old tune. It's me. I didn't know I remembered it.
The children here dance when I hum. I let them. I sit on the bench and my leg taps along.
I think my sister would like it here. I talk to her, sometimes, by the well. She never answers. That's all right.
You carried a letter to a stranger for an old fool who limps. The mountain may not have been listening, but I was.
hearthbound.persona.tale_unpaid_tune.epi: Now the village always pays its musicians in full, and on quiet nights someone by the well hums a very old tune.
hearthbound.persona.tale_unpaid_tune.sou: The Pied Piper of Hamelin — Robert Browning (1842)
hearthbound.persona.tale_unpaid_tune.sta: Little grey things are crawling out of the cellar stones. I won't call a piper this time. Would you deal with them?
Gone, and paid for in full. Here, and don't argue.
A travelling musician played at our feast and the council paid only half. Not in my village. Bring me emeralds for the rest.
The musician wept when I paid. Said nobody ever pays the second half. They should.
A piper in motley was seen in the next village. It can't be him, I know. Carry my letter anyway?
He read it and smiled, they say, and played a tune about a child who limps. I'll take that.
hearthbound.persona.tale_unpaid_tune.tal: I still hear a tune some nights. Nobody else does.
Rats? No. I keep cats. Three of them. Very well paid.
I think the other children were happy, wherever he took them. I have to think that.
I came from the sea. I gave my voice to a sea witch for legs, and every step on land felt like knives. All for someone who married another.
My sisters brought me a knife to go back home: his heart for my tail. I threw it in the waves. The foam didn't take me. This village did.
Sorry, I speak slowly. I learned words late. Twice. Please be patient with me.
You smell of rain and road dust. On land, everyone smells of somewhere. I like guessing where.
Every step on land felt like walking on knives. I smiled anyway. That was the bargain.
Some nights I miss the sea so much I can taste salt on my tongue, and wake up crying without a sound.
My sisters' gardens were full of kelp swaying like green hair. I used to hide in it from my grandmother.
Kelp is the taste of home. Dried, raw, in soup, I don't care. It's green and salty and it remembers.
Would you bring me some kelp? A good armful. I want to taste my sisters' gardens again, just for one night.
Walking still hurts a little. Dancing hurts less. Strange, isn't it? I dance in the kitchen when nobody looks.
I sit on the pier most evenings. The boards are warm, and the water is close enough, but not too close.
Fire still amazes me. Where I grew up, nothing ever burned. Things only drifted.
I had five older sisters. Each of us had a little garden, and mine was round and red, like the sun seen from below.
When I turned fifteen, I rose to the surface for the first time. There was a ship full of lanterns and music.
A storm broke the ship. I pulled a young man from the waves and laid him on the sand. He never knew it was me.
The sea sings at night. I don't answer anymore. But I listen, the way you listen to an old letter.
I paid a sea witch for these legs. The price was my voice. She cut it out like a thread from cloth.
Salty and green. For a moment I was home. Thank you. I didn't expect to cry again, but it was the good kind.
I made a soup with it. The children said it tasted like the beach. That's exactly right.
My voice came back word by word, like shells washing up. First 'bread'. Then 'thank you'. Then my own name.
I use it only for true things now. I spent too long unable to say them.
But the sea witch doesn't like losing a bargain. I think she's still watching me.
The drowned in the river stand very still when I pass. They face me. Always me.
I'm sure they serve her. They watch from the water at night. Please, make them stop.
Now I'll tell you the rest. I gave everything for a man who danced with me, called me his little foundling, and married someone else.
He thought another girl had saved him from the sea. I couldn't tell him the truth. I had no voice to tell it with.
The witch had warned me: if he marries another, you turn to sea foam at dawn. I watched the wedding ship's lanterns all night.
Then my sisters rose from the waves. Their long hair was gone. They had traded it to the witch for a knife.
His heart for my tail, they said. Strike before sunrise and come home. I held the knife over him while he slept.
I threw it into the waves. Where it fell, the water turned red for a moment. Then it was just the sea.
The tale says I became foam. I thought so too. But dawn came, and I was still here, shivering on the sand.
A fisherwoman from this village found me and wrapped me in her shawl. She asked no questions. I couldn't answer anyway.
The river is silent. Let her find someone else to watch. I walked by the water today without looking over my shoulder.
I slept the whole night through. I'd forgotten what that felt like. Like floating, but warm.
My grandmother told us that when we were small, so we could always find each other, even far apart.
I've tried ordinary shells from the beach. They only whisper. I need the great spiral ones, pearly inside.
Nautilus shells, the fishers call them. They wash up rarely, or the drowned carry them.
My dream is so simple: to hear my sisters laugh, and to tell them, in my own voice, that I'm happy here.
Find me a couple of those great shells. Please. It's the only way I can reach home without leaving this one.
Now I can tell you my fear. It's not the witch. It's that my sisters paid with their hair, and I never thanked them.
They gave the most beautiful thing they had, and I threw their knife away. Do they think I chose him over them?
I didn't. I chose not to become someone who kills for love. I hope they understand that.
My grandmother wore twelve oysters on her tail, because she was noble. I think she'd scold me, then hug me.
The youngest of us always sang the best. They said my voice was the sweetest in the sea. It's rougher now. I prefer it.
Sometimes I dream I'm swimming, and I wake and my legs are tangled in the sheets like a net.
I wonder if the prince is happy. I think he is. I hope he is. It stopped hurting, one day, without my noticing.
Here's a secret: great shells hold the sea's voice. If you press one to your ear, my sisters can speak through it.
Hear it? Not the sea: my sisters, singing. I pressed the shell to my ear and they were already calling my name.
I told them everything. They cried. Then they laughed, because I said 'dinner' and 'bread' and they don't know those words.
My grandmother spoke through the shell yesterday. She said: 'You chose well, little one.' I sat on the pier until dark.
I talk more now. You may have noticed. I'm making up for lost years, word by word.
Thank you for listening when I was slow. Most people finish my sentences. You never did.
The sea still sings at night. Now I sing back, softly, from the shore. Both of us are home.
Come to the pier some evening. I'll let you hold the shell. Say hello to them from me, and from you.
Their hair has grown back. The eldest says it's longer than ever, and she's insufferable about it.
The helm I gave you was theirs to give. They'd want you to visit them. They'd like you, I think.
Wear it when you swim. My sisters will know you by it and keep the currents gentle.
I sit on the pier every calm evening now, shell to one ear. People think I'm odd. I am, happily.
The kelp soup is famous now. The innkeeper asked for my recipe. I said: miss someone, then add salt.
Remember those drowned in the river? A child asked me if I was scared of them. I said: not anymore, I had help.
My legs still hurt a little when it rains. I dance anyway. The pain is part of the music now.
I've started teaching the children the sea songs. They sing them wrong. It's perfect.
Now, on calm evenings, a quiet figure sits on the pier with a shell pressed to one ear, laughing at something only the sea can say.
Fairy Tales Told for Children — Hans Christian Andersen (1837)
Some nights I miss the sea so much I can taste it. Bring me kelp; it tastes of my sisters' gardens.
Salty and green. For a moment I was home. Thank you.
A taste of home
The drowned in the river serve the sea witch, I'm sure of it. They watch me from the water. Make them stop.
The river is silent. Let her find someone else to watch.
The witch's servants
My sisters can speak through great shells, if you hold them to your ear. Find me some.
Hear it? Not the sea: my sisters, singing. Take this helm; it's how they'd want you to visit.
A shell to listen
Sorry, I speak slowly. I learned words late. Twice.
Walking still hurts a little. Dancing hurts less. Strange, isn't it?
The sea sings at night. I don't answer anymore.
My voice came back word by word. I use it only for true things now.
A voice for legs
hearthbound.persona.tale_wolf_in_the_bed: Years ago I heard snoring from a grandmother's cottage, far too loud for an old woman. Inside was a wolf with a full belly, and two people still alive in it.
Everyone thinks I hate wolves. I don't. I hate lies dressed up as grandmothers. A wolf in the woods is just a wolf.
Stay on the path. Not a rule, just good sense. The woods don't forgive shortcuts.
What big ears I have? All the better to hear trouble coming. I've heard you coming since the bridge.
The child in red is grown now. She brings me cake every year, on the day I opened that door.
And now she has a little daughter of her own, just old enough to walk the forest path alone.
That scares me more than any wolf. I know what waits in the woods for children who stand out.
But I also know what saves them: being seen. So I want to give the girl a red cloak, like her mother's.
Would you bring me red wool? Six should make a cloak bright enough to find from the top of any hill.
I walk the forest road twice a day. Morning for the tracks, evening for the shadows.
A red cloak is easy to spot among the trees. That's the whole point of red.
You'd be surprised how many creatures pretend to be something they're not. Most of them aren't wolves.
Years ago, on a round like this one, I passed an old woman's cottage and heard snoring.
Far too loud for a grandmother. Rattling the shutters. I knew something was wrong before I opened the door.
Inside, in her bed, wearing her nightcap, lay a wolf with a belly like a barrel.
And in that belly, still alive, were the grandmother and a little girl in a red hood.
I won't tell you how I got them out. Let's say I was quick, and the wolf slept very soundly.
Bright as a poppy. Nobody will lose her in the woods now. Thank you, friend.
She twirled in it until she fell over. Her mother laughed and then cried. That's how it goes with mothers.
It isn't a wolf. Wolves don't groan like that. Wolves don't drag their feet.
The girl in the new cloak has to walk that path to visit her great-grandmother. Yes, she's still alive, and stubborn.
I've fought them alone for a week. There are more every night, and my arm isn't what it was.
The dead don't pretend to be grandmothers, at least. They're honest in their own way. Rotten, but honest.
Clear them out with me? Eight of them, at least. I want the path quiet before the girl walks it again.
Now let me tell you something people get wrong about me. Everyone thinks I hate wolves.
I don't. A wolf in the woods is just a wolf. Hungry, proud, honest about what it wants.
What I hate is lies dressed up as grandmothers. A creature wearing a nightcap and a sweet voice.
That wolf didn't just eat. It pretended. It asked the child to come closer. That's the part I can't forgive.
When I tell the story in taverns, men cheer when the wolf dies. I never cheer. I just drink.
Some nights I dream the door was locked and I walked on, thinking the snoring was just an old woman.
I've come to believe the real danger in the forest is anything that smiles too much.
Lately there's something new on the grandmother's path. It shuffles along at night.
The path is quiet again. Only owls and honest wolves now. I slept a whole night for the first time in weeks.
You fight like someone who has something to protect. I recognise that. It's how I learned too.
Here's my dream, and it's a strange one: a wolf. A tame one, walking the grandmother's path, guarding it.
A wolf to protect a grandmother. Justice, of a sort. The forest balancing its own debts.
The girl's mother laughed when I told her. Then she said, 'Only you would think of that.' I took it as praise.
There's a young grey one who follows me at a distance. He's hungry and curious. That's a good start.
Bring me bones, twelve of them. Patience and bones: that's how you make a friend of a wolf.
Can I tell you the thing I've never said, not even at a tavern? I was late that day.
I'd stopped to argue with a miller about a debt. Ten minutes. If I'd come sooner, the wolf might never have eaten them.
Everyone calls me a hero. I think of those ten minutes every time someone says it.
That's why I walk the path twice a day, rain or snow. I'm paying back ten minutes, one step at a time.
The grandmother forgave me before I even asked. She said, 'You came. That's the part that counts.'
But I'm getting old. Someday my knees will quit, and who will walk the path then?
I keep thinking about the old tales from the other side of the mountains. The wolf always gets there first, in the tales.
I want to change that. I want something at the cottage door that gets there first, every time.
Look at him, guarding the cottage door. He growls at strangers and rolls over for the girl in red.
I hope you're using the lead I gave you. A friend like that makes every road shorter.
You helped me turn an old nightmare into a new habit. That's a rare gift. Better than a hood or a cake.
The girl in the red cloak asked who you were. I said: someone who stays on the path, but not always.
If you ever hear snoring that's too loud, you come and get me. Old habits.
Life goes on in the woods: owls, wolves, a red cloak between the trees. The way it should be.
Go on, stay on the path. Or don't. Either way, Nightcap and I will be watching for you.
The great-grandmother named him Nightcap. I think she has a darker sense of humour than people realise.
He walks the path every dusk. I follow him now, instead of the other way round. My knees are grateful.
No child in red has been lost since. No child in any colour, actually.
The girl's mother brought me the anniversary cake. Two slices this year: one for me, one for the wolf.
He ate his in one gulp. I ate mine slowly, thinking about ten minutes, and for once they didn't sting.
The dead have stayed off the path. I think Nightcap scares them. He's very convincing when he howls.
The miller still owes me that debt, by the way. I've decided he can keep it.
I tell the story differently in taverns now. It ends with a wolf at the door, and everyone safe inside.
Now a tame wolf walks the path to grandmother's cottage, and no child in red has been lost since.
Children's and Household Tales — Brothers Grimm (1812)
The child I saved has a daughter of her own now. I want to give her a red cloak, like her mother's. Bring me red wool.
Bright as a poppy. Nobody will lose her in the woods.
A new red cloak
Something shuffles along the grandmother's path at night, and it isn't a wolf. It groans. Clear them out.
The path is quiet again. Only owls and honest wolves now.
Things that aren't wolves
I'll tame a wolf to walk the grandmother's path. Justice, of a sort. Bring me bones.
Look at him, guarding the cottage door. Take this lead; you may want a friend like that too.
A wolf for the path
Stay on the path. Not a rule, just good sense.
A red cloak is easy to spot among the trees. That's the point.
The child in red is grown now. She still brings me cake every year.
What big ears I have? All the better to hear trouble coming.
The wolf in grandmother's bed
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.bio.0: They say you can tell a village by its tavern. Mine has the best stew for ten leagues around.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.bio.1: My mother's recipe book burned in a fire. I remember most of it... but not the honey stew. Her best.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.bio.2: Every traveller who sits at my table leaves a story. I collect them like others collect coins.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.dialogue: Sit, sit! You look like you haven't eaten in days. Here, bread first. Questions later.
The secret is patience. And a bit more salt than you think. No, more than that.
Her honey stew. Her best. I've tried it forty times. Close. Never quite. Something's missing.
Don't look so sad. We have a festival to plan! The harvest one, the biggest night of the year.
Every year the whole village crams in here, and every year I run out of something. Last year, spoons.
This year I want baked potatoes for everyone. Golden, crackling, with butter melting in.
Can you help? I need lots of them. Lots. The guards alone eat a field's worth.
The guards eat like wolves, the elder like a bird. You? Like a bear after winter.
They say you can tell a village by its tavern. Ours has the best stew for ten leagues.
See that nail by the door? Every traveller who tells me a good story gets a knot in the string.
Forty-three knots. A sailor with no boat, a juggler with one arm, a shepherd who married a baker.
My mother ran this kitchen before me. I learned to walk holding onto that table leg.
She had a recipe book. Thick as a brick, stained with every sauce she ever made.
Seven years ago a spark from the hearth caught the curtains. The book was on the shelf beside them.
I remember most of it. My hands remember more than my head. But not all of it.
The festival! They'll talk about it for years. The elder had four potatoes. Four! Like a bird, ha.
Thank you. You carried those potatoes like treasure. In my kitchen, they are.
I've tried chicken, mutton, beef. It's always wrong. Too heavy, too tame.
Last week a trapper told me a story at the counter, and I remembered something. Rabbit!
She'd buy rabbits from the hunters in autumn. The kitchen smelled of thyme and fur.
I think that's it. The heart of the stew. But the hunters have gone south this year.
Bring me some fresh rabbit? Tender ones. I'll cook and try to remember the rest.
After everyone left, I sat by the hearth and cried a little. Good tears. Mostly.
It was the first festival since the fire that felt like hers. Loud, warm, too much food.
