Let me tell you about her. She sang while she cooked, badly. The soup never minded.
She'd hide a spoon of honey in everything. Bread, sauce, porridge. 'A little sweet for the road,' she said.
The night of the fire, I ran back in for the book. The guards pulled me out by my collar.
I got out with a burnt sleeve and one page. Just one. The recipe for turnip soup. Nobody likes turnip soup.
I kept the page anyway. It's in her handwriting. That matters more than the turnips.
The honey stew... I close my eyes and I can almost smell it. Earthy. Sweet. Something wild in it.
Yes... yes! It's starting to smell like her kitchen. Can you smell it? Tell me you can smell it.
I made a pot last night with your rabbit. I stood over it for an hour, just breathing.
'A little sweet for the road.' She said it every time. It was in front of me the whole time.
Just a few spoons at the end, stirred in when the fire's low. That's the final touch.
But not any honey. Real honey, straight from the hive. The kind the bees fight you for.
I can't leave the kitchen. The guards would riot. And the bees don't like me anyway.
Bring me honey, and then sit down and taste it with me. I don't want to taste it alone.
It's close. Closer than ever. But there's a hole in the flavour, right at the end.
Do you know what scares me? That I'll get old and forget even this much. Her whole kitchen, gone.
People come here for warmth. If I can't keep her recipe, what am I keeping?
The nail by the door got two new knots this week. One for you. You didn't even notice.
Your story? The one about the potatoes and the festival. Every story is someone's feast.
I dream of putting it on the board by the door: 'Mum's Stew'. In chalk. Big letters.
Last night I found her old wooden spoon, behind the flour barrels. Sticky. Still sticky, after all these years.
I licked it. Don't laugh. It tasted of smoke and honey. Of course. Of course it was honey!
It's her stew. After all these years. I still can't say it without my voice going funny.
It's on the board by the door now: 'Mum's Honey Stew'. In chalk. Very big letters.
Sometimes I sing while I cook now. Badly. Just like her. The soup still doesn't mind.
The trapper came back and I gave him a free bowl. He cried into it. Didn't ruin it.
Next festival, potatoes again. And stew. And maybe spoons enough for everyone this time.
There's always a seat for you here. The one by the fire. I've chased three people out of it already.
Now sit. Eat. The road will still be there after the second bowl. A little sweet for the road.
And the first bowl of every pot is yours. That's a rule. Kitchen rules are sacred.
The guards order it twice a day. The elder finishes a whole bowl. A whole bowl! A bird no more.
I've started a new recipe book. Thick paper. I keep it in a tin box, far from any curtain.
The first page is the turnip soup. Her handwriting. Glued in. Nobody still likes it.
The second page is the honey stew. My handwriting. With a little note in the margin about you.
Travellers taste it and ask for the recipe. I smile and say it's a family secret. You're family.
The nail by the door is full now. I had to put up a second one. Most knots are yours, I suspect.
Remember when I said you eat like a bear? You still do. It's the best compliment a cook can get.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.epilogue: "Mum's honey stew" is now on the tavern menu, and the first bowl of every pot is always yours.
The harvest festival is coming and I need baked potatoes. Lots of them. Can you help?
The festival will be talked about for years!
My mother's stew had rabbit. Fresh, tender rabbit. Bring me some and I'll try to remember the rest.
Yes... yes! It's starting to smell like her kitchen.
I remember now: the final touch was honey. Just a few spoons. Bring it and taste it with me.
It's her stew. After all these years... Take some for the road. There's always a seat for you here.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.talk.0: Sit, sit! You look like you haven't eaten in days.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.talk.1: The secret is patience. And a bit more salt than you think.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.talk.2: The guards eat like wolves. The elder, like a bird. And you? Like a bear.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.talk.3: I tried to recreate mum's stew again. Close. Not quite.
hearthbound.persona.tavern_cook.title: Tavern Cook
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.bio.0: I founded this village with six families and a cart. Now look at it.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.bio.1: I've buried friends, blessed weddings and settled more disputes about goats than I care to count.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.bio.2: Before I go, I want to leave the village at peace with its neighbours. Old grudges are poor inheritances.
Sit down, sit down. My knees are old, but my ears still work. Better than most, in fact.
The young ones want everything now. The land teaches patience. So do knees.
I used to know every settlement for three days' walk. Who traded fairly, who watered their milk.
Now I hear nothing. Travellers pass and tell me about roads, never about people.
Are there other villages like ours, grown from a cart and some stubbornness? Are they well? Lonely?
An old founder wonders about such things. Whether we did it right. Whether others did it better.
Visit a village I haven't heard of, and bring me news. Tell me about its people, not its walls.
You've done a lot for us already. More than you think. I notice these things.
When I'm gone, remember: a village is its people, not its walls.
That tree in the plaza? I planted it the first spring. It was a twig. So was I, in a way.
I founded this village with six families and a cart. The cart had three wheels. We pushed a lot.
The first winter we lived in one barn, all of us. Babies, goats, grudges. Mostly grudges.
I've buried friends here, blessed weddings, and settled more disputes about goats than I care to count.
Every stone of the well, every fence post, I remember who set it and what they argued about while doing it.
My legs don't carry me past the fields anymore. The world has shrunk to this bench.
So others have grown too. Good. The world is less lonely than I thought. I slept well after that.
Thank you. I asked the baker to make your story into a toast at supper. It was a long toast.
I've watched you. You have it. Not the loud kind. The kind that stays until dawn.
If they see you hold the line, they'll learn. Not from speeches. From your back, in front of them.
I'm asking a great deal. Nights are long and the dead don't tire.
But I'd rather ask you than bury another young one who wasn't ready.
Protect the village while the young ones learn to do it themselves. Stand with us through the nights.
You described their elder sitting on a bench. I laughed. We're all the same, us old benchwarmers.
Now let me tell you what keeps me awake. It's not the neighbours far away. It's the nights here.
The dead walk more often now. Creepers in the lanes. Arrows from the dark. Every season, worse.
When we founded this place, I stood at the gate with a pitchfork every night for a year.
My shoulder still aches from it. I can predict rain with it. That's the one gift the dead gave me.
Now the young ones should take the gate. But they've never seen a real night. They flinch.
I don't blame them. I flinched too, once. Old Marta pushed me forward, and I learned.
Courage isn't taught with words. It's caught, like a cold. From standing beside someone who has it.
You stood with us. The young ones saw it. They'll remember. I watched from the window, every night.
The miller's son took the gate alone last night. His hands shook. He didn't leave. That's your doing.
I've written an apology. Plain words. No excuses. It took me forty years and one afternoon.
Their new elder is her daughter. She might tear it up. She'd have every right.
But I can't walk the ridge anymore. And I want it carried by someone who builds bridges.
You've already shown both villages what it looks like to stand beside someone. Show them once more.
Take them my apology. It's time. It's been time for a very long while.
Now I can tell you the thing I'm most ashamed of. It's older than the gate, older than the tree.
Forty years ago, a dry summer. We and our neighbours across the ridge shared a well at the boundary.
We quarrelled over it. Who drew first, who drew more. Foolish, thirsty words. I said the worst ones.
We built our own well. So did they. We haven't spoken since. Forty years of silence over water.
Their founder was my friend. We carried the same cart up that hill. We laughed at the same jokes.
She died last winter. I heard it from a trader. I didn't go. I didn't know if I'd be welcome.
That's what haunts me. Not the dead in the lanes. The living I stopped speaking to.
Old grudges are poor inheritances. I don't want to hand this one to the young ones with the keys.
They accepted. After forty years. I cried in front of the whole village. Nobody pretended not to notice.
Her daughter came over the ridge last week. She has her mother's laugh. We drew water together.
I've started planning my own farewell. Don't make that face. It's far off. I'm just tidy.
When the time comes, I've asked for both villages at the table. And you at the head of it.
Remember what I told you. A village is its people. You're one of ours now. Walls or no walls.
Sit a while longer. The sun's warm on this bench, and I've a story about a three-wheeled cart.
Or go, if the road is calling. The bench will be here. And so will I, a while yet.
How does the mantle sit? It belonged to the founders. Now it belongs to someone who builds bridges.
The old boundary well has a bucket again. Children from both villages fight over who turns the handle.
That's a good kind of quarrel. The kind that ends in splashing, not in silence.
The young ones hold the gate now. Taking turns. They even argue about who gets the worst shift.
I spend my evenings telling the children about the traveller who helped mend an old grudge.
They always ask whether you were scared. I tell them yes. That's what makes it a good story.
The tree in the plaza bloomed early this year. I'm choosing to believe that means something.
My knees are worse. My heart is lighter. On balance, a fine trade.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.epilogue: The elder spends the evenings telling the children about the traveller who helped mend an old grudge.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.stage.0.a: My legs don't carry me far anymore. Visit a village I haven't heard of and bring me news.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.stage.0.d: So others have grown too. Good. The world is less lonely than I thought.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.stage.1.a: The nights are getting worse. Protect the village while the young ones learn to do it themselves.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.stage.1.d: You stood with us. The young ones saw it. They'll remember.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.stage.2.a: Long ago we quarrelled with our neighbours over a well. A foolish thing. Take them my apology; it's time.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.stage.2.d: They accepted... after forty years. Take this mantle. It belonged to the founders; now it belongs to someone who builds bridges.

hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.talk.1: The young ones want everything now. The land teaches patience.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.talk.2: You've done a lot for us. More than you think.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.talk.3: When I'm gone, remember: a village is its people, not its walls.
hearthbound.persona.wise_elder.title: Village Elder
hearthbound.persona.young_dreamer.bio.0: I've never been further than the old mill. Everyone here was born, lives and dies in the same ten fields.
hearthbound.persona.young_dreamer.bio.1: At night I climb onto the roof and look at the lights of the other villages. I want to see them all.
hearthbound.persona.young_dreamer.bio.2: My parents want me to take over the farm. I love them. But my heart is already on the road.
hearthbound.persona.young_dreamer.dialog: You're not from here! I can tell. Your boots have mud I've never seen. What colour is that?
What's it like out there? Tell me everything. Everything! Start with the smells.
Mother says I'll fall off the roof one day. Father says I'll fall off the world.
They want me to take over the farm. It's a good farm. I love them. That's what makes it hard.
But I need to know those lights are real. That there are people there, eating supper, telling stories.
You travel. You could go where I can't, yet. Just once. For me.
Go somewhere you've never been. Find another village and come back to tell me what it's like.
Is it true there are villages where people have pointy ears? Or is that just a tavern story?
I've drawn a map of the village. Look. It fits on one page. The world must be enormous.
One day I'll write a book about my travels. You'll be in the first chapter. Maybe the prologue.
I've never been further than the old mill. I walked there once and my knees shook the whole way back.
Everyone here is born, lives and dies in the same ten fields. My grandparents never saw the river's end.
At night I climb onto the roof and look at the lights of other villages. Tiny orange dots.
I've counted them. Four on clear nights. Five if the east wind blows the smoke away.
I give them names. The Blinking One. The Sleepy One. The One That's Always Late.
Towers? Strange songs? I knew it! The world is wonderful! Tell me again, slower.
I wrote down every word you said. Look, three pages. I drew the towers. Are they right?
The problem is, I get lost going to the well in the fog. Truly. Twice last winter.
The trader who came through last spring had a little box with a needle that always knew north.
I held it for a moment. It shivered and turned, like it was alive. I haven't forgotten it.
If I'm going to travel, I need one. It would be the first in the family. The very first.
Could you get me a compass? Then nobody would have to cry about me getting lost.
Last night I found their light from the roof. I think it's the Sleepy One. It'll need a new name.
Thank you. You don't know what that did. My heart's been running laps all morning.
Can I tell you a secret? I've been packing a bag. Just a little one. Under the bed.
A spare shirt, a knife, some bread that's gone hard, and my map. That's all I have.
My parents found it. Mother cried. Father said nothing and went out to the fields until dark.
I felt terrible. But I didn't unpack it. I just pushed it further under the bed.
Grandmother understood. She told me she wanted to see the sea when she was young. She never did.
She said, 'Go, but go smart. Fools who get lost make mothers cry twice.'
It points north! It always points north! I've walked in circles all day just to watch it.
I showed Mother. She held it a long time. Then she said, 'Well. At least you'll come home.'
I've written a letter to the neighbouring village. The one with the towers you told me about.
I asked if they need an apprentice. Anything. Builder, farmer, stable-hand. I'll learn.
I've rewritten it eleven times. The last one has no ink blots. Almost none.
If I carry it myself and they say no, I don't think I could walk back. Not with everyone watching.
Will you take it to them for me? I'll wait on the roof and watch their light.
That's almost a blessing, isn't it? I'm taking it as one.
I sleep with the compass under my pillow. It ticks a little when I turn over. Like a heart.
Can I tell you my biggest fear? Not the dead, not the creepers. Being ordinary somewhere else.
What if I get there and I'm just as small, only lonelier? What if the world doesn't want me?
Then I think of you. You go everywhere and you're still you. That helps.
Father came up on the roof last night. First time ever. He looked at the lights and didn't speak.
Then he said, 'That's a lot of fields out there. They'll need people who know how to work.'
I think he meant yes. In father-language, I think that was yes.
They said yes! I leave in spring. I've said it a hundred times and it still sounds like a song.
Do you like the spyglass? It was grandfather's. You'll find the next horizon before I do.
The compass still ticks under my pillow. North, always north. And home is always south of it.
I've started the book. Chapter one: 'The Traveller With Strange Mud'. Guess who that is.
When I'm out there, and someone asks where I'm from, I'll say the village with the best friend.
Thank you. For the stories, the compass, the letter. For believing the lights were real.
See you on the road someday. I'll be the one grinning at everything and asking too many questions.
Promise you'll tell me what you see through it. Every mountain. I'll compare notes.
My map has your name on the first page now. In the corner. With a little drawing of your boots.
The bag's not under the bed anymore. It's by the door. Mother packed extra bread in it herself.
Father has been teaching me to mend a fence properly. 'They'll ask,' he says. He's probably right.
Grandmother gave me a shell she's kept for fifty years. 'For when you see the sea,' she said.
I've renamed the lights. The towers one is called 'Spring' now. I look at it every night.
Do you think I'll be homesick? I think I will. I think that's all right.
I'll come back for the harvest festival. I promised. The farm can't do without my bad carving.
hearthbound.persona.young_dreamer.epilog: The young dreamer is packing for spring. Their map already has your name on the first page.
Go somewhere you've never been. Find another village and come back to tell me what it's like.
Towers? Strange songs? I knew it! The world is wonderful!
If I'm going to travel, I need a compass. Mine would be the first one in the family.
It points north! It always points north! Thank you, thank you!
I've written to the neighbouring village asking whether they need an apprentice. Will you take it to them for me?
They said yes! I leave in spring. Take my spyglass: you'll find the next horizon before I do.

hearthbound.persona.young_dreamer.talk.3: One day I'll write a book about my travels. You'll be in the first chapter.
